short_definition: The chloride-resistant grade of the common stainless family. It adds molybdenum to what 304 has, which is why it turns up on marine, pool and fountain work.
explanation:
304 is the common general-purpose grade and 316 is the one specified where chlorides are expected. Both of them are stainless and neither of them is corrosion-proof.

They are indistinguishable by eye, which is what makes a substitution so easy and so slow to show up. Swapping one in because the right one is not on the truck is a decision with a several-year fuse on it.
example: A bracket is replaced with an off-the-shelf part from the bin because it fitted. It looks identical to the ones either side of it, and it is the one that pits first.

short_definition: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene. The black plastic used in some drain, waste and vent piping. It takes its own cement, not PVC cement.
explanation: Mixing materials and cements is one of the specific things the can governs. If the pipe in your hand is not a material the can lists, the joint is not rated whatever it looks like afterwards.
example: A black drain stub left by another trade needs tying into your overflow. Before it gets cemented, the question is what that stub actually is.

short_definition: How much water a unit or a stone takes up, normally published as a percentage of its dry weight.
explanation:
It is the number behind most of what a material does in permanent water: how it behaves frozen, how much salt it will move, how long it takes to dry before anything is applied to it.

You cannot tell it by looking, by tapping, or by what the last job used. Manufactured units carry a figure. Natural stone varies piece to piece, which is a problem of its own.
example: Two pale pavers look identical on the pallet. One data sheet gives a low absorption and lists submerged service; the other says exterior paving only. Nothing on the paver itself separates them.

short_definition: In code language: able to be reached and worked on without taking apart or damaging the structure around it.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English it just means easy to get to, or reachable by somebody with a disability — a matter of degree rather than a rule.
explanation:
Every junction box and every splice must stay accessible. No box under a stone coping, none mortared in, buried under soil in a planter, tiled over, or hidden behind a panel that was then caulked.

On a finished fountain a box is ugly, and that is exactly why this rule gets broken in the last week of a job by somebody who is not thinking about the technician who arrives three winters later.
example: The coping is being set and one box lands directly under a stone. The stone does not go down; either the box moves or an accessible cover gets designed into the coping.

short_definition: The gradual physical adaptation that lets a body cope with working in heat.
explanation: It is real and it is not fitness. The body builds it over days of graded exposure and loses it after time away — so the people most at risk on any crew are the newest person and the one back from leave or illness, not the weakest or the oldest. A disproportionate share of heat fatalities happen in somebody's first days on a job.
example: A new hire who runs marathons starts on a heatwave week and is given the same workload as everybody else on day one. His fitness is not the thing his body is missing.

short_definition: Removing scale from a finish by removing a thin layer of the finish it is stuck to.
ordinary_meaning: "Washing" suggests cleaning — something you can do as often as it needs doing. This one spends the surface each time, and there is a limited number of them in a finish's life.
explanation:
Taking material off is the mechanism, not a side effect. A plaster finish can only take so many acid washes before there is no finish left, and that number belongs to the finish, not to the schedule.

It is a serious hazard job in its own right: acid handling, fumes in what may be a poorly ventilated basin, respiratory and burn protection, and effluent that has to be neutralised and disposed of as a regulated discharge rather than pushed into a storm drain. It is planned work for people equipped to do it.
example: A basin has been acid washed every couple of years because it keeps chalking up. Nobody has fixed the index that keeps putting the scale there, and the plaster is running out of life.

short_definition: Starting a motor by connecting it straight to full voltage, so it goes from stopped to full speed immediately.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like crossing a boundary, or a phone line, or being out of order. It refers to the supply line - the motor is thrown straight onto it.
explanation:
An across-the-line start is the simplest and cheapest way to run a motor and the hardest on everything attached to it. The pump goes to full flow in an instant, which is a sudden change presented to a column of water - a classic water-hammer source - and the motor draws a large inrush current.

A VFD ramping the pump up and down over a set period never presents that sudden change at all.
example: A feature with three across-the-line pumps thumps audibly through the plaza slab each time the controller brings one on. The same feature after a drive retrofit comes up without a sound.

short_definition: A threaded rod or a length of rebar bonded into a drilled hole with injected epoxy or acrylic.
explanation:
It puts no expansive force into the concrete, so it works closer to an edge and fills an irregular hole. In exchange it needs full cure time at the actual temperature before any load goes on, and its strength is entirely a bond to the wall of the hole.

Overhead adhesive anchors under sustained load have failed and killed, which is why the adhesive, its hole-cleaning procedure and its sustained-load qualification all have to be the ones in the evaluation report for that exact product.
example: A bracket goes in on epoxy at four on a November afternoon and the crew bolt it up at eight the next morning. The cure table for that product at that temperature is the only thing that says whether that was long enough.

short_definition: Automated External Defibrillator: a portable unit that analyses a casualty's heart rhythm and delivers a shock if one is needed, guided by spoken prompts.
explanation: The thing worth knowing in advance is simply whether there is one on the property and where — a hotel, an office lobby or a plaza very often has one in a cabinet nobody on the crew has noticed. That is a question to ask on arrival, not during.
example: A technician working in a corporate atrium walks past a green cabinet by the reception desk every week. Knowing what is in it costs one look.

short_definition: A nozzle that deliberately draws air into the water as it passes through, so the jet comes out white and foamy instead of clear.
explanation:
The white look is air, and the air is what gives the jet its body and its sound. It also makes the nozzle sensitive to pressure: above what it was selected for, an aerated jet goes thin and loud instead of fuller.

Chemically it is also a CO2 stripper, which is part of why spray features climb in pH.
example: A client says the centre jet 'sounds angry' since the filter was cleaned. It looks thinner than it used to and it is noisy - the filter coming clean gave the whole ring more pressure than the nozzles were picked for.

short_definition: Mixing air into water - by throwing it into the air, breaking it over an edge, or bubbling it through.
explanation:
Aeration drives carbon dioxide out of water, and water losing CO2 rises in pH. A tall spray, a weir, a cascade and an aerated nozzle are, chemically speaking, machines for stripping CO2 as efficiently as possible.

So a fountain climbs in pH by design. That is a condition to manage rather than a fault to chase, and it is the clearest argument for getting the buffer right first.
example: A pool and a spray feature share a plant room and the same fill water. The pool sits where it is put; the spray feature is up again every visit. Only one of them is throwing its water through the air all day.

short_definition: Water broken into droplets fine enough to hang in the air and be breathed in.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a spray can — a can of paint or deodorant with a propellant in it. Here it just means water in the air as a fine mist, made by the feature itself.
explanation: Any feature that makes aerosol — spray jets, misters, splash, a waterfall landing in a basin — puts whatever is in the water into the air people are breathing. It is what changes a water quality question into a public health one.
example: A misting feature at the entrance of a building runs all day past people queueing beside it. Everything in that basin is being delivered straight into the queue.

short_definition: Water that is chemically under-saturated, so it takes calcium out of whatever it touches — plaster, grout, stone, tile. On the LSI it is the negative side of zero.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, aggressive describes a person looking for a fight, or a hard sales approach.
explanation:
Water wants a certain amount of calcium in it. If it does not have enough, it goes and gets it from the surfaces it is in contact with, all day, every day. The damage is slow and cumulative and it never announces itself — by the time plaster is etched or grout is soft, the water has been aggressive for a long time.

A fresh spring fill is very often on the aggressive side, which is exactly when a feature's finish gets quietly damaged and nobody connects it to start-up day.
example: A feature refilled in April from a soft municipal supply and left to run. By late summer the plaster under the returns feels rough and the grout lines are recessed. Nothing ever went wrong on a test strip.

short_definition: Water whose chemistry makes it attack the materials it runs through, pulling metal and minerals out of the system.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a description of someone's temper, or of fast-moving water.
explanation:
It etches plaster, softens grout and mortar, leaches the surface of concrete, corrodes metals and dulls polished stone. The damage is permanent and expensive, which is the argument against treating a scale complaint as a licence to push chemistry as far the other way as it will go.

The target is balance, not the absence of scale.
example: A basin is chased hard with acid all season to stop it scaling. By autumn the nozzles are clean and the plaster is rough underfoot where it used to be smooth - a deposit you could have removed, traded for damage you cannot.

short_definition: Authority Having Jurisdiction: the body that adopts the code for its area, interprets it, issues the permit and inspects the work — usually a building department, sometimes a health department or a state agency.
explanation: Their interpretation is the operative one on this job, including where you believe the printed model text reads differently — and arguing the printed code at an inspector is not a strategy. Two AHJs an hour apart can genuinely reach different conclusions about the same feature, and both are right where they stand.
example: An inspector reads a section differently from how the crew has always read it. Whatever the book says, the inspection is what has to pass, and the conversation to have is with the project manager.

short_definition: A small valve at the high point of a system, opened while filling so trapped air can escape ahead of the water.
ordinary_meaning: Bleeding is blood. In plumbing it means letting air or fluid out through a deliberate small opening — the same word is used for bleeding a radiator or brakes.
explanation:
Fill slowly from the lowest point with the bleed wide open, and leave it open until a steady, unbroken stream comes out. A spitting, spluttering stream is air still coming through.

Skipping this does not just risk an air lock. Trapped air compresses and dissolves under pressure, and that moves a needle — so a badly filled line fails a test for a reason that is not a leak, and the fix is to fill it properly rather than argue about the result.
example: The bleed runs clear water for a second, then spits, then runs clear again. That spit is the reason to keep it open rather than the moment to close it.

short_definition: Air trapped at a high point in a line, blocking or choking the flow of water past it.
ordinary_meaning: The sealed chamber on a submarine or spacecraft that you pass through. Here it is a bubble stuck in a pipe.
explanation:
Water will not push a trapped bubble uphill out of a high spot on a gravity line, so the flow stalls and the basin or splash pad deck backs up instead of draining.

The same physics is why a hydrostatic test is filled slowly from the low point with the bleed wide open: trapped air both hides leaks and compresses.
example: An overflow line with a flat section in the middle drains fine at a trickle and backs up over the deck in a storm, which is the one time it was needed.

short_definition: The small manual valve on top of a filter lid that lets trapped air out, and on restart stays open until water comes out instead.
explanation:
It runs the procedure in both directions. Opening a vessel: relief open, wait until nothing more escapes. Closing one up: valves open, pump on, relief held open until a solid stream of water comes out, because a vessel buttoned up full of air is the same spring you just let down.

A filter that repeatedly builds air is reporting a suction-side leak. Fix that rather than managing it with the relief every visit.
example: The first spring start-up gives a good ten seconds of air out of the filter relief before any water shows. That whole pocket was sitting under the lid making the gauge read high.

short_definition: A product dosed specifically to kill or suppress algae, separate from the sanitiser.
explanation:
Sapphire's document gives one firm rule for architectural fountains: verify the product is a non-foaming formulary type. Standard low-cost pool algaecides contain surfactants, and a fountain drives water through high-pressure nozzles — an excellent way to make foam.

They are also not interchangeable. Copper-based products stain and carry a real upper limit on how much copper a body of water may hold; quaternary ammonium products behave differently again. Whether either is compatible with the sanitiser already in that water is a label and treatment-design question.
example: A pool-supply algaecide goes into a plaza fountain on a Friday. By Saturday lunchtime there are mounds of soap-like foam spilling down the stonework in front of the client, and the dose has left the basin with it.

short_definition: The temperature of the surrounding air at the time and place of the work.
explanation:
It is recorded with a pressure test because water and pipe both expand and contract: a line pressurised in the sun and read in the shade will have moved on the gauge for reasons that are not a leak.

It is also an input to the cure chart on a cement can, and the temperature that counts there is the one the joint actually cured at, not the one at noon.
example: A test starts at 8 a.m. in shade and ends at 10 with the sun full on the exposed section. The temperature at both readings is worth writing down beside the pressures.

short_definition: A plastic whose molecules have no ordered crystalline structure. PVC is one.
explanation:
It explains both ends of this module. Solvent can penetrate and soften the surface of an amorphous plastic, which is what makes solvent welding possible at all.

The same structure is why it fails brittle rather than stretching: under stored energy PVC shatters instead of tearing.
example: Cut a failed PVC fitting out of a trench and the break is sharp-edged and clean, not stretched or necked down the way a ductile material would be.

short_definition: How a unit is physically held down: dowels, anchors or adhesive, and how deep and how far from an edge those fixings sit.
explanation:
Whichever the drawing shows is there because somebody decided what this edge has to resist. A coping detailed with anchors is not a piece to set loose and grout later.

The anchor is also a metal living in water, so everything from the metals lesson applies to it. Its alloy is specified, and a substituted anchor is a galvanic couple buried in a stone you would have to break to reach. Where a fixing is structural, or holds something that could fall or be stood on, the anchor, its embedment and its edge distance are designed together.
example: Two dowels per stone are shown on the detail. The run goes down without them because the mortar has it. Putting them in afterwards means lifting a set run of coping.

short_definition: The sensor that measures wind speed, so a controller can drop the height of a feature or shut it down before the wind carries water out of the basin.
explanation:
Three problems at once are being prevented: water loss, a wet and slippery walking surface, and a complaint from whoever was standing there.

Like the freeze interlock, it only works if somebody proved it works. An anemometer that has seized reads a calm day in a gale.
example: A plaza feature soaks the paving on the first windy day of autumn. The cups on the sensor have not turned since a bearing gave out in July, and the controller has been reading dead calm ever since.

short_definition: The ring-shaped gap left around a pipe where it passes through a sleeve or a cored hole.
explanation:
The seal is sized for one specific combination of pipe and opening, so the sizing question is answered by measuring rather than by naming pipe sizes.

Nominal sizes do not answer it. A 4 inch pipe is not 4 inches across the outside, PVC is made in both steel and ductile-iron sizing standards, and a cored hole is not the same size as a sleeve of the same nominal size. Measure both, then take the model and the link count from the manufacturer's table.
example: A seal is ordered off the drawing's pipe callout, turns up on site, and does not close on a cored hole that came out a little over size. Somebody would have known that with a tape.

short_definition: The rated cover over a suction outlet, shaped and sized so that a body, a limb or hair cannot be held against it by the flow. It carries a rating and a service life.
explanation:
This is a life-safety device, not a grille. A suction outlet with no cover, a cracked cover, a loose one or a substituted one can hold a person underwater against flow they cannot pull away from. The rating is specific to the flow and the fitting, so an ordinary grate that fits the hole is not a replacement.

Cracked, missing, loose or substituted means the feature does not run. There is no version where you open for the season and deal with it later.
example: A start-up turns up one cover with a hairline crack across two screw bosses and a second held down with two screws out of four. That feature stays off until both are right, whatever the calendar says about the opening event.

short_definition: A compound put onto threads at assembly so the two thread faces never touch as bare metal and cannot fuse to each other.
explanation:
The film of compound is exactly the barrier the oxide layer is failing to be, which is why it is the main defence against galling.

It brings two decisions with it. Most compounds are loaded with metal, copper, nickel or aluminium, and that introduces a third metal into a joint that will sit in treated water, so metal-free formulations exist for exactly that reason. And compounds differ in what they are approved for: potable water, plastics, elastomers and oxygen service are each their own compatibility question.
example: Two identical stainless risers, fitted a week apart by two people. Four seasons later one comes out with a wrench and a bit of patience; the other was assembled dry and is not coming out at all.

short_definition: A shock boundary: how close an unqualified or a qualified person may get to exposed energised parts.
explanation: These are the shock family of boundaries, separate from the arc flash boundary, which is about burns rather than contact. Two hazards, two sets of distances — and an unqualified person's boundary is further out than a qualified one's, which is the whole reason the roles are defined.
example: An open panel is being worked on by an electrician and a technician wanders over to watch from a couple of feet away. Being a spectator does not change where he is standing.

short_definition: A water feature regulated as a place people get into — a splash pad, a wading basin, anything designed for human contact.
ordinary_meaning: "Venue" sounds like a booking — a hall or a place people gather. Here it is a regulatory category, and the label changes what the law requires of the water.
explanation:
An interactive feature is commonly regulated under a local adoption of a pool and spa code, with mandated chemistry, mandated testing frequency and an inspected log. A display fountain nobody touches may be under none of that and run on a completely different treatment program.

Find out which one you are standing in front of before you dose anything.
example: Two features on the same campus, one hundred metres apart. One is a sculptural basin and the other has children running through jets. Only one of them has a log an inspector will ask for.
see_also: International Swimming Pool and Spa Code

short_definition: An electrical fault that turns into an arc through the air, releasing an intense burst of heat, light and pressure.
explanation: It is electricity's second way of hurting you, and it does not require contact — it can ignite clothing and throw a person who was simply standing in front of the equipment. The cheap habit that costs nothing: when operating a disconnect or a breaker, stand to the side of the door rather than square in front of it, and turn your face away.
example: A technician stands square in front of a switchboard and pulls a disconnect handle with his face a foot from the door. Nothing happens, which is the usual outcome and not the reason to keep doing it.

short_definition: The distance from equipment within which somebody would receive a serious burn if an arc flash happened while they were standing there.
explanation: Where the distances have been worked out by an arc-flash study, they go on a label on the equipment itself. Where there is a label, that label is the instruction for that piece of equipment, and no general figure printed in a training course could replace it. If a panel carries no label, that is a finding to report rather than a reason to guess at a distance.
example: A technician finds a fountain plant-room panel with no arc-flash label anywhere on it. The right response is to say so to the project manager, not to work out his own comfortable distance.

short_definition: How much the relative size of the two metals matters in a galvanic pair. A small piece of the corroding metal joined to a large piece of the other is eaten quickly.
explanation:
It is why fasteners are so often the casualty. The fastener is almost always the small part in the pair, so if it is also the less noble one, it takes the whole load of the cell.

The reverse pairing is far more forgiving: a stainless bolt in a carbon steel frame spreads the same attack over a large area.
example: A stainless frame gets two carbon steel bolts as a temporary fix. They are gone long before the frame shows a mark.

short_definition: The part of the National Electrical Code that governs pools, fountains and the electrical work in and around the water.
explanation:
It is where the equipotential bonding requirement comes from, and it covers underwater and in-ground luminaires, their bonding, grounding, entries and splices. Nothing in that scope is relaxed because the job you came to do is a data job or because a circuit happens to be low voltage.

How far the bonding has to extend on a particular feature is engineered from the article and then inspected — the engineer designs it and the AHJ signs it off.
example: Somebody argues that a 24 V fixture is outside all this because it is only 24 volts. The metal parts around the water do not become exempt at any voltage.

short_definition: A drawing corrected after construction to show what was actually installed, rather than what was designed.
explanation:
Between design and handover a valve gets added, a line is rerouted around an obstruction, a filter is swapped for a different model, somebody ties a new feature into a spare port. None of that appears on the original sheet unless a proper as-built was produced.

So on an existing feature the schematic is what was meant to be there. Verify by tracing actual pipe before you rely on a valve to isolate anything - then mark up what you found and hand it back. A marked-up drawing is worth more than the clean one you were given, and a correction nobody files gets made again next year.
example: The drawing shows one isolation valve on the return. There are three, one of them behind a fixed access panel, and the middle one is the only one that actually holds.

short_definition: The state something was in when you arrived, saved and labelled as such. As-left is the state you leave it in.
explanation:
Upload what is actually in the controller and save it with a name and a date before the first edit. Without that, undo is your memory of what the rung used to say.

And do not assume the file on somebody's laptop is that copy. On a site that has been running for years, the version in the controller very often contains a field change that was never sent back to anybody.
example: A technician saves the running program before touching it, makes one change, tests it, and saves again under a second name. Two files and a date, and anybody can see exactly what moved.

short_definition: The standard that sets out what a water management program for a building water system is and what belongs in one.
explanation:
ASHRAE is the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers. Standard 188 is the reference people mean when they talk about a written program for managing waterborne pathogen risk in a building.

Whether the feature in front of you needs such a program, and who writes it, is a question for the design and the health authority — not one to answer at the basin.
example: A facilities manager asks whether the lobby fountain is "covered by the building's plan". The honest answer is that you do not know, and it is a question worth putting in writing to whoever holds the plan.
see_also: International Swimming Pool and Spa Code

short_definition: A time switch that works out sunrise and sunset for its location through the year, so a schedule tied to darkness does not have to be reset each month.
explanation: The value is that nobody has to remember. A lighting schedule set against clock times drifts out of step with the season and gets quietly wrong; one set against sunset does not.
example: Deck lighting is meant to come on at dusk. On an astronomic clock it does that in December and in June without anybody visiting the panel in between.

short_definition: The person who stays outside the space for the whole entry, keeps contact with the entrants, watches conditions, and orders evacuation.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English an attendant is someone who helps or serves — a parking attendant, a flight attendant — which makes the role sound like a spare pair of hands rather than a safety position with two absolute rules.
explanation: The attendant does not leave, and the attendant does not enter. That is the whole point of the role, and it is the rule that breaks first under stress — because the moment it matters is the moment when going in feels obviously right. They know who is in there and how many, and they watch conditions outside the space as well as inside it, since a truck pulling up beside the hatch changes the air in it.
example: An attendant is asked over the radio to run and fetch a fitting from the van, sixty seconds away. The answer is no, and somebody else goes — that is the job.

short_definition: The office that actually enforces the code on this job: the building department, the health department, or the inspector who signs it off.
explanation:
Codes are model documents until somebody adopts and interprets them locally. The AHJ is who does that, and their answer can differ from the next county's.

Questions about classification, compliance, and where backwash water may legally go are theirs, and they go up through the project manager rather than round the site.
example: Backwash goes to the storm system on one site and to sanitary sewer on the next, ten miles away. Neither crew chose that; the AHJ did.

short_definition: The official or office that interprets and enforces the adopted codes on this particular job.
explanation:
Codes are written documents, but somebody has to decide what they mean here. That person is the AHJ, and their reading is the one that counts - including how a feature is classified and what extra they have already required on this job.

Arguing the text of a code with an inspector is not a winning strategy. Finding out early what this AHJ expects is.
example: An inspector requires a bonding connection at a point the engineer did not show. It is added, because the inspection is the gate the pour has to get through.
see_also: International Swimming Pool and Spa Code

short_definition: A valve that tops the water level back up on its own as evaporation and wind-blow take it away.
explanation:
The water level is the skimmer's operating range, and on an outdoor fountain that level moves every single day. Auto-fill exists for exactly that reason.

A failed auto-fill is a common root cause behind 'the pump keeps losing prime'. A working one that nobody watches will equally well hide a leak for a whole season.
example: A feature has been losing prime every hot afternoon for a fortnight. The auto-fill solenoid is stuck shut, and the skimmers have been gulping air at the bottom of each day.

short_definition: A valve or float device that tops a basin up automatically, holding the level where it is set.
explanation:
It is useful and it is also the reason big leaks run for months. A working autofill holds the level no matter how much water is going out, so the symptom a client would have noticed never appears.

What appears instead is a water bill, chemistry that drifts one way forever, and eventually scale. And it has to be isolated before a bucket test, or the basin cannot drop and the test measures nothing.
example: A basin that has never once looked low turns out to be running a meter on the fill line steadily all week. Nobody had read the meter, because nothing looked wrong.

short_definition: American Wire Gauge — the numbering system for conductor size. The number runs backwards: a smaller number is a larger wire.
explanation: The backwards numbering is where mistakes happen. Sapphire's bonding conductor is bare, solid copper no smaller than 8 AWG — and no smaller means the number does not go up. Ten is thinner than eight, not thicker.
example: A crew is short on 8 AWG and there is a reel of a higher-numbered wire on the truck. That is thinner wire, and it is not a substitute for the minimum.

short_definition: Flat-trowelling a layer of thinset directly onto the back of a tile before it goes up, in addition to the mortar already combed onto the wall.
explanation:
It fills the keying pattern moulded into the back of the tile and wets the surface, so the mortar on the tile and the mortar on the wall join as one body rather than meeting as two skins.

It is one part of Sapphire's Back-Butter Rule, which sets 95 to 100 per cent mortar coverage behind every single submerged tile. The rest of it is combing the wall in one direction, setting the tile across the ridges and working it back and forth to collapse them rather than dropping it in place, then pulling a tile back up while everything is fresh to see what the coverage actually is.
example: A tile is lifted off a freshly set wall and turned over. Whatever the back of that one looks like is what the whole wall looks like.

short_definition: A circuit that can be energised from a source other than the breaker you opened.
explanation: One open breaker proves one open breaker. A generator, a transfer switch, a control transformer, a UPS, a second panel, or a circuit somebody added years ago can all put voltage on conductors downstream of a breaker that is definitely off. This is why verification is a measurement at the point you will touch rather than a look at a panel schedule.
example: A technician opens the breaker labelled for a fountain lighting circuit and finds 120 volts still on one conductor at the junction box, fed from a landscape panel on the other side of the property.

short_definition: Pushing water backwards through a blocked part so the blockage comes back out the way it went in.
explanation:
It works because most blockages arrive from the upstream side and are wider than the hole they lodged in. Driving them further forward jams them; bringing them back the way they came releases them.

It is the first thing to try on a blocked nozzle, and it costs nothing but a little time.
example: A nozzle is short and splitting. Out it comes, held under a tap the wrong way round, and a wood chip the size of a grain of rice drops out of the back of it.

short_definition: A second wrench held on the pipe or fitting behind a joint, so the turning force is taken between the two wrenches instead of travelling on into whatever the pipe is attached to.
explanation:
Force has to go somewhere. Pull on one wrench and it travels down the line until it reaches something that gives - a manifold, a pump port, a valve body. Hold the back-up wrench and it never gets past the joint you are working on.

Never pull on a single wrench where the fitting is attached to a manifold or a pump housing.
example: A stuck nipple in a pump port finally moves - and it moves because two wrenches were working against each other six inches apart, rather than because one of them was working against the pump.

short_definition: Running water backwards through a filter to flush out what it has trapped, and sending that waste to drain.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary speech it is what goes back into a bottle when somebody drinks from it, or the wash of water behind a boat. Here it is a deliberate maintenance operation.
explanation:
It matters most in the step after a shock that everybody abandons. Killing algae does not remove it — it turns a living green problem into a suspended dead one the filtration has to physically take out of the water.

The water typically goes grey or milky first, which looks like the treatment failed and is actually the sign it worked. Filter pressure climbs as it loads; clean or backwash according to the equipment's instructions and keep going.
example: Wednesday morning the water is milky and somebody reports the shock as unsuccessful. It worked. What is in the water now is dead, and it needs to come out through the filter, not out of a bottle.

short_definition: Cleaning a sand filter by reversing the flow through the bed and sending what comes out to waste.
explanation:
It needs a legal, planned discharge point, and it costs a quantity of treated water every time, which is why cartridges are common where discharge is restricted.

The cycle runs on BACKWASH until the sight glass is clear, then RINSE for thirty seconds to resettle the bed and clear the dirty water left standing in the pipe. Every handle movement starts with the pump off.
example: Sight glass runs the colour of coffee, then tea, then clear at about two and a half minutes. Pump off, handle to RINSE, thirty seconds, pump off, handle to FILTER, and write down the new clean baseline.

short_definition: A separate tank plumbed to the feature that holds the water displaced when the system starts, stops or surges, and that the pumps draw from.
explanation:
It is a hydraulic buffer, and that means two things at once. It has to hold enough volume to fill every pipe and every nozzle at the moment the pumps start, and enough room spare to take all of that water back when the system shuts down and the decks drain into it.

A tank sized only for the running state overflows at every shutdown. Its level, not anything under the deck, is what the controller watches.
example: A splash pad floods its vault every evening at shutdown. Nothing is leaking. The tank was sized for the system running and not for the whole system coming back down into it.

short_definition: A throttling valve on a branch, set once during commissioning so that branch takes its designed share of the flow.
explanation:
Water divides between parallel branches according to how much resistance each offers, not according to the drawing. Left alone, the near branch off a manifold takes more than its share and the far branch starves.

A balancing valve fixes that by deliberately adding resistance to the easy branches until every branch reads its designed flow. The work is done against flow readings, not against how the jets look - eyeballing nozzle heights gets you a display that is even on a still day and wrong on every other one.
example: Three of eleven jets on a runnel run visibly higher than the rest. The flow meter on the main says the system is exactly where it should be, because all the water is there - it is just in the wrong three branches.

short_definition: A quarter-turn valve with a drilled ball inside it, either fully open or fully shut. On a test manifold it isolates the water intake.
explanation:
Low loss, positive shut-off, and you can read its position from across the room by looking at the handle. That last point is genuinely useful on a site.

Two cautions. Partly open, the jet squeezing past the ball cuts the seats, so it is not a throttling valve. And because it goes from open to shut in a quarter turn, it is the easiest thing on a site to slam - which makes it a common source of water hammer.
example: A technician shuts a two-inch ball valve on a live line with one quick flick of the wrist. The bang travels the length of the vault and something upstairs rattles.

short_definition: A brand of cementitious fluid-applied waterproofing, named in Sapphire's document as an example of the kind of material used on a submerged shell.
explanation:
The brand names in the course tell you what class of material is meant. They do not tell you the mix water, the primer requirement, the recoat window or the cure time for the pail on your job.

Products that look identical in the bucket differ on every one of those, and mixing components between systems — one maker's primer under another's membrane — is a real incompatibility, not a paperwork problem.
example: The job hands you a pail, the spec sheet says a different brand, and somebody says they are the same stuff. They may well behave the same way, but the recoat window on the can in front of you is the one that governs what time you can put the second coat on.

short_definition: The reading a particular system produced when it was known to be working correctly, written down so later readings have something to be compared against.
explanation:
Every diagnosis made with a gauge depends on one. "The filter pressure is high" says nothing at all until there is a clean number for it to be high against, and the same goes for suction vacuum, the normal operating level, the balanced chemistry and the sequence timings.

Start-up is the one visit where the whole system is clean and right at the same moment, which is why the whole set is taken then — and re-taken after every filter clean. Record them where the site's records actually live: a reading the next technician cannot find is a reading nobody took.
example: Two identical features on one plaza. One has a start-up sheet in the site file with six numbers on it, and a caller reporting weak flow gets an answer in a minute. The other has nothing, and the same call costs half a day.

short_definition: The ring of squeezed-out cement that appears around the outside of a joint when the pipe is pushed home.
ordinary_meaning: A small round ball on a necklace, or a drop of sweat.
explanation:
A continuous, uniform ring of purple and gray around the whole joint is what a finished Sapphire joint looks like, and the excess gets wiped off.

Be careful how much you read into it. A bead confirms that cement reached the mouth of the socket. It says nothing at all about whether the socket walls further in were wetted or scraped dry, which is the failure a missing chamfer causes.
example: Two joints on the same rack look identical from the outside — same clean purple and gray ring. One was chamfered and one was not, and no amount of looking at the bead will tell you which.

short_definition: The prepared layer placed along the trench floor for the pipe to sit on, put in before any pipe goes in.
ordinary_meaning: Sheets and blankets, or plants being bedded in. Here it is a graded layer of clean washed sand or pea gravel.
explanation:
Its job is to give a level and forgiving base along the whole length of the run, so support is continuous. PVC never goes straight onto native rock or dirt.

Sapphire's figure for the layer is a minimum of 4 to 6 inches, and the trench floor underneath it has to be continuous and clear of rock, jagged shale, roots and debris first.
example: A trench bottom is raked level and looks fine, but there is a fist-sized cobble sitting proud at the twelve foot mark. Bedding exists so that cobble is not what the pipe rests on.

short_definition: A pocket dug out of the bedding so a fitting or a joint has somewhere to sit without the pipe being lifted off the bed.
explanation:
A coupling is fatter than the pipe. Without a pocket for it, the fitting carries the run and the pipe either side of it hangs.

The pocket has to be refilled and worked in before backfill, or you have deliberately built a void at the joint — the one place you least want one.
example: The bedding is perfect except at three couplings, where somebody scooped hollows and nobody filled them back in.

short_definition: A dip in a buried pipe run where the line falls, rises, and falls again. Water sits in the bottom of it and gravity cannot get it out.
ordinary_meaning: A stomach. In the trade it is a defect in a pipe run and always a criticism.
explanation:
Gravity drains a line that falls all the way to its drain point. It does not drain one that dips, and no amount of leaving the valve open changes that — the water in the sag stays there. The sag is then precisely where the split happens, because it is the one place holding water when the frost arrives.

A belly is a grade problem, not a winterizing problem. If the same run splits in the same place two winters running, say so, so somebody can fix the actual thing.
example: One run out of six always needs extra blowing and always comes up milky long after the others are dry. It crosses ground that was backfilled late in the build. That is a belly, and it will be there next year too unless it is reported.

short_definition: Below the finished level of the surrounding ground. Grade here means ground level.
ordinary_meaning: Grade normally means a mark at school or a quality level — and confusingly, this same module uses grade in that second sense too, in engineering-grade cement and underwater-grade sealant. Below-grade has nothing to do with quality: it means buried.
explanation:
Below-grade is a flag for a set of problems arriving at once. Groundwater pressure from outside, uplift under the slab, restricted access, and often a confined space.

The same basin above grade raises none of them.
example: Two basins on the same site take the same membrane and the same detailing, and only one of them requires anybody to think about the water table before it is drained. That one is the buried one.

short_definition: A physical point on the job whose elevation is known and agreed, that every other elevation is measured from.
ordinary_meaning: A standard to compare performance against, as in benchmarking a competitor. Here it is an actual spot on an actual object you can put a rod on.
explanation:
On a fountain it is typically the finished concrete coping or the absolute top edge of the weir wall. It has to be something that will not move and that everybody uses.

Two people working from two different benchmarks produce two sets of numbers that are each internally consistent and disagree with each other.
example: The morning crew shoots from the coping and the afternoon crew, arriving later, shoots from a stake somebody drove near the spoil pile. Both runs are perfect and they do not meet.

short_definition: A living layer of microorganisms growing on a wetted surface - slippery to the touch rather than hard, and it wipes off with a cloth.
explanation:
It is the slipperiness on a basin wall, the slime behind a weir, the film inside a filter, and — the part you cannot see — the coating inside the pipework and on the pump impellers.

Three consequences: it eats sanitiser continuously, so the residual crashes between visits and the dose gets blamed; it protects what lives inside it from the sanitiser in the water; and it re-seeds the water as fast as you treat it, from a place your chemistry is barely reaching.
example: A white-ish coating in a shaded corner of a basin turns out to wipe away under a thumb and feel slick rather than gritty. That is not the scale the ticket says it is.

short_definition: A single on-or-off value in a controller's memory. Contacts ask about bits; coils write them.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a small piece of something, or a drill bit.
explanation: Everything in a ladder program is bits. An input bit reflects what the controller read from the field at the start of the scan; an output bit is what it intends to write at the end. A fault bit that has not been cleared is one of the commonest reasons a condition is genuinely false and everything else looks fine.
example: A feature will not start and the screen shows no active alarm. A latched fault bit from a trip last week is still set, and the rung is waiting on it being clear.

short_definition: Algae appearing as dark dots or streaks on a basin surface.
explanation:
Two things about it defeat chemistry. It grows a hard protective outer shell, so sanitiser reaches the outside and nothing else. And it embeds root-like structures into porous concrete or grout, so the living part is inside the finish rather than on it.

Sapphire's document says it plainly: exceptionally difficult to kill without mechanical scraping. Spots that keep coming back in the same place are usually telling you the surface there is damaged or porous enough to hold roots, which makes it a repair question as much as a chemistry one.
example: Four dark spots on a concrete floor return in exactly the same places after every shock. The dose was never the problem — nothing you poured in ever reached the part that was alive.

short_definition: A plug that closes an enclosure entry no cable is using, so the opening is sealed to the same standard as the rest of the box.
explanation:
A rating describes an enclosure as tested, with every entry made up the way the maker intended. One unused opening with nothing in it and the rating is gone — not degraded, gone.

Tape or a smear of silicone does not restore it. Neither does the opening ending up above the water line, on a box that was rated for submersion.
example: A four-entry box is installed with two cables. Nobody had the plugs on the van and the plan was to come back. It went under water that afternoon and looked exactly like a box that was right.

short_definition: What happens when chlorine in a sample is so high that it destroys the test's indicator dye as fast as it develops, and the sample turns clear.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like the chlorine itself bleaching away, or being used up. It is the reverse — the chlorine is winning, and the thing being bleached is your test.
explanation:
Sapphire's document puts the threshold above roughly 10 to 15 ppm of free chlorine. A clear sample reads as zero chlorine, so the instinct is to add more, on water that already has far too much.

The fix: dilute the sample with 50% distilled water, re-test, and multiply the result by 2. A near-zero result on freshly shocked water is never a reason to add more.
example: You shock a basin hard on Monday night, come back Tuesday morning and the DPD-1 test reads almost nothing. Nothing has been consumed. The dye never had a chance.

short_definition: To let trapped air escape from a high point of a filled system, usually through a small relief fitting, until water rather than air comes out.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English it is what a cut does.
explanation: Air rises to the high points as a system fills and stays there. Until it is bled off, every gauge on the system is describing a mixture rather than water, flow is down, and the first time the level moves the pocket can travel and cost you prime.
example: The pumps are running, the filter gauge is jumping about, and a fine shimmer of bubbles keeps arriving at the wall inlets. Cracking the relief at the top of the filter gives a long hiss before it spits water, and the gauge steadies as soon as it does.

short_definition: To plug the surface of a filter so completely with fine material that water can no longer pass through it.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like it has to do with sight, or with covering something over. In filtration it means clogged solid at the face — the filter has not torn or failed, it has been sealed shut by what you sent it.
explanation: A cartridge blinds rather than fills. Coarse debris loads it gradually and it keeps working; a slug of silt lays a skin across the pleats and the pressure goes up in minutes. The filter is not damaged, but it is finished until it is cleaned, so vacuuming fines through a cartridge buys you a cartridge clean instead of a vacuum — and the dirt is still in the system.
example: You vacuum a grey post-treatment film through a cartridge filter because there is no multiport. Within a quarter of an hour the pressure is up and the flow has dropped, and the afternoon becomes a cartridge strip-down.

short_definition: A rapid growth of algae in a body of water, to the point where it is visible.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like flowers opening — a pleasant word for a slow, seasonal thing. Here it names an outbreak, and it can happen in days.
explanation:
Algae needs light, warmth, water and nutrients, and three of those are what a fountain is. Spores arrive constantly on wind, rain, birds, people and equipment moved between sites — exposure is not what decides whether a feature blooms.

What decides it is whether the sanitiser is winning. A bloom is a symptom, not the disease. Something is short: free chlorine, circulation reaching that part of the basin, filtration, or chlorine that is present on the test but parked behind too much stabiliser.
example: A feature greens up between two visits in warm weather. Treating the colour buys you the interval to the next visit; finding out which of the four is short is what stops it.

short_definition: The manufacturer's exact hole-cleaning sequence for an adhesive anchor: a specified number of compressed-air blows and brush passes, with a brush of a specified diameter.
explanation:
Drilling concrete produces a fine dust that coats the walls of the hole. Adhesive injected onto that dust bonds to dust, not to concrete, and the anchor can pull straight out at a fraction of its rated load.

The sequence is part of the anchor's published rating. Doing three-quarters of it does not give you three-quarters of the strength, and it is not 'give it a blast with the compressor'.
example: Twelve holes to clean and the compressor is on the far side of the plaza. The temptation is one quick pass each, and that is the number one cause of adhesive anchor failure in the field.

short_definition: Pushing air through the plumbing to drive out the water that gravity could not reach, working from the manifold outwards to the nozzles.
explanation: Connect a high-volume compressor or blower to the main manifold test ports and run air through at low pressure, under 15 PSI, but high CFM. The finish line is neither a time nor a gauge reading: keep going until a clean, mist-free stream of air comes out of every field nozzle tip. Mist means water is still being carried out of that line, and a line still carrying water is a line you have not finished.
example: Zone three has been blowing for a while and the tips look dry from twenty feet away. Up close the stream is still faintly milky. Another minute and it goes hard and clear — and that is the difference between a finished zone and one that splits.

short_definition: Something that stops two layers sticking to each other. Sometimes a contaminant that does it by accident, sometimes a strip deliberately installed at a joint so the membrane is free to move there.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like the name of a fault — the thing that ruined your bond. Half the time it is, but the other half it is a real component you are supposed to install on purpose, and reading the deliberate one as a defect is how the movement-joint detail gets skipped.
explanation:
Accidental bond breakers are the whole point of the Rule of Clean: dust, laitance, release agent, curing compound, loose sand. Each one sits between the membrane and the concrete and stops the bond happening there.

The deliberate kind is at a movement joint, where you want the membrane unbonded across the gap so the movement is taken up by slack instead of by stretch.
example: You sweep a cured membrane before the tile crew arrives and a fine layer of unbonded sand comes off it. That loose sand was an accidental bond breaker: the mortar would have bonded to the sand, and the sand to nothing.

short_definition: A mortar bed placed onto a prepared substrate with a bond coat, so that bed and substrate act as one piece.
explanation:
It can be thinner than the alternative, because the slab underneath is carrying it. The trade-off is that it inherits everything the substrate does: a crack that opens in the slab travels straight up through the bed and into the tile.

Bonded means the substrate has to be genuinely clean. Laitance, release agent or curing compound left on it makes a bonded bed an unbonded bed that is far too thin.
example: A hairline crack appears in the finished tile in a dead straight line, and it is exactly over the crack that was in the slab before anybody tiled it.

short_definition: This word does two unrelated jobs on a fountain site. Electrically, bonding ties metal parts together with a conductor so they all sit at the same voltage. In tiling and masonry, a bond is simply one layer sticking to another.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, bonding is gluing things together, or two people getting close. The electrical meaning has nothing to do with either.
explanation:
Bonding does not carry fault current anywhere and it is not trying to. It removes the voltage difference between things a person can touch at the same time - the water, the wet deck, the coping, the reinforcing steel, a handrail, a light housing. If all of those are tied together they rise and fall together and there is nothing to drive current through a body.

Around water this is an engineered, inspected grid governed by NEC Article 680, much of it buried in concrete. Never cut, extend, shorten, relocate or tidy up a bonding conductor. It is frequently bare copper and it looks exactly like scrap.
example: A stainless grate in a new splash pad has a green wire clamped to a lug underneath it. That is not an offcut somebody left behind - remove it as tidying up and the next fault in the feature has somewhere to go that it did not have this morning.

short_definition: The point at which added chlorine has destroyed all the combined chlorine, so further chlorine starts staying in the water as free chlorine.
ordinary_meaning: "Breakpoint" sounds like the point where something fails or gives way — the last straw. Here it is a target you are aiming to reach, not a limit you are trying to avoid.
explanation:
The shape of the curve is the lesson. Below breakpoint, added chlorine forms more chloramines rather than destroying them — so an under-dose is worse than doing nothing. The feature smells worse and irritates more, and the usual conclusion is that shocking did not work and next time should be gentler.

Sapphire's document gives the dose: free chlorine must reach ten times the combined chlorine, plus 5 ppm. There is no credit for getting close.
example: A basin tests at 1.5 ppm combined. Someone doses to what feels like plenty, stops, and walks away having manufactured more of exactly the thing they came to remove.

short_definition: The point at which a chemical has worked its way through a glove material and reached the skin underneath.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English a breakthrough is a great discovery or a big step forward. On a glove it is a failure, measured in minutes.
explanation: Glove materials are selected against a specific product, using the breakthrough data the glove manufacturer and the safety data sheet provide — a glove that is right for one product can be permeated in minutes by another, with no visible change to warn you. That is the silent-failure property PPE is famous for: a permeated glove and a glove doing its job look and feel identical.
example: A technician wears the same nitrile gloves for every chemical on the truck because they have never let him down. A glove that has been permeated does not look any different afterwards, so he would not know if they had.

short_definition: To throw loose material by hand so it scatters and lands evenly over a surface, rather than pouring it in a heap.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like radio and television. The older meaning is the farming one — scattering seed by hand across a field — and that is the sense the trade kept.
explanation:
Product tipped in one place lands as a concentrated slug: it bleaches, etches or stains the finish under it, and the rest of the basin gets nothing.

The method: a clean bucket filled with water first, product added slowly into the water, stirred with something dedicated to the job, then poured in slowly around the perimeter with the circulation running. Some products say explicitly not to pre-dissolve — the label decides that, not the habit.
example: A technician working alone on a small basin is tempted to pour from the bag and push the sand around with a brush. That drags the wet coat, thins it in streaks and leaves the sand sitting loose on top. Throwing it takes the same five minutes and leaves a coat still worth having.

short_definition: A water-loss test in which a bucket of basin water is stood in the basin, both levels are marked, and the two drops are compared after a set period.
explanation:
The bucket is the control. It sits in the same sun, the same air and the same water temperature as the basin, so a still surface in the bucket and a still surface in the basin lose water at the same rate. Anything the basin loses beyond that is something evaporation does not explain.

What it cannot reproduce is the extra evaporation a running display creates by throwing water into the air - which is why the test is repeated with the feature off.
example: Tuesday morning, a bucket weighted down on the basin step, both levels marked with tape at the same minute, the autofill isolated and the weather written on the ticket. Thursday the basin is well below its mark and the bucket has barely moved.

short_definition: Something dissolved in the water that absorbs acid or base additions, so the pH moves less than the dose on its own would move it.
ordinary_meaning: A buffer in everyday use is a polishing machine, or a gap you leave between two things for safety. In water it is a chemical effect: the thing that decides whether a pH you set stays where you put it.
explanation: When people say the chemistry on a feature is unstable, this is usually what they mean without knowing it. Unstable pH is not a mysterious property of the basin - it is the measurable absence of a buffer, and it has a number attached to it.
example: Two basins get the same correction from the same jug. One moves a little and settles; the other overshoots past the target and is back where it started by Thursday. The difference is not the product.

short_definition: A liquid of known, stable pH that a probe is calibrated against.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a cushion between two things, or a polishing pad.
explanation: Calibration is the only way a probe's reading is tied to anything real. Which buffers, and how often, comes from the probe manufacturer's instructions and the site's own schedule.
example: A technician brings two bottles to a service visit, dips the probe in each, and finds the reading needs a nudge in one direction at both points — which is the probe ageing, not the water changing.

short_definition: The barrier between the cargo area and the cab.
explanation: It is what an unrestrained load hits before it reaches the people. Useful, and not a substitute for securing the load — a bulkhead is sized for an accident, not for a habit.
example: A hard stop at a light slides an unstrapped toolbox the length of the bed. It stops against the bulkhead with a bang everyone in the cab feels through their seat.

short_definition: A quick check that exposes a gas monitor to a known test gas to confirm the sensors and the alarm actually respond.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like knocking or jolting the instrument to see if it still works — the way you might thump a radio. It is nothing physical; it is a dose of test gas.
explanation: Calibration adjusts what the numbers mean; a bump test only proves that the thing reacts at all. It matters because of how a gas meter fails: an uncalibrated or dead-sensored meter does not read nothing — it reads a plausible number, and a plausible number is exactly what talks somebody into the hole.
example: A monitor that has been rattling around a truck all summer shows a tidy 20.9% oxygen and zeros across the board at the hatch. So would the same monitor with a sensor that stopped responding in June.

short_definition: A valve with a disc on a shaft that rotates within the bore, common in large pipe sizes because it is compact and cheap.
explanation:
A butterfly will isolate and it will throttle over part of its range, which makes it a useful compromise on large lines. It is not a precision control device.

Near the closed end of its travel the flow past the disc becomes unstable and it can cavitate, which is noisy and eats the disc and seat.
example: An eight-inch butterfly on a main feed is nudged nearly shut to quiet a feature down for an evening event. It starts making a sound like gravel in the pipe, which is the disc cavitating, not debris.

short_definition: A short parallel pipe around a piece of equipment, with valves, so flow can be split around it or diverted past it entirely.
explanation: It lets the heater see the flow it wants while the rest of the system runs at its own rate, and it lets the heater be isolated for service without draining anything.
example: The heater wants less flow than the circulation pump moves. Two valves and a loop, and both get what they want, plus the heater comes out in spring without a drain-down.

short_definition: The fitting that seals a cable where it passes into an enclosure, sized to the cable's actual measured outside diameter. It also takes the strain, so the jacket is never dragged through the seal.
ordinary_meaning: A gland in ordinary English is an organ in the body. The mechanical sense is old and unrelated — a gland is a part that is tightened down to compress packing around something passing through it, and the same word is used for the seal on a pump shaft.
explanation:
Almost every wet enclosure that fails, fails at an entry. The body is a moulding or casting with no way through it and the lid has one large well-understood gasket, but the entries are small, numerous and made up by hand on site.

One gland tightened onto a cable it was never sized for cannot close around it, however tight the nut goes. One cable per gland, unless the gland is specifically made for more.
example: The cable measures a shade under the gland's stated range, so it goes in and the nut spins up nicely with nothing gripping the jacket. Pull on it and it slides. That is not a seal; it is a hole with a fitting in it.

short_definition: A moulded cover laid over a hose or cord where it crosses a walking surface, so people walk up and over it instead of catching a foot on it.
explanation: A trip over a hose or a cord is the injury this trade causes more often than any other, and the person who goes down is usually a member of the public who was not watching their feet. Tape is not a ramp — it changes the colour of the lump and nothing else, and now the cord is also stuck to the ground when somebody catches it.
example: A discharge hose has to cross a lobby walkway. The crew picks the narrowest point, runs straight across it, drops a ramp over the top and cones the ends, rather than running the hose diagonally to the door because that is shorter.

short_definition: The compound that forms when calcium coming out of the water binds with carbon dioxide. It is what fountain scale is made of, and what limestone, travertine and marble are made of.
explanation: Knowing the deposit and the stone are the same compound explains the whole acid rule in one line. An acid that dissolves the crust has no way of knowing it should stop at the stone, because the stone is chemically the same thing.
example: The same bottle that cleans a granite spillway beautifully will put a permanent cloudy patch on the limestone step beside it, and the tech will have done nothing differently.

short_definition: How much dissolved calcium the water is carrying. It is one of the factors in the LSI, and it is a property of the water itself rather than of anything you can feel.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like how hard or firm something is, or how difficult the water is to deal with. It is simply a count of dissolved calcium — a soft-water feature is not an easy one.
explanation:
Too little dissolved calcium and the water goes and gets its own, out of grout, mortar, plaster and copper fittings. Too much and it drops calcium back out as scale on stone, tile, nozzles and quartz sleeves.

Unlike pH it does not wander on its own, so a hardness change holds — it is the slower lever and often the more honest one. It only rises by itself, though: evaporation concentrates it, and bringing it down means diluting the water.
example: Two features on opposite sides of town are filled on the same day from different supplies. One comes up balanced almost by itself. The other needs work before it is safe to leave running, and the difference is what came out of the hose.

short_definition: A granular chlorine product, one of the two Sapphire's document names for shock dosing a fountain.
explanation:
It is alkaline, so it pushes pH up — a feature that was balanced before a shock is not balanced after it. It is also an oxidiser: combined with trichlor in a bucket, a feeder or even on a damp scoop it can ignite. Sheds have burned down from this.

Granular product thrown into a basin sinks and lands as a concentrated, chemically extreme pile on the finish, which is why the protocol says pre-dissolved and broadcast uniformly.
example: A ring of white marks on a dark basin floor, all the same size. Somebody two seasons ago tipped the bucket in dry and walked off.

short_definition: Adjusting an instrument against a known reference so its readings mean what they say, on the schedule the manufacturer sets.
explanation: Sapphire's pre-entry rule names a calibrated four-gas monitor specifically. An instrument drifts quietly over time — nothing about the display changes — so the calibration date is part of whether the reading is evidence or decoration.
example: Before an entry the technician checks the calibration due date on the monitor's label the same way he would check the date on a fire extinguisher, and finds it expired two months ago.

short_definition: A structure supported at one end only, with the far end carrying itself.
explanation:
A cantilever is in tension along its top, all the way out, which is the opposite of what most people expect. A basin wall standing off its footing is one. A coping slab projecting past the wall it sits on is another.

It also means the steel in the top of that section is the thing holding it up, so cutting or coring near it is not a field decision.
example: A coping slab overhangs the wall by a hand's width. Somebody sits on the outer edge to eat lunch. Everything keeping that person up is in the top inch of that slab.

short_definition: A component that stores electrical charge. It can hold that charge after the circuit around it has been switched off.
explanation: Motor-start capacitors and power supplies both hold charge, and a discharged capacitor can recover some of it on its own afterwards. Capacitance is also why long wire runs leak a little current to earth all by themselves, which is one of the genuine causes of a spurious GFCI trip.
example: A very long lighting run with several fixtures on one device has been marginal since it was built. Its capacitive leakage adds up, and on a damp week it is enough to put the device over the edge.

short_definition: Liquid travelling along very narrow gaps by surface tension alone, with nothing pushing it — including uphill, and over long distances.
explanation:
Inside a cable there are narrow gaps everywhere: between the strands of a conductor, and between the conductors and the jacket. Those spaces are called the interstices, and they behave like a wick.

So water gets into a cable at a nicked jacket or a wet splice somewhere else entirely and arrives inside an enclosure whose lid has never been off and whose glands are perfect. The useful tell is volume: condensation leaves a box damp, but a wicking cable fills it.
example: A submersible junction box is pumped out in spring and full again by midsummer. Every seal checks out. The cable was nicked by a trowel during the tile work two years ago, forty feet away and above the water line, and it has been feeding the box ever since.

short_definition: A colourless, odourless toxic gas produced by anything burning, and one of the four a pre-entry test measures.
explanation: Sapphire's safe operational figure is below 25 ppm. There is nothing to smell and nothing to see, and the source is usually something the crew brought: a generator, a compressor, a pressure washer, or a vehicle idling near the hatch. It is also the reason a purge must draw fresh outdoor air — a blower sitting beside a running generator feeds the vault exactly what you are trying to clear out of it.
example: A gas-powered pressure washer is left running ten feet upwind of an open vault hatch while a technician works below. Everything about the scene looks ordinary from the deck.

short_definition: Stone made mostly of calcium carbonate: limestone, travertine and marble. Acid dissolves it.
explanation:
This is the single most expensive thing to get wrong in a cleaning job, because the stone is chemically the same family as the deposit you are trying to remove. An acid strong enough to take the crust off does not stop politely when it gets to the stone.

And you cannot always tell what you are standing in front of. A pale slab is limestone or it is a dense manufactured unit; the two take opposite treatments. If nobody can say which it is, that is a stop and ask.
example: A tech wipes a splash of scale remover off a travertine coping with a wet rag. Next morning there is a dull, lighter patch exactly the shape of the wipe.

short_definition: The pipe actually carrying water through a penetration — the inner one, the thing the seal grips.
explanation: The word exists to keep two pipes apart in conversation. Once there is a sleeve in a wall and a pipe inside it, saying just the pipe is ambiguous and the ambiguity gets built.
example: Ordering a seal over the phone, it matters which of the two diameters you are reading out. The carrier is the one with water in it.

short_definition: The pleated fabric cylinder inside a cartridge filter that the water passes through.
ordinary_meaning: 'Element' sounds like a chemical element, or the heating element in a kettle.
explanation:
There is no backwash. You shut down, isolate, bleed, open the vessel, pull the element and clean it, which uses far less water than backwashing.

Hosing removes debris from the pleats. It does not remove oils, scale or mineral deposits, and an element that is hosed but never soaked loses capacity while looking perfectly clean. A high-pressure washer tears the engineered fibres, after which the element passes water freely and filters nothing.
example: An element gets blasted with a pressure washer every spring because it comes up so white. Three seasons later the water never quite clears and the element still looks brand new.

short_definition: A filter that strains water through a pleated fabric element in a housing. It is cleaned by pulling the element out and washing it, not by backwashing.
explanation: Two things follow for service work. It filters finer than sand, which also means fine material blinds it. And most cartridge installations have no multiport, so there is no waste position to vacuum to — leaving you the choice of filtering and then cleaning, or reaching for one of the portable rigs that discharge outside the system by design.
example: A courtyard feature on a cartridge filter has a silt film on the floor. There is no waste valve anywhere in the pit, so the Jet Vac comes off the truck rather than the vacuum pump.

short_definition: A vessel poured on site in its final position, as opposed to pre-cast, which is cast at a yard and delivered.
explanation:
Strong, permanent, and entirely unforgiving about anything you forgot to put in before the pour. With pre-cast the same constraint exists, moved earlier and further away: the penetrations were decided at the casting yard.

This is the root of how sequencing-heavy fountain work is.
example: The pour is Tuesday. Everything that belongs in that wall - sleeves, niches, conduit, drain bodies - is either in the formwork on Monday afternoon or it becomes a core drill and an engineer's signature.

short_definition: Measurement categories describing how much fault energy a meter and its leads are built to survive if the circuit flashes over while they are connected. A commercial or industrial panel is a CAT III or CAT IV environment.
explanation:
A cheap or unrated meter in that panel is not a worse measurement — it is the thing that turns a fault into an arc flash across your hands. The category comes with a voltage rating, and both have to suit the installation in front of you.

The rating covers the leads as well, and that is where it is usually lost. Cracked insulation, an exposed strand, a probe tip that has been filed — those leads get binned, not taped.
example: A meter in the van is correctly rated, but one lead has a split near the probe from being shut in a door. That measurement is no longer a rated measurement, whatever the badge on the meter says.

short_definition: Vapour bubbles forming in water where the pressure falls very low, then collapsing violently when they are carried back into a higher-pressure region.
explanation:
A restriction on the suction side drops the pressure at the eye of the impeller. Drop it far enough and the water reaches its vapour pressure and boils at ambient temperature. The bubbles are then flung outward into higher pressure, where they collapse against the metal - thousands of tiny collapses a second.

That is both the noise and the damage: it pits and erodes the impeller from the surface inward. The fault is upstream; the damage is to the pump.
example: A pump has been making an odd rattling sound for three weeks and everybody has been working around it. The basket underneath it was packed solid, and the impeller that comes out is pitted like it has been sandblasted.

short_definition: The standard water pump on a fountain system. A vaned wheel spins inside a housing and throws water outward, and that is what produces both the suction at the inlet and the pressure at the outlet.
explanation:
Nearly every pump in a fountain equipment room is one of these. It moves water well and it moves air badly, which is the source of most of its troubles: it has to be full of water before it will do anything at all.

The wet end is the part that holds water; the motor is bolted to the back of it and the shaft passes between them through a seal.
example: Two pumps on the same manifold sound identical from the door, but one has been drawing on an empty basket for a minute. From ten feet away there is nothing to see — which is exactly why the rule is to stop the pump the moment the note changes rather than finish the pass first.

short_definition: Cubic feet per minute — how much air a compressor or blower actually moves in a minute, as distinct from how hard it pushes.
explanation: The blow-out pairing is low pressure with high CFM, and the reason is that volume moves the water and pressure only stores energy in the pipe. A big tank compressor turned up is not a better blow-out, it is a more dangerous one. What clears a long line is a lot of air passing through it, not a lot of force behind it.
example: A small trim compressor is on site and it will happily reach 100 PSI, but it takes forever to shift the water out of one zone because it delivers very little air per minute. The blower on the truck does the whole manifold at a fraction of the pressure.

short_definition: A small plastic or steel support that holds a reinforcing bar off the form at the right height while concrete is placed around it.
ordinary_meaning: Something you sit on.
explanation:
Chairs and spacers are how cover stops being a number on a drawing and becomes a real dimension in a wall. They are the reason bars are tied off the form rather than laid against it.

Which is why a bar that has been walked down or pulled to the face during a pour is not a cosmetic issue to be patched over later.
example: A tech kicks a loose chair clear because it is in the path of the vibrator. The bar it was holding drops an inch, and nobody finds out until the wall tells them years later.

short_definition: A 10 to 15 degree angle cut around the outside edge of a pipe end, made with a chamfering tool or a fine rasp before the pipe goes into a fitting.
explanation:
Sapphire's own document calls this the non-negotiable step, and it is the one that gets skipped because a cut end already looks finished.

A square, unchamfered end behaves like a scraper blade on the way into the socket. What it does to the cement inside is invisible once the joint is together, and the outside bead looks perfect either way.
example: A 3 inch return line is cut clean with a wheel cutter, and the crew skips the bevel because the edge looks smooth. The test passes that afternoon. The joint weeps two summers later, under the slab.

short_definition: Any line where a surface turns a corner — floor to wall, an inside corner, a step nosing, the lip of a drain.
explanation:
