These lines collect every problem at once. They are where the structure moves, where a coating is being asked to bridge a crack, and where a brush or roller pulls the material thin over an edge.

That is why reinforcement goes in at every one of them — fabric bedded into a liquid system, preformed pieces in a sheet system. It is part of the system, not an upgrade somebody can decide to skip.
example: You look at a finished first coat on a raking afternoon light. The flat areas are even, and every inside corner has a slightly paler line where the brush stretched the material round the angle. That pale line is the thin spot, and it is exactly where the reinforcement is supposed to be.

short_definition: One value slot in a DMX universe. A fixture consumes as many consecutive channels as its functions need.
explanation: A single dimmer takes one channel, an RGBW fixture takes four, and one with dimming, strobe and effects takes more. How many a given fixture consumes depends on which mode it is set to, which is why the mode and the address have to be recorded together.
example: Someone plans a layout assuming four channels per fixture, and half of them are actually in a mode that takes more. Every address after the first few is now wrong by a growing amount.

short_definition: To cut a crack open into a clean, wider groove with a grinder or saw, so a repair material can be packed into it properly.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English, to chase something is to run after it. In the trade it means to cut a channel — so chasing a crack means deliberately making it bigger before you fix it, which sounds backwards until you have tried to fill a hairline.
explanation:
A hairline crack has nowhere for repair material to go. Chasing it open gives the hydraulic cement a real section to fill and clean faces to bond to, instead of a skim across the top.

Sapphire's document is explicit about the sequence: chase it out, fill it with an engineering-grade waterproof hydraulic cement, let it cure, then coat over it. A crack that is simply painted over is a crack with a film stretched across it, and the film is the part that tears.
example: A shrinkage crack runs three feet across a basin floor, hairline the whole way. You could rub membrane into it in two minutes. Instead you open it with a grinder, pack it, and leave it until the next day — and that is the version that is still sealed next year.

short_definition: A length of pipe slipped over a wrench handle to multiply the force applied to a stuck fitting.
ordinary_meaning: The name makes it sound like a clever shortcut - cheating the problem. What it actually does is apply far more force than the weakest part of the assembly can survive, and the weakest part is rarely the fitting you are turning.
explanation:
The instinct when a fitting will not move is to find more leverage, and it is almost always the wrong instinct. The cheater bar does not break the nipple - it breaks the pump housing, the valve body, the filter port, or a female fitting cast into something that cannot be replaced on site.

More force is not the next step on the ladder. Penetrant, a back-up wrench, heat on an all-metal joint, and then cutting are.
example: Four o'clock on a Friday, one fitting left, a metre of scaffold tube over the wrench. It moves - and what moved was the port it was threaded into, which is now a new pump.

short_definition: A valve that lets water flow one way and closes against flow in the other direction. It has no handle and no position you set.
ordinary_meaning: Check in ordinary English means to inspect or verify something. A check valve inspects nothing - here check means to stop or restrain, as in checking a fall.
explanation:
Direction is the whole point. On a schematic, a check valve is telling you which way the designer expects water to move through that line - and by implication, that reverse flow there would be a problem.

It is not an isolation valve. Debris on the seat lets it dribble backwards, so you never rely on one to hold a line you are working on. And a check valve that only closes after the flow has already reversed gets slammed shut by the returning column, which is hydraulic shock every single time.
example: A metering pump's feed line is found full of fountain water all the way back to the tank. The check valve at the injection fitting has been weeping closed for months and the tank has been quietly diluting itself.

short_definition: A salt ion carried in treated water. It is the thing that attacks reinforcing steel and stainless steel alike.
explanation:
Chlorides break the passive film that both kinds of steel rely on. They also concentrate over time, because water evaporates and the dissolved solids it was carrying do not, and then the feature gets topped up with more.

This is why fountain corrosion is a different problem from building corrosion. The water is the delivery system.
example: A system runs for three summers on top-ups alone. Nothing was added to the water that anyone remembers, and the water is far saltier than it was on day one.

short_definition: A yellow-green toxic gas produced when acid and chlorine products are mixed, and the reason those two are never carried or stored where they can reach each other.
explanation:
It is released when an acid meets a chlorine product: in a container, in a feeder, in a puddle on a vault floor, or in a shared spill tray. A lungful in an enclosed equipment room is a life-changing injury.

Hence separate storage, separate containment, separate transfer equipment. Chemicals go into the system, never into each other, and it is always acid into water rather than water into acid.
example: A jug of acid tips against a bucket of cal hypo in the back of a van on a Tuesday afternoon. The driver opens the rear doors at the next site into a cloud, and the correct next move is upwind and a phone call, not a grab for the jug.

short_definition: The protective device in a panel that opens a circuit when the current in it exceeds what that circuit's conductors are rated to carry.
explanation:
A breaker is sized to the wire, not to the appetite of whatever is plugged in at the far end. This is the single most misunderstood sentence in the panel.

Which is why fitting a larger breaker to stop repeated tripping is a way to start a fire: the wire in the wall did not get any bigger, and you have removed the only thing that was going to notice the fault.
example: A pump circuit trips every second or third day and a larger breaker would make that stop. It would also let the damaged conductor that is causing it keep heating up, unreported, inside a wall.

short_definition: The tension in a fastener that actually holds a joint together. It is the thing a bolted joint needs; torque is only the crude way of reaching it.
explanation:
A tightened fastener is a very stiff spring under tension, and the clamp load is what that tension does to the joint. A joint with enough clamp load does not move, and a joint that does not move does not fatigue and does not shake loose.

Too little and the joint moves, the fastener works loose or fatigues, and the gasket weeps. Too much and the fastener is taken past its yield point.
example: A flange that weeps only when the pump is running has enough bolts and not enough clamp load - the joint is breathing a fraction of a thousandth every cycle and the gasket has given up.

short_definition: The classification of a GFCI intended to protect people, which trips on a leakage of roughly 4 to 6 milliamps.
explanation: The figure is not arbitrary. It sits below the current at which a person loses muscle control: a few milliamps is already a painful shock, a little more takes the choice away, and more again puts the heart at risk.
example: Somebody asks why the device is so sensitive when the pump it feeds draws amps. It was never watching the pump's current — it is watching for the fraction of an amp that would go through a person.

short_definition: A ground-fault circuit interrupter that trips at roughly 4 to 6 mA of ground-fault current. Class A names that sensitivity level.
explanation:
The 4 to 6 mA threshold is chosen against human physiology, not equipment protection. It is set just below the level at which a person's muscles lock up and they cannot let go, and far below what it takes to stop a heart.

That is why it is required around water, and why a device that protects equipment at a much higher trip level is not a substitute for it.
example: A protective device on a fountain circuit trips at a level intended to save a pump motor. It will do that reliably and it will not do anything at all for the person in the basin, because the current that matters to them is a tiny fraction of it.

short_definition: The regulatory category a water feature is placed in, which decides which set of rules applies to it.
explanation:
A decorative basin nobody is meant to touch, an interactive feature children are designed to run through, and a swimming pool are three different regulatory objects. Requirements step up sharply: treatment and residual, turnover rate, testing frequency and records, suction entrapment protection, barriers and signage, and in some jurisdictions operator certification.

The same physical basin can land in a different class depending on whether people can get into it. So changing how a feature is used changes its classification - and telling a client that is part of the job.
example: A client mentions cheerfully that the ornamental pool is where the children paddle in summer now. That is a regulatory change, not an operational one, and it goes up the line the same day.

short_definition: The pressure a particular vessel shows with completely clean media, at normal operating speed, with the valves in their normal positions, written down so later readings can be compared to it.
explanation:
Recorded at commissioning and recorded again after every clean. Without it nobody can tell a dirty filter from a system that has always run at that pressure; with it, the call takes ten seconds.

The same discipline applies to the suction and discharge gauges, and to the operating speed and valve positions they were read at.
example: The handover folder lists both gauges, the pump speed and the valve positions on the day the fountain was commissioned. Three years later a tech who has never seen the site can read the filter instantly.

short_definition: A sheet laid between a mortar bed and the substrate so that the bed can slide rather than being tied to it.
explanation: It is not waterproofing and it is not there to keep anything dry. Its entire job is to stop two layers gripping each other.
example: A slip sheet is left out because it seemed to be doing nothing. The first season of movement in the slab is printed straight into the tile.

short_definition: Two different things in this module. In a ladder program, the output instruction at the right-hand end of a rung. On a relay, contactor or solenoid valve, the actual winding of wire that makes the device move.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a loop of rope or wire — and in ladder logic, a coil is not a physical object at all, just a symbol borrowed from the relay it replaced.
explanation:
A program coil is energised while the rung is true and drops out the instant the rung goes false. It has no memory — a momentary button wired to a plain coil gives you a momentary output, which is what a seal-in exists to fix.

A physical coil is a length of fine copper wire that can melt shut or snap open, and it is measured in ohms.
example: Somebody says the coil is fine. Ask which coil: the bit on the screen and the winding in the vault fail in completely different ways.

short_definition: The line where one placement of concrete meets another that had already stiffened before it arrived — typically where a floor pour meets a wall pour.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a joint that is cold, or one that opens up in cold weather. Temperature is not what the word is about.
explanation:
The two placements do not become one piece. There is a plane in there, and a plane is a path for water.

Planned construction joints are a different thing entirely and are perfectly fine, because they are detailed with keyways, waterstops and continuous reinforcement. A cold joint is the unplanned version, produced by a pour that stalled, and it has none of that.
example: You are running the first coat across a basin floor and you reach the line where floor meets wall. That line gets worked, reinforced and gone back over — it is not a place to keep the roller moving at the same pace as open floor.

short_definition: Chlorine that has already reacted with ammonia and nitrogen compounds and is spent. It is found by subtracting free chlorine from total chlorine.
ordinary_meaning: "Combined" sounds like the total — everything added together. That is total chlorine. Combined chlorine is only the used-up part.
explanation:
The nitrogen comes from sweat, urine, skin, leaves, birds and dust. What is left after chlorine reacts with it is a weak sanitiser and a strong irritant — it is the byproduct, not the product.

It is also the sharp chemical smell and the stinging eyes that everybody blames on there being too much chlorine. Very often the water is saying the opposite. And it is the number the breakpoint dose is calculated from, which is why a kit that reports only total chlorine cannot tell you what to do.
example: Office staff report that the lobby feature smells strongly of chlorine each morning and it makes their eyes sting. The instinct in the room is to cut the dose. The subtraction says the water never had enough free chlorine to finish the reaction.

short_definition: The air a gas appliance must draw in to burn its fuel, supplied through openings of an engineered size.
explanation:
Clearances, vent material, termination location and the free area of the openings supplying air are all engineered together for that appliance.

Put a gas heater into a tight vault, an enclosure, or a room that was later sealed up, and it produces carbon monoxide. Gas piping and appliance venting are licensed work in most jurisdictions; if the installation does not match the manufacturer's instructions, it stops there.
example: A louvre gets boarded over one winter to keep the room warm for the plumbing. The heater in that room is now burning inside a sealed box.

short_definition: Bringing a system into service deliberately: proving each part works, running the whole program through, and recording what it reads when it is right.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English, commissioning means ordering something made — a commissioned painting — or the percentage a salesperson earns. Here it has nothing to do with money; it is the act of proving a system and writing down what it does.
explanation:
The word carries the distinction between switched on and proved. A feature that is running is not commissioned; a feature is commissioned when the flow was observed, the safety devices were tested, the chemistry was balanced from today's measurements and the readings were recorded somewhere the next technician will find them.

What counts as commissioned on a given site — which baselines, on which form, signed by whom — is Sapphire's call. If the site has a commissioning sheet, that sheet is the authority for the visit.
example: A branch is found wildly out of balance. The question that decides whether this is a half-hour job or a half-day one is whether a commissioning record exists saying where that valve used to be.

short_definition: The documentation produced when a system is first set to work — settings, addresses, setpoints and the state everything was left in.
explanation: It is the first document to open, before the first fixture comes out of the water. If the record does not match what is in the basin, that mismatch is the finding — report it and get the record corrected rather than working around it.
example: A technician opens the record, finds the address for the fixture that is misbehaving, and checks it against the number physically written on the fixture. Those two disagreeing is itself the answer.

short_definition: Packing a dry mix down until it is dense. In a dry-pack bed, density is where the strength comes from.
explanation:
Under-compacted mud is crumbly at the edges, sounds hollow, and crushes locally later under anything concentrated: a coping stone, a bench leg, a ladder foot, a scaffold pad.

Compact the same way across the whole bed, not harder near the rails where it is easy. Inconsistent compaction gives a perfect plane on the day and a dished area a year later.
example: The plate compactor runs the length of the trench, and the only thing between it and the 2 inch line below is 6 inches of pea gravel and whatever is in the fill.

short_definition: In excavation work, a specifically designated person who can identify hazards and has the authority to stop work and remove people.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a compliment — somebody reasonably good at the job. It is a formal role with named duties and the power to shut the work down.
explanation:
Trench and excavation work has its own OSHA standard and its own protective systems — sloping, benching, shielding. Which one applies is that person's decision, made on site, not a crew consensus.

The point for this module is simple: getting into a trench is not a plumbing decision. A trench that looks stable is the one people die in.
example: The trench walls are dry and vertical and the joint is three feet down. Whether anybody goes in is not settled by how it looks to the person holding the cement.

short_definition: A gauge that can read both positive pressure and vacuum, fitted on the suction side of a pump.
explanation:
Read on its own it says little. Read as a pair with the discharge gauge it splits the whole system at the impeller, because restriction shows up as pressure building against it: a restriction after the impeller makes the discharge pressure climb, one before it makes the suction vacuum climb, and a pump that has stopped doing work produces neither.

A gauge that has seized, corroded or plugged does not read zero and does not read off the scale - it parks on a believable number and never moves again. Prove it before you trust it.
example: You want to know whether a gauge is alive before you believe it. Close a valve part way and watch: a needle that does not move while the system does is not measuring the system.

short_definition: A steel or aluminium bottle holding gas under high pressure, with a removable cap that protects the valve.
explanation: The whole hazard is the pressure inside and the valve on top. A cylinder that falls and snaps its valve off becomes a rocket — that is a literal description of what happens, not a figure of speech. So cylinders travel secured, upright, with the valve protection cap fitted, and never loose or in an enclosed cab.
example: A cylinder is laid in the bed on its side 'just for the drive back' and rolls into the tailgate at the first junction. The cap is in the toolbox where somebody put it that morning.

short_definition: The finned coil on a chiller that dumps the heat it has taken out of the water into the surrounding air, with a fan pulling air through it.
explanation:
Airflow is a performance specification, not a preference. Fence it in, plant a shrub in front of it, or stack crates beside it, and it recirculates its own hot exhaust and loses capacity.

Then somebody diagnoses it as low on refrigerant, and the actual fault is a landscape decision.
example: A chiller performed perfectly for two summers and struggles through the third. The hedge that was planted for screening is now a foot from the coil.

short_definition: The pipe that carries electrical conductors. The wire runs inside it; the conduit itself carries no current.
explanation:
Conduit does two jobs. It protects the conductors from being cut, crushed, dug up or chewed, and it leaves a path so the wire inside can be pulled out and replaced later without breaking concrete.

The second job is the one people forget and the one that costs money. A fountain is full of things that get changed, and a raceway that is still a raceway turns a rewire into an afternoon instead of a demolition job.
example: A client wants a bigger pump three years after handover, and the new motor needs larger conductors. Because the run to the equipment pad was left as a usable path, the crew pulls the old wire out at the pad, pulls the new wire in, and nobody touches the stone.

short_definition: A small fitting with a removable cover, spliced into a conduit run so a pull can be reached, redirected or restarted at that point.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the body or shell of the conduit itself — the pipe.
explanation: It is a device, not a length of pipe. Opening the cover gives you access into the raceway partway along a run, which lets you break a long or heavily bent pull into two shorter, straighter ones. Like every other box holding a splice or a pull, it has to stay accessible afterwards.
example: A run to the far basin needs one more turn than the bend limit allows, so a conduit body goes in at the wall. The crew pulls up to it, feeds through, and pulls the remainder as a separate, easy pull.

short_definition: The limit on how much of a conduit's inside cross-sectional area the conductors are allowed to occupy.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like how much you can physically stuff in before it will not go — a question about whether it fits.
explanation: Whether the wire fits is not the question fill answers. There are two real reasons for the limit. A pull that is too tight drags insulation across the conduit wall and across the other conductors and scrapes it. And current-carrying conductors make heat, which has to leave; bundle enough of them in one raceway and each one has to be derated to account for the heat of its neighbours.
example: Two of you get the last conductor into a run by leaning on it, and it goes. Nothing looks wrong. Months later the circuit is intermittent, and the reason is a stripe of insulation left behind on a coupling at the second bend.

short_definition: A space big enough to enter and work in, with limited ways in and out, that was never designed for a person to occupy. Entry is governed by a formal OSHA standard and a written program.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a description of how tight it feels. It is a formal classification with a written program behind it, not an opinion formed at the hatch.
explanation:
The hazard is not usually the space being small. It is the atmosphere: oxygen displaced by heavier gases, fumes with nowhere to go, or something released by the work itself. People who go in to help someone who has collapsed are a large share of the casualties.

Entry has a formal standard and a written program behind it. If somebody has to go into a vault to look at a wet patch, that is a confined-space question before it is a waterproofing one, and it is not a decision the person holding the torch makes on their own.
example: A basin has been drained for a liner repair. It is open to the sky and looks like a courtyard with no water in it — but the only way out is one aluminium ladder at the deep end, which is what makes it a confined space rather than a big shallow room.

short_definition: A deliberate stopping point in a concrete pour, detailed in advance so that the two placements still act as one and still keep water out.
explanation:
A construction joint is not designed to move — that is a movement joint. It is simply where the concrete work was broken into placements, and the two placements did not become one monolithic piece.

It is therefore a predictable leak path, and the defences for it are cast in: a waterstop, a hydrophilic strip, a prepared and roughened surface before the next pour.
example: You are given a basin whose wall was poured in two lifts because a delivery ran late. That horizontal line half way up the wall is a joint nobody designed, and it is the first place to look when the flood test loses water.

short_definition: In a ladder program, an instruction that asks a question about a bit in memory: is this on, or is this off?
explanation: It is a question about a bit, not a picture of the device in the field. Getting comfortable with that distinction is most of learning to read ladder — and failing to is how a program and a replaced field device end up disagreeing without anybody noticing.
example: A rung shows a normally-open instruction on the low-water bit, meaning all is well. The float in the basin is a normally-closed device. Both are correct, and they only stay correct together.

short_definition: How long an organism is exposed to a given concentration of sanitiser. Killing something depends on both the strength and the duration, not one or the other.
explanation:
A high concentration for an instant and a low one for a long while are not equivalent, and organisms differ enormously in how stubborn they are. Some are dealt with almost immediately; some resist a normal residual for a very long time.

This is the reason a sanitiser target is a band held continuously rather than a dose. A slug of chemical that spikes and then disappears has given very little contact time to anything.
example: A basin is shocked on a Friday and reads zero by Sunday. Anything that arrived on Saturday got a high concentration for no time at all, and then nothing.

short_definition: A relay built for load current — larger contacts made to switch motor and heater loads repeatedly and to handle the arc each time.
explanation: Coil on the control side, contacts on the power side. A contactor that chatters, buzzes or shows burnt, pitted contacts is on its way out, and it fails in one of two unhelpful directions: welded closed, or no longer pulling in at all.
example: A pump starts on some mornings and not others, and the panel is buzzing when it does. The contactor is dropping in and out on a weak coil pull-in, and the contacts are already pitted from it.

short_definition: A meter function that confirms there is an unbroken electrical path between two points, usually by sounding a tone.
explanation:
Continuity answers a smaller question than you think. The beeper says there is a path. It does not say the path can carry load current — a conductor down to a few surviving strands, a corroded terminal or a contact with a film on it all beep happily and then drop voltage under load.

If a circuit beeps but does not work, measure the voltage at the load while it is running.
example: Following a hundred-foot underground run from a field junction box back to the panel, one conductor rings and the other is silent. The silent one is the job now, and it is a much smaller question than the one you started with.

short_definition: The rating on a bag or a data sheet saying a product is approved to live under water permanently, rather than merely to get wet.
explanation:
These are the words to look for: continuous submersion, or pool. If they are not on the bag it is the wrong bag, however good the product is at everything else.

The same question applies to sealers, and the answer is usually no. Assume nothing is approved for submerged service until the manufacturer has said so in writing.
example: Two pails on the same pallet. One lists pool and submerged applications on the side; the other is a first-class interior product that will not survive a basin.

short_definition: The low-current part of a panel that carries decisions — controller outputs, float switches, buttons — as opposed to the power circuit that carries the load.
explanation:
The split is the shape of nearly every fountain panel: something small and safe is used to turn something large and dangerous on and off. On a Sapphire panel the control side includes the 24 VDC a Splash Wizard puts out to cycle the manifold solenoids.

Both worlds sit in the same enclosure, frequently on the same DIN rail. The control side being dead tells you nothing at all about the power side.
example: A technician opens a panel, finds the 24 V control wiring reading zero, and reaches past it to a terminal that is still at line voltage from a breaker in a different room.

short_definition: The stone or precast unit that caps the edge of a basin wall. It is the visible architectural edge, and on a negative-edge feature it is frequently the weir itself.
ordinary_meaning: Dealing with something difficult, as in coping with stress.
explanation:
Coping stones are heavy and they are set on a thick, non-sag mortar bed, full and continuous. Not dabs, not a mound at each end. The bearing has to be even along the whole piece, because a stone that rocks will keep rocking and break its joints open, and a piece bearing on two high points carries all its own load, and all the load of anybody who sits on it, at those two points.

Anchorage is a detail, not a habit. Dowels, anchors, adhesive, slip sheets and expansion allowance at joints are whatever the drawing shows, and the anchor is a metal sitting in water, so its alloy is specified too.
example: The membrane was stopped an inch below the underside of the coping because that was above the normal water level and the coping was going to cover it anyway. The first heavy rain lifts the basin above normal level, and the water goes straight over the top of the membrane and into the wall.

short_definition: Cutting a clean round hole through hardened concrete with a hollow diamond bit.
explanation:
The expensive answer to a missed embed. Through a structural element it means locating reinforcement first, getting engineering approval to cut anything you find, and then making the hole watertight through a structure never detailed for one.

A rebar strike is a stop, not an obstacle.
example: Halfway through a basin wall the bit stops biting and starts smoking. That is steel. The drill comes out and the question goes up; it is not a bit change.

short_definition: A round opening cut through finished concrete with a diamond core barrel, as opposed to a sleeve that was cast in when the wall was poured.
explanation:
A cored hole is not the same diameter as a sleeve of the same nominal size, so it gets measured like anything else.

Coring also leaves concrete dust, slurry and a ragged lip at the edges, and every one of those gives the rubber somewhere to bypass. Clean it before the belt goes in.
example: A penetration cored on Friday is sealed on Monday without anybody wiping the inside, and the seal is bulging evenly against a film of dried slurry.

short_definition: The thickness of concrete between a reinforcing bar and the surface. It is a specified dimension, not whatever is left over.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English a cover is a lid or a blanket. Something laid over the top, that could be lifted off without changing what is underneath.
explanation:
Cover does two jobs at once. Concrete is strongly alkaline, and steel sitting in that alkalinity forms a passive film and does not rust. Cover also physically keeps water and chlorides away from the bar.

Lose it and both jobs fail together. The bar rusts, and rust occupies several times the volume of the steel it came from, so the expansion breaks the cover off from the inside. The sequence on a wall is always the same: a rust stain, a hairline crack following the line of a bar, a flake, then a piece of the face on the floor.
example: During a pour somebody stands on the mat to reach across. The wall looks perfect when the forms come off. Three winters later a brown line appears, then a crack along it.

short_definition: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation — chest compressions and rescue breathing for somebody whose heart has stopped. A trained skill, taught with an instructor and a manikin.
explanation: Reading about it does not confer it, which is why this module says so plainly rather than printing a procedure. Get certified. It is a short course, it is available everywhere, and the person it is most likely to matter for is somebody you work beside.
example: A crew realises during a toolbox talk that nobody present holds a current certificate. That is a fact worth discovering on a Tuesday morning rather than at an incident.

short_definition: Chlorinated polyvinyl chloride. A close relative of PVC rated for higher temperatures, and it takes its own cement.
explanation: It looks enough like PVC to be picked up by mistake, and the cements are not interchangeable. The can states which materials it is rated for.
example: A tan-coloured length of pipe turns up in a bundle of white and somebody welds it in with the gray cement off the truck. The can never claimed to bond it.

short_definition: A design condition an anchor is tested and approved against: concrete assumed to have hairline cracks running through it in normal service.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like damaged concrete nobody should be anchoring into. It is a normal design assumption, not a defect.
explanation:
Concrete in tension cracks; that is expected and designed for. An anchor approved for cracked concrete keeps a rated capacity in it. One approved only for uncracked concrete does not.

Which condition applies is a design decision, and it is a quiet thing to get wrong because both anchors install identically.
example: An anchor rated only for uncracked concrete goes into a basin wall that is in tension. It tests fine on the day, and two winters of thermal movement later it is holding a fraction of what the drawing assumed.

short_definition: A network of fine cracks opening in the surface of a plastic fitting.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like going mad.
explanation:
Tapered pipe threads seal by wedging, so a plastic female fitting keeps being pushed open for as long as you keep turning. The failure is not immediate. The fitting crazes and opens up weeks later, long after the pressure test passed.

Metal male into plastic female is the combination that does it. Prefer plastic male into metal female, or a transition designed for the job.
example: A galvanised nipple was driven into a plastic adapter and given one more pull with the wrench. It passed the fill test. A month later there is a hairline star round the hub and a steady drip.

short_definition: Corrosion that starts inside a tight gap between two surfaces rather than out on the open face.
explanation:
A crevice supplies the stagnant, oxygen-starved condition for free, so the attack does not need a chloride to find a weak spot first. Under a washer, under a gasket, inside a threaded joint, under a scale deposit, under a leaf, behind a fitting flange.

Two things follow. A feature shut down while still full of treated water is harder on stainless than one that is running, because circulating water is oxygenated and moving. And a deposit on a stainless surface is not cosmetic. It is a crevice being built.
example: A fixture is unbolted after two seasons. The exposed face is perfect and the ring of metal that was under the washer is brown and rough.

short_definition: Applying the second coat of a membrane at right angles to the direction the first coat was run.
explanation:
The direction is the point of the second coat, not just the extra material. Two coats brushed the same way repeat the same misses twice, in the same places, and end up looking like a thorough job.

Sapphire's sequence is specific: the second coat goes on at ninety degrees once the first is dry to the touch.
example: You run the first coat on a basin floor north to south, working out towards the steps. When it is dry to the touch you start the second coat east to west, and any line your brush edge left in the first pass now has a full coat running across it.

short_definition: Starting a fastener at an angle or on the wrong thread form, so it cuts across the existing thread instead of following it.
explanation:
Cross-threading destroys the hole, and the hole is usually in something far more expensive than the bolt. Fine threads cross-thread more easily than coarse ones.

There is one rule that prevents nearly all of it: if a fastener does not run in freely by hand for several turns, it is the wrong fastener or it is going in crooked. Stop and find out which.
example: A cover bolt on a strainer housing feels slightly tight from the first turn. Somebody leans on it, and the repair becomes drilling out and fitting a thread insert in a cast bronze lid.

short_definition: A thread started at a crooked angle, so the male and female threads cut into each other instead of meshing.
explanation:
A cross-threaded joint jams tight, will go no further in, and refuses to back out - because the threads are now mechanically destroyed rather than merely stuck. It is the other case that reaches the cutting step.

Caught on the first turn it costs nothing. Forced home it is a cutting job, and the female half is usually the half you cannot buy.
example: A fitting fights from the very first turn and somebody decides it is just tight and reaches for a wrench. Six turns later it is immovable in both directions, in a port cast into a pump.

short_definition: A waterborne parasite that chlorine at ordinary levels barely touches.
explanation: It is the reason a UV loop exists on a feature people contact. The residual in the basin handles most things; this is one of the ones it does not, and the lamp is what deals with it.
example: An interactive feature with toddlers in it has a UV system on the return. That is not a luxury item on the submittal — it is there for the one pathogen the chlorine cannot reach.

short_definition: A material batched into the concrete mix itself that forms crystals in the pores of the hardened concrete and reduces how much water can pass through it.
explanation:
This is waterproofing that is part of the concrete rather than applied to it — so, like a waterstop, it is a decision made at the batching plant and it cannot be added later.

It reduces permeability; it is not a substitute for a membrane on a submerged basin, and it does nothing about a joint the pour left behind.
example: Somebody says the concrete is waterproof because there was an admixture in the mix. That may well be true of the concrete itself and it says nothing about the cold joint, the tie holes or the penetrations, which is where the water is going.

short_definition: What the vehicle weighs on its own, ready to drive, with nobody in it and nothing loaded.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a limit that curbs — restricts — how much you may carry, or something to do with weight allowed at the kerbside.
explanation: It is simply the weight of the truck as it stands at the kerb. It matters because payload is GVWR minus curb weight: everything you add to the truck permanently — racks, boxes, a liftgate — raises curb weight and takes the same amount straight off what you may carry.
example: Two identical-looking trucks sit side by side. One has a steel service body and a crane; its curb weight is far higher, so even though both share a GVWR, it can legally carry much less than the plain pickup beside it.

short_definition: The chemical reaction by which concrete, a coating or a resin develops its strength and its final properties over time. It is a reaction, not a drying-out.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English, to cure is to heal an illness — and in everyday DIY, people use cure and dry interchangeably. Both readings mislead here. Concrete does not harden by losing water; it hardens by reacting with it, which is why a coating can be dry to the touch and nowhere near cured.
explanation:
Once you separate cure from dry, several rules in this module stop looking arbitrary. A new pour needs a minimum of 28 days because the reaction takes that long to get far enough, not because it takes 28 days to dry. A cementitious membrane on a bone-dry slab loses its mix water into the concrete and cannot finish reacting — so it ends up chalky and weak while looking fine.

Dry to the touch, the trigger for the second coat, is a different and much earlier state than cured.
example: A patch of hydraulic cement in a chased crack is hard enough to walk on within the hour. Somebody coats over it that afternoon. It had not finished reacting, and the membrane over it is now bonded to something that is still changing.

short_definition: The longer of the two waiting periods on a solvent cement can. The manufacturer publishes it as a chart rather than a single number.
explanation:
The chart has three inputs: pipe diameter, ambient temperature and the pressure the joint will see. Bigger pipe, colder weather and higher pressure all make it longer — often dramatically so.

Read it for the size, the temperature and the pressure you actually have, not the shortest number printed on the can. It is the gate on two separate things: putting water in a system, and putting load on it.
example: A run is welded at seven in the morning in November and the crew wants to fill it at noon. The temperature column they need is the cold one, and it is not the number anybody remembers from July.

short_definition: The treatment and the waiting period after a pour that let concrete reach its designed strength. It is an active job, not simply time passing.
ordinary_meaning: Elsewhere, curing is what happens to an illness or to bacon. Most people hear the word and picture something drying out, which is the opposite of what it means here.
explanation:
Cement does not dry, it hydrates: a chemical reaction with water that keeps producing strength for as long as there is water to react with. Take the water away and the reaction stops, and it does not pick back up where it left off. Treat strength lost to early drying as gone.

The surface dries first and the surface is what you look at forever, so a badly cured slab can test fine through its body and still dust, craze and wear through at the top. Sapphire's floor for a new pour is a minimum of 28 days before the shell counts as cured at all, and the data sheet or specification wins where it asks for longer.
example: A slab is poured on a hot, windy Thursday and left open over the weekend. It tests acceptably and it powders under a broom for the rest of its life.

short_definition: A liquid sprayed onto fresh concrete that forms a film to hold moisture in while the concrete cures.
explanation:
There is a trap built into this product. The compound that protected the slab while it cured is also the film that will stop the next layer sticking to it.

So doing the right thing at the pour leaves you something to remove later, and nobody removes it by accident. It has to come off along with laitance, form-release agents, dirt and dust before waterproofing or a bed goes on.
example: The concrete sub sprayed the floor the day after the pour, as good practice, and nobody wrote it down. Four weeks later the membrane goes over a surface that has a curing film on it, and the bond is to the film.

short_definition: Gloves or soles made from materials that resist being cut or pierced — for sheet metal, glass, blades, demolition debris and open trenches.
explanation: Different hazard, different glove: cut resistance has nothing to do with chemical resistance, and a glove good at one is not automatically good at the other. And the rule that overrides both: no gloves at all near rotating machinery, where a glove is something for the machine to grab.
example: A technician pulls a torn liner out of a basin wearing chemical gloves and finds the edge of a broken tile with his palm.

short_definition: A chemical that shields free chlorine from sunlight. It is not consumed and does not evaporate, so it leaves the water only by dilution.
ordinary_meaning: Called "stabiliser", it sounds like something that makes the chlorine steadier or stronger. And "acid" suggests something corrosive you would dose to bring pH down. Neither is what it does.
explanation:
Ultraviolet light destroys unstabilised free chlorine fast — dose in the morning, nothing left by afternoon. Cyanuric acid prevents that by binding the chlorine, which is also the catch: the bound share is in reserve, not at work. Push the level high enough and the water reads a fine free chlorine number and will not hold against anything.

It also has to be mathematically subtracted from total alkalinity before the saturation index is calculated, because it registers as alkalinity on the test and does not buffer like it.
example: A plaza fountain has been dosed on trichlor tablets all summer. The free chlorine reading is respectable, the ORP is sitting well under the band, and the water keeps greening. Nothing is wrong with the dose; the reserve has swallowed it.

short_definition: Wiring devices one after another in a single line — out of the controller into the first fixture, out of that one into the next.
explanation: It is a chain, not a star. Splitting one output with a Y so it feeds three fixtures creates branches that reflect signal back into each other. When a run genuinely has to branch or go a long way, that is what a splitter or repeater is for.
example: Three fixtures around a basin are fed from one point with a home-made split because it saved cable. All three flicker, and none of them is faulty.

short_definition: The plate fixed to a motor or a piece of equipment carrying its own ratings - voltage, full-load current, speed, service factor.
explanation: It is the authority a measurement is compared against, and it belongs to that specific machine. A figure remembered from a different pump proves nothing, which is why this course prints none of them.
example: A clamp meter reading means nothing on its own until you have wiped the mud off the plate on the side of the motor and read what this particular machine is supposed to draw.

short_definition: The small container of liquid chemical a metering pump draws from, sitting near the equipment in its own containment.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a tank that only runs during the day, or one you fill each morning.
explanation:
It is named for holding a working supply close to the point of use, rather than a bulk store.

Acid and chlorine products get separate storage, separate containment and separate transfer equipment. Never a shared tray and never a shared measuring jug.
example: Acid day tank on one side of the room in its own tray, chlorine product on the other in its own. Nothing is carried between them and nothing is rinsed in the same bucket.

short_definition: The internal reservoir of direct-current energy inside a drive. It stays at a dangerous voltage after the supply is removed.
explanation:
Power off is not energy gone. Capacitors hold charge after the supply is removed, and a drive's DC bus can sit at a voltage that will kill you long after the disconnect has been opened and the display has gone dark.

The drive's own label and manual give the wait time. Wait it, then verify with the meter at the terminals the manual names — the lights going out is not a measurement, and a capacitor can recover some charge after being discharged.
example: A drive display goes black the instant the disconnect is opened, and somebody reaches for the cover screws. The label on that cover has a wait time printed on it for exactly that moment.

short_definition: To remove electrical supply from equipment so that nothing on it is live. Energised is the opposite - power present.
explanation:
De-energising is the first move on any electrical concern around water, and it is the immediate response to a report of a tingle: get people out, de-energise the feature, keep it out of service, and escalate.

De-energised is not the same as locked out. If somebody is going to work on the equipment, the supply has to be isolated and locked under the site's program, not just switched off at a panel anyone can switch back on.
example: A display is due to run for an event in an hour and a contactor needs replacing. The pressure to do it hot is real, and it is not one of the two justifications.

short_definition: A length of pipe where water sits without moving — a capped branch, an abandoned run, or a line that only flows on a schedule.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a numb or dead leg on a person, or a wasted trip. It is a piece of plumbing, and it is where the trouble lives.
explanation:
Dead legs appear when a feature is modified: a branch is capped, a piece of equipment is removed, a valve is shut permanently and the pipe behind it is left in place. The water in there is never treated, never turned over and never tested.

They matter because they are invisible on a running system and because a trace of an unexplained line on a schematic is not proof that it is one. A line you cannot follow back to the basin means you missed something or the drawing is incomplete - it does not mean the line is dead and can be ignored.
example: A capped branch left from a nozzle that was removed at handover still holds a foot of water from last September. Every start-up pushes a little of it back into the system.

short_definition: Running a pump against a closed or blocked discharge, so it is turning but moving no water.
ordinary_meaning: In gardening it means snipping spent flowers off a plant; in trucking it means driving a leg with an empty trailer.
explanation:
The dangerous part is what it does to the current. A centrifugal pump moving no water takes less power, not more, so the overload stays perfectly satisfied while the pump cooks itself on the heat it is stirring into trapped water.

Dead-heading is caught by proven flow, by pressure and by temperature. It is never caught by the overload.
example: Somebody closes the discharge valve to do a quick repair and forgets to reopen it before the schedule starts the pump that evening. Nothing trips, nothing alarms, and the seal is gone by the morning.

short_definition: A trigger that only runs the tool while it is held, so the tool stops the moment it is let go.
ordinary_meaning: The name sounds like something to do with a person dying, or a booby trap. It just means the control has to be actively held by a live hand.
explanation: The safety is in the releasing, not the pressing. A lock-on catch defeats that on purpose, and a jammed one defeats it by accident — either way the tool keeps running after a hand comes off it, which is exactly the situation the trigger exists to prevent. A trigger that does not return to off puts the tool out of service.
example: A technician drops a running grinder when it snags. With a working dead-man trigger it is a wheel spinning down on the deck; with a jammed lock-on it is a wheel still under power, walking itself along the paving.

short_definition: Taking the loose burrs and shavings off the inside edge of a cut pipe, with a deburring tool or medium-grit sandpaper.
explanation:
A burr is the curl of plastic a cutter or a saw leaves behind. It is attached well enough to survive handling and not well enough to survive water.

What breaks loose goes downstream on the first system flush and lodges in the smallest things on the job — nozzle orifices and wedge-action valves — where it stays and where nobody looks for it.
example: A splash pad commissions with one jet running noticeably lower than the other eleven. The orifice has a crescent of PVC in it that came off a cut made weeks earlier.

short_definition: A stiff sand-and-cement mix with very little water in it, used to build up and shape a floor or basin surface.
explanation:
It has almost no bonding strength of its own. It works by being compacted into a dense mass and confined, the way a compacted road base works, so density is everything and water is the enemy.

It is also how pitch gets built into a surface. A bed that varies in thickness lets you screed a true plane at whatever fall the drawing asks, off a substrate that is whatever it is.
example: A handful squeezed out of the mixer looks far too dry to be useful, screeds into a dead-flat plane, and cures like rock.

short_definition: Removing chemical from clothing, equipment or a person — or disposing of what cannot be cleaned.
explanation: Contaminated clothing comes off at work. Chemical on a shirt or in a pair of boots does not stop being chemical in the truck, on the sofa, or in a family wash. Change, bag it, and follow the product's instructions for decontamination or disposal.
example: A technician gets a splash on his trouser leg, rinses it at the hose and finishes the day in it. It dries, he forgets, and it goes in with the household laundry that evening.

short_definition: Having lost more fluid than you have taken in.
explanation: It makes heat worse in two directions at once: less fluid to sweat with, and less blood volume to carry heat out to the skin. Thirst lags behind dehydration, so drinking when you are thirsty means drinking late — drink through the day rather than at it. Water, rest and shade are controls, and taking the rest in the shade rather than in the truck cab is part of the control working.
example: A technician notices at three o'clock that he has not needed a drink all afternoon and takes that as a good sign.

short_definition: Two bonded layers separating from each other — the mortar bed coming away from the membrane, or the membrane from the concrete.
explanation:
Delamination is a bond failure, and the useful diagnostic question is always which bond let go. Turn the failed piece over and read the back of it.

Clean membrane on the back of a mortar bed means the bed never had a grip — no keyway. Concrete stuck to the back of the membrane means the membrane held fine and the surface under it was not sound. Those are two different mistakes made by two different people.
example: Tap along a tiled basin wall with a knuckle and part of it rings hollow. The tile is intact, the grout is intact, and a whole area of bed is no longer attached to anything.

short_definition: The rate at which something in the system consumes sanitiser as fast as it arrives.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a request or a requirement — what the design demands. It is the opposite: something in the water is eating your chemical, and the demand is how fast.
explanation:
Leaves, dust, birds, skin, biofilm inside the pipework and algae all consume chlorine. Where demand is high the residual crashes between visits and the dose gets blamed.

This is why a run of readings beats a single reading. A rate of change tells you there is a consumer somewhere; one number just tells you today's position.
example: Every visit for a month the residual is near zero and the dose goes up. The basin is fine. The film inside the return lines is not, and it is eating the chemical before it reaches the water anybody tests.

short_definition: A link between two pieces of work where one cannot start until the other has finished.
explanation:
You cannot pressure test until the joints have cured. You cannot backfill until the test has passed. You cannot pour until the bonding grid has been inspected. You cannot commission until power is energised and the water is in. That chain is the schedule.

So the important question about your own work is not only when it is due - it is who is waiting on it. A task with nothing behind it can slip cheaply. A task three trades are queued against cannot slip at all without moving every one of them, and moving a trade off a site is not the same as moving it back on.
example: A half-day delay on a pressure test pushes the backfill, which pushes the pour, which loses a concrete booking and a week - because the slab crew had one other job to go to and took it.

short_definition: Reducing the current a conductor is allowed to carry because of the conditions it is installed in, such as heat from the other conductors sharing its raceway.
explanation: A conductor's rating assumes it can shed the heat it makes. Crowd several current-carrying conductors into one conduit and each one is now sitting in the others' heat, so each has to be treated as capable of less than its standalone figure. The derating factor is a design calculation, not something a technician picks in the field.
example: A designer wants four more circuits in an existing raceway. On paper the wire sizes look fine, but once the conductor count in that conduit goes up, the engineer comes back with a larger size for every circuit in it.

short_definition: One specific condition drawn much larger than the rest of the set, so the parts of it can actually be shown.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a detail is a small or minor point - just a detail. On a drawing set it is often the most important sheet you will use.
explanation: A detail bubble on a plan or section names the sheet the enlargement is drawn on. Where a small-scale plan and a large-scale detail disagree, the detail is usually the one that was drawn with knowledge of the condition - but which governs is stated in the documents, not decided by you.
example: The plan shows a nozzle in a basin floor. The detail shows the sleeve, the sealing arrangement, the clearance to the finish and how the whole thing is supported before the pour - which is the drawing you actually build from.

short_definition: Lowering the groundwater around a structure — with pumps and wells outside it — rather than pumping the structure itself out.
explanation:
The distinction is the whole point. Emptying the basin removes the weight holding it down and leaves the outside pressure unchanged. Dewatering removes the outside pressure first, so the basin can then be emptied safely.

Which approach a given vessel needs is an engineering answer that comes from the geotechnical report and the structural drawings.
example: A below-grade basin cannot be emptied safely on its own, so well points go in around it and run for a while before anyone touches the valve inside. Slower, more equipment, and the structure is still where it was put.

short_definition: A valve that uses the line pressure in the pipe to do the work of opening and closing, with a small solenoid only controlling the pilot. Fast-acting valves are the alternative, used where an effect has to snap.
explanation: Both kinds turn up on our manifolds and they are chosen for the effect, not for the electrics. A diaphragm valve borrowing line pressure is gentler on the piping; a fast-acting valve gives you a crisp start and stop, and gives the pipe a sharper shock each time it closes.
example: A row of jets is meant to fire in a chase, crisply. Fast-acting valves go on that manifold, and the designer is asked about surge at the same time.

short_definition: A hardened cutting tool that cuts an external thread onto a rod or a pipe end.
ordinary_meaning: Die in ordinary English means to stop living, or a single dice. Here it is a threading tool, and it is the outside-thread counterpart of a tap.
explanation:
Taps and dies are the pair: tap for the hole, die for the rod. Both remove metal and both need cutting fluid, squareness and the discipline of backing off to break the chip.

A die is also how a bruised end on a threaded rod gets brought back far enough to start a nut - but if the thread is only dirty rather than damaged, a chaser is the right tool.
example: A length of threaded rod cut to size has a burred end that will not start a nut. A die run on squarely by hand cleans the first few threads up in under a minute.

short_definition: A fitting with a non-conducting insert, used where two different metals join so that current cannot pass between them.
explanation:
Dielectric simply means non-conducting. The union, the bushing and the plastic washer all do the same job: they break the electrical half of a galvanic cell while still making a mechanical and watertight connection.

What they are never allowed to do is compromise equipotential bonding. Isolation is designed in with the bonding intact.
example: A brass fitting threads into a stainless manifold through a dielectric union, so the two metals are plumbed together and electrically apart.

short_definition: Two wires carrying a signal as the difference between them, so interference picked up equally by both cancels out.
explanation: The cancellation only works if both wires are exposed to the same interference, which is what the twist is for. Splitting the pair, or running one leg separately, throws away the protection you were relying on.
example: A run is extended with two random conductors out of a spare multicore rather than a twisted pair. It works on the bench and misbehaves the moment it is beside anything electrically noisy.

short_definition: The difference between the influent and effluent gauge readings on a filter. It is the only thing in the equipment room that reports directly on how loaded the media has become.
explanation:
A reading still means nothing on its own. What means something is how far it has moved from this vessel's clean baseline.

Sapphire's service threshold is a rise of 8 to 10 PSI over that baseline. At that point the media is choked, the system's flow rate is suffering for it, and the filter is serviced immediately rather than noted for next time.
example: A vessel that read 12 PSI clean now reads 21. Nothing else in the room would have told you, and the gauge does not look alarming to anyone who does not know where it started.

short_definition: Removing part of a feature's water and replacing it with fresh, to bring down something that cannot be removed any other way.
explanation:
It sets the limit of what chemistry can do. You can add things to water; you cannot subtract most of them. Stabiliser, hardness and dissolved solids all leave only with the water.

It is a water-use, discharge and design decision rather than something to start with a hose — a decision to bring back, not to make at the feature.
example: The stabiliser reading has climbed all season and no dose will bring it down. What comes back to the office is the reading and the question, not a running hose and a half-empty basin.

short_definition: The standard metal mounting strip inside a control panel that relays, terminal blocks, breakers and small devices clip onto.
explanation: Worth knowing because of what it does not tell you. Control devices and power devices clip onto the same rail and look alike from the front, so physical position in the panel is no guide to what is behind a given terminal.
example: Four identical-looking grey blocks sit in a row. Two are 24 V control relays and two switch line voltage to the lighting circuit, and the only way to tell is the schematic and the meter.

short_definition: The pressurised pipe leaving the pump outlet and feeding the feature.
explanation: Sized at design to keep velocity below 7 feet per second — a higher allowance than the suction side, but still a limit, and for the same reason: less velocity means less energy available to become a shockwave.
example: Squeezing a run of discharge through a smaller pipe to get past an obstruction saves an afternoon of digging and raises the velocity in that section for the life of the feature.

short_definition: The pressure measured downstream of the pump, on the side the pump pushes into - usually read at the filter.
explanation:
On its own the number means nothing without something to compare it with: this system's own clean baseline, recorded when it was known to be right. There is no universal pressure a filter should run at.

How it moves is the useful part. A slow climb over weeks is a filter loading up, which is maintenance. A jump since the last visit is a debris event, which is a different lesson.
example: A gauge reads well above what the start-up record shows for this system, the suction vacuum looks normal, and there is barely any water at the feature - the pump is getting water and cannot push it anywhere.

short_definition: A switch that removes power at the equipment, mounted within sight of it, so the person working on a machine controls the power to that machine.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a verb — to unplug or detach something. Here it is a noun: a specific device on the wall.
explanation: The reason it is within sight is trust. Without it, the person with their hands in a pump is relying on a panel in another room and a text message. It is also not the whole answer: the line side of a disconnect stays live with the disconnect open.
example: A technician opens the disconnect beside the pump, locks it, and gets on with the seal — instead of asking somebody in the plant room to switch off breaker fourteen and hoping it was breaker fourteen.

short_definition: Any point where a run of pipe is interrupted - a joint, a fitting, a penetration, or a place where the pipe is held fast while something around it moves.
explanation: It is the organising idea behind a leak search. Sound, undisturbed pipe in the middle of a straight run is the least likely thing in the system to be leaking, so you do not walk the pipe - you go to the list of places where it stops being just pipe.
example: A buried line is leaking somewhere along thirty metres of run. The two ends, the elbow under the planter and the point where it passes through the vault wall account for almost all of the ways it could fail, and they are the four places you dig.

short_definition: The one-way digital lighting protocol used to control show fixtures. A controller broadcasts values and fixtures listen; nothing reports back.
explanation: The one-way part explains most of the troubleshooting. The console has no idea whether a fixture received anything, so a fixture doing nothing and a fixture that never got the message look identical from the desk.
example: A light is stuck on the last colour it understood. The console still shows it as commanded, because the console has never had any way of knowing otherwise.

short_definition: The manufacturer's label inside the driver's door opening that carries the vehicle's ratings, including the combined weight of occupants and cargo.
explanation: This is where the numbers actually live for the vehicle in front of you. Read this truck rather than remembering the last one — two trucks that look identical are frequently rated differently, and a trailer carries its own plate with its own figures.
example: Before hooking up an unfamiliar truck from the yard, the technician opens the driver's door and reads the placard rather than assuming it matches the one he drove all last week.

short_definition: A tool built with two independent layers of insulation instead of an equipment ground, so it comes with a two-pin plug by design.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a tool with extra-thick insulation — a bonus feature — rather than a different and complete design decision about how the tool protects you.
explanation: The protection comes from the construction, not from a ground path, which is why the plug legitimately has no ground pin. That is not the same as a tool whose ground pin somebody cut off. One was built that way and tested that way; the other has had its only fault path removed and looks identical at the plug end.
example: Two drills in the same van both have two-pin plugs. One carries the double-insulation marking on the housing. The other has a fresh cut where the third pin used to be, and only one of them is safe to use.

short_definition: A chlorine test reagent, supplied as a tablet or a powder pillow, that develops a pink colour in the sample. The number after DPD says which chlorine the result refers to.
explanation:
DPD-1 is the one Sapphire's document tells you to reach for when you want free chlorine. DPD-3 is for combined chlorine only. They sit next to each other in the kit, they look alike, and a DPD-3 result logged as free chlorine is not a slightly wrong number — it is the wrong quantity.

The test has one hard failure mode: above roughly 10 to 15 ppm the chlorine bleaches the indicator dye out and the sample reads clear.
example: A technician grabs the wrong strip of tablets at a truck tailgate, logs the figure as free chlorine, and the whole day's dose calculation is built on a reading that was answering a different question.

short_definition: The DPD reagent used when what you actually want is the combined chlorine figure.
explanation: There is exactly one place it belongs: getting the combined chlorine number that the breakpoint dose is calculated from. Anywhere else it is the wrong reagent.
example: You are about to shock a basin, so you need the combined baseline. This is the one moment in a routine visit that DPD-3 comes out of the case.

short_definition: Water in pipes and basins above the equipment running back down through the system when something is opened or shut off.
explanation: It is the mechanism by which head actually reaches you. Drain-back is why an isolated, de-energised pump can still deliver several hundred gallons into a vault, and why the valves get isolated and locked as well as the electrical supply.
example: A technician cracks a flange to swap a gasket, expecting a cupful. The riser above it holds a great deal more than a cupful and it all arrives at once.

short_definition: The slow movement of a sensor's reading away from the true value as the sensor ages, with nothing about the reading looking wrong.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily wandering aimlessly, or snow piling up against a wall.
explanation:
This is why a number on a screen is not evidence. A drifted probe still reports confidently, and the value it reports is usually plausible — which is exactly the condition in which a wrong number looks right.

Treat a reading that has not moved at all as suspicious too. A stuck sensor and a stable process look identical from the control room.
example: A basin temperature has read within a degree of the same figure all summer. Everyone assumes good control until a hand thermometer in the water reads several degrees off.

short_definition: A deliberate downward loop in a cable before it enters an enclosure from above, so water running down the jacket falls off the bottom of the loop instead of reaching the entry.
explanation:
It costs nothing, needs no parts, and it works purely on gravity. Water follows the cable down, reaches the low point of the loop, and leaves.

A cable that runs straight down into the top of a box delivers every drop that has landed anywhere along it straight onto the gland.
example: Two identical boxes on the same wall, both with the same gland and the same cable. The one whose cable dips below the entry and comes back up stays dry through a winter of rain; the one whose cable runs straight in does not.

short_definition: The total vertical distance a gravity line descends from one end of the run to the other.
ordinary_meaning: To let go of something. Here it is a measurement you work out on paper before any pipe is set.
explanation:
On pipe under 4 inch the arithmetic is the run length in feet multiplied by 0.25 inches. At 4 inch and larger the same sum uses 0.125 inches per foot.

Work it out first. Discovering at the far end of a long run that the drop puts your invert below the structure you have to reach is a design problem, and it is cheaper to find on paper.
example: A 40 foot run of 3 inch drain needs 10 inches of fall end to end. The tie-in at the far end is 7 inches lower than where you started, which is a conversation to have before the trench is dug.

short_definition: Pushing the pipe into the fitting with nothing applied, to see how far it goes in before anything is committed.
explanation:
A PVC socket is tapered, so a correctly sized dry pipe wedges partway in and stops. How far it goes is a direct reading of the tolerance between the two parts.

It is a test of the fitting, not a rehearsal of the assembly. It has a pass and a fail, and the fail has a consequence.
example: Out of a box of ten couplings, one lets the pipe slide straight through to the stop with no resistance at all. That coupling is telling you something about itself.

short_definition: A cast iron pipe material with its own sizing standard — its outside diameters differ from steel and PVC of the same nominal size.
explanation: It matters in this module for one reason: PVC is manufactured in both the steel sizing and the ductile-iron sizing. Two pipes labelled the same nominal size can measure differently across the outside, and a seal chosen on the label will be wrong for one of them.
example: Two coils of 6 inch PVC on the same yard rack, from two suppliers, and a tape across the ends says they are not the same pipe.

short_definition: The flow and pressure a particular pump was selected to deliver on this particular system, read off the pump's curve and recorded in the submittal.
ordinary_meaning: 'Duty' in ordinary English is an obligation, or a shift at work. Here it means the working load the machine was picked for.
explanation:
Which pump, at which speed, against how much head, is an engineering decision made before anything was ordered. It is not something to substitute on site because what arrived is close enough.

A bigger pump is not a safer choice either: it lands somewhere else on its curve and pays for it.
example: A pump is swapped for a bigger one to cure a height complaint. The display is now wrong in a new way, the nozzles are noisy, and nobody checked the curve against what the feature was designed to receive.

short_definition: Drain, Waste and Vent: the class of plastic pipe and fittings made for household-style gravity drainage plumbing.
explanation:
It looks like pressure pipe, it glues like pressure pipe, and it costs less. It carries no pressure rating at all, because it was never meant to see any.

The markings on the pipe and the fitting say what they are. Read them rather than matching by eye, because this is a mistake that becomes invisible the moment the cement is on.
example: A tee from the drainage pile gets used on a return line because it was the right size and within reach. It holds while the system is filled and splits on the first full-speed start.

short_definition: Throttling valves used on a suction manifold to set how much draw each leg takes. The eccentric type carries its seal off-centre so it seats without dragging.
ordinary_meaning: 'Eccentric' in ordinary English describes an odd or unconventional person.
explanation: These are set to a position and left there. The position is the balance between the skimmers and the main drains, and it was found by watching the water rather than by counting turns.
example: A new tech finds three half-closed valves on the manifold and opens them all, reasoning that a pump wants all the water it can get. The surface looks better for a day and the pump has lost prime by Thursday.

short_definition: The minimum distance a table requires between an anchor and the edge of the concrete, with a matching minimum between one anchor and the next.
explanation:
Too close to an edge is the common field failure. Expansion anchors suffer worst because they push outward, and near an edge that force blows a cone of concrete out sideways rather than holding.

Like everything else about an anchor, it is in a table and it is not adjustable on site.
example: A bracket does not quite line up, and the obvious fix is to shift both anchors an inch toward the edge of the curb. The table for that anchor is what says whether an inch is the difference between held and not held.

short_definition: A white salt deposit left at the face of masonry by water that travelled through the assembly, dissolved salts on the way, and evaporated at the surface.
explanation:
It looks like scale and it is not. Scale comes out of the water onto the surface; efflorescence comes out of the surface itself, which is why it keeps returning as long as water keeps moving through the material.

That makes it a waterproofing question rather than a chemistry one, and correcting the water balance will not touch it.
example: A white bloom keeps coming back on the outside face of a basin wall - the dry side. No amount of adjusting the water in the basin will change it, because the deposit is being pushed out from within the wall.

short_definition: The water coming out of a piece of equipment, and the name of the gauge on its outlet.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English 'effluent' means sewage or waste discharge.
explanation: Here it only means 'flowing out'. The effluent from a filter is the cleanest water in the system.
example: A client overhears 'effluent pressure' on the radio and assumes something has gone badly wrong. It is the reading on the clean side of the filter.

short_definition: A drowning caused by electric current in the water: the shock takes away muscle control, and the person cannot swim or hold on.
explanation: It is the failure equipotential bonding exists to make impossible. Current leaks into the water, a person bridges two zones at different potential, becomes the path between them, loses muscle control, and drowns. The shock itself does not have to be the thing that kills them.
example: A child standing in an inch of water in a basin, one hand on a metal rail. If the rail and the shell are bonded together there is no difference for them to bridge, and if they are not, there is.

short_definition: A person carrying current through their body because they are touching something energised.
ordinary_meaning: 'Shock' in everyday English is emotional — a nasty surprise, bad news. The trade sense is a physical current through the body, and how bad it is has nothing to do with how startling it felt.
explanation: What injures a person is current through the body, and that depends on voltage and on your resistance. Wet skin and wet footing leave very little resistance and an excellent path to earth through both feet, so the contact that would be an unpleasant jolt on a dry shop floor can be the one that stops a heart on a fountain deck. Low voltage is not the same thing as safe voltage. If somebody is still in contact, do not touch them — isolate the power and confirm it is off first. An electrical casualty needs medical assessment even when they look unhurt, because the damage is internal and the heart rhythm is the concern.
example: A technician gets a buzz off a light fitting while standing in six inches of water and laughs it off. The same fitting on a dry deck in dry boots would not have delivered anything like the same current.

short_definition: A liquid that conducts electricity. Fountain water is one, and everything added to it makes it a better one.
explanation:
Sanitiser, salt, pH and scale chemicals, and the dissolved solids that concentrate as water evaporates and gets topped up all raise conductivity.

So the corrosion risk in a system is not fixed at handover. Changing a sanitiser or raising a salt level changes the electrical environment every metal in the system is sitting in.
example: A feature is converted to a salt system and the hardware it has run with for six years starts showing rust at the fixings within a year.

short_definition: A drawing that looks straight at one face of something from outside, with no perspective, showing heights and what the face looks like.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English elevation means height above sea level, or raising something up. On a drawing set it is a viewpoint.
explanation:
Plan looks straight down and gives you the horizontal arrangement. Elevation looks straight at a face and gives you heights and appearance. Section cuts through and shows what is inside.

Confusingly, the word is also used for a level in feet on a survey - so read which sense a sheet means from its context. On a fountain, the elevation is where the coping heights, weir heights and waterline relationships are usually shown.
