example: The plan shows a rectangular basin with a wall along one side. The elevation is the sheet that tells you the wall is a scupper wall with three spouts in it, and how high off the water they sit.

short_definition: Any part deliberately cast into concrete so that it is already there when the concrete sets: a sleeve, an anchor plate, a light niche, a drain body, a run of conduit.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary use 'embed' is a verb, and usually about putting a video on a web page. Here it is a noun: a physical object sitting in the formwork.
explanation:
Every embed has exactly one cheap moment, and that is before the truck arrives. Afterwards you are core drilling a structural element.

Which is why the layout review before a pour is worth more than any day of work after it.
example: Two light niches were on the drawing and one went in. The second now costs a rebar scan, engineering approval to cut anything the scan finds, and a watertight penetration through a wall that was never detailed for one.

short_definition: Anything cast into the concrete and left there — an anchor, a bracket, a sleeve, a niche body, a waterstop.
explanation:
Every embedment is a boundary between two materials that expand and contract differently, so every one of them has to be sealed and detailed into the membrane rather than coated up to and left.

They also share the waterstop problem: if it was not in the pour, it is not in the wall.
example: A stainless bracket for a weir plate was cast into a basin wall a year ago. When the membrane goes on, that bracket is a detail with a perimeter to reinforce, not a piece of hardware to brush around.

short_definition: The engineer who designed and takes responsibility for the installation, and whose specification and drawings say what this client actually bought.
explanation:
Nobody in the field knows what a given bar is carrying. It might be crack control, or it might be the tension steel holding a cantilever up. The consequence of guessing wrong is not a leak, it is a collapse, and it can arrive years later under a load nobody was thinking about.

Cutting, bending, relocating, drilling through or coring a reinforced section is their question. So is discovering after the fact that somebody already did it. That gets reported, not buried under the patch.
example: A sleeve misses by two inches and a drain lands squarely on a bar. Cutting it takes ninety seconds and moves the decision from a designer to whoever happened to be holding the grinder.

short_definition: A physical change that removes or contains a hazard — a guard, a ventilation system, a barrier — and that works whether anybody is paying attention or not.
explanation: Engineering controls sit above procedure and PPE because they do not rely on a person remembering, and they protect everybody in the area rather than just the person wearing the equipment. A guard on a tool, a ventilation blower in a pit and a hatch cover are all engineering controls.
example: Rather than telling a crew to hold their breath while they glue joints in a pit, a blower goes in and runs. Nobody has to decide anything for that to keep working.

short_definition: Being surrounded and captured by a flowable material — water, silt, sludge, loose debris — that can drown or crush a person.
explanation: It is one of the things that turns a confined space into a permit-required one. On a water feature the flowable material is usually water arriving from somewhere else on the system: a basin above the vault, a line somebody opens at the far end of the site, a header draining back through whatever you have just taken apart.
example: A technician is kneeling in the bottom of a vault when a crew member three hundred feet away opens a valve to check a nozzle. The vault takes the drain-back, and there is one ladder.

short_definition: The person who goes into the confined space, and one of three defined roles on a permit entry.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English an entrant is somebody who has entered a competition or a contest.
explanation: The entrant knows the hazards, uses the equipment the permit specifies, stays in contact with the attendant, and evacuates immediately when told to, when the monitor alarms, or when anything feels wrong — without waiting to be convinced and without finishing what they were doing.
example: A technician is halfway through a coupling when the monitor on his belt alarms. The right move is to leave the wrench where it is and go up the ladder, which is a harder thing to do than it sounds when the job is nearly finished.

short_definition: The covers, grates and split-suction arrangements that stop a person or their hair being held against a suction outlet.
explanation:
A pump pulling through a single small opening can generate enough suction to hold a body or a limb against it hard enough that nobody can pull it free. Entrapment protection exists to make that impossible - by covering the outlet, by splitting the suction between two widely separated points, or both.

It is required wherever the public can reach the water, and it is not optional or adjustable. A missing or broken suction cover takes a feature out of service immediately.
example: On an interactive splash feature you find one of the two suction covers cracked and lifted at a corner. The feature goes off and stays off - not at the end of the visit, now.

short_definition: The person who authorises a confined space entry, verifies that the permit's conditions are actually in place before it starts, and terminates the entry when the work is done or conditions change.
explanation: A signature here is a statement that somebody checked — not that somebody was told. The permit is the written record of that check: the space, the hazards, the readings, the equipment, who is filling which role, and the rescue arrangements.
example: The permit on the clipboard has the gas readings blank and a signature at the bottom. The signature does not mean anything until those boxes are full.

short_definition: The conductor that gives fault current a route back, so that the overcurrent device upstream sees enough of it to operate.
explanation:
Grounding is about clearing a fault. It is a different job from bonding, which is about making sure two things a person can touch at once are at the same voltage, and a different job again from a GFCI.

Fiddling with an equipment grounding conductor to make a GFCI trip go away is disabling a life-safety device, not a fix.
example: A circuit will not hold and somebody suggests lifting the ground at the fixture, because the trips stop when they do. The leak that was causing them is still there, and now nothing is watching it.

short_definition: The below-grade chamber housing a fountain's pumps, filters, valves and controls.
ordinary_meaning: Vault suggests a bank or a strongroom — a secure place to keep valuables. Here it just means a buried concrete box you have to climb down into, and the security is not the point. What the word should bring to mind is the hazard of going into it.
explanation:
A vault is where leak evidence collects, so it is on the inspection list for any flood test. It is also, very often, a confined space: restricted entry and exit, poor ventilation, and the possibility of an atmosphere that will not support life.

Going down to look at a wet patch is a confined-space decision before it is a waterproofing one, and not one the person holding the torch makes alone.
example: You are three days into a flood test and want to check the vault under the basin. That is the point to stop and find out who the entry is authorised by — not the point to lift the lid because you will only be a minute.

short_definition: Tying the metal parts around a body of water together so there is no voltage difference between anything a person can touch. It is required work under NEC Article 680.
ordinary_meaning: Bonding in everyday English is forming a relationship. And even inside this module the word has a second, completely different trade sense — a membrane bonding to concrete, a mortar bed bonding to sand. Electrical bonding is neither: it is about removing voltage differences, and it is not the same thing as grounding or providing a path to earth.
explanation:
NEC Article 680 requires it, the engineer designs how far it extends, and the AHJ signs it off. On Sapphire work the conductor is bare, solid copper no smaller than 8 AWG, and it reaches the reinforcing steel in the shell, metallic pump frames and filter bodies, stainless steel light niches, underwater pipe penetrations, and metal ladders and rails within 5 feet of the water perimeter.

A severed grid has no symptom — nothing stops working and nothing trips — so it is proved by measurement while the connections are still reachable, and never assumed.
example: Someone reads bonded on a drawing and thinks of the membrane bonding to the slab, because that is the sense the rest of the job has been using all week. Two different words that happen to be spelled the same, and only one of them is about keeping a person alive.

short_definition: The engineered network around a water feature that ties the reinforcing steel, shell metal, fittings, rails, equipment, nearby conductive surfaces and where required the water itself into one electrically continuous system.
explanation:
Conductor sizes and connectors are specified, much of it is cast into concrete, and it is inspected before the pour because afterwards nobody can see it. Two consequences follow: it is never a field improvisation, and you cannot verify it by looking.

The thing a technician can do is notice when metal has been added to a finished feature - an aftermarket handrail, a sculpture, a metal grate, a new light. New metal near water that nobody bonded is a new potential difference waiting for a person.
example: A client has had a decorative steel sculpture set into the basin floor over the winter by a landscaper. Nothing about it is tied into anything, and it is now the most interesting piece of metal in that pool.

short_definition: A feeder that dissolves solid chemical by running a controlled stream of water past it, so the water carries the chemical into the system.
explanation:
A feeder is the one part of the system that can add chemistry between your visits, which makes it the first thing to verify when the water has moved without you.

Left wide open, running when it should not, fed with the wrong product, or sitting behind a stuck check valve, it will comfortably outpace anything you do on a Tuesday afternoon.
example: Chemistry that swings in the same direction every single week on a feature nobody visits between services. The feeder had been opened up by somebody chasing a cloudy basin in July and never turned back down.

short_definition: A dull, lighter patch where acid has dissolved the surface of a stone. The material is gone, not dirty.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English an etching is decorative: a design deliberately cut or burned into glass or metal, and something somebody paid for on purpose.
explanation:
People treat an etch as a stain and attack it harder, which does nothing, because there is nothing sitting on the surface to remove. The stone that used to be there has been dissolved.

It is refinished by a stone specialist, or the piece is replaced. Those are the only two answers.
example: A polished marble surround shows a cloudy footprint-shaped mark where a bucket of acid wash was set down for two minutes on a Tuesday afternoon.

short_definition: The glycol used in automotive antifreeze and engine coolant. It is poisonous, and it never goes into a water feature.
explanation: It works as an antifreeze, which is why it gets reached for, and it is toxic to people, to pets and to the aquatic ecosystem you are about to refill and hand back in the spring. There is no version of this where the jug already in the truck is close enough.
example: The last of the marine glycol runs out with three deck drains still to do. The right answer is another trip, not the jug behind the seat.

short_definition: The third-party document listing what one specific anchor product is approved for: hole size, embedment, edge distance, cure times, cracked or uncracked concrete, sustained load.
explanation: It belongs to that exact product. Two anchors that look identical in your hand have different reports and different numbers, and none of those numbers are interchangeable or adjustable on site.
example: Two buckets of wedge anchors, same diameter, different brands, and somebody tips them together because they look the same. Only one of them is qualified for what this bracket is doing.

short_definition: Water leaving an open surface into the air. It costs a filled vessel real depth with nothing at all wrong with it.
explanation:
The rate is driven by sun, wind, dry air and the gap between the water temperature and the air temperature — so it is not a constant, and it cannot be read off the clock. It slows at night without stopping, because water warmer than the air goes on evaporating in the dark.

The way to separate it from a leak is a floating reference: float a container of water in the vessel and mark that too. It loses evaporation and nothing else, so the gap between the two marks is the leak.
example: A basin drops a visible amount over a hot, dry, windy Tuesday and everyone assumes the worst. The floating container next to it dropped by the same amount. Nothing is leaking; the weather took it.

short_definition: A conduit fitting that lets a run get longer and shorter with temperature instead of pushing against whatever it is clamped to.
explanation: PVC conduit moves with temperature far more than the concrete and steel it is strapped to. A long exposed run clamped hard at both ends bows, buckles, or pulls a joint apart. How much movement to expect, and therefore which fitting and how far open it is set at the temperature you install it, is a design figure for that run and that climate.
example: An exposed PVC run along the south face of a plant room is installed on a cold morning. The fitting is set to the opening the drawing calls for at that temperature, so that in August it has somewhere to go.

short_definition: The flexible material that fills a movement joint at the finished surface. Sapphire's document calls for an approved underwater-grade polyurethane or silicone expansion sealant.
explanation:
The sealant's job is to close the joint against water while still letting it open and close. It is what goes across a structural joint instead of tile, so the shell can flex safely without shattering the tile lines.

Underwater-grade is not a decorative qualifier. A sealant that performs well on a facade can soften, discolour or lose adhesion after months of continuous immersion in treated water.
example: A joint in a basin floor gets filled with a general-purpose exterior sealant because it is what was on the van. It holds through the flood test and goes chalky and loose after a season underwater, and now the joint is open in a basin that is full.

short_definition: Equipment built so that its own sparks and heat cannot ignite a flammable atmosphere around it.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like 'able to survive an explosion' — armoured, bomb-proof. It actually means the opposite direction of protection: the equipment is built so it cannot start one.
explanation: It matters for a purge blower because the thing you are blowing out of a vault may be flammable, and an ordinary motor makes sparks. Using a shop blower to clear an atmosphere that alarmed on LEL is putting an ignition source into the exact space you already know can burn.
example: The nearest blower on the truck is a plastic carpet dryer. It will move air beautifully and it is the wrong tool for a vault that alarmed, however much faster it would be than fetching the right one.

short_definition: A fixed or portable supply of clean water for flushing a chemical out of somebody's eyes immediately.
explanation: The first seconds decide how much damage there is, so the important thing about an eyewash is knowing where it is before you open a chemical — from where you will actually be standing. On a site with no plumbed water, what is provided instead is a question for Sapphire rather than something to work out at the time.
example: A technician opens an acid jug in a plant room and could not say where the nearest clean running water is. That is a question with a five-second answer at nine in the morning and no answer at all thirty seconds after a splash.

short_definition: A clear screen covering the face, worn over primary eye protection — never instead of it.
explanation: A shield protects the face but does not seal around the eyes, and things get behind it. For chemical handling that means goggles underneath; for grinding it means safety glasses underneath. The shield is the second layer, always.
example: Somebody pulls a face shield down over bare eyes to decant a chemical because it covers more. It covers more of the face and less of what matters.

short_definition: Arranging a circuit so that the state a failure puts it in is the harmless one, rather than the one that lets the machine carry on.
ordinary_meaning: Reads as a promise that something cannot fail — safe from failure — rather than a design choice about what happens when it does.
explanation: It does not mean the device will not break. It means that when it breaks, the machine ends up somewhere safe. The question that matters on the job is: which state does the circuit have to be in for the machine to be allowed to run, and what happens to that state when the wire breaks?
example: A cutoff cable gets chewed through by something in the vault over the winter. Because the circuit was wired to be closed while all was well, the break reads as no water and the pump refuses to start in spring.

short_definition: Equipment and physical measures that stop a person falling, or stop the fall — covers, guards, guardrails, and a harness attached to a rated anchor.
explanation: The hazards here are basin edges, open vaults and hatches, scaffolds, ladders and lifts. The open hatch you left behind you while you fetched a tool is the classic one, and the answer is a cover or a guard, every time, not memory. A harness is only protection if it is attached to an anchor rated for it — a harness clipped to nothing, or to a handrail somebody assumed was strong enough, is costume.
example: A technician opens a vault hatch, walks to the truck for a fitting and comes back to find a guest photographing the fountain two feet from the hole.

short_definition: A mud mix with lime in it, which makes it sticky enough to stay put on a vertical surface.
explanation: Deck mud and fat mud are both called mud and they are not interchangeable. One is designed to be compacted flat underfoot; the other is designed to hang on a wall.
example: A tech grabs the floor mix to pack out a vertical face and spends the morning watching it slide off in slabs.

short_definition: The loss of attention, judgement and coordination that comes from long hours, short sleep, heat and dehydration.
explanation: Look back at every failure in this module — the wedged guard, the meter that did not get re-checked, the hand in the sump, the cord that got taped instead of tagged. Those are not knowledge failures; everybody involved knew better. They are what a tired, hot, dehydrated brain does at the end of a long day: it takes the short version, and the short version is the one without the safety step in it. The impairment is measurable, and it includes behind the wheel on the way home.
example: A technician says at four o'clock that he is running out and would rather finish the vault work tomorrow. That sentence is information the crew needs, the same as saying a fitting is the wrong size.

short_definition: The internal thread - the one inside a port, a hub or a socket - that a male thread screws into.
explanation:
On a fountain the female half is very often moulded or cast into something large: a pump volute, a valve body, a manifold, a filter port. That makes it the half you cannot buy, and it is the reason the removal ladder runs least-destructive first.

It is also what splits when a tapered thread is over-tightened, because the taper is a wedge and the hub is what gives.
example: A cracked hub on a moulded manifold turns a fitting change into a component replacement, and the part is on a lead time. The fitting that was stuck in it cost a few dollars.

short_definition: The loose material inside a sand filter that does the actual straining: graded sand, or crushed glass.
ordinary_meaning: 'Media' in ordinary English means newspapers and television.
explanation:
Over years the grains round off and channels form, so water takes a short cut through the bed and filtration quality falls quietly. Nothing breaks and nothing leaks.

Media has a service life. A filter that has stopped performing after years is often due a media change rather than a repair.
example: A ten-year-old sand filter backwashes clean, holds a sensible baseline, and the water is still faintly hazy. Nothing is broken. The sand is worn round and the bed has channelled.

short_definition: The pressure reading on the filter, which rises as the filter loads with dirt. The gap between the pressure into a filter and out of it is its pressure drop.
explanation: "The filter pressure is high" is not a statement about anything until there is a clean number to be high against. That clean number is the baseline, taken at commissioning and re-taken after every filter clean.
example: A gauge reads fourteen and the technician shrugs, because nobody knows whether this system runs at eight clean or at thirteen. One line on a start-up sheet last April would have settled it in a second.

short_definition: Removing suspended particles from water by passing it through a medium. It is what makes water look clear.
explanation:
Filtration is one of three separate jobs people lump together under the word treatment. It takes out grit, debris, dead algae and the fine material that makes water look hazy.

It kills nothing. A filter has no effect at all on living organisms or on dissolved material - those are sanitation and oxidation, and they are measured separately.
example: A client points at a basin you could read a newspaper through and says the water must be in great shape. It is beautifully filtered. Nobody has tested the sanitiser residual in a fortnight.

short_definition: The layers that sit on top of the membrane — mortar bed, tile, grout, stone, coping. The word names the visible surface of the job, not the last task on the schedule.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English, finish means the end of something — the point where you stop. So people hear finish trades as the ones who wrap the job up, and treat the finish itself as the completed article rather than as one layer with a specific and limited job.
explanation:
The finish is there to be looked at, walked on and cleaned. It is not holding the water in, and a crew that believes it is will make decisions accordingly — skimping the membrane because the tile is going on anyway, or bridging a joint because the tile pattern looks better unbroken.

The other half of the trap: because the finish is the visible part, a failure in the layer under it is only ever seen as damage to the finish.
example: A client points at a hairline crack running through four courses of tile and asks for the tile to be repaired. The tile is fine. It is sitting over a structural joint that somebody tiled across, and the repair is the whole run plus the joint detail underneath it.

short_definition: A formal test that proves a particular respirator, in a particular size and model, actually seals on a particular person's face.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like trying it on to see whether it fits comfortably — the way you would size a boot. It is a measured test with a pass or fail, and comfort is not what it measures.
explanation: A respirator that feels snug can leak badly, and you cannot tell by wearing it. That is why fit testing is a requirement rather than a courtesy, why it is tied to the specific make and size, and why facial hair at the sealing surface rules it out — there is nothing to seal against.
example: A technician borrows a half-mask from a colleague because it is the same brand he was tested on. The size is one step different, and nothing about wearing it would tell him.

short_definition: Any moulded part that joins, turns or branches pipe — a coupling, an elbow, a tee, a reducer.
ordinary_meaning: Suitable or appropriate, as in a fitting tribute; or trying clothes on.
explanation: Fittings are where a piping system does all of its interesting work and where nearly all of its failures live. They are also the part with manufacturing tolerance in it, which is why a dry fit checks the fitting rather than the pipe.
example: A manifold with fourteen fittings in ten feet has fourteen chances to be wrong and one long piece of pipe that almost certainly is not.

short_definition: When a solvent evaporates out of a freshly applied coat and leaves the surface dry.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like something igniting, or a flash of light. It is just evaporation.
explanation:
Primer and cement are both solvents and both start leaving the moment they hit the pipe. Heat, wind and direct sun make it happen much faster than you expect.

It matters on primer because the cement has to go onto a surface that is still wet with it.
example: Priming a run on black asphalt in August, the first socket you primed is dry before you have finished the fourth. Prime in smaller batches, or prime again.

short_definition: A buried pipe that changes shape slightly under the weight above it instead of resisting it rigidly. Buried PVC is one.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a bendy hose you can coil up. A 20 foot stick of Schedule 80 is a flexible pipe in this sense, and you cannot bend it by hand.
explanation:
The word describes how the pipe behaves under soil load, not how it feels in your hands. A flexible pipe is not designed to span anything or to carry the fill above it on its own.

It squats slightly under load and pushes out sideways, and what happens next depends entirely on what is beside it. That is why the trench detail is part of the pipe system rather than a separate job.
example: A perfect weld on a run laid straight onto native clay fails the first time a concrete truck crosses the line, in the middle of a stick rather than at any joint.

short_definition: A level-sensing device in a tank: either a float that trips at a set height, or an ultrasonic sensor that measures the surface without touching it.
explanation:
This is how the controller knows what is in the balance tank. Multi-tier means several trip points on one suspended assembly, which is how a single string reports the refill level, the operating level and the cut-off.

Everything the controller does about water level is only as true as these are.
example: A make-up valve has stopped filling. The float is fine electrically; it is hooked on a bracket in the sump, sitting at the top of its travel, insisting the basin is full.

short_definition: Filling a finished vessel with water, marking the level against a fixed reference and holding it, to find out whether the waterproofing actually holds.
explanation:
Everything else in this module is process. A flood test is evidence — the only point where the membrane is asked the question that matters, under the conditions it will actually live in.

Looking underneath is part of it: the slab soffit, the equipment vault, the penetrations, the ceiling below. Staining and damp are as much a result as a number on a tape.

It happens before anything covers the membrane. The same failure found after the mortar bed, tile, grout and coping are on is demolition.
example: You plug the outlets, fill the basin on a Monday, and mark the level against a screw head set in the wall rather than a pencil line on a plank that somebody will move. Then you go and look at the vault ceiling underneath, twice a day, and write down what you see.

short_definition: An arrangement where the pump sits below the water level, so water runs down to it by gravity and its suction line stands at positive pressure whenever the pump is off.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a fault report - something has flooded and somebody should come and deal with it. It is a normal and often preferred way to set a pump, and the word describes where the pump sits rather than anything going wrong.
explanation:
The easy case, and what most fountains are designed for. The pump does not have to get the air out of the suction line because there was never any in it.

It also gives you a free diagnostic: with the pump stopped, a joint on the suction side is under static pressure instead of vacuum, so a leak that pulled air in while running will weep water once it is off.
example: A vault pump is a metre below basin level. The night guard reports a wet floor; by the time you arrive at ten in the morning the floor is bone dry and the spray is surging. One split union, two different symptoms.

short_definition: A worn buoyancy device for work over or in water deep enough to drown in.
explanation: It stops being optional where the water is deep enough to drown in, where a current or a suction outlet could hold somebody, or where a fall would put you in water you could not climb out of. Two rules go with it: nobody enters water alone, and somebody on the bank knows you are in it.
example: A technician wades a deep basin to free a floating debris screen, alone, at the end of the day. The water has not changed since the morning; who would notice has.

short_definition: A device in the pipe that proves water is actually moving, and lets equipment run only while it does.
explanation:
On chemical feed it means nothing can be dosed into a system that is not circulating; a feeder that keeps running after the pump stops builds a concentrated plug in the pipe, and the next start-up delivers that plug all at once, out to the feature.

On a heater it is what stops the burner firing into an exchanger with no water in it. Either way it is never jumpered to test. If a heater will not fire, the honest first question is whether it is right not to.
example: A strainer basket clogs while a heater is running. The pump is still energised and the controller still believes everything is fine, so it is the flow switch — and nothing else in the panel — that shuts the heater down.

short_definition: Deliberately overriding an input or output in a controller so the program acts on a value you have imposed rather than the real one.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily just means making something happen by effort — pushing harder.
explanation:
It is a diagnostic instrument with a hazard attached. It makes the controller act on something that is not true: it starts pumps, and it satisfies the exact interlocks that exist to stop things happening.

Force with people clear and the equipment in a state where movement is safe, force one thing at a time, and remove every force before you leave. A forgotten force is a machine that will run with an interlock permanently satisfied, long after everyone has forgotten it is there.
example: A force put on a flow input to test a heater on a Tuesday is still there in November. The heater now fires whenever it is commanded, whether or not anything is moving through it.

short_definition: An oil or wax sprayed onto formwork so the concrete will let go of it when the forms are struck. Some of it stays on the concrete face.
explanation:
The product's entire purpose is to stop things sticking to concrete, which is exactly the wrong property to leave under a membrane. It is on every formed face — that is, every wall — unless somebody removed it.

It is usually invisible. Water beading on a wall that should be soaking it up is one of the few cheap tells.
example: You flick water at a basin wall before starting the SSD soak. Half the wall darkens and half of it beads. The half that beads has release agent on it and is not ready for anything.

short_definition: The hole left straight through a concrete wall where the metal tie holding the two faces of formwork together was removed or broken off.
explanation:
Every formed wall has a grid of them, and each one is a route from one face to the other. They are supposed to be patched by a specified method, which is not the same as smearing something over the recess.

They are easy to overlook because a patched hole and an unpatched one look similar once the wall is grey and dusty.
example: A basin wall loses water in a flood test with no crack anywhere. On the outside face, a neat row of damp spots appears at regular spacing, exactly where the ties were.

short_definition: A portable instrument that measures oxygen, hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide and combustible gas at once, and alarms when any of them is out of range.
explanation: Sapphire's rule is that the calibrated monitor is lowered down into the vault before the hatch is cracked completely — the instrument goes in ahead of you. The reading you want is of the air as it has been sitting, not of the air after you have stood over an open hatch stirring it about with your head in the worst possible place. Test at the top, the middle and the bottom, lowering slowly, because gases stratify.
example: A technician ties the monitor to a length of cord, opens the hatch a few inches, lowers it to the floor of the vault and waits, watching all four readings settle before he opens anything further.

short_definition: The chlorine still available in the water to kill pathogens and algae. The working number.
ordinary_meaning: "Free" sounds like free of chlorine, or like chlorine that is spare and idle. It means the opposite — the chlorine that is still free to do the job.
explanation:
Free chlorine is a quantity, not a strength. The same reading does far less work in high-pH water, and less again when a large share of it is bound to stabiliser. It has very little smell of its own — the sharp smell people blame on it is the spent kind.

It is measured with a DPD reagent, and at the very high levels reached during a shock that test can fail outright.
example: A reading comes back respectable but the ORP is on the floor. The chlorine is there; it is just not working — pushed into its weak form by high pH, or parked behind a season's worth of stabiliser.

short_definition: Carbon steel particles left on a stainless surface by tooling, sparks or a steel bench. They rust; the stainless underneath has not failed.
explanation:
The sources are all ordinary: a grinding wheel or flap disc previously used on carbon steel, a steel wire brush, laying the part on a steel table, sparks from steel work landing on it, mild steel clamps, even steel wool. The particles embed in the soft austenitic surface and do what steel does in water.

It is not only ugly. The rust holds moisture against the surface and shields it from oxygen, which is the one condition the passive film cannot survive, so a contamination stain grows a genuine pit underneath it. This is why stainless work gets dedicated tooling used on stainless and nothing else.
example: A bracket is cut on the same bench as the mild steel work and dressed with whatever flap disc was on the truck. Three weeks later it is streaked orange and everyone blames the supplier.

short_definition: The empty space left above the water in a tank: room for more water to arrive without it going over the top.
explanation: At operating level, a balance tank needs enough freeboard to take back everything standing in the pipes, the nozzles and the decks when the system shuts down and it all drains home.
example: A tank filled to the brim looks generous and healthy right up to the moment the pumps stop and the whole system comes back down into it.

short_definition: Damage caused by water inside a material freezing and expanding, over and over through a winter.
explanation:
Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes. A pore that is half full has somewhere to put that. A pore that is full does not, so the ice pushes the material apart from the inside.

Saturated masonry and saturated stone are the two things a freeze is hardest on, which is why a material's freeze-thaw grade is a published figure and not something you judge by looking.
example: A brick coping that stood in a garden wall for forty years gets reused at a basin edge because it matched. One winter later the top course is flaking off in sheets.

short_definition: The pressure a system spends simply pushing water through pipe, fittings and equipment.
explanation:
It rises steeply with velocity, so a smaller bore costs more than people expect, and every fitting adds its share. Two 45s instead of a hard 90 is a cheaper path where the space allows.

It is a large part of what the pump is working against, which is why it turns up again as a component of Total Dynamic Head.
example: A line gets rerouted round a new planter with four extra elbows. Nothing leaks, nothing looks wrong, and the fountain is an inch shorter than it was the week before.

short_definition: The depth to which the ground freezes in a given climate. Local code states it.
explanation:
In a freezing climate the lines sit below it. Water trapped in a line above that depth freezes, expands and splits the pipe.

It comes from the local building code. It is not a judgement made in the trench, and it is not the same number in the next county.
example: A return line is run shallow across a planting bed to dodge an irrigation main, and the split shows up the following spring some distance from anything anybody touched.

short_definition: Plumbing slang for a fitting completely immobilised by heavy corrosion or lime scale. It means the same thing as seized and carries no extra information.
ordinary_meaning: It has nothing to do with ice, cold weather or a winterised system. A fitting can be frozen solid in August, in full sun, on a feature that has never seen a frost.
explanation: Worth knowing mostly so it does not send you down the wrong road. Somebody saying a fitting is frozen is telling you it will not turn - not that anything froze, and not what is holding it.
example: A ticket reads 'valve frozen, needs replacing' on a job in Phoenix in July. Nothing was ever cold; the bonnet had scaled up over three seasons.

short_definition: The current a motor draws when it is doing the full work it is rated for. It is printed on the data plate, and it is the figure a measured current is compared against.
explanation: Current is the most direct measure of how hard a motor is actually working, which makes it far more informative than listening to it. It also cuts the other way: a motor at low supply voltage draws more current to deliver the same power, and the extra current is heat.
example: A motor that sounds completely normal is drawing well over what its plate says. Nothing is audible, nothing is visibly wrong, and it has been quietly cooking itself since the supply problem started.

short_definition: A fastener seizing solid partway down its thread, on stainless, aluminium or titanium. It will not tighten, it will not come off, and it never reached its seat.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, galling means irritating or humiliating: it was galling to lose.
explanation:
As a nut runs down a bolt, the threads slide under load and scrape the thin oxide film off in patches. Clean stainless pressed hard against clean stainless with no oxide between them does what clean metal does. It sticks. The two surfaces cold-weld, tear, and weld again, friction climbs, heat climbs, and heat makes the next patch worse. It is welding, not overtightening.

Once two threads have cold-welded there is no penetrating oil, no heat cycle and no longer wrench that reliably separates them. They are not stuck together, they are joined, and they come out by cutting, grinding, drilling or extracting. The damage lands on the expensive thing the fastener was holding.
example: A stainless nipple goes into a stainless coupling dry, turns easily for two turns, and locks solid well before the joint is made up. It will not go in and it will not come out, and it was ruined in about four seconds.

short_definition: Corrosion driven by an electrical cell rather than by a chemical attack on a surface. One metal is consumed as part of a circuit, protecting the other.
explanation:
It needs three things present at once, and removing any one of them stops it. Design breaks the liquid path with coatings and gaskets, or breaks the electrical path with dielectric unions, isolation bushings and non-metallic washers.

Fountain water is an excellent conductor and everything done to it makes it better at the job, so a pair of metals that coexist happily in a dry building can be a live cell in a basin.
example: A brass nozzle body that has sat in a stainless riser for four seasons will not move at all, while its neighbour - fitted in the same week, same water, same everything, but brass into brass - comes out by hand.

short_definition: The assembly of valves, regulator and controls that delivers gas to a burner in the correct amount and shuts it off safely.
explanation: Named here so you can recognise where your work stops. The water side of a heater is service work. The gas side — the train, the combustion setup, a pilot that will not stay lit — belongs to a qualified gas technician, and that is a person, not a task.
example: The heater lights, runs for a few seconds, and drops out again. It is tempting to have a look at the pilot assembly while you are standing there. That is the point to stop and make a call.

short_definition: A compressible ring or strip squeezed between two mating parts of an enclosure to close the gap between them.
explanation:
A gasket only works when it is compressed evenly, all the way round, in the groove it was made for. Pinched under a lid, twisted in its groove, or left off because it stuck to the bench, it seals nothing — and the closed box looks identical either way.

Pulling a lid down one corner at a time compresses the gasket on one side and opens it on the other, which is why cover fasteners get drawn up progressively and to the maker's torque figure.
example: A lid goes back on a submersible box in fading light. The gasket has a half-inch twist near one corner that you would only see by running a finger round the whole groove before the lid went on. It is underwater by the time anyone could have noticed.

short_definition: An isolation valve that opens and closes by raising and lowering a flat wedge across the bore of the pipe.
explanation:
Fully open, a gate valve is close to a plain piece of pipe and costs almost nothing in head loss. Fully shut, it seals. Those are its two positions.

Left part way, the wedge sits in the middle of a fast stream and the flow chatters and erodes across it - and the surfaces being damaged are the sealing surfaces, the ones that have to mate perfectly for it to shut. It was never good at throttling anyway: nearly all of the flow change happens in a small part of the travel.
example: A gate valve on a return line has been used as a flow trim since the feature was commissioned. Closed hard against the seat it still passes enough water to keep the vault wet.

short_definition: Gross Axle Weight Rating: the most one axle is allowed to carry.
explanation: Each axle has its own rating, and a load can be legal on total weight and still overload one end. Piling everything at the tailgate keeps you under GVWR while pushing the rear axle past its GAWR — and lifting weight off the front axle takes away steering at the same time.
example: The crew loads two drums right at the back of the bed. Total weight is comfortably under the truck's GVWR, but everything is sitting behind the rear axle, so the rear GAWR is the limit they have actually run into.

short_definition: The OSHA provision requiring an employer to provide a workplace free of recognised hazards likely to cause death or serious harm, even where no specific standard covers the situation.
explanation: It is the catch-all behind the specific standards. The practical meaning for a technician is that 'there is no rule about this exact thing' does not make an obviously dangerous arrangement acceptable — a recognised hazard is a hazard whether or not a standard names it.
example: A hazard on site does not match any standard anybody can point to, and everyone agrees it is plainly dangerous. That agreement is the recognised part, and it is enough.

short_definition: The engineer's report on the ground at a site: what the soil is, how it behaves, and where the water table sits.
explanation:
Every question in this module that begins with how wet is the ground is answered here, along with the structural drawings and the waterproofing submittal.

Which waterproofing system, on which face, whether a vessel may be emptied and under what conditions, and how it is filled and tested — none of those are field decisions.
example: Before a below-grade basin is drained, somebody has to be able to say where the water table is. That number is not something you can estimate from how the excavation looked last summer; it is written down in a report somebody already paid for.

short_definition: Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupter. A protective device that compares the current going out to a load with the current coming back, and opens the circuit when a small amount does not come back.
explanation:
A Class A device acts on roughly 4 to 6 milliamps, deliberately set below the current at which a person's muscles lock and they cannot let go of what is shocking them. The breaker feeding the same circuit is rated in amps — thousands of times larger — so a person can be electrocuted by a current the overcurrent device will never notice, while the lights stay on and nothing looks wrong.

It does nothing to prevent a fault. It detects one that already exists, and it does not stand in for bonding.
example: A ring of submersible uplights has been in the basin for four seasons. One fixture's cord has been rubbing on a rough edge of the sleeve. Nothing is visible, nothing smells, nothing is warm - and the GFCI is the only thing in the whole feature that knows.

short_definition: Ground-fault protection of equipment — a device that trips on leakage, but at a much higher level than a Class A GFCI. It protects equipment and wiring, not people.
explanation: The acronyms look alike and the devices do not do the same job. Something protected by GFPE is not personnel-protected, and treating one as the other around water is a serious mistake.
example: A panel schedule lists ground-fault protection on a circuit and somebody records it as GFCI protection for the basin. Two letters apart, and a completely different trip level.

short_definition: A throttling valve in which a plug closes onto a seat and the flow turns through the body on its way past.
explanation:
This is the valve built to sit part way. The control is smooth and spread across the whole travel, and the internals are designed for the stream squeezing past them rather than being wrecked by it.

The price is head loss even wide open, because the water has to change direction twice inside the body. That is a fair trade when you need control and a waste when you only need a shut-off.
example: A branch that needs fine adjustment gets a globe valve. The one next to it, which is only ever open or shut so the pump can be pulled, gets a gate valve - and putting them the other way round would ruin one and frustrate everybody using the other.

short_definition: Gallons Per Minute: the unit flow rate is given in, and the horizontal axis of a pump curve.
explanation: Almost everything in the system is sized in GPM: pipe, filter, heater, nozzles, the rating on a suction cover. That is why reading it off the curve matters when there is no flow meter to ask.
example: No flow meter on site. TDH off the two gauges, across to the pump's line, straight down, and there is the GPM.

short_definition: How steeply a pipe run rises or falls, expressed as drop per foot or as a percentage.
ordinary_meaning: A school mark, or a quality grade as in grade A. In the field it also means ground level, as in below grade — so context does a lot of work.
explanation:
Sapphire's minimums on non-pressurised gravity-return, overflow and deck drain piping are 1/4 inch of drop per foot under 4 inch pipe, and 1/8 inch per foot at 4 inch and above.

They are minimums. A drawing or a code asking for more wins; nothing allows less. And the usual reason a line ends up wrong is not that somebody picked the wrong grade — it is that the grade moved between setting it and backfilling it.
example: A 3 inch deck drain is set beautifully on Tuesday morning and haunched in that afternoon. Nobody re-shoots it, and one hanger has dropped a quarter inch under the weight of the gravel.

short_definition: The marks on a fastener head that say what strength class it belongs to - radial lines on an inch bolt, a number on a metric one.
explanation:
The grade and the torque figure belong together, because the figure was written for a fastener that can take it. Substituting a same-size bolt out of the bin can be a dramatic downgrade that nothing about the fit will reveal.

And stainless is a corrosion choice, not a strength choice. Plenty of stainless fasteners are weaker than a decent alloy steel bolt, and stainless running on stainless galls and seizes.
example: A bracket bolt shears on a feature that vibrates. The replacement that somebody fitted last year was the right size, the right pitch, and two strength classes below what the original was.

short_definition: Letting water run out of a line under its own weight by opening a low point, with no pump and no air involved.
explanation: It is the first move of a winterizing pass and it is free, but it only works where the pipe falls continuously to the point you opened. It cannot lift water over a high spot or out of a sag, and it cannot empty a pump volute that sits below the pipes feeding it. Everything gravity misses is what the blow-out and the drain plugs are for.
example: A valve has been open at the low end of a run for two hours and the drip stopped long ago, so the line reads empty. Air through it still throws a slug of water out of the far tips — that was sitting in a dip forty feet back.

short_definition: Concrete that has been placed but has not yet reached the age where it can be built on or coated. On a new pour Sapphire's document sets that at a minimum of 28 days.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a colour, or like environmentally friendly concrete with recycled content. It means neither. Green here means young — the same sense as green timber or a green apprentice.
explanation:
Green concrete is still shrinking. A membrane applied to it is a thin film stretched over a surface that has not finished moving, so the film is put in tension by the substrate itself and tears where it is thinnest.

Nothing about a green slab looks different from a mature one. The date on the pour record is the only evidence you get.
example: The pour went in on the 3rd. The schedule wants the membrane on the 20th. Seventeen days looks close enough to a month on a calendar, and it is eleven days short of the rule.

short_definition: Current escaping a circuit to earth by a path it was never meant to take — through damaged insulation, wet equipment, or a person.
explanation:
A large ground fault trips the breaker and clears itself. The dangerous ones are the small ones: a fault can be far too small to operate any overcurrent device and still be far more than a person can survive.

That gap is why GFCI protection exists at all, and why a fountain that has never tripped anything is not thereby proved safe.
example: A run installed in July is fine all summer. The first sustained rain of October fills the conduit, the damaged spot finds earth, and the device starts dropping out every evening.

short_definition: A device that compares the current going out on a circuit with the current coming back and opens the circuit when they do not match.
explanation:
A mismatch means current is getting back by some other route - through water, through earth, through a person. A Class A device trips at roughly 4 to 6 milliamps of that leakage.

A GFCI protects people; the breaker beside it protects the wire. It is a device and devices fail, which is exactly why it has a test button on it.
example: You find a GFCI in a fountain panel replaced with a plain breaker, with a note on the door saying it kept tripping. It kept tripping because something is faulted, and what is there now is a lethal modification that looks like a perfectly normal fountain. The feature comes out of service.

short_definition: The neutral — the circuit conductor that current returns on. It is a current-carrying conductor, not a safety ground.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the earth or safety wire, because it has the word grounded in it.
explanation: Three names sit one word apart and mean three different things: the ungrounded conductor is the hot, the grounded conductor is the neutral, and the equipment grounding conductor is the safety path. Only the last of those is a ground in the sense most people mean.
example: Somebody treats a neutral as safe to handle because it is called grounded. It is carrying the circuit's return current, and opening it under load is not a harmless act.

short_definition: Providing a low-impedance path from equipment metal back to the source of supply, so that a fault makes a protective device operate.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English being grounded means being sensible and level-headed, or being punished by having your privileges taken away. Neither is this.
explanation:
Grounding's job is to clear a fault. When an energised conductor touches a metal enclosure, a large current flows down that path, and the overcurrent device or the GFCI sees it and disconnects.

What grounding does not do is make things safe to touch. It is not the same wire and not the same mechanism as bonding, and a perfectly grounded feature with a broken bond can still shock somebody standing in it - because there may be no fault large enough to trip anything, just enough of a difference to kill.
example: A technician points at a green conductor on a pump and calls it the bond. It is the equipment ground; the bond is the separate conductor tying the pump, the shell, the handrail and the water together.

short_definition: The third, round pin on a plug, which connects the metal body of a tool back to earth through the cord.
explanation: It is the fault path the tool relies on: if a live conductor touches the housing, current goes down that pin instead of through the person holding it. Cutting the ground pin off to make a plug fit is the same decision as removing a guard from a saw — the tool still works, and the protection is simply gone. A bent or missing pin is damage, and no amount of tape or careful use puts it back.
example: Somebody snaps the ground pin off a cord end so it will go into an old two-slot receptacle in a plant room. The grinder runs perfectly and will keep running perfectly until the day it faults to its own housing.

short_definition: Water held in the soil and rock around a buried structure, including water that simply sits in the ground for a while after heavy rain.
explanation:
Groundwater does two separate things to a vessel, and it is easy to think about only one. It pushes water in through the walls, and it pushes the whole structure up from underneath.

Ground that holds water after rain counts, even where the permanent water table is well below the slab.
example: A basin in heavy clay is nowhere near the permanent water table, and after two days of rain the excavation around it holds water for a week. For that week the structure is behaving exactly like one built below the water table.

short_definition: A box that holds the keys to the isolation locks, with each worker's own padlock on the box, so the keys cannot come out until every worker has removed their lock.
explanation: It does the same job as a scissor hasp for a crew too big to hang every padlock on every device. The principle does not change: the equipment cannot be restored while any individual still has a lock in place.
example: A six-person crew works on a plant room shutdown. Two isolation keys go in the box, and six padlocks go on its lid.

short_definition: The material that fills the joints between tiles once they are already stuck down. It is a filler, not an adhesive.
explanation:
Grout is porous and tile joints are not a seal, so water gets past it. That is expected. It is why the waterproofing membrane sits under the bed and not under the tile.

Two things grout is never doing: holding a tile on, and filling a movement joint. Grout in a movement joint is a rigid strut across the one gap that was supposed to close.
example: A void behind a loose tile is filled by working grout into it from the front. It is now a void with a plug in the doorway.

short_definition: The fixed or moving part fitted to a tool or machine that keeps a person away from the moving edge — a blade guard, a wheel guard, a coupling guard.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English a guard is a person who guards something, or 'to guard' means to be generally careful. Here it is a specific physical part with a specific job, and it either works or the tool is out of service.
explanation: Guards are the parts people remove, because they are in the way — and being in the way is the mechanism. The lower guard on a circular saw retracts as the cut starts and springs back the instant the blade leaves the work, so wedging it open leaves the blade exposed while the saw spins down in somebody's hand. A grinder's guard is positioned so that if the wheel comes apart, the pieces go somewhere other than the operator's face. A tool with a defeated guard does not go back in the truck — it goes out of service with a tag on it.
example: A crew member zip-ties the lower guard of a circular saw open because it keeps snagging on the coping stone he is cutting. The correct response is not 'be careful with it' — it is a tag on the saw and a different tool for the cut.

short_definition: Gross Vehicle Weight Rating: the most the whole loaded vehicle is allowed to weigh, set by the manufacturer.
explanation: GVWR covers everything at once — the truck itself, the fuel, the crew, the racks and the cargo. It is a structural and braking limit, not a target. Going over it means the brakes, tyres, springs and frame are being asked for something nobody certified them to do, and it is the number an enforcement officer weighs you against.
example: A technician looks at the door-jamb placard on the service truck and reads the GVWR there. It is the ceiling for the truck plus everything and everybody in it, so it is not the number that tells him how much more pump he can load.

short_definition: The clear-lidded strainer housing bolted to the inlet side of a pump, holding a removable basket that catches debris before it reaches the impeller.
explanation:
Because the lid is clear, the pot is also the best instrument in the pump room. A pot running full and steady is a pump with prime; a pot half empty, or churning with bubbles, is telling you about air on the suction side before any gauge does.

It is also the thing you fill by hand at start-up, and it holds water over winter, so it carries a drain plug of its own.
example: Halfway through a vacuum the clear lid goes from solid water to a swirl of foam. You have not looked at a gauge and you do not need to — something is letting air in, and the pump comes off before anything else happens.

short_definition: The clear-lidded housing on the suction side of a pump, with a removable basket in it that catches debris before it reaches the impeller. Often just called the pot.
ordinary_meaning: 'The pot' sounds like a cooking pot or a plant pot. It is the pump's own strainer housing.
explanation:
This is where priming starts: the housing is filled completely, to the top lip, with clean water before the pump is ever switched on.

The lid O-ring gets inspected for debris and cracks, lubricated with a silicone-based sealant, and hand-tightened. Not wrenched. A full basket starves the pump as effectively as a closed valve.
example: 'The pot is full' on a work order does not mean somebody left a bucket out. It means the strainer housing has water in it up to the lip, which is the step before the pump is started.

short_definition: The three-position selector on a panel: hand runs the equipment directly, off stops it, auto hands control to the controller.
ordinary_meaning: Hand sounds like manual as in careful or by feel. It actually means the equipment is running on a switch, with the controller and often its interlocks out of the picture.
explanation:
A selector left in hand is one of the classic reasons an output arrives and nothing happens the way the program expects — or worse, something runs that the program believes is stopped.

Before you leave a controller, selectors, hand-off-auto and bypass switches all go back where they belong.
example: A pump ran all weekend and the schedule shows it should not have. Somebody left the selector in hand on Friday afternoon while testing, and the controller has had no say since.

short_definition: A flexible extension cord built with a tough jacket for rough outdoor and wet use, rather than the light indoor type sold for a lamp.
explanation: The difference is in the jacket and the rating, not the length or the colour. An indoor extension lead borrowed from a house looks identical coiled on a truck and is not built to be dragged over stone, driven on, or left lying in a wet plaza.
example: A technician sets up temporary power beside a fountain basin and finds a thin brown household lead in the bin of cords. It goes back in the bin — not because it is broken, but because it was never rated for where he is standing.

short_definition: A protective circuit built physically in wiring rather than in software, so that it works whatever the controller is doing.
explanation: A safety function that must stop machinery is generally not permitted to depend on ordinary PLC logic, because a program can be edited, forced or left in the wrong mode. Whether a given interlock is allowed to live in software is an engineering decision, not a convenience.
example: Somebody suggests moving an emergency stop into the program so it can be logged with everything else. That is not a housekeeping change; it removes the one path that works when the controller does not.

short_definition: The amount of dissolved calcium the water is carrying. It is a measured chemistry value and one of the inputs to the saturation index.
ordinary_meaning: Nothing to do with how hard a surface is. You cannot feel hardness by touching the tile, and hard water is not water that is difficult to work with - it is water carrying a lot of dissolved calcium.
explanation: It arrives with the fill water and it does not leave with evaporation, so on a feature that is topped up rather than drained it only goes one way. That makes it the quiet link between a water-loss problem and a scale problem.
example: Two identical features on the same street: one is drained and refilled seasonally, the other has been topped up continuously for two years. Only one of them has a white band at the waterline.

short_definition: Working bedding material in under the lower curve of the pipe on both sides, so it is supported around the bottom and not just beneath it.
ordinary_meaning: A haunch is a hip or a hindquarter. Related by shape only — it is the curved lower flank of the pipe.
explanation:
Dropping material into a trench leaves loose pockets under the two lower curves of the pipe, because that is where the material does not naturally fall. Somebody has to push it in.

This is the step people leave out, and it is the one that puts material where the pipe pushes when it deflects.
example: A 6 inch line is bedded and backfilled without anybody kneeling down to work the gravel under the flanks. The bottom of the pipe is supported, the sides are sitting in air, and the run goes oval over the next two seasons.

short_definition: Air inside a space that could harm or kill someone — too little or too much oxygen, a toxic gas, or a flammable concentration.
explanation: None of the four things a meter looks for can be seen, and only one of them reliably smells — and that one deadens your nose at the concentrations that matter. The air in a closed vault is not information you can gather by leaning over the hatch and sniffing.
example: A vault that has been shut since autumn smells faintly of rotten eggs when the hatch is cracked. That smell is data; the absence of a smell would not have been.

short_definition: A way of expressing pressure as the height of a column of water it would support, measured in feet.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the top of your body, the head of a nail, or a shower head.
explanation:
Pumps are rated in feet of head rather than PSI because the figure stays meaningful whatever the pipe is doing. Vertical lift and friction both show up in it.

It is not a statement about how high a jet will go. Friction in the pipe eats a large part of it before any water reaches a nozzle.
example: A tech reads the head figure off a pump's nameplate and assumes that is how high the jet will go. It is not. It is the resistance the pump can work against, expressed as a column of water, and the friction in the pipe run takes its cut before any water reaches a nozzle.

short_definition: The energy water gives up to friction and turbulence as it moves through pipe, fittings and equipment, expressed as a height of water.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like losing your head, or losing a head count, or a head of hair. Head here is a measure of pressure written as a height.
explanation:
Every foot of pipe, every elbow, every filter and every part-closed valve takes something out of what the pump produced. Add enough of it and there is nothing left at the nozzle.

This is also why the far branch of a manifold starves: it has more pipe, more elbows and more loss than the near one, so less water goes that way. And it is why a globe valve costs something even wide open - the flow has to turn twice inside the body.
example: A feature was extended by forty feet of pipe and four elbows to reach a new pair of jets. The pump was never changed, and the new jets have never matched the old ones.

short_definition: The part of a heater where the heat crosses into the water — typically a coil or bundle of tubes with water inside and the heat source outside.
explanation:
Water temperature is a term in the saturation index and warmer water is more scale-forming, so the same water that calculates out balanced at basin temperature can be firmly on the scaling side against a heat exchanger.

That is why scale turns up inside the equipment first while the tile still looks perfect, and why a heater can fail on a feature whose test results have been filed as fine all season. Deposition is fastest where the water is hot and slow.
example: A heater is allowed to fire during a spring start-up while an isolation valve downstream is still shut. It sounds like a kettle for a few seconds, and that noise is the exchanger being destroyed.

short_definition: The heat illness that comes before heat stroke: heavy sweating, cool pale clammy skin, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, a fast weak pulse, muscle cramps.
ordinary_meaning: 'Exhaustion' in everyday English just means being very tired — something a coffee and a sit-down fixes. This is a medical condition with a defined set of signs, and the person who has it is finished working for the day.
explanation: Get them into shade or air conditioning, loosen clothing, cool them, give fluids if they are fully alert, and they are done working for the day — not back out after twenty minutes. If it does not improve, treat it as heat stroke and call.
example: A technician on a plaza in July goes grey and clammy and wants to sit in the van for ten minutes and then carry on. The ten minutes is fine; the carrying on is not.

short_definition: Heat illness that has gone past the body's ability to control its own temperature. A medical emergency that kills.
ordinary_meaning: 'Stroke' usually means the brain event, and 'heat stroke' can sound like a bad afternoon in the sun. It is neither — it is a core temperature out of control, and it is a 911 call.
explanation: The thing that separates it from heat exhaustion is a change in how the person is thinking — confusion, slurred speech, agitation or odd behaviour, staggering, unconsciousness or seizures. Not whether they are sweating: the old rule that heat stroke means dry skin is unreliable, and somebody working hard can be soaked and in heat stroke at the same time. Call 911, get them out of the heat, and begin cooling with whatever is available. Nothing by mouth for somebody confused or not fully awake. If you are standing there debating which one it is, treat it as heat stroke and call.
example: A crew member who has been fine all morning starts giving muddled answers about which basin he is working on and where he left his tools. That, and nothing else, is the sign.

short_definition: The ranking of ways to deal with a hazard: eliminate it, substitute something less dangerous, engineer it out, control it administratively, and only then PPE.
explanation: The ranking is about how much each option depends on a person doing the right thing. Elimination and engineering work whether anybody is paying attention or not; procedure and training work while people follow them; PPE works only while one person wears it correctly. That is the entire reason for the order.
example: A hazard is 'controlled' by a line in a method statement telling everybody to be careful near an open hatch. A cover over the hatch would have removed the need for anybody to remember anything.

short_definition: Fluorescent and retroreflective clothing worn so that drivers and equipment operators can see you.
explanation: It is worn wherever vehicles, equipment or public traffic move near the work — which on a plaza or a hotel forecourt includes delivery vans and guest cars, not just construction plant. It protects you from somebody else's attention, which is the one variable you cannot manage any other way.
example: A technician kneels beside a hatch in a hotel drop-off lane in a dark blue shirt at dusk. Every driver arriving is looking for the entrance, not for him.

short_definition: A place a coating was missed — a gap, a streak or a thin run where the brush or roller did not leave material behind.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a holiday is time off. In coatings it is a defect: the spot where the coating took a holiday. New hands hear it in a sentence like check it for holidays and have no idea what is being asked of them.
explanation:
Holidays are normal. Nobody applies a perfect coat, which is precisely why the second coat goes on at ninety degrees to the first — a miss running one way gets covered by a coat running the other.

What makes them dangerous is that they are almost invisible on a wet grey coat over a grey slab, and completely invisible once the finish is on.
example: Standing at the wrong angle, a coated basin wall looks flawless. Move so the light rakes across it and you can see two faint vertical streaks where the brush lifted. Those are holidays, and the cross coat is what deals with them.

short_definition: Voids in hardened concrete where the mix did not consolidate around the aggregate, leaving a coarse, open, stony texture. It shows up most often at the base of a wall.
ordinary_meaning: A honeycomb is what bees build, and it sounds almost decorative. Here it is a defect nobody wanted.
explanation:
Honeycombing is an open path through the concrete, and it is at the wall base because that is where the mix had the furthest to fall and the most steel to get past.

Coating over it does not fill it. The repair is a specified patching method that reaches the sound concrete behind, done before any membrane goes near it.
example: You are grinding a basin wall and one strip along the floor line crumbles under the wheel and keeps going. That is not a bad patch of surface. That is a section of wall that never got consolidated.

short_definition: Work that produces flame, sparks or heat — welding, cutting, grinding, soldering, torch work.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like working in the heat, which in a module that also covers heat illness is an easy thing to mishear. It means work that makes heat and sparks, whatever the weather.
explanation: Hot work carries its own training and authorisation requirements, and inside a confined space it is doubly serious: it consumes oxygen, produces fume, and puts an ignition source into a volume whose atmosphere you have measured once. It is a reason the air is monitored during an entry, not only before it.
example: A bracket needs a quick grind in the bottom of a vault that tested clean at eight o'clock. The grinder is an ignition source and the vault is a different space at half past nine.

short_definition: Water short of dissolved calcium, which dissolves calcium out of whatever surfaces it is touching.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a figure of speech — a colourful way of saying the water is thin or empty. It is a real, testable condition, and it is consuming the feature while you look at it.
explanation:
Water is a solvent. Water that is short of calcium carbonate takes it out of masonry grout, stone mortars, plaster linings and copper fittings.

Note the failure direction. Hungry water tests as almost nothing in it, which reads as clean: no cloudiness, no smell, no deposit, nothing alarming on a strip. Hardness that is too high announces itself as scale. The hungry side is expensive precisely because it is invisible, and a finish that has gone does not come back — it gets replaced.
example: A courtyard basin is topped up from a line that runs through the building's water softener. The water looks immaculate all season. Two years later the plaster is pitted, the grout has washed out of the joints and the tile is loose.

short_definition: The chemical reaction between cement and water that produces strength. It runs for as long as water is available to react.
ordinary_meaning: Everyone knows hydration as drinking enough water to stay well. Applied to concrete, the word means a chemical reaction in which the water is consumed and locked into the material, not simply absorbed and later given back.
explanation:
This is the single most misunderstood thing about concrete and mortar. Nothing is drying. Water is being consumed by a reaction, and the water still in the mix is the fuel for it.

It also explains why adding water to a stiffening mix is destructive rather than helpful. Once hydration has begun, extra water does not rewind it.
example: Two identical test patches of the same membrane go down an hour apart, one on a properly damp floor and one on a floor that dried out in the sun. The second one rubs off under a thumbnail when it has cured. Same mix, same day, one of them never got to finish reacting.

short_definition: A cement that hardens by reacting with water rather than by drying out, so it will set inside a damp or actively wet crack. The grade Sapphire's document calls for is an engineering-grade waterproof hydraulic cement.
ordinary_meaning: Hydraulic sounds like hydraulics — rams, hoses, fluid power, high pressure. It has nothing to do with machinery. Here it describes the chemistry: water is what makes it set, not what stops it setting.
explanation:
This is why it is the specified crack repair and ordinary filler is not. You are working on a shell that is damp by design, and a material that needs a dry surface has no chance in a chased crack in a basin floor.

It is not caulk and it is not a substitute for a movement joint. It is a rigid repair for a crack that is not supposed to move again.
example: A chased crack in a basin floor still has a damp sheen in the bottom of the groove on a cool morning. That is the condition this material is for. Packing it into a damp groove is the job, not a compromise.

short_definition: A drawing that shows what is connected to what and in which order, using symbols rather than shapes and positions.
explanation:
A schematic answers one question extremely well: the order things sit in. Is the filter upstream or downstream of the chemical injection? Which valve isolates which branch? Where is the sample point taken from?

It is not a picture of the equipment room. It is not to scale, the lines are not where the pipe runs, and two items drawn touching may be in different rooms. Do not measure it, do not count fittings off it, and do not decide where to stand from it.
example: On the sheet the heater sits a thumb's width from the pump. In the vault it is round a corner and up a ladder, and the two are joined by forty feet of pipe with a bypass in the middle that nobody drew.

short_definition: A vacuum rig with no motor and no moving parts, driven by a high-pressure garden hose. Sapphire calls it a Jet Vac.
explanation:
The incoming hose stream creates a localised low-pressure vortex at the base of the head, and that lifts debris straight up into a mesh silt bag. Because there is no impeller anywhere in the path, there is nothing for a stone to jam and no prime to lose, and because the debris leaves in the bag it never reaches the feature's filter either.

This is the tool for the cases that defeat a portable pump: deep architectural vaults and features carrying heavy sediment.
example: A sunken vault under a plaza has a winter's worth of leaves and a layer of grit on the floor. The portable rig clogs within a minute of the head touching down. The Jet Vac goes on a hose bibb at the wall and clears the vault in passes, bag by bag.

short_definition: A toxic gas given off by stagnant organic decomposition, and one of the four a pre-entry test measures.
explanation: Sapphire's safe operational figure for it is 0 ppm — not 'low', zero. It smells of rotten eggs at small concentrations and then deadens your sense of smell at larger ones, so the smell going away is the wrong kind of good news. The conditions that produce it are an exact description of the bottom of a fountain vault that has been shut since autumn, with a few inches of water and leaf litter in it.
example: A technician cracks a vault hatch in April, gets a strong rotten-egg smell, and notices a minute later that he cannot smell it any more. That is not the vault clearing.

short_definition: A strip laid into a construction joint that swells when it gets wet, closing the joint against itself.
explanation:
Hydrophilic means water-attracting, and this is a rare case of a material that is designed to be got at by water — that is what activates it.

Like a waterstop, it belongs in the pour. It also has to be kept dry and protected on site before the concrete goes in, because a strip that has already swelled and dried once has already spent part of what you bought it for.
example: A roll of strip is left out in the rain on a Friday and installed on the Monday. It looks much the same and it has already done its trick once.
