short_definition: A valve set into the floor of an in-ground vessel that lets groundwater in when the outside pressure exceeds the inside, so the two equalise instead of the structure lifting.
explanation:
It works by deliberately letting the thing you normally keep out come in — which is the correct trade, because a basin with some groundwater in it is intact and a floated basin is not.

The danger is that a seized valve looks exactly like a working one. It sits in the floor, quietly, for years, and nobody finds out until the basin is emptied.
example: A basin has a relief valve in the floor, so draining it is assumed to be safe. The valve has been silted in since the last resurfacing and has not moved in five years. The protection everybody was relying on has not existed for a long time.

short_definition: A seal that holds against standing water pressure rather than only against splashing or damp.
explanation:
Hydrostatic means the pressure of water simply sitting there, which rises with depth and never lets up. A seal that sheds a hose-down is not the same class of thing as one that holds back a water table.

That is what a modular seal is for, and it is why the bolt heads face the dry side: pressure pushes the belt into the annulus rather than out of it.
example: Groundwater standing against the outside of a vault wall all winter pushes on that penetration every hour of every day, whether or not the feature is running.

short_definition: Filling a section of pipe with water, raising it to a set pressure, isolating it and watching the gauge for a set time.
explanation:
It asks one question: does this system hold pressure? It does not tell you whether the system was designed right and it is not a substitute for building it correctly.

It happens while the trench is open, on purpose, because that is while a bad joint is an hour's work rather than a day and a machine. Sapphire's order is bed, lay, test, shade, backfill. It runs on water, never air.
example: A run is welded on Monday, tested Wednesday once the cure chart allows it, and shaded the same afternoon. Nothing gets covered in between.

short_definition: The upward force groundwater exerts on the underside of a buried structure that displaces it. Water weighs about 62.4 pounds per cubic foot, so each foot the water table stands above the slab underside puts roughly that much force on every square foot of it.
ordinary_meaning: Uplift in ordinary English is encouragement — something that lifts your spirits. And hydrostatic sounds like it should describe something static and therefore harmless. The force is neither gentle nor static in its effects: across a basin floor it adds up to tons.
explanation:
This is genuinely counter-intuitive and it injures people. Full of water, an in-ground vessel is heavy enough to stay put — the water you are about to pump out is part of what is holding it down. Drained, the same structure can lift, tilt, crack its floor or shear at the wall-to-slab joint, and it can do it with people standing in it.

So draining an in-ground vessel is a structural decision, not a housekeeping one.
example: A basin needs emptying to chase a repair, in ground everybody knows goes soft after rain. Before the pump starts, somebody has to know where the water table is and what the structure was designed to survive empty. If nobody knows, that is a stop, not a guess.

short_definition: Readily absorbing moisture out of the air.
explanation:
Test strip pads are hygroscopic, which is why a lid left off, a wet hand in the bottle, or a summer in a hot truck kills the whole bottle at once.

The problem is that a dead strip still produces a colour. It fails by giving you an answer rather than by refusing to.
example: Somebody reaches into the strip bottle with a wet hand at the first stop of the day. Every reading taken off that bottle for the rest of the week is fiction, and all of it looks plausible.

short_definition: The chlorine-releasing chemical family used to sanitise water — liquid bleach and the granular or tablet forms of it.
explanation: On its own it is a routine product handled with routine precautions. Mixed with acid it releases chlorine gas immediately, which is the single most common chemical accident in this trade and the reason acid and chlorine products are kept physically apart rather than merely kept tidy.
example: A technician sets a jug of muriatic acid down on the same shelf as an open bucket of granular hypochlorite because there was nowhere else to put it while he unloaded. Nothing happens that day, which is the part that makes it feel fine.

short_definition: One of the two forms free chlorine takes in water, and the strong one. The other, the hypochlorite ion, is far weaker.
explanation:
The balance between the two is set by pH, and it shifts toward the weak form as pH rises. So the same free chlorine reading does substantially less work in high-pH water.

This is the mechanism behind a sentence you will hear often: the test reads the concentration, it does not read the strength.
example: Two basins both read the same free chlorine. One holds clear all week and the other greens up by Thursday. The difference is not the chlorine number — it is which form that chlorine is sitting in.

short_definition: The body losing heat faster than it can make it, to the point where its core temperature drops.
explanation: It does not need snow. Wet plus wind does it at temperatures well above freezing, and standing in a basin in March doing a startup is wet, windy and stationary all at once. Early signs are shivering, cold hands and clumsiness — then the giveaway: shivering that stops while the person is still cold is not improvement, it is the body losing the ability to do it. As with heat, confusion and slurred speech are the emergency marker.
example: A technician in soaked clothing on a breezy March morning stops shivering an hour in and says he has warmed up. He has not.

short_definition: A powered wrench that drives a fastener round in rapid hammering bursts — very fast, and with almost no feel for how tight it is getting.
explanation:
It tightens far too rapidly for the belt to load evenly, which warps the rubber links and snaps the composite or stainless hardware.

The module document calls the hand tool a mandatory tool choice — socket wrench or hand torque wrench, and nothing else.
example: Someone runs the bolts up in under a minute with a cordless impact and one link is visibly pinched before anybody notices.

short_definition: A cable's opposition to a signal travelling along it. Data cable is made to a defined impedance so that signals behave predictably on it.
explanation: Matching matters at the ends. A terminator of the right value looks to the signal like more cable, so the signal is absorbed rather than reflected. A mismatch — the wrong resistor, no resistor, or the wrong cable entirely — sends part of the signal back down the line.
example: Somebody extends a DMX run with ordinary two-core flex from the shelf. It is the right number of wires and the wrong cable, and the far end of the run is where you will notice.

short_definition: The vaned wheel inside a pump that spins and actually moves the water. Everything before it is suction; everything after it is pressure.
explanation: For chemistry it matters because biological films grow on it, out of sight and out of reach of anything you do in the basin. That is part of why Sapphire's protocol keeps the circulation running continuously for 24 hours after a shock — the point is to scrub the plumbing and the impellers, not the basin.
example: A fountain has lost half its display height with clean baskets and a clean filter. Pulling the wet end apart shows the impeller vanes pitted and rounded off. It is still spinning; it is just no longer throwing much.

short_definition: The central opening of an impeller, where water enters before it is flung outward. It is the lowest-pressure point in the pump.
ordinary_meaning: Not a body part, and not a hole you can look through from outside. It is the inlet at the middle of the impeller, and calling it the eye is just what the shape is called.
explanation: It is worth having a word for because it is where the pressure is lowest in the entire system. Anything that restricts the suction lowers it further, and that is where cavitation starts.
example: A half-closed suction valve nobody noticed does its damage at one spot the size of a coin, in the middle of a wheel spinning inside a sealed housing, where nothing can be seen or heard except a noise like gravel.

short_definition: Clothing that liquid and vapour cannot pass through — chemical suits, waders, rain gear.
explanation: The body sheds heat mainly by sweating and letting the sweat evaporate, and impermeable clothing takes that away entirely — your sweat has nowhere to go. That makes protective clothing a heat hazard in its own right, and it is why somebody in waders can be in trouble on a day nobody else finds hot.
example: A technician spends a mild afternoon in chest waders cleaning a basin. Everyone else is comfortable in shirtsleeves, and he is the one who has to sit down.

short_definition: The unit a vacuum gauge reads in, written inHg.
explanation:
Multiplying the reading by 1.13 converts it to feet of head, so it can be added to the converted discharge reading.

Leaving the suction side out is the usual way people come up short on Total Dynamic Head. The work of getting water in is as real as the work of pushing it out.
example: The suction gauge reads 5 inches of mercury. Times 1.13 is 5.65 feet of head: small next to the discharge side, and still part of the total.

short_definition: A fluid that barely changes volume when it is squeezed. Water is effectively incompressible; air is very compressible.
explanation:
This one property drives two separate rules in this module. A water-filled line at pressure stores almost no energy — when it fails it squirts and the pressure is gone. A line full of compressed air is a loaded spring, and PVC is amorphous, so under air it does not split, it explodes into razor-sharp shrapnel. People have been killed doing this.

The same incompressibility is what makes moving water able to generate water hammer: the energy in the moving mass has nowhere to go when it is stopped.
example: A pinhole in a line under a water test produces a thin jet and a dropping needle. The same pinhole under air produces nothing at all, right up until the pipe lets go somewhere else.

short_definition: A voltage a meter picks up on a conductor that is not connected to any supply, produced by other live conductors running alongside it.
explanation:
A high-impedance digital meter draws almost nothing to take a reading, which is what lets it display a voltage that has no source behind it. The reading is real - the meter is not faulty - but it is not a supply and it cannot do any work.

The point for troubleshooting is the converse: a number on a screen is not by itself proof of anything, in either direction. That is what the proving procedure is for.
example: You disconnect a spare conductor in a pull box, meter it out of habit, and it shows a reading. Nothing is feeding it - it has spent ten years in a conduit beside a pump feeder, and that is all the meter is seeing.

short_definition: The water going into a piece of equipment, and the name of the gauge on its inlet.
explanation: Always paired with effluent. On its own an influent reading tells you very little; its whole value is the difference between it and the reading on the other side.
example: Two gauges on the filter, one each side. The one on the inlet is the influent gauge, and by itself it is close to meaningless.

short_definition: The spring-loaded valve where a chemical feed line threads into the main fountain plumbing, letting chemical in and nothing back out.
explanation:
Acid injection lines frequently clog with scale deposits, and a partly blocked injection point fails the same way a tired squeeze tube does: the controller calls, the pump runs, and less arrives than anybody thinks.

Clearing them also prevents chemical backing up under pressure in the feed line, which is its own hazard.
example: Everything in the loop checks out — fresh tube, good calibration, controller calling correctly — and the dose still is not landing. The check valve is half shut with a ring of scale.

short_definition: The housing plumbed into the circulation that a controller's pH and ORP probes sit in, so they read moving water.
explanation:
The probes are glass sensing bulbs, and in moving water they gather an organic microfilm. The film slows their response and drifts their calibration — so the controller goes on dosing accurately against a number that is no longer true.

Sapphire's document makes it a monthly job: remove the probes, soak them in a 5% muriatic acid solution for five minutes, scrub gently with a soft toothbrush, rinse with clean water, then calibrate.
example: A controller has been holding its setpoint perfectly for six weeks and the water is green. The setpoint is real; the reading it is holding is not.

short_definition: A circle with letters in it on a schematic, marking an instrument. The first letter says what is measured and the rest say what is done with the reading.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a soap bubble or an air bubble in the water - which is a real thing you chase on a fountain, and not this.
explanation:
PI is a pressure indicator, FI a flow indicator, TI a temperature indicator. A bubble marks a spot where somebody designing the system expected a reading to be taken.

That makes bubbles useful for a reason beyond decoding the drawing: they tell you where the designer thought the diagnostic information was. If a bubble exists and there is no gauge there any more, that is worth reporting.
example: The schematic shows a PI either side of the filter. In the vault there is one gauge and a plugged half-inch port where the other used to be, which is why nobody has been able to say what the filter's pressure differential is doing.

short_definition: A measurement of how well a conductor's insulation is resisting current leaking out of it, taken with a test instrument before an assembly is closed up or potted.
explanation:
It is the test that finds damage a visual inspection cannot: a nick in a jacket, moisture already inside a cable, a strand touching where it should not.

It belongs before the pour, along with pulling on every connection and confirming polarity and conductor identification against the drawing. After the resin cures there is no getting a probe onto anything.
example: Everything looks right, the fixture lights on the bench, and the insulation reading on one core is markedly worse than its neighbours. That is the last moment anybody will ever be able to act on that information.

short_definition: A wiring arrangement that cuts power to the chemical dosing controllers and pumps the instant the main circulation pump stops.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds mechanical — parts fitting into each other, like interlocking bricks or paving. Here nothing touches anything; it is an electrical condition.
explanation:
With no circulation, nothing carries the chemical away, so a highly concentrated pocket of acid and chlorine builds at the injection point. When the pump restarts, that pocket is fired into the basin in one slug — dangerous to anyone in or around the water, and corrosive enough to eat copper nozzles.

A bypassed or failed interlock is a finding to report, not something to work around for the afternoon. And if you find a controller dosing while the pump is off, do not simply restart the pump — that is the event you are trying to prevent.
example: A feature keeps dropping out on windy afternoons and somebody suggests raising the wind setpoint so it stops being annoying. The right move is to report it, because the wind has not changed and something else may have.

short_definition: The organisation that publishes the International family of model codes, including the ISPSC.
explanation: It writes and publishes; it does not enforce. Nothing it prints is law anywhere until a jurisdiction adopts it, and the body that then interprets and enforces that text is the authority having jurisdiction, not the council.
example: A specification cites an ICC code by edition. Which edition the local building department actually adopted is the question that decides what has to be built.

term: International Swimming Pool and Spa Code
short_definition: A model code for pools and spas that jurisdictions adopt locally, setting requirements for water treatment, testing and records at features people get into.
explanation:
What matters on site is the local adoption, not the model document — plus whatever the health authority with jurisdiction requires on top of it. Targets, testing frequency and the re-entry criterion after a treatment are very often written down by that authority and are not negotiable.

A figure remembered from another feature is not a substitute for finding out which rules apply here.
example: A technician recalls a chlorine re-entry figure from a splash pad in a different county and applies it. Different county, different adoption, and a log that now records the wrong decision.

term: International Swimming Pool and Spa Code (ISPSC)
short_definition: A model code covering pools, spas and many water features, published for jurisdictions to adopt. A model code has no force until a state or city adopts it.
explanation:
Model codes are written nationally and adopted locally - selectively, in different editions, and usually with local amendments on top. So what the code says always means what your jurisdiction adopted, as amended, as this inspector reads it.

Which is why a feature that complied in one city does not automatically comply in the next, and why assuming the last city's rules apply here is the habit that reliably causes trouble.
example: A design that passed without comment in one county is rejected across the line because that jurisdiction adopted a different edition and amended two sections of it.

short_definition: The inside bottom of a pipe — the surface the water actually runs on. Gravity lines are read and specified at it.
ordinary_meaning: To turn something upside down. Nothing here gets turned over; it is a fixed part of the pipe.
explanation:
Read at the invert unless the drawing says otherwise, and then be consistent for the whole run.

Top-of-pipe and invert differ by the pipe's diameter, so mixing them on one line is how a fall quietly becomes a rise. Mixing them between two different pipe sizes on the same run is worse.
example: A 6 inch line is shot at top of pipe at the head end and at the invert at the tail, and the sheet says it falls. It does not.

short_definition: Ingress Protection: a two-digit rating on an enclosure. The first digit is protection against solid objects, the second against water. Each digit is earned by a specific test.
explanation:
The digits are not a ladder where a higher number covers everything below it. A device tested for immersion has not automatically been tested against pressure jetting, so an enclosure can legitimately carry IPX7 and not IPX5. Every claim needs its own test.

An X in place of a digit means that property simply was not tested, not that it failed.
example: A supplier says a fixture is IP rated. That is not information. Which two digits, and declared at what depth and for how long, is information.

short_definition: The IP water rating for temporary immersion: the enclosure survived being submerged at a stated shallow depth for a stated short time.
explanation:
Temporary is the operative word. IPX7 describes surviving a dunk, which is a completely different duty from sitting underwater permanently.

A submerged enclosure sees constant pressure on every seal, day and night, plus a heat cycle that makes the air inside expand and contract. It breathes — and what it breathes in at the end of a hot afternoon is water.
example: A junction box marked IPX7 goes into the bottom of a basin because the rating mentions immersion and the basin is not deep. It is now doing a job it was never tested for, every hour of every day for years.

short_definition: The IP water rating for continuous immersion. The depth and the duration are whatever the manufacturer declares, so the marking alone is not a number.
explanation:
IPX8 is a pointer to the manufacturer's statement rather than a fixed specification. Two products both marked IPX8 can be declared for wildly different depths and durations.

So the marking is the start of the question. The declared depth and duration for the part in your hand is the answer, and it lives on the data sheet or the submittal.
example: Two fixtures on the shelf both say IPX8. One is declared for continuous use at a depth greater than your basin and one is declared for a fraction of it. The carton does not tell you which is which; the data sheet does.

short_definition: Breathing a gas or vapour that attacks the airway — on our sites, most often chlorine gas from an acid-and-hypochlorite mistake in a pump room or a vault.
explanation: Get out, upwind, into fresh air, take everybody with you, and do not go back in for anything or anybody — that is the confined space rule again. Then get medical attention even if the person says they feel fine: respiratory injury from an irritant gas can develop hours later, and feeling all right early is not reassurance.
example: Two technicians get a lungful in a pump room, walk out into the car park, stop coughing after ten minutes and want to finish the job. Feeling better at ten minutes tells you nothing about how they will be at bedtime.

short_definition: Disconnected from the rest of the circuit, so that what a meter measures is only the component you meant to measure.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily just means alone or cut off — here it names a specific physical step: lifting one end of the thing under test.
explanation:
De-energised is not the same as isolated. With power off but the component still wired in, a parallel path through some other part of the circuit returns a resistance that is completely real and completely useless to you.

For a solenoid coil the isolation step is disconnecting the valve leads from the controller's terminal block. Without it you are measuring the controller as well.
example: A coil reads a figure well outside the healthy band, and the technician is about to condemn it. The leads were never lifted off the terminal block, and the reading was the coil plus everything else on that block.

short_definition: A valve whose job is simply to shut a section of pipework off from the rest of the system, so it can be worked on or taken out of service.
ordinary_meaning: Isolate in ordinary English means to keep somebody apart from others, or to feel alone.
explanation:
Isolating and throttling are two different jobs and most valves are built for one of them. Ask an isolation valve to sit part way and control flow and you either get no useful control or you destroy the valve - and you find that out on the day you actually need to isolate something.

A check valve is not an isolation valve, whatever it looks like it is doing. Never rely on one to hold a line you are about to open.
example: A feature loses water with everything switched off. Shutting the far ring out at its valve and watching the gauge on the remaining leg overnight takes half the system out of the search before anybody lifts a paver.

short_definition: The International Swimming Pool and Spa Code — a model code covering pools, spas and aquatic vessels: barriers and access, suction entrapment protection, circulation and filtration, water quality, and how these are built and maintained.
explanation: It is aimed at the vessels people are meant to get into, so whether it reaches a given decorative fountain depends on how the jurisdiction classified that feature and what it amended in. That classification changes whether barriers, entrapment provisions and water-quality requirements are mandatory — which is a project manager and engineer question, settled before the work is priced.
example: Two nearly identical splash decks in two states. One is regulated as an aquatic venue with everything that implies, the other is not. The difference is the classification, not the hardware.

short_definition: To energise a motor for a moment and switch it straight back off, just long enough to see which way the shaft turns.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like going for a slow run.
explanation:
It is the rotation check before a real start. Swap any two phases on a three-phase motor and it runs the other way, and a centrifugal pump running backwards still moves some water and still sounds like a pump.

So nothing looks obviously wrong. The pump just never makes its numbers, and everybody spends the day chasing a hydraulic problem that does not exist.
example: New pump, first start. The tech taps the starter and watches the shaft against the arrow on the motor casing. It is turning the wrong way, the electrician swaps two phases, and it is right. Thirty seconds instead of a wasted day.

short_definition: A piece of wire bridged across a safety switch so the circuit reads closed whether or not the condition it watches is actually true.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a jumper is a sweater, or somebody who jumps.
explanation: It is how a heater ends up firing without flow, and how an interlock gets defeated 'just to test'. The switch is not the fault; it is the messenger.
example: A flow switch gets jumpered on a Friday to prove the heater works. It proves it, and the exchanger is finished by Monday because nobody took the jumper back out.

short_definition: An enclosure that holds splices, keeps them dry, and contains the arc if one of those splices ever fails.
explanation: A splice is the most likely place for a circuit to fail, so a box exists to protect the splice and to let somebody reach it later. Covers on, gaskets in, connectors listed for the location, and every unused knockout plugged — an open knockout in a wet location is a direct path to a splice.
example: A light circuit goes intermittent. The box in the planter is where the technician starts, because it is the one place on that run where two conductors were joined by hand.

short_definition: A groove, ridge or texture that gives the next layer something to grip mechanically, instead of relying on adhesion alone.
explanation:
The word turns up three times in this module and means the same thing each time: a shape to hold on to. A keyway cast into a construction joint, the sandpaper texture a sand broadcast gives a smooth membrane, and the moulded keying pattern on the back of a tile.

Mechanical grip is what you fall back on when chemical bond is unreliable, which underwater it always is.
example: You run a hand over the broadcast wall and it catches like coarse sandpaper. That catch is the whole reason the bed will still be there in ten years.

short_definition: The tool or the workpiece being thrown back along the line of the cut when the blade binds.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a kickback is a bribe — money paid back under the table. Nothing to do with it.
explanation: It is worst when you are pushing hard, which is why a dull blade causes it. A sharp edge cuts at the pressure it was designed for; a dull one does not, so you lean in, the tool is more likely to bind, and when it binds it releases all that stored force at once into somebody who was already leaning into it. Support the work so it cannot pinch the blade, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.
example: A technician is cutting a bracket with a worn blade, pushing steadily with both arms. The blade catches, the saw comes back along the cut, and his forearm is exactly where it was going.

short_definition: A partly stamped disc in the wall of an enclosure, punched out to make an opening for a conduit or fitting.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a boxing blow, or a striking person.
explanation: Every knockout you open and do not use has to be plugged. An open knockout in a wet location is a direct, unobstructed path to a splice — which is the one thing the box existed to protect.
example: A box is opened for two conduits and three knockouts come out because the punch caught. Two get filled with fittings; the third gets a plug before the cover goes back on.

short_definition: The programming language drawn to look like relay wiring: a left rail, a right rail, and rungs of conditions ending in an output.
explanation: If there is an unbroken path of true conditions from the left rail to the coil, the coil is on. That is the whole language. Contacts in series are AND — all of them have to be true. Contacts in parallel are OR — any one of them will do. Everything else is those two ideas stacked up.
example: Reading a rung out loud is a real technique: if the controller is in auto, and the low-water float is satisfied, and the wind interlock has not tripped, and start has been pressed, then the pump contactor comes on. Whichever clause is false is your fault.

short_definition: The weak, dusty layer of fine cement particles that floats to the surface of concrete as it is placed and finished.
explanation:
It looks like the concrete because it is made of the concrete, and it has almost no strength. Anything bonded to it is bonded to a layer that will let go.

It has to be gone before waterproofing, a bed or a tile assembly goes on, together with form-release agents, curing compounds, dirt and dust. Whether the concrete is clean is a separate question from whether it is structurally sound, and both have to be answered.
example: A section of membrane lets go on a basin wall and comes away in a sheet. Turn the piece over and the back of it is furred with a thin grey skin of concrete. The membrane did not fail. It took the top of the slab with it.

short_definition: Water moving in smooth parallel layers rather than tumbling and swirling.
explanation:
The impeller wants water arriving at the eye evenly. A fitting hard against the suction port delivers it to one side of the eye and unevenly around it, and the pump never makes its numbers.

The same physics is used deliberately elsewhere in the trade, in the glass-rod jets that throw a clear unbroken arch.
example: The elbow was glued straight onto the pump inlet because the pad was cut short. The pump runs, sounds perfectly healthy, and has never once reached the display height on the drawing.

short_definition: A single number worked out from pH, temperature, calcium hardness, total alkalinity and total dissolved solids, describing which way a water is inclined to go with respect to calcium.
ordinary_meaning: "Saturation" sounds like how wet or soaked something is. Here it is about how much calcium the water is already carrying compared with how much it can hold.
explanation:
Water wants to be perfectly balanced at 0.0, and Sapphire's document gives the band: below -0.3 is corrosive, hungry water; above +0.3 is scale-forming; between the two is balanced. Sapphire's method works from five live site readings — pH, water temperature, calcium hardness, total alkalinity and cyanuric acid, with the cyanuric acid subtracted from the alkalinity rather than added as a factor of its own.

You are not deriving anything by hand: a slider rule app or a matrix chart turns each measured value into its factor. The skill is knowing which five to measure and what each does to the answer.
example: Two basins on the same plaza show an identical pH and sit on opposite sides of balance. One is chalking the tile line and the other is eating its grout, and no single reading on either log would have told you.

short_definition: A single calculated number that says whether water is under-saturated or over-saturated with calcium carbonate. Balanced water sits near zero.
explanation:
It is assembled from pH, plus a temperature factor, plus a calcium hardness factor, plus an alkalinity factor, minus a total dissolved solids constant. Negative is aggressive and positive is scaling.

It is a design parameter rather than a diagnosis reached for when something looks wrong. The target is chosen so the water is compatible with everything it touches - stone, plaster, coloured concrete, grout, copper, stainless and the internals of the equipment - and the band around it comes with the finish.
example: A basin with a natural stone lining and one with a plain plaster finish on the same site are held at different targets, because the stone will not tolerate what the plaster is happy with.

short_definition: The overlap where one reinforcing bar continues into the next. The two run past each other instead of meeting end to end.
explanation:
Two bars that simply butt together transfer nothing. Force moves out of one bar into the concrete around it and back into the next, and that takes length. How much length depends on bar size, concrete strength, coating, spacing and whether the bar is in tension there, so it is a figure off the drawing and never a habit carried from the last job.

Where the laps fall matters as much. The drawing staggers them and keeps them away from the points of highest stress. And a splice only works if there is sound concrete all around it.
example: A bar run comes up a foot short. The quick answer is to butt a new length on and wire the ends together. That joint carries nothing at all, and it looks exactly like one that does.

short_definition: The detector that clamps to a graded rod and beeps or displays when it is sitting in the laser plane, so you can read a height at that point.
explanation:
The rod is the measuring stick and the receiver tells you where the plane crosses it. Stand the rod on the benchmark first to get the plane height, then every later reading is a subtraction.

Hold the rod plumb. Leaning it makes the reading longer than the true height, and always in the same direction.
example: A tech checks elevations every 10 feet down a trench, resting the rod against the trench wall for balance each time. Every reading is off by a consistent amount nobody notices.

short_definition: Levelling instruments accurate enough to work a long edge as a single plane instead of checking it piece to piece.
explanation:
A spirit level off a bucket will not resolve 1/16 inch over a long run, and matching each piece to its neighbour lets a tiny error accumulate down the whole length.

Sapphire's method on a weir is a machinist level or a digital smart level used alongside a laser transit, working the length as one edge, and checking it again after the bed has taken the weight.
example: Every joint in a coping run checks level against the stone beside it. The laser, set once and read at both ends, says the far end is a quarter of an inch down.

short_definition: The senior field role at Sapphire who signs off a technician's Module 6 practical demonstrations.
explanation:
Reading the module is not the qualification. It is signed off on six things done with the equipment in your hands and observed — measuring a live supply with correctly rated gear, diagnosing a solenoid coil from its resistance, isolating a broken control path on a long run with the continuity chime, building a bonding mesh loop on a mock rebar grid, isolating a simulated leak on a tripping GFCI, and producing a void-free potting pour.

Every one of them is a measurement or a physical result somebody can observe, not an opinion about whether you understood the lesson.
example: A technician can describe the potting protocol perfectly. The sign-off is the pour itself, and whether it comes out void-free.

short_definition: The panel on a drawing that lists the symbols and abbreviations used on that set and says what each one means.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a legend is a famous person or an old story that may not be true.
explanation:
Symbol conventions are not universal. Different design offices draw the same valve differently, and the same symbol can mean two things on two sets.

So the legend is the authority for that set and only that set. If a symbol and your memory of the last job disagree, the legend wins.
example: A hatched circle you are certain means a strainer turns out, on this set's legend, to be a basket filter with a magnetic trap. The last office you worked for drew it the other way round.

short_definition: A bacterium that people catch by breathing in contaminated water droplets, or by water going down the wrong way into the lungs — not through the skin.
explanation:
The combination associated with it is warm stagnant water, biofilm, and anything that throws water into the air as fine droplets: spray, misters, splash, a waterfall into a basin. Decorative fountains have caused documented outbreaks.

This is not a technician's judgement call and not something to treat your way out of on the day. What is yours to do is report it as a finding — heavy biofilm, a feature that has stood stagnant and warm, or a system that will not hold a residual — and stop rather than improvise.
example: You arrive at a lobby feature that has been off for six weeks in warm weather, with slime you can feel on the walls, and somebody asks you to fire up the misters for a photograph. That is the moment to stop.

short_definition: Lower Explosive Limit: the concentration at which a flammable gas in air will burn. A meter reports its reading as a percentage of that concentration, not as a percentage of the air.
explanation: Sapphire's safe operational figure is 0%. The scaling is what catches people. A reading of 10% LEL does not mean the air is 10% fuel — it means the atmosphere is one tenth of the way to burning. So a small number here is not a small problem, it is a fraction of the distance to an explosion. The source in this trade is usually methane from decomposition or vapour from a fuel or solvent.
example: A meter dropped into a vault reads a few percent LEL and somebody calls it negligible because it is a small number. It is not a small number — it is a detectable flammable atmosphere in a hole somebody is about to climb into.

short_definition: One layer of backfill placed and compacted before the next layer goes on. Its thickness is specified on the drawings.
ordinary_meaning: To pick something up, or an elevator. It is a layer, and thickness is the whole point of the word.
explanation:
Fill compacts properly only in layers thin enough for the compactor to reach through. Dump three feet in one go and the top gets dense while the bottom stays loose, so the trench settles later and takes the surface with it.

Lift thickness and required compaction come from the project's civil drawings, not from custom.
example: A trench across a car park backfilled in two big pushes rather than measured lifts looks identical on the day and shows as a long depression in the asphalt a year later.

short_definition: The recessed housing cast or set into a basin wall or floor that a submersible light fixture mounts into.
ordinary_meaning: Niche in everyday use means a small specialised corner of a market, or a role that suits somebody. The physical sense — a recess in a wall — is the older one and the one meant here.
explanation:
The niche carries the conduit, the cord grip and, on metal niches, a bonding connection. That bond is the part people forget: a light gets replaced, the fixture goes back in, and the bonding conductor that was landed on the niche never gets reconnected.

Everything to do with a niche is Article 680 work - the wiring method, the junction box position relative to the water line, the listing of the fixture itself.
example: Coating a basin goes quickly until you reach the niches, and then a two-foot square of wall takes as long as the rest of the elevation. That is the correct ratio, not a sign you are being slow.

short_definition: The supply voltage of the building distribution — on our work usually 120 VAC — as opposed to the reduced voltage of a control or lighting circuit.
explanation: VAC and VDC are worth keeping straight because the meter setting depends on them. A Splash Wizard takes line voltage in at its main line input, which is diagnosed on the meter's AC range, and puts 24 VDC out to the solenoids, which is diagnosed on its DC range. Mixing those up wastes an afternoon.
example: A controller output reads nothing on the AC range, and the technician starts writing up a dead controller. The output was never AC.

short_definition: A belt of interlocking rubber segments bolted around a pipe inside a wall opening. Tightening the bolts squeezes the rubber lengthwise, which makes it swell outward and seal the gap.
explanation:
It does two opposite jobs on a fountain: keeping groundwater out of a dry equipment vault, and keeping feature water from escaping past a tank wall.

It beats grout or sealant for three reasons. It stays elastic, so it tolerates the pipe moving, the structure settling and everything expanding in heat. It seals against standing water pressure from the wet side. And it can be taken apart and reused if the pipe ever comes out.
example: The suction line through the vault wall is sealed with a link belt rather than packed with mortar, so when the pump is repiped in five years that penetration is a wrench job rather than a demolition one.

short_definition: Sodium hypochlorite in solution — the liquid chlorine product used for dosing and shocking.
explanation:
Like calcium hypochlorite it is alkaline and pushes pH up, so check pH after a shock.

The critical rule is the one Sapphire's document flags as the error to avoid: never allow liquid chlorine and muriatic acid to mix directly. The mixing rarely looks like mixing — a shared jug, a re-used container, two feed lines injecting into the same dead section of pipe, or two drums stored where one can leak into the other's bund.
example: One clean dry scoop, one container, one product. The five-gallon pail that held acid last month does not get re-used for anything, ever.

short_definition: A waterproofing material brushed, rolled or trowelled on as a liquid, which cures into one seamless film. Sapphire's document specifies this type.
explanation:
The advantage is that it goes round drains, steps, radii and odd shapes with no joint anywhere, so there is nothing to seam. The cost of that is thickness: the film is exactly whatever you put on, and nobody can put on an even film by eye.

That single fact is why the whole procedure is built around measurement — a wet film gauge, two coats crossed at ninety degrees, and a flood test at the end.
example: Two technicians coat opposite halves of the same basin floor out of the same pail on the same morning. One has been rolling a fraction heavier than the other all day. Both halves look identical when they are wet and identical when they are cured, and only the gauge readings tell you they are not the same membrane.

short_definition: Equipment that has been tested and certified by a recognised laboratory for a particular use, and comes with instructions that are part of that certification.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like it just means written down on a list — a catalogue entry, or something the supplier stocks.
explanation: A code generally requires listed equipment to be installed according to its listing, which makes the manufacturer's instruction sheet enforceable rather than advisory. It is also where every number this course refuses to print actually lives — cure times, torques, dose rates, clearances, the wait time on a drive.
example: A tube of general-purpose lubricant in the truck would make the pull easier, but its label says nothing about conductor insulation. It stays in the truck, because a jacket it quietly attacks will not show the damage for years.

short_definition: The three-step proof that a conductor is dead: test your meter on a known live source, test the conductor, then test your meter on the known live source again.
explanation:
Step three is the one people skip and the one that saves them. A meter with a flat battery, a blown fuse, a broken lead, or a dial left on the wrong function reads zero volts on a live bus and is completely convincing while it does it.

This is the measurement taken inside a lock-out, not a replacement for one. Module 9 and the employer's program own the sequence around it, and say who is authorised to do it at all.
example: A technician proves the meter on a known outlet, reads zero on the conductors in the panel, then goes back to the outlet and gets nothing. The fuse blew between the two, and the zero in the panel meant nothing.

short_definition: In a circuit, the thing at the far end that actually uses the power - a motor, a light, a heater. More generally, the amount of work or material something is being asked to handle.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a load of material in the back of the truck. In electrical work it means the equipment being fed, and 'under load' means while that equipment is running and drawing current - which is when several faults appear and at no other time.
explanation:
The distinction that matters on a fault call is at rest versus under load. A loose lug or a corroded terminal carries no current at rest, so it reads perfectly normal. Put current through it and it drops voltage across itself, and the motor at the end of the run starves.

That is why a measurement taken with everything switched off can be completely true and completely useless.
example: A pump that will not start gets metered at the disconnect with the system idle: correct voltage, both legs. Metered again with somebody holding the starter in, the voltage falls away as the motor tries to turn. The fault is in the run, not in the motor.

short_definition: The controlled procedure for putting a machine into a state where it cannot be energised, and marking it so nobody restores power while somebody is working on it.
explanation:
Sapphire's rule is that lock-out and tag-out come before any sub-panel or control enclosure is opened, every time. The rule is not turn it off: panels routinely have more than one source, and switching off the one you found leaves parts of the enclosure energised and looking exactly like the rest of it.

The sequence itself, and who is authorised to work it, lives in Module 9 and in the employer's written programs. Nothing in this module is a reason to skip either.
example: A pump sub-panel is fed from the main disconnect, but its controller comes off a separate breaker in the building panel. Locking only the disconnect leaves the controller terminals live.

short_definition: A formal procedure for putting an energy source into an off state and physically locking it there, with a tag naming who applied the lock, so that nobody can restore power while work is going on.
explanation: It exists because equipment that is switched off is not equipment that is safe: somebody else flips a breaker, a timer fires, a level switch calls for a pump, a control system resumes after a fault. Sapphire's six steps are switch off at the local panel, find the main breaker upstream, flip it off, snap a scissor-hasp over the toggle, add your own padlock with a signed dated DANGER: DO NOT OPERATE tag — and then verify: try the breaker, then prove 0 volts at the target terminal block with a meter. The key stays in your pocket until the repair is finished.
example: You are changing a seal on a plaza pump. The disconnect is around a corner in a room the building engineer also uses. Locked and tagged, your lock, your key in your pocket - because the only thing standing between you and that motor starting is somebody else's assumption that the switch was off for no reason.

short_definition: The formal written program for isolating a machine's energy sources and physically locking them off so it cannot be started while somebody is working on it.
explanation:
Locking out is not the same as switching off. It means the energy source is isolated, a lock is applied, the lock has one key and the person doing the work holds it, and a tag says who and why.

It is a certified program with training and written procedures behind it, covered properly in Module 9. What matters here is knowing when a job needs it and who is permitted to apply it - servicing an ozone system, for instance, is not work you improvise around a switch.
example: A pump needs its strainer housing opened. The controller could start that pump on a schedule at any minute, so the breaker is isolated and locked with your own lock, and the key stays in your pocket until the lid is back on.

short_definition: A threaded plug or small valve at the bottom of a piece of equipment, put there so the last of the water can be let out of it.
explanation:
Pumps, strainer pots, filter bodies, heater coils, UV chambers and sight glasses all carry them. They come out for the winter and they stay out — a drain valve closed for the winter is a trap, not a drain. Sapphire's rule for where they go is specific: store the plugs safely inside the pump basket, at the equipment they belong to, in the one container the spring crew opens first. Write down that you did it.

In spring the threads are coated with silicone lubricant and the plugs re-torqued securely back into their own equipment blocks, checked off against the winterizing record.
example: A start-up in April stops dead because there are five plugs in the basket and the record says seven were pulled. Nobody knows which two are missing or which housings they came out of, and the fill cannot start until somebody does.

short_definition: The critically low tank level that a controller treats as a stop condition rather than as a normal operating state.
explanation:
At that level the pumps would be drawing in air, cavitating and running dry, and a dry mechanical seal has fifteen seconds. So power to the feature pumps and the circulation pumps is cut instantly.

A feature that has shut itself off on low water has done exactly what it was built to do.
example: Monday call-out: the fountain will not start. The tank is low, the cut-off is holding the pumps off, and the actual job is finding where the water went over the weekend.

short_definition: The interlock that stops a pump when the water level falls below the point where it can safely run.
explanation: It is the reason a pump does not run dry, and it is only worth as much as its wiring convention. Wired so the circuit is closed while the water is there, a broken cable produces the stop. Wired the other way round, the same broken cable reads as water present, forever, and the pump runs dry.
example: A feature loses water overnight through a stuck fill valve. At three in the morning the cutoff drops the pump out, and the morning's job is a valve rather than a burnt seal.

short_definition: Langelier Saturation Index — a single figure that says whether water is in balance overall: pH plus a temperature factor plus a calcium hardness factor plus an alkalinity factor, minus a total dissolved solids constant. Near zero is balanced.
explanation:
It exists because no one reading answers the question on its own. Water can have a perfectly respectable pH and still be eating the plaster, because the calcium and alkalinity behind it are low. The index combines them, and the sign tells you the direction: negative water is aggressive, positive water scales.

At spring start-up you balance from what you measure today. Last season's numbers describe water that is no longer there.
example: A spring fill reads fine on pH, and the index comes out clearly negative because the fill water is soft and the basin was drained to nothing over winter. The water looks perfect and is quietly working on the finish.

short_definition: The metal terminal that clamps a conductor to a piece of equipment or structure and makes the electrical connection.
ordinary_meaning: To lug something in ordinary English is to carry it with effort. A lug is also the ear-shaped tab on a casting.
explanation:
On a bonding system the lug is where the copper meets the steel, and it is the part that corrodes. Wet, chlorinated, dissimilar-metal environments are exactly where a connection goes green, then powdery, then open.

A conductor that has corroded off at the lug looks like a loose wire and is a broken bond. It is a reason to take a feature out of service, not a reason to twist it back on.
example: Behind a pump you find a bonding lug with a copper conductor still under the screw and a white bloom of corrosion filling the gap between them. Mechanically attached, electrically gone.

short_definition: The trade word for a complete light fitting — the lamp or LED module, its housing, its lens and its wiring, as one unit.
explanation:
Underwater and in-ground luminaires sit inside the scope of NEC Article 680 like everything else around the basin, and their bonding, grounding, entries and splices are not relaxed because the job you came to do is a data job.

Open one and it goes back together with the seals and gaskets the manufacturer specifies, fitted the way the instructions say. A reused, pinched or omitted gasket is a leak, then a flooded fixture, then a ground fault, in that order.
example: A submittal lists six luminaires for a basin. On site they are the underwater lights, and the section of the code that governs how they are installed is the one that also covers the bonding around them.

short_definition: A submerged outlet in the floor of a basin that the circulation system draws through, and usually also the only route that can empty the vessel.
ordinary_meaning: The word 'drain' suggests water leaving down a hole. Most of the time this one is an intake: the pump is pulling water in through it while the feature runs.
explanation:
A bottom outlet lets you draw from the coldest, dirtiest layer and turn over the whole volume rather than just the top. It is also the route that empties the basin for service, which links straight back to whether the floor actually falls to it.

Because it is submerged and it pulls, it is the fitting entrapment happens at.
example: A client asks why the drain is running while the fountain is full. Nothing is emptying. The pump has been drawing through it all summer.

short_definition: Water added automatically to a basin to replace what it loses to evaporation, splash-out and drift.
ordinary_meaning: 'Make-up' sounds like cosmetics, or like making up a story.
explanation:
Water leaves a feature as vapour and everything dissolved in it stays behind. Make-up water arrives carrying its own minerals and leaves those behind too when it evaporates in turn.

So hardness, alkalinity, stabiliser and total dissolved solids all concentrate over a season while the level looks constant and nobody changed anything. Knowing what the make-up water carries matters, because you are concentrating it continuously all summer.
example: You write down the make-up meter every visit. In March it reads a steady rise, and the weather has been cool and still the whole month. The basin has not visibly dropped, because the fill valve is quietly keeping up with a crack in the buried return line.

short_definition: The header that splits one supply into several branch lines, each with its own isolation. Its test ports are threaded take-offs used for gauges — and for connecting the air supply at winterizing.
ordinary_meaning: Many and varied, as in manifold blessings. Unrelated, though a manifold does have many branches.
explanation:
A test manifold goes at the highest physical point of the section, because air collects at the high point and that is where it has to be let out.

It carries three things: a pressure gauge, a ball valve for the water intake, and a dedicated air-bleed valve. The gauge is chosen so the target pressure sits in the middle 50% of the dial — a needle at the bottom of its range cannot show a small drop, and a small drop is the only thing the test is looking for.
example: A splash pad manifold in a vault with eight branch valves. You close seven, blow one to a clean stream at its tips, and step along the row. Blowing all eight together would push a little air down each and clear none of them.

short_definition: The highest pressure the system is designed to run at in normal service. It is the designer's number.
explanation:
Sapphire's test is 50 PSI or 1.5 times this figure, whichever is greater — so 50 PSI is a floor rather than a cap, and on a high-pressure feature the multiplier wins.

Get the figure from the drawing, not from what the pump happens to read on the day. What a pump reads is one operating condition, not the design maximum.
example: A feature whose drawing states a maximum operating pressure well above 33 PSI gets tested at 1.5 times that number, not at 50.

short_definition: A deliberately textured or grooved surface that a later layer physically locks into, instead of relying on adhesion alone.
ordinary_meaning: Keyway sounds like a slot for a door key, or the machined groove that holds a key on a shaft. The sense here is the builder's one: to key a surface is to roughen it so the next material gets a grip.
explanation:
Sand broadcast into a wet coat cures with its lower half locked in the film and its upper half standing proud. That is the keyway — a sandpaper-like face the mortar can hook onto.

Mechanical grip and chemical adhesion are two different things, and on a smooth cured membrane you have very little of the second, so the first is what you are building.
example: Run a bare hand across a properly broadcast wall the next morning. It should feel like coarse sandpaper, evenly, everywhere — not smooth in patches where the sand went on thin and not gritty-loose where it never bonded.

short_definition: The pair of polished faces where the pump shaft enters the wet housing. They keep water in, and the water itself is what cools and lubricates them.
explanation:
This is the part that dies when a pump runs dry. With no water going through, the two faces run against each other with nothing between them, they heat, and the polished finish is gone. It does not take long — far less time than it takes to work out what caused the loss of prime and put it right.

So the rule is the order of operations: stop the pump first, diagnose afterwards.
example: A tech starts a pump on a system that has not been filled, hears it scream, and kills it in what feels like no time at all. The next day it drips steadily from behind the wet end. The seal was gone before he got back to the panel.

short_definition: A million ohms. The megohm range on a meter is used to look for current leaking through insulation — a measurement from a hot line to structural ground.
explanation:
Sapphire's GFCI procedure ends on this range, and a low reading there is the answer: water has found a pinhole in the insulation and that cable run gets replaced.

What a handheld meter cannot do is clear a cable. Insulation fails under voltage, and a handheld is asking the question with a few volts from its own battery, so a clean reading is not proof the insulation would hold at line voltage. A megohmmeter applies a high test voltage on purpose — and has a habit of destroying any electronics still connected.
example: A technician reports that the pump ohms out fine, so the pump is not the ground fault. It might still be: the meter never asked the question at a voltage that would find the fault.

short_definition: The continuous layer of waterproofing material applied to a basin shell. It is either liquid material that cures into a film in place, or a factory-made sheet.
explanation:
A membrane is a system, not just a bucket of material: the coating or sheet, plus the reinforcement at corners, plus the details at every drain, sleeve and joint. Miss one of those and the rest of it is still doing nothing, because water only needs one place the barrier is not.

Its thickness, its continuity and its bond to the concrete are the three things that decide whether it works, and none of the three can be judged by looking at a finished job.
example: You finish a basin floor and walls, and the coat looks even and glossy all over. Behind the light niche, where you could only get the brush in at an angle, it is half the thickness of everywhere else. Nothing about the surface tells you that, and that is where the first pinhole shows up.

short_definition: An adjustable stop on a balancing valve that marks the commissioned position, so the valve can be shut for service and reopened to exactly the same setting.
ordinary_meaning: Memory sounds like recollection or computer storage. Here it is a small mechanical collar and screw.
explanation:
The stop is how a commissioned setting survives maintenance. Shut the valve to pull a nozzle, open it back until it meets the stop, and the branch is back where the engineer put it.

Which is exactly why you never move the stop. Move it and the record of that setting is gone, and putting it right is a rebalancing exercise with flow readings, not a guess.
example: A valve was closed to change a fitting and somebody backed the stop off to get a bit more flow while they were at it. Nothing on the site now records where it used to be.

short_definition: The curved top surface of water sitting in a narrow tube or vial. You read the fill line against it.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday use it is a piece of cartilage in your knee — the thing footballers tear. Same word, unrelated thing.
explanation: Read it at eye level. From above, the water looks higher than it is, so you stop short of the line; from below, you fill past it. Either way the reagent-to-sample ratio is wrong, and on a titration that is the whole result.
example: You are crouched at the edge of a basin with the vial down by your knee, filling by eye from above. The vial goes back in the case under-filled and every reading off it reads high.

short_definition: The fabric collection bag hung on a hydro-vac head. Water passes through the weave and the solids stay in the bag.
explanation: It is what makes a hydro-vac a closed answer to a dirty basin: the debris is captured where you can lift it out and carry it away, without going through a pump, a filter, or a drain. The water it passes goes straight back to the basin, so the level does not fall while you work.
example: Two bags into a leaf-packed vault the bag is heavy and the lift rate has dropped off. Not a fault — the weave is loaded. Empty it and carry on.

short_definition: A small pump that injects liquid chemical at a controlled rate, drawing from a day tank.
explanation: Precise where an erosion feeder is approximate. It needs a working check valve at the injection point, and it must be interlocked with circulation so it cannot dose a system that is not moving water.
example: The acid pump ticks once every few seconds while the system runs. When the circulation pump stops, it stops too. If it does not, the interlock is what you go and find.

short_definition: A leak too small to see as running water — it shows as a slow loss of pressure rather than as a puddle.
explanation:
Certifying a network free of these while the trench is still open is the whole purpose of a hydrostatic test.

A drop on the gauge with no water visible anywhere deserves more attention, not less. On a buried line the water has somewhere to go, and gravel takes a great deal of it before anything shows at the surface.
example: Two hours, a couple of PSI gone, and the trench looks bone dry. That is not evidence the test was fine.

short_definition: One thousandth of an inch. It is the unit coating thickness is specified and measured in — Sapphire's document gives typically 30 to 40 mils per coat.
ordinary_meaning: It reads as a shortening of millimetre, and sometimes as short for million. Both are badly wrong in this context. A millimetre is about 39 mils, so reading 30 mils as 30 millimetres overstates the target by a factor of nearly forty.
explanation:
Thirty to forty mils is roughly the thickness of a credit card, give or take. That is not a thickness anyone can judge by eye, from any distance, in any light — which is the whole reason a wet film gauge exists.

If a specified figure ever seems absurdly thin or absurdly thick, check which unit you are reading before you change anything.
example: A new hand is told 30 to 40 mils and rolls the first coat on heavy enough to see the ridges, on the reasonable assumption that a few millimetres was meant. That pail covers a fraction of the floor it should have, and the coat is still curing solid two days later.

short_definition: A named point on a project schedule marking that the job has reached a particular state - basin watertight, power energised, feature handed over.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a milestone is a significant achievement worth celebrating - a birthday, an anniversary.
explanation:
A task is work: it takes time, it consumes somebody's day, and half done is real progress. A milestone is different in kind. It is reached or it is not, and half of one is nothing.

Milestones are drawn on a schedule because they are what other people are waiting on. That is the only reason anybody put one there.
example: The commissioning milestone slips by two days. Nothing about it was half finished on the Wednesday - the electrician had not energised the panel, so the state simply had not been reached.

short_definition: A thousandth of an amp. The unit GFCI trip levels are expressed in.
explanation: The whole safety case is a matter of scale. A Class A GFCI acts on a few milliamps; the breaker on the same circuit is rated in amps. A current a thousand times too small for the breaker to care about is more than enough to kill somebody.
example: A technician reads 4 to 6 mA on a spec sheet and reads it as a small number. It is small compared with the breaker and large compared with a person.

short_definition: A thousandth of an amp — the unit small enough to describe the current that hurts a person rather than the current that runs a tool.
explanation: The scale is the point. A power tool draws amps; the leakage a GFCI trips on is a handful of milliamps; and the current that injures a human being sits in between. That is why a device protecting people has to be far more sensitive than one protecting wiring.
example: A technician sees 'Class A' on a GFCI and knows that means it opens in the 4 to 6 mA region — thousandths of the current the saw plugged into it is drawing.

short_definition: A slotted guide that holds a saw at a fixed angle so a cut comes out square.
explanation:
The cut has to be 90 degrees. An angled cut reduces the welded surface area inside the tapered socket and leaves a wedge-shaped void on one side.

A freehand hacksaw cut is out of square more often than it is not, and you cannot see it once the joint is together.
example: A tech cuts six 2 inch stubs freehand on a bucket lid because the wheel cutter is in the other van. All six look fine on the bench.

short_definition: The proportion in which the two parts of a resin must be combined. It is the chemistry of the product, not a guideline.
explanation:
Off-ratio resin cures soft, cures slowly, or never cures at all. There is no version of the failure where a bit extra hardener makes it tougher.

Mixing has to include the sides and the bottom of the cup. An unmixed streak stays liquid forever and leaves a soft channel running straight through the middle of a pot that looks perfect from outside.
example: A pot is poured, left overnight, and is hard on top. Push a screwdriver into it and it goes through into something that is still tacky — a rope of unmixed resin that came off the side of the mixing cup and went straight into the pour.

short_definition: A code published by a standards organisation as text offered for adoption, rather than as law in its own right. The ISPSC and the NEC are both model codes.
ordinary_meaning: 'Model' sounds like the exemplary or official version — the one everybody follows. It means almost the reverse: a template with no force of its own until somebody adopts it.
explanation: A state or local jurisdiction adopts a particular edition of a model code, and very commonly amends it on the way in — striking sections and adding their own. So 'the code says' is half a sentence. The other half is which edition, adopted where, amended how. Two towns an hour apart can be on different editions with different amendments, and the answer that was right on last month's job is not automatically right on this one.
example: A technician quotes a requirement he learned on a job in the next county. The department here is on an older edition and struck the section he is quoting, so he is precisely and confidently wrong.

short_definition: A cement, sand and water mix used to set masonry units or bed a stone, proportioned for bond and workability.
explanation:
Mortar, grout, deck mud and fat mud get called mud on site and they are four different materials with four different jobs. Using one where another belongs does not usually fail on the day.

On this work every mortar is polymer-modified and rated for continuous submersion or pool use, without exception.
example: A bag labelled for interior walls gets used to bed a coping because it was open. It is the right consistency, the right colour, and the wrong product.

short_definition: The layer of sand-and-cement mortar laid over the membrane to carry the tile or stone and to give the finished surface its shape and falls.
ordinary_meaning: Its other name on site is a mud bed, and mud sounds like wet dirt — something you would clean off a job rather than deliberately install. It is a precisely proportioned, barely damp sand-and-cement mix that is packed and screeded, not slopped on.
explanation:
The bed is a finish layer. It carries no waterproofing duty at all, and it will happily stay wet — which is fine, because the membrane under it is what is holding the basin.

What it needs from you is something to grip. A bed sitting on a smooth film delaminates under water pressure, and that is a tile job coming off a wall that was correct in every other respect.
example: A stone bench inside a basin lifts as one slab a year after handover. The membrane under it is undamaged and perfectly smooth on the back of the bed — smooth, because nobody broadcast sand into it.

short_definition: A contactor plus an overload, packaged as the device that switches a motor on and off and watches what it draws.
explanation: Two things in one box doing two jobs: the contactor makes and breaks the motor current, and the overload trips when that current has been too high for too long.
example: A pump will not run and the panel is silent. The contactor never pulled in, because the overload beside it has tripped and is holding the control circuit open.

short_definition: A deliberate gap built through a structure so that thermal, shrinkage, settlement or seismic movement happens in one designed place instead of wherever the structure is weakest.
explanation:
Run a membrane bonded straight across a joint like that and you have handed all of that movement to a film you can barely measure. It tears in a line, exactly along the joint — the one crack you can predict before the job starts.

The detail is always the same idea: the membrane is deliberately not bonded across the joint, with extra material there — a loop, a bond breaker, joint tape, a preformed profile — so the movement is taken up by slack instead of stretch. More coats over the joint is not that detail, and it is the substitution people reach for.

And the joint has to line up all the way through: structure, waterproofing, mortar bed, tile and grout, with a compressible sealant at the surface.
example: A tile setter reaches a structural joint and the pattern would need an ugly break in it to carry the joint through. Tiling across it hides the joint for one season and then reappears as a crack through the finish in exactly the same line, and the repair is the whole run.

short_definition: The valve on a sand filter whose handle selects which way water runs through the vessel: FILTER, BACKWASH, RINSE and the rest.
explanation: The handle is depressed, rotated and locked into position, and it is never turned while a pump is running. That is not padding in the sequence: the running pump is what has the vessel under pressure, and the handle is being dragged across its ports.
example: Somebody spins the handle to BACKWASH with the pump going, to save a minute. It costs the valve's internal seal, and then it costs an afternoon.

short_definition: The handheld instrument that measures voltage, resistance and continuity. The three functions work in two completely different ways.
explanation:
Voltage is a difference between two points, so it is measured across them, in parallel, on a live circuit — and it is the only one of the three that belongs on an energised circuit.

Resistance and continuity work the opposite way round: the meter supplies its own small current and measures what comes back, so they are valid only on a circuit that is de-energised and isolated.
example: A technician wants to check a cable and leaves the dial on ohms with the circuit still live. The reading is nonsense, and on a bad day the meter is scrap.

short_definition: A single valve with a handle that selects between several flow paths through a filter — filter, backwash, rinse, waste, recirculate, closed.
explanation: The handle drives a diverter down onto a gasket, and the gasket is what keeps the ports separated. Turn it against full pump pressure and that gasket tears, after which the valve leaks internally in every position — a fault that looks like a filter problem and costs the next person a morning. Stop the pump before the handle moves, every time.
example: A filter will not hold pressure and a trickle keeps running out of the waste line with the valve set to filter. Nobody has touched the filter in months. What happened is that somebody switched to waste on a running pump last autumn.

short_definition: Hydrochloric acid, sold under this name for construction cleaning. Strong enough to strip scale off a hard surface and strong enough to destroy a soft one.
explanation:
It depresses pH and alkalinity together, so one dose moves two terms of the saturation index at once — that coupling is the lever a balancing correction uses, and the reason to re-read both afterwards.

Two absolute rules. Acid into water, never water into acid: water poured into concentrated acid flashes to steam at the contact point and throws boiling acid out of the container. And never near a chlorine product or its feed line — the two together produce lethal, greenish-yellow chlorine gas.
example: The crust on a granite spillway fizzes the moment the diluted solution touches it. The fizzing stopping is how you know the crust is gone, which is also when you stop.

short_definition: A yellow-brown powdery film, usually found on the shaded walls of a basin, that brushes away easily and returns in the same place.
explanation:
It returns because it is resistant to normal chlorine baselines. A residual that holds green will not hold mustard; Sapphire's document says it needs high shock levels — the breakpoint protocol, not a top-up.

And it survives on anything that touched the water: nets, brushes, hoses, vacuum heads, wetsuits, the test kit. Treat the feature perfectly, put an untreated brush back in it, and you have re-inoculated it yourself.
example: The same shaded wall goes yellow-brown a fortnight after every treatment. The treatment was fine. The brush that went back in the van damp and went back in the basin next week was not.

short_definition: The manufacturer's data label on a piece of equipment, carrying the figures that particular unit is rated for.
explanation: An overload is set from the motor nameplate. Not from memory, not from the last job, and not from a figure somebody wrote in a notebook. If the nameplate and the panel drawing disagree, that is a question to raise rather than a difference to split.
example: A replacement motor goes in and looks identical to the old one. The nameplate says otherwise, and the overload setting changes with it.

short_definition: An incident that could have caused injury or damage and happened not to.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English 'near miss' sounds like two things nearly missing each other — an almost-collision. In safety it means an event that did happen, and simply did not hurt anybody this time.
explanation: A near miss is the only free information a jobsite ever gives you: the same circumstances with slightly different timing is an injury. How one gets reported and to whom is Sapphire's to define, and the reason to report is that the arrangement that produced it is still in place.
example: A length of pipe slides off a rack and lands where somebody was standing four seconds earlier. Nobody is hurt, so nobody says anything, so the rack is loaded the same way tomorrow.

short_definition: The National Electrical Code — the model code for electrical installation. Article 680 is its section for pools, spas, fountains and other bodies of water.
explanation:
Adopted and sometimes amended state by state and city by city, so the governing version is a local question rather than a universal one. What it settles for this trade is bonding, grounding, equipment ratings, and what may be installed where in relation to the water.

When a question is a code question, it is not a matter of experience or preference - somebody reads the article.
example: A client wants a receptacle moved closer to the basin so the holiday lighting reaches. That is not a judgement call about how far is far enough; it is a clearance printed in Article 680, and it is what the inspector will read.

short_definition: The section of the US National Electrical Code that covers pools, fountains and other permanently installed water features — bonding, GFCI protection, wiring methods and clearances around water.
explanation:
Article 680 governs how power gets to and around water: ground-fault protection, equipotential bonding, listed luminaires, specific wiring methods, and where junction boxes may sit relative to the water line.

It is licensed work. Do not do electrical work you are not qualified and permitted to do, however simple it looks - and like every code, it applies in the edition your jurisdiction adopted.
example: A client asks whether a small decorative basin really needs all the bonding, since it is only ankle deep. Depth is not the test. If it is a fountain, the article applies, and the answer comes from the code and the qualified person, not from how big the basin looks.

short_definition: A detail where water runs over the top of a wall and down the far face out of sight, into a catch basin below.
explanation:
The whole effect is a uniform sheet of water, so the edge is doing architectural work, hydraulic work and finish work at once. It is the least forgiving thing in the module.

It is also usually made of coping stones, which means a heavy unit installation and a precision levelling job are the same task.
example: From the terrace the water looks like it ends at the horizon. From the side, one corner of the edge is dry.

short_definition: The face of a wall or slab opposite to where the water pressure is coming from. A membrane on the inside of a basin is on the negative side with respect to groundwater outside.
