ordinary_meaning: It reads as a criticism, as though negative-side waterproofing were the poor way of doing it. It is a description of geometry, not quality — and negative-side work is a legitimate engineered choice, just a different one with its own specific products.
explanation:
On the negative side the water pressure is trying to push the membrane off the wall instead of onto it. That is a harder job, and it is not solved by applying the same tub of material to the other face.

Plenty of fountains are both cases at once: a basin holding water in, sitting in ground that is trying to push water back through it.
example: A below-grade basin is coated on the inside and holds its flood test perfectly. Two winters later the ground gets wet and the coating starts blistering off the wall from behind, pushed by pressure it was never on the right side of.

short_definition: The NEMA enclosure type meaning prolonged submersion, as against Type 6 which covers occasional temporary submersion. NEMA types also account for corrosion and ice, which IP does not.
explanation:
NEMA and IP describe overlapping ideas from different systems, and they do not convert cleanly into each other. The extra things NEMA covers — corrosion and ice — matter in a fountain, where the water is chemically treated and the equipment sits outdoors through a winter.

The 6 versus 6P distinction is the same distinction as IPX7 versus IPX8: a dunk, or a life underwater.
example: An enclosure marked Type 6 is fine for a vault that floods occasionally in a storm. Bolt the same box to the floor of a basin and you have chosen the temporary rating for a permanent job.

short_definition: Adding a chemical to counteract another one. On skin and in eyes it is the thing you do not do.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English to neutralise something is to make it harmless — so it sounds like exactly the right first aid response, and it is the wrong one.
explanation: A neutralising reaction generates heat, and it generates it inside the burn. Flushing with clean water beats everything: get to the eyewash or the nearest clean running water immediately and keep flushing while somebody else makes the call. Do not stop to look up the product, do not go and find the safety data sheet first, and get contaminated clothing off while flushing.
example: Somebody reaches for a jug of neutraliser kept for spills when a colleague takes acid on the forearm. The right thing is already running out of the hose bib six feet away.

short_definition: The US standard for electrical safety in the workplace: what makes somebody a qualified person, what protective equipment is required, and when work may be done on energised equipment at all.
explanation:
Which electrical work a technician may carry out, and which requires a licensed electrician, is set by state and local law and by Sapphire's own policy — not by confidence or by how long the drive back is. 70E and the employer's written electrical safety program sit over the top of that.

The working boundary is short and holds even where the law is unclear: if you cannot lock it out and verify it dead, you are not opening it.
example: Two technicians disagree on whether a panel cover comes off with the feed live. It is not a matter to resolve between themselves in the equipment room; the answer is written down, and until somebody has read it the cover stays on.

short_definition: A short length of pipe threaded on both ends, used to join two female fittings together.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English it means a part of the body. In plumbing it is simply the short threaded pipe between two fittings, and it is very often the part found seized into a pump port or a manifold.
explanation: It matters in the removal ladder because the nipple is the cheap half. It is a fitting off a shelf; the female half it is stuck in is cast into a pump, a valve or a manifold. So when cutting becomes necessary, the nipple is what gets destroyed, carefully, to save the threads around it.
example: A metal nipple seized into a plastic manifold - nothing that would shift the metal is survivable by the plastic. It comes out with a hacksaw blade worked down the inside of it, and the manifold lives.

short_definition: A metal's position on the galvanic scale. Of two connected metals in water, the less noble one is the one that corrodes.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, noble means high-born or honourable, so it sounds like a judgement about quality.
explanation:
It says nothing about how good, strong or expensive a metal is. It only predicts which of a given pair loses.

And it is always about a pair. A metal is not noble on its own; it is more or less noble than the thing it is bolted to.
example: An aluminium bracket and a stainless fixing look like a sturdy pair. Six months in the water the bracket is chalky and pitted around every hole, and the fixings look brand new.

short_definition: The size a pipe is called — 2 inch, 4 inch — which is a label rather than a measurement of anything on the pipe.
ordinary_meaning: Nominal usually means small or token, as in a nominal fee. Here it means in name only, which is closer, but it still catches people.
explanation:
A 4 inch pipe is not 4 inches across the outside and usually not across the inside either. The nominal number is a naming convention that lets parts on the same sizing standard fit together.

It is enough to order pipe by and not enough to select a penetration seal by, which is why the seal job starts with a tape measure on both diameters.
example: Someone reads 4 inch off the drawing, reads 4 inch off the seal catalogue, and never puts a tape on either the pipe or the hole.

short_definition: The name a pipe goes by rather than a measurement of it. A 3-inch pipe is called 3-inch; neither its inside nor its outside is exactly three inches.
ordinary_meaning: 'Nominal' sounds like 'small' or 'token', as in a nominal fee. It means 'in name only'.
explanation:
The outside diameter is fixed for a given nominal size so that fittings fit, whatever the schedule. The inside diameter is whatever is left after the wall thickness.

This is why hydraulic calculations use the actual bore from a table and not the name on the pipe.
example: A drawing calls for a 3-inch suction line, so the straight run before the pump is five times three: fifteen inches. The rule uses the nominal size, and the friction calculation behind it does not.

short_definition: A product that oxidises organic contamination without adding chlorine.
ordinary_meaning: The name suggests a chlorine-free alternative that does the same job. It does one half of the job — it oxidises, and it does not sanitise.
explanation:
It is genuinely useful indoors, where a chlorine spike is not tolerable, and where the water is needed back quickly. But it does not replace a sanitiser residual and it does not kill algae, so it is not a substitute for the breakpoint protocol.

And it interferes with DPD combined-chlorine testing: for a period after dosing, the monopersulfate itself registers as combined chlorine. Since the breakpoint dose is ten times the combined reading, a false combined reading is a large false dose.
example: An indoor atrium feature is dosed Friday afternoon, tested Saturday, and the combined number is alarming. Somebody multiplies it by ten. The water was never full of chloramines; the test was reading the product.

short_definition: A mortar stiff enough to hold a heavy unit at the height you set it, instead of letting it settle out of line while you work down the run.
explanation: It is what makes a coping bed a full and continuous bed rather than a compromise. A mix that sags forces people towards dabs and mounds, which is the failure the full bed exists to prevent.
example: The first three stones are dead level when they go down. By the time the eighth is set, the first has dropped a hair and the whole run has to come back up.

short_definition: A description of a contact at rest, unactuated, sitting on the shelf: normally open means its contacts are apart, normally closed means they are together.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like it describes the contact in normal running — how the device sits while the machine is working properly.
explanation:
It is a fact about the device on the shelf, not yet a fact about your machine. Confusing the two is how interlocks get defeated by accident.

It gets worse in software: a ladder instruction drawn as a normally-open contact is a question about a bit in memory, not a picture of the device in the field. Two separate conventions that have to agree, and swapping either one without the other lets the machine run in exactly the condition that was supposed to stop it.
example: A float is replaced with one of the other contact configuration because that is what the van had. The program is not touched, and the pump now gets its permission to run from an empty basin.

short_definition: A trowel with square or V-shaped teeth that leaves adhesive on the wall in parallel ridges of a set height.
explanation:
The ridges are not decoration and the direction they run is not arbitrary. Combed in one direction, they collapse sideways when the tile is pressed down and the air between them has a straight path out. Swirls and arcs trap air in the curve of every loop, and no amount of pressing gets it out.

The trowel pattern is a ventilation design.
example: A tiler works in comfortable arcs because it is faster on a big wall. Every loop on that wall has an air pocket in it that nothing later will remove.

short_definition: The precisely sized opening a display nozzle shapes its water through.
explanation: It is the smallest passage in the whole system, so it is where anything loose in the water ends up and stays. That is what makes deburring a cut pipe end a display-quality issue rather than a tidiness one.
example: One jet in a row of twelve stands visibly shorter than the rest, and what comes out of it during service is a curl of PVC.

short_definition: A protective device tripping with no real fault behind it. Genuine ones exist, and they are far rarer than the phrase suggests.
ordinary_meaning: The word nuisance makes it sound settled — an annoyance with nothing behind it — which is a conclusion rather than a diagnosis.
explanation:
Real causes exist: long wire runs have capacitive leakage, several loads sharing one device add their leakage together, and a soaked but undamaged luminaire can push a device over the edge.

But the great majority of GFCIs that will not reset are reporting a real fault — water in a fixture or a junction box, a conductor nicked during a hard pull, a failing pump seal that has wet the windings, a heater element gone to ground. Assume a real fault until you have isolated the loads and proved otherwise.
example: Three tickets in a row on the same feature say nuisance trip, reset. The fourth technician pulls the loads off one at a time and finds a junction box in the planter with an inch of water in it. It had been reporting itself since spring.

short_definition: The unit of electrical resistance, written with the symbol for omega. On a meter's ohms range it tells you how hard a path is to push current through.
explanation:
Resistance is measured on a de-energised, isolated circuit, because the meter supplies its own current. Isolation matters even when nothing is live: a parallel path through some other part of the circuit gives you a resistance that is completely real and not the one you asked about.

A solenoid coil measured this way tells three different stories — a healthy steady figure, near zero, or OL.
example: A coil is measured with its leads still on the controller terminal block, and the figure that comes back is the coil in parallel with whatever else that block connects to. Lifting one lead changes the answer.

short_definition: What a meter displays on the ohms range when the resistance is beyond what it can measure — in practice, when there is no complete path at all.
explanation: On a solenoid coil, OL means the coil wire has snapped and the circuit path is broken. Nothing is shorted, nothing blew, and nothing happens — which is why an open coil is the quiet failure and a shorted one takes a fuse with it.
example: A valve has stopped operating but the controller is otherwise healthy and no fuses have gone. The coil reads OL with its leads lifted, and that is the whole story.

short_definition: A timer instruction that produces its output only once its input has been continuously true for a set time. An off-delay does the opposite, holding its output on for a time after the input goes false.
explanation: The word that matters is continuously. A timer that never reaches its preset is usually being reset every scan by a condition that is flickering — a bouncing switch, a sensor sitting right on its threshold, a pressure hunting around a setpoint.
example: A heater is supposed to come on after flow has been proven for a short while, and it never does. The flow switch is chattering right at its threshold, and the timer restarts from zero every time it blinks.

short_definition: A break in the return path of a circuit, so current cannot complete its loop even though voltage is still present at the equipment.
explanation:
Voltage is only half a circuit. Current has to get back, and if the neutral or the second leg is open then full voltage sits at a load that can do nothing with it.

This is one of the two readings that routinely fools people, because the meter says the supply is fine and it is telling the truth about the half it measured.
example: A basin light reads full voltage at its terminals and stays dark. The lamp gets swapped, and it is still dark. The neutral had corroded off in a junction box nobody had opened, twenty feet back.

short_definition: How long a mortar or adhesive can still bond after it has been mixed and spread.
explanation:
It is shorter in direct sunlight and in wind, which between them describe most of a working day on an open site. It is shorter again in dry air and over a thirsty substrate.

Which reduces to one habit: mix what you can place, spread only what you can set, and place what you mixed.
example: A full wall is combed out before lunch so the afternoon can be all tiling. The last third of that wall is already past its open time before a tile touches it.

short_definition: The clause in the contract documents that says which document wins when two of them conflict.
explanation:
There is no universal rule that the drawings beat the specification or the other way round. It is written into each contract and it differs from job to job - and on top of it, the approved submittal is what is actually being installed and can be a different model from either document.

The useful habit is to stop rather than to pick. Installing the wrong thing correctly is still installing the wrong thing.
example: A conflict between the drawing and the spec over a valve type gets settled in ten minutes by the project manager reading one clause in the front of the project manual. Guessing would have cost a wall.

short_definition: The amount of living and once-living material in the water - leaves, pollen, algae, birds - all of which reacts with the sanitiser and uses it up.
ordinary_meaning: Nothing to do with food labelling or farming, and it is not a good thing. Organic here means carbon-based material, and a high organic load is a basin full of leaves rather than anything virtuous.
explanation: It is why a sanitiser that will not hold is very often a debris problem wearing a chemistry costume. You dose, the organic material consumes it, and by the next visit the reading is back where it was - and nothing was wrong with the product or the dose.
example: A basin under a mature tree will not hold a sanitiser reading for a fortnight in October and holds it perfectly in February. Nothing about the dosing changed; the tree did.

short_definition: The machined hole a nozzle sprays through. Its size, its shape and the condition of its edge are what produce the nozzle's pattern.
explanation:
An orifice is a dimension, not just a hole. The bore, the edge, and the swirl or aeration passages behind it were chosen together to give a particular pattern at a particular flow.

That is why a blockage is removed rather than drilled out. Anything that changes the bore changes the display permanently, and leaves a nozzle that is genuinely clear and still wrong.
example: A nozzle that has furred up gets lifted out, soaked, and back-flushed until the deposit lets go. It goes back into the ring looking identical to the other nineteen, because it is identical to the other nineteen.

short_definition: Oxidation-reduction potential — a millivolt measurement of how strongly the water is able to oxidise, used by a controller as a live reading of sanitiser effectiveness.
explanation:
Sapphire's document sets the band: a healthy commercial fountain should hold 650 to 750 mV. A respectable free chlorine reading sitting next to a low ORP is information, not a fault — it means the chlorine present is not doing much.

ORP also moves with pH on its own, so a controller steering on ORP can spend a week chasing what is really a pH problem. And a reading is only as good as the probe behind it.
example: The controller doses steadily all week and the readings on the panel look settled, while the water tells a different story in the basin. The probe went through a winter out of solution and has been reading plausible nonsense ever since.

short_definition: The federal agency and body of law covering worker safety in the United States, and the source of the specific standards for confined space, lock-out/tag-out, fall protection, excavation, hazard communication and protective equipment.
explanation: The word to hold onto is minimum. An OSHA standard is a floor, never a ceiling — a manufacturer's instruction, a project specification, a state plan or Sapphire's own program can all require more, and where two requirements differ the stricter one governs. 'OSHA does not require it' is not an argument against doing it. It also gives you rights worth knowing you have: to see the safety data sheets and written programs for hazards you work around, to be trained in a language you understand, and to raise a hazard without retaliation.
example: A crew member points out that a task has no written procedure. Saying it at the time, to a supervisor, is the move that is always available and always protected — and it is more useful at eight in the morning than at four in the afternoon.

short_definition: A tag fixed to a damaged tool or cord saying it is not to be used and who took it out of service.
explanation: The tag goes on the item and the item goes somewhere separate. Both halves matter: a broken tool returned to the same shelf as the good ones will be used by somebody who trusted the shelf, and a tag alone tends to get read as 'somebody meant to look at this'.
example: A cord with a crushed section gets a tag and goes in the cab footwell to come back to the shop, rather than back into the cord bin where it will be dug out in the dark at the end of a long day.

short_definition: The measurement across the outside of a pipe, over the wall. It is what a seal, a clamp or a coupling actually fits.
explanation:
Outside diameter belongs to the sizing standard the pipe was made to rather than to the material. Steel and PVC of the same nominal size share one OD, and schedule changes the wall thickness rather than the outside — so Schedule 40 and Schedule 80 measure the same across the outside.

Ductile iron and copper are each on a different standard, and PVC is made in both the steel and the ductile-iron sizes. Which means you measure rather than reason about it.
example: A tech assumes the heavier gray pipe must be fatter outside than the white and orders a different seal for it. Both measure the same over the wall.

short_definition: Clean, graded quartz sand that has been dried in an oven and bagged, used for broadcasting into a wet membrane coat.
explanation:
Two properties are being bought here, and both matter. Dry, because damp sand clumps and will not scatter evenly. Clean, because whatever the sand is carrying goes into the coating with it — and dirty sand is a bond breaker in its own right.

A bag of builders' sand from the yard is neither of those things, however similar it looks in the hand.
example: The bagged sand has been sitting in the back of an open truck through a rainy night. It will still pass through your fingers and it will still look like sand. Broadcast it and it goes on in clumps, and the clumps sit on the coat rather than in it.

short_definition: A coiling method that alternates a normal forward loop with a reversed one, so the twist each loop puts into a hose or cord is cancelled by the next.
explanation:
Wrapping a hose or a heavy cord around your forearm and elbow puts a full 360 degree twist into the casing with every loop, and the twist does not go anywhere. It comes back as kinks, knots and a choked line, and the casing has been worked in a direction it was never built for.

Alternating the loops cancels the torsion instead of accumulating it, so the coil lies flat and pulls apart in a straight line. Secure it with a hook-and-loop strap or a cord tie — never a knot, which is a permanent crush point.
example: Two identical 50 foot wash hoses, one coiled each way for a season. In April one pulls straight out across the deck and the other has to be walked out and fought with.

short_definition: The breaker or fuse that opens a circuit when the current through it rises above what that circuit is rated to carry.
explanation: It protects the wiring, not the equipment and not the person - that is a different device's job. Fitting a larger one because the existing one keeps operating does not remove the condition it was reacting to; it raises the level at which anybody finds out about it.
example: A breaker feeding the equipment room trips every warm afternoon. Pulling the loads off it one at a time and resetting between each puts the trip on one pump - the one standing in full sun with its cooling fan packed with cottonwood.

short_definition: A gravity line that carries away water above the intended level — storm water, a stuck fill valve, a deck washing down.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the event of something spilling over the edge - a failure. Here it is a piece of hardware whose job is to make sure that never happens.
explanation:
Make-up and overflow are the two ends of the same level control: one adds water and the other sets the ceiling. Rain, a passing fill valve or a hose left running all end up going out of the overflow instead of across the deck.

Which also means a blocked overflow plus a stuck fill valve is a flooded plaza, and that a level set too close to the overflow quietly wastes treated water and the chemical in it.
example: After a heavy storm a client reports water across the walkway. The overflow grate is packed with bark mulch off the planter beds, so the basin had nowhere to put the rain.

short_definition: The device in a motor starter that watches how much current the motor is drawing and trips when it has been too high for too long.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the condition — the motor being asked to do too much — rather than a specific piece of hardware in the panel that trips.
explanation:
It is a device, and it is not the breaker. The breaker protects the conductors from a short circuit or a gross overcurrent, and it acts fast. The overload protects the motor from slowly cooking itself at a current the breaker is perfectly happy with. Two devices, two jobs, and neither does the other's.

It is set from the motor nameplate, never from memory.
example: Debris jams an impeller on a Tuesday afternoon. The motor stalls, current climbs, and the overload trips after a few seconds — while the breaker upstream, rated in amps for the wire, never notices anything at all.

short_definition: Chemically destroying dissolved organic material in the water - the invisible load a filter cannot catch.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like rusting, or metal going dull in air. That is one kind of oxidation, but here it is a water-treatment job done deliberately.
explanation:
Third of the three jobs, after filtration and sanitation. Sweat, sunscreen, leaf tannins, bird droppings and pollen dissolve rather than float, so no filter touches them. They are what makes water smell tired and look dull even when it is clear and sanitised.

Ozone systems are oxidisers. So, in part, is chlorine - which is why a basin under heavy use consumes far more sanitiser than the maths for killing organisms alone would suggest.
example: A courtyard basin under a lime tree goes slightly brown-tinged every spring even though the filter is spotless and the residual is on target. The colour is dissolved tannin, and it comes out with oxidation, not with a backwash.

short_definition: Air holding less oxygen than the safe operational range the employer has set, and the first of the four things a pre-entry test looks for.
explanation: Sapphire's safe operational range is 19.5% to 23.5%, and below it you are in an oxygen-deficient atmosphere. Oxygen is read first for two reasons: it decides whether anybody can be in the space at all, and the combustible sensor in most meters needs oxygen to work. In a low-oxygen atmosphere that sensor reads low, which is the worst possible direction for an instrument to be wrong. Oxygen can be consumed quietly by rust on the inside of a steel tank, or displaced by a heavier gas that has settled in the bottom.
example: A monitor lowered into a vault reads 18.2% oxygen with zeros elsewhere. The zeros are not reassurance — the flammable channel is reading through an atmosphere it cannot measure properly.

short_definition: Air holding more oxygen than the safe operational range, which is an alarm condition rather than a comfortable one.
ordinary_meaning: 'Enriched' sounds like an improvement — extra oxygen, so easier breathing. It is an alarm condition, not a bonus.
explanation: The top of Sapphire's range is 23.5%, and above it the space counts as enriched. Enriched oxygen makes materials that normally smoulder burn fiercely — clothing included — and it turns a small ignition source into a serious fire. It usually means something is leaking oxygen into the space, which is itself a problem to find rather than to work around.
example: A meter at a hatch reads 24.1% oxygen. Nobody is short of breath and nothing smells wrong, and the entry still stops there.

short_definition: A gas generated on site and injected into the water as a powerful oxidiser. It is used up in the process and is toxic to breathe.
explanation:
Like UV, ozone acts only where the water passes through the equipment, and it leaves nothing behind in the basin. Its job is to reduce the load the residual sanitiser has to carry, not to replace it.

The safety point is the important one. Ozone systems are built with contact vessels, off-gas handling and destruct units because the gas hurts people who breathe it. Opening, venting or servicing one is work for somebody trained on that equipment, with the system isolated under the site lock-out/tag-out program.
example: You walk into an equipment room and get a sharp, electrical-smelling bite at the back of your throat. That is a reason to walk straight back out and call it in, not a reason to look for the leak.

short_definition: Piping and instrumentation diagram — a schematic drawing of a system showing every pipe, valve, pump, filter and instrument as a standard symbol, and how they connect.
explanation: It is not a plan view and it is not to scale. It shows connection and sequence rather than position, so a valve drawn an inch from a pump on the sheet may be twenty feet away in the vault. What it buys you is the ability to trace a flow loop — where water goes from here, what it passes through, and what can shut it off — without walking the whole system. Module 10 teaches the symbols.
example: You need to know whether the UV chamber is upstream or downstream of the heater before deciding what to isolate. The sheet answers it in five seconds; the vault takes twenty minutes and a torch.

short_definition: A U-shaped dip in a drain line that holds a permanent puddle of water. That standing water is the seal that stops sewer gas coming back up the pipe.
explanation: A p-trap works because it holds water, which means it cannot be drained and cannot be blown out without destroying the thing it is for. That is the whole reason antifreeze exists in a winterizing procedure: marine-grade, non-toxic propylene glycol goes into all sub-grade p-traps and perimeter drains so the residual puddle cannot freeze.
example: A deck drain on a splash pad has been blown through and reads dry at the grate, and there is still a cupful of water sitting in the bend under the paving where the air went straight over the top of it.

short_definition: A concentration unit: one part of a substance dissolved in a million parts of water.
explanation:
In water, one part per million is the same as one milligram per litre — the units are interchangeable and kits label them either way.

It matters mostly because every dose calculation in this module is in ppm, and the arithmetic only works if the reading you feed it is the same unit and the same quantity you think it is.
example: The breakpoint target you write down is in ppm and the photometer reports in ppm, so the sum is straightforward — provided the number you multiplied was the combined reading and not the free one.

short_definition: A chemical treatment that dissolves free iron off a stainless surface and leaves the protective film to re-form clean.
explanation:
It is both the cure for a contaminated part and the preventative step after fabrication.

It is not the same as polishing, and this is the part people get wrong. Mechanical cleaning can make a contaminated part look perfect while leaving every embedded particle exactly where it was.
example: A rust-streaked handrail is buffed until it gleams and is streaked again a month later. Nothing was removed; it was just spread around.

short_definition: The invisible chromium-oxide skin on stainless steel that gives it its corrosion resistance. It is a few atoms thick and re-forms by itself where oxygen can reach it.
explanation:
Everything good about stainless comes from this film, and everything bad that happens to stainless is the film being prevented from re-forming. It needs oxygen, so wherever oxygen runs out the alloy is defenceless.

Reinforcing steel relies on the same trick by a different route: the alkalinity of sound concrete keeps a passive film on the bar.
example: A scratch across a stainless panel in open, moving water heals itself and never rusts. The same scratch under a gasket does not.

short_definition: The weight of occupants and cargo a vehicle is rated to carry, on top of its own weight. It is GVWR minus the truck's curb weight.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like the load you are being paid to haul — the pump and the pipe in the back — as though the truck itself and the people in it were not part of it.
explanation: Payload counts the crew, and it knows nothing about anything bolted on after the truck left the factory. A ladder rack, a headache rack, a toolbox and whatever has been living in the bed since spring all come out of it before the first pump goes on. A built-out service truck has spent much of its payload before you load anything. That is why the honest answer to 'can we take this too?' is often no on a truck that looks half empty.
example: The placard on a service truck gives an occupants-and-cargo figure. Subtract a two-man crew, the rack, the ladder, three toolboxes and a hose reel, and the amount left for the submersible pump and a tote of water is a fraction of what the bed looks like it could swallow.

short_definition: Small, rounded, washed stone used with clean sand as bedding and shading material around buried pipe.
explanation:
Rounded and washed is the whole specification. Rounded stone has no edges to press into the pipe wall, and washed means no fines or clay lumps riding along with it.

Screened site spoil is not a substitute, however clean it looks in a bucket.
example: The yard is out of pea gravel, so somebody suggests running the excavated material through a screen. What comes out is still angular, and the angular bits are the reason bedding is bought rather than made.

short_definition: A deck of pavers carried on adjustable supports with open joints between them, built over a reservoir so water falls through the joints and returns below.
explanation:
Letting water through is the whole point of the construction, and it works. The consequence is that everything else on the plaza goes through it too - leaves, grit, cigarette ends, coins, winter sand, drink spills. There is no filter between the plaza and the water: the deck is the inlet.

So the fix for a debris problem here is almost always on top of the deck rather than in the equipment room.
example: A reservoir nobody has looked into for three years is found carrying a layer of grit and wrappers across the whole floor. Not one thing in the equipment room was ever at fault - the plaza had been swept toward the feature by somebody trying to be helpful.

short_definition: A walkable deck of stone pavers, tile or grating carried on heavy-duty adjustable plastic pedestals above a waterproofed sub-slab, with the jets coming up through it and no visible basin edge.
explanation:
The joints between the pavers are entirely open on purpose, so water drains instantly through the floor grid instead of standing on it. Nozzle supply lines and light conduits run in the void below, carrying none of the foot load.

Service is a lift rather than a demolition: you take out the surrounding pavers, work on the plumbing, and put them back. That only works if whoever set the equipment put it where pavers can actually be lifted over it.
example: A pump under the deck needs four pavers lifted and a structural pedestal cut out to reach it. That pump will not be serviced properly for the rest of its life, and the decision that caused it was made during installation.

short_definition: A thin oil formulated to wick down into a thread and break a corrosion or scale bond, given time to work.
explanation:
It is the first step of the removal ladder and the step people skip. The course's method is to apply it - a proprietary penetrant, or a 50/50 mix of acetone and automatic transmission fluid - then tap the fitting lightly with a wrench so the vibration helps it wick deeper, then wait 10 to 15 minutes.

That wait is the cheapest thing in the whole lesson.
example: A seized union gets a dose, a few light taps, and a quarter of an hour while you eat lunch and write up the last call. It comes free with a back-up wrench and no drama at all.

short_definition: Anywhere something passes through the shell — a drain, a return, a jet, a light niche, a sleeve, an anchor — together with the hole it passes through.
ordinary_meaning: The everyday sense is the act of piercing something, which makes it sound like damage or a breach. In construction it is a noun for an ordinary, planned feature: the pipe or fitting going through the wall, and the detail around it.
explanation:
Every penetration is a place where the concrete was cast around something that expands, contracts and vibrates differently from concrete. So the shell and the fitting are always trying to part company at that line.

The membrane has to wrap each one, and every penetration is on the look-at list during a flood test.
example: A basin with one floor drain, four returns, two jets and three light niches has ten penetrations. Nine of them can be perfect and the tenth still empties the basin, and the water will be tracking sideways under the finish by the time you see it.

short_definition: The drain line or channel running round the edge of a basin or deck that collects splash-out and surface water.
explanation: Perimeter drains are easy to leave off a winterizing list because they are not part of the circulation system, and they are full of exactly the low spots and traps that hold water. They get glycol along with the sub-grade p-traps.
example: A trench drain along the plaza edge collects a winter's leaf litter and a persistent puddle at one end where the channel is flat. That end is what freezes and lifts the channel.

short_definition: A chemical dosing pump that moves liquid by rollers squeezing a flexible tube, so the chemical never touches the pump's own workings.
explanation:
The tube is the wearing part, and Sapphire's document sets rebuild or replacement of the internal squeeze tubes on a six-month cycle. A tired tube loses elasticity and the flow output drops, so the controller calls for a dose the feature never receives — the chemistry drifts while the screen says everything is being done.

A tube that splits rather than fades is worse: it sprays concentrated acid or chlorine inside the equipment room.
example: The controller log shows it has been calling for acid every day for a month and the pH has not moved. The pump has been running the whole time; the tube stopped delivering in July.

short_definition: What has happened when a gasket or seal has been compressed for long enough that it stops springing back and keeps the squashed shape.
ordinary_meaning: Set in ordinary English is a collection of things, or the act of putting something down. Here it means a permanent deformation — the material has given up its elasticity, which is the one property it was installed for.
explanation:
A gasket that has taken a set no longer pushes back against the lid, so it stops following any movement in the joint and stops closing small gaps.

This is a genuine ageing failure mode, and it is why gaskets are inspected and replaced rather than reused indefinitely. It is also a plausible-sounding diagnosis that gets reached for too early — a box that is filling right up is more likely to be fed by something else.
example: You take the lid off a vault box after several seasons and the gasket has a flat, glazed band round it where the lid has been bearing. Press it with a thumbnail and it does not come back. That one is finished.

short_definition: A confined space that also carries a hazardous atmosphere or the potential for one, an engulfment risk, a shape that could trap or asphyxiate, or any other recognised serious hazard.
explanation: Most of that list is about what the space could do, not what it is doing while you look at it — which is why the determination is made in writing, by the employer, before anybody goes near it, and not by a technician at the lip of the hole. Sapphire has already made that call for the commonest case: its below-ground concrete equipment vaults are classified as permit-required, on the grounds of toxic gas accumulation and oxygen depletion. A vault starts permit-required and stays that way unless somebody with the authority to reclassify it does so in writing.
example: A vault is pleasant and breezy on a March morning and a technician is tempted to call it fine. It is the same vault that fills with solvent vapour when somebody glues a line two hours later, which is precisely why the classification is not his to make.

short_definition: Equipment worn to protect the person rather than to do the work - eye protection, gloves, face protection, and whatever else the chemical or the task calls for.
explanation: What is required is not a matter of preference or of how routine the job feels. It comes from the chemical's own safety data sheet and from the standard covering the task, and it is the last line rather than the first - it protects you when everything else has already gone wrong.
example: Decanting acid on a windy plaza with the basin drained is exactly the routine, boring, done-it-a-hundred-times job where the gloves and the face protection stay in the truck.

short_definition: The operating profile a DMX fixture is set to, which decides how many channels it consumes and what each one does.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily somebody's character — the sort of person they are.
explanation: Two physically identical fixtures in different personalities are different devices as far as the address map is concerned. Which personality a fixture should be in comes from the fixture manual and the lighting design, not from whatever it was shipped in.
example: A replacement fixture goes in on the correct address and behaves strangely from the first show. It came out of the box in a different mode and is reading a different number of channels than the map assumes.

short_definition: A measure of how acidic or basic water is, on a scale running from 0 to 14. It is the reading that moves almost everything else in the water.
explanation:
pH decides how much of your chlorine sits in its strong form, whether the water deposits minerals or dissolves them, and whether the water stings people's eyes. The scale is logarithmic, so each whole number is a tenfold change — a reading one unit off target is ten times off, not slightly off.

That is also why a confident correction overshoots. And pH will not hold at all if the alkalinity underneath it is wrong, which is why alkalinity is corrected first.
example: You read a plaza basin, find the pH high, and add acid until it looks right. Next Tuesday it is back where it started, and somebody suggests the client is dosing it. Nobody is. There is nothing in that water holding the pH still between visits.

short_definition: The sensor that a controller reads the water through. A pH probe senses through a thin glass membrane; an ORP probe reads against a reference junction. Both are wet-contact instruments.
explanation:
Both parts have to stay wet to survive, which is why a probe is the one thing in a winterizing pass that does not get stored dry. A dry probe is instantly ruined — and it does not go dead and obvious, it goes plausible, so a ruined probe can mislead a whole controller for a season.

In spring they come straight out of their storage caps and onto the system. A probe found dry is treated as a dead probe rather than one to try.
example: A probe is found in the shop in April sitting in an open box, cap off, tip chalky. It powers up and gives a reading. That reading is the most expensive thing in the pump room.

short_definition: The indicator used in a liquid drop kit to read pH — it changes colour across the pH range.
explanation:
Sapphire's document names it alongside a digital photometer as the way pH is taken. It is a colour comparator, so your eye is doing the measuring, and it drifts with age like every other reagent.

Whichever method you use, read the pH immediately after the sample is drawn. Air exposure changes the water's carbon dioxide and moves the true pH.
example: The vial gets filled at the basin, carried back across the plaza, and read on the tailgate ten minutes later. That is no longer the water you dipped.

short_definition: Dissolved compounds that act as fertiliser for algae. Phosphate and nitrate are the two that matter in a fountain.
explanation:
They arrive from decaying leaves and organic debris, from lawn fertiliser and irrigation runoff draining into an outdoor basin, from some source water, from birds, and from certain treatment products themselves.

Chlorinating hard against a feature that is being fed continuously is a losing arrangement — you pay for chemicals to treat a symptom on every visit while the cause keeps arriving. That is a site and design conversation to raise, not a bottle to pour.
example: A basin sits at the low point of a lawn that gets fertilised every spring, and blooms every spring a fortnight later. Nobody had connected the two until somebody walked the grade.

short_definition: An instrument that reads the developed colour of a treated sample and reports a number instead of asking your eye to match a chart.
explanation:
It is the first method Sapphire's document reaches for on pH and free chlorine, and the module's own performance check asks you to demonstrate it. Taking your eye out of the loop is a real improvement and makes results repeatable between technicians.

It removes nothing else. Expired reagent, an unrepresentative sample, a scratched or fingerprinted vial, water too cold for the reaction, or an instrument that has drifted out of calibration all produce a confident number to two decimal places that is simply wrong — and a display is much harder to disbelieve than a smudgy colour.
example: The screen says 0.42 and everybody writes it down. The vial had a thumbprint across the light path and nobody looked at it.

short_definition: A more aggressive acid treatment of stainless that removes a little of the metal itself, along with surface contamination and the discoloured band left beside a weld.
ordinary_meaning: Everywhere else, pickling is preserving food in vinegar or brine.
explanation:
Pickling and passivation are often spoken about together, and they are not the same. Passivation cleans iron off the surface; pickling takes surface metal away with it, which is what it takes to remove heat tint at a weld.

Neither is a mechanical process, and neither is achieved with a wire wheel.
example: A welded stainless frame comes back from the fabricator with straw and blue bands either side of each weld. Those bands are not decoration and they are not cleaned off with a brush.

short_definition: Anywhere two parts close on each other — a belt and pulley, a coupling, a clamp, a lid.
explanation: It does not need to be fast or powerful to take a finger; it needs to close. A slow actuator and a hand-tightened clamp both qualify, and so does a hatch cover coming down on the edge of a vault.
example: A technician steadies a pump coupling with his fingers while somebody else bumps the starter to check rotation. The shaft turns a quarter of a revolution, which is all it needs.

short_definition: A tiny hole right through a cured coating film, often too small to see without looking for it.
explanation:
Pinholes form where the film is thinnest — over the high spots of an uneven slab, over the top of an aggregate particle, along an edge where the material was pulled thin. Water under standing pressure does not need more than that.

A membrane can be continuous to look at and pinholed in fact. Cross-coating is the control for it, and a flood test is the check.
example: A basin holds its level for the first hours of a flood test and then loses a steady trickle overnight. There is no damage anywhere, no visible defect, and the whole loss is going through holes you would need to kneel down and hunt for.

short_definition: Water entering a cable through a tiny break in its insulation, giving the current a path out of the circuit.
explanation:
It reads as a low resistance from the hot line to structural ground on the megohm range, and it is the usual reason a GFCI will not stay in. That sub-component cable run gets replaced — it is not dried out and put back.

The pinhole often started as a scrape from a hard pull months or years earlier.
example: A light run keeps tripping the device. The meter on the megohm range shows a low reading hot to ground on that run, and the answer is a new cable, not a hot-air gun and optimism.

short_definition: A paste sealant brushed onto pipe threads before assembly.
ordinary_meaning: 'Dope' in ordinary speech is a drug, or an insult.
explanation: Some pipe dopes attack plastic, so the one the fitting maker calls for is the one that goes on. Thread tape is the alternative: it goes on the male thread, wound in the direction the thread turns so it does not unwind as you assemble.
example: A half-used tube from the bottom of the van gets brushed onto a plastic female fitting. It seals beautifully. Six weeks later the fitting is crazed all round the thread and weeping.

short_definition: The wall-thickness class of a pipe, written as a number after the word: Schedule 40, Schedule 80.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a timetable, and on a drawing the 'equipment schedule' really is a list. Pipe schedule is wall thickness and nothing else.
explanation:
Same nominal size, same outside diameter, which is why fittings interchange between them. What changes is the wall: a higher schedule means a thicker wall, a higher pressure rating and a smaller inside diameter.

A smaller bore means more velocity for the same flow and more friction loss, so swapping schedules is a hydraulic change as well as a strength change. Pressure ratings also fall as temperature rises.
example: A run gets patched with Schedule 80 because that is what was on the truck. It fits perfectly, holds pressure easily, and quietly adds friction to a line that was sized in 40.

short_definition: The deliberate slope built into a surface so water runs where you want it. Also called fall.
ordinary_meaning: Everywhere else, pitch is throwing a ball, a sales pitch, a musical note, or the black tar on a roof.
explanation:
A flat slab does not drain and no finish laid parallel to it will either. Fall comes from the structure or it comes from the bed, and on most of this work it comes from the bed, which is the real reason deck mud exists.

The required fall is on the drawing. A pitch remembered from the last job is a pitch you are about to tile over.
example: A basin floor looks dead level, and it is. After a drain-down there are four puddles that somebody will be looking at for the life of the feature.

short_definition: Corrosion that attacks one small spot and drives downward, through a surface that still looks polished a millimetre away.
explanation:
A chloride ion breaks the passive film at a point. Inside the pit the water goes stagnant and oxygen-starved so the film cannot re-form there, and the chemistry inside becomes more aggressive than the water outside. The attack accelerates itself.

The classic presentation is a pinhole leak in a bright, clean-looking stainless part, which is why a visual check is a poor test.
example: A polished nozzle body weeps a thin bead of water from a hole you can barely see, and the metal either side of it is flawless.

short_definition: A programmable logic controller — the industrial computer that runs a sequence, reading inputs and driving outputs.
explanation:
It is the brain and not the muscle. Its output is a signal; something downstream — a relay, a contactor, a solenoid coil — does the actual switching.

It also does not watch its inputs continuously. It loops, and that loop has consequences.
example: An output is commanded on and the pump does not run. The controller has done its whole job at that point, and the next place to look is the relay, the contactor, the overload or the disconnect.

short_definition: Pressurising a closed, capped line with air and holding it to look for leaks. On plastic pipe it is forbidden. A hydrostatic test does the same job with water instead, which is why it is the safe one.
explanation:
Air compresses and stores energy; water does not, in any amount that matters. A plastic pipe full of pressurised air is a spring that fails all at once and sends fragments, and that is why Module 1's rule exists.

A winter blow-out looks similar and is a different operation: you are moving water out of an open line, not building and holding pressure in a closed one. The far end stays open, nothing is capped, and the under-15-PSI setting means there was never much energy to store. The moment somebody caps the end to push harder, it has become a pneumatic pressure test on plastic pipe. Stop.
example: A zone is blowing slowly and somebody suggests capping the last two heads so the air "goes where it is needed". That single suggestion turns a routine winterizing job into the thing the rule is about.

short_definition: All the weight above a length of pipe ending up concentrated on one small spot instead of spread along it.
explanation:
Leave a rock, a lump of clay or a piece of the old system in the trench and the pipe bridges across it. Everything above then presses down through that one contact point.

Under compaction a sharp stone does not merely load the wall — it punctures it.
example: A short length of the demolished old line is left lying in the trench under the new 4 inch. It is doing nothing at all until the first vehicle crosses the lawn.

short_definition: A cement product with polymers built into it, which fill the microscopic pores that cement otherwise cures with.
explanation:
Sapphire's rule has no exceptions written into it: always use polymer-modified mortars, thinsets and grouts specifically rated for continuous submersion or pool use. Not where the specification happens to call for it, always.

The mechanism is the reason. A plain cementitious bed lets water travel its own pore network, and the polymers seal those pores so water cannot work its way through the bed and break down the structural bond over time. A bed that is holding perfectly today and has quietly let go a few years from now is usually this.
example: An excellent interior floor product is used on a basin wall. It holds through the first fill, the first season and most of the second.

short_definition: One of the tiny voids running through brick, stone, concrete or mortar. The network of them is what lets water into a material.
explanation:
A porous material does not just hold water, it moves it, and everything dissolved in the water rides along. The water evaporates at the face and the salts stay behind in the pore and crystallise there.

Porosity is not fixed either. Extra water in a mix leaves a more open pore structure behind when it cures, so a wet batch is a thirstier bed than the one that was designed.
example: Two coping stones come off the same pallet. One dries out overnight and the other is still dark three days later. Same quarry, different porosity.

short_definition: The face of a wall or slab that the water pressure comes from. On a basin holding water in, that is the inside face.
ordinary_meaning: Positive and negative sound like good and bad, or like an assessment of how well something is done. They are not a judgement at all — they simply name which side of the structure the pressure is on, relative to the membrane.
explanation:
Waterproofing belongs on the positive side wherever it can be, because the water pressure then presses the membrane onto the substrate. Defects stay local and the pressure is working with you.

This is why the membrane on a basin goes on the wet face, which is also the face everything else has to be built over.
example: A basin above the water table has its membrane on the inside, under the mortar bed and tile. Every foot of water in it is holding that membrane against the concrete rather than trying to lift it off.

short_definition: How long a mixed two-part resin stays pourable after the two parts are combined. It is a property of the product, and it is not the same number as cure time.
explanation:
Pot life shortens as the temperature rises, and it can shorten a lot. The same product that gave you comfortable working time indoors in the spring will go off noticeably faster in a van in the sun.

Mix only what you can pour inside it. Resin that has started to thicken will not flow into the corners of a cavity, which leaves exactly the voids the pour was supposed to eliminate.
example: You mix a full batch, then spend several minutes repositioning the assembly and re-checking a drawing. By the time you pour, it is noticeably stringy and it bridges over a gap instead of filling it. The pot looks full from the top and has a void underneath.

short_definition: The electrical level of something relative to something else. Two objects at the same potential have no voltage between them, whatever their voltage relative to earth.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily means possibility or promise — somebody with potential.
explanation: Current flows because of a difference. If a pump shorts and leaks into the water, a person bridging two zones that sit at different potentials becomes the path between them. Bond everything together and every zone sits at the same potential, 0 volts relative to each other, and there is no differential left for a person to bridge.
example: Somebody standing in a basin with one hand on a handrail is touching two things at once. Whether that hurts them depends entirely on whether those two things are at the same potential.

short_definition: Filling a junction box with a compound that surrounds and seals every splice inside it, so there is nothing left for water to bridge.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like something you do to a plant — putting it in a pot. The sense here is the container one: the cavity is the pot, and you are filling it. Potted in this trade means embedded in cured resin, not housed in a container.
explanation:
Potting does not hold water back at a boundary the way a gasket does. It works by occupying the volume: there is no void for water to collect in and no air gap for it to travel along. It also supports the joint mechanically and takes the vibration and flex out of a connection that would otherwise work-harden and break.

The rule that catches people is that whatever is in the cavity when you pour stays there — a damp splice, condensation, flux residue, water in the strands. Potting over moisture does not dry it out; it seals it permanently against copper, in the warm.
example: A splice is made up on a cool morning and there is a faint mist of condensation on the metalwork. Pour now and that moisture is sealed against the conductors for the life of the assembly. Warm it, dry it, and pour after lunch.

short_definition: Personal Protective Equipment: the gear worn on the body to protect the person wearing it — eye, hand, foot, hearing, respiratory, flotation and fall protection.
explanation: PPE is the last line in the hierarchy of controls, and that is not a slogan. It protects exactly one person; it works only while it is worn, worn correctly and undamaged; it does nothing to the hazard, which is still there waiting for the next person who is not wearing any; and it fails silently. When the answer to a hazard is 'wear more PPE', the honest question is whether anybody asked the first four.
example: Two techs dilute acid on a deck. One is in a face shield and chemical gloves; the other is holding the jug in a T-shirt. The splash does not care which of them opened it.

short_definition: Parts per million — the unit used for gas concentrations far too small to express as a percentage.
explanation: One part per million is one ten-thousandth of one percent. The unit exists because the gases measured in it do damage at concentrations that would round to zero on a percentage scale, which is also why a figure like 'below 25 ppm' is a meaningful limit rather than a rounding error.
example: A monitor reads 30 ppm carbon monoxide. On a percentage display that is 0.003% and would look like nothing at all, which is precisely why the meter does not use one.

short_definition: How repeatable a measurement is. Accuracy, which is a different thing, is whether it is true.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary speech precise and accurate are the same compliment. In measurement they are two independent properties, and an instrument can have one without the other.
explanation:
An instrument gives you precision for free — it will hand you the same wrong figure every time, to two decimal places. Accuracy comes from the reagent being in date, the sample being representative, the vial being clean and the instrument being calibrated against a standard.

Precision without accuracy is the dangerous combination, because consistency reads as reliability.
example: A meter reports the same pH to two decimals on three consecutive samples, so the crew trusts it. Its calibration drifted in June and it has been confidently wrong ever since.

short_definition: Any closed tank that operates with its contents under pressure. In an equipment room it is the filter housing.
explanation:
Air trapped inside one is a compressed spring. Opening or loosening a clamp band on a vessel with trapped air under pressure can launch the lid, and that has killed and maimed people in this trade.

The sequence never changes: shut down all system pumps and lock them out, isolate the vessel at its inlet and outlet valves, open the air relief, and wait until nothing more comes out of it. Only then does the locking ring come off.
example: A lid gets cracked open on a vessel that was isolated but never bled. The clamp band ends up across the room.

short_definition: A pump is primed when the pump body and the whole suction line are completely full of water, with no air in them. To prime a pump is to get it into that state before it is switched on.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the first coat of paint you put on bare wood, or 'prime' meaning best quality.
explanation:
A centrifugal pump cannot pull air. It moves water by flinging it outward, and air is far too light for that to work, so the moment the suction side is holding air instead of water the pump keeps spinning and stops pumping. Worse, the water passing through a pump is also what cools and lubricates it, so a pump that has lost prime is not sitting there idling — it is wearing itself out.

This is why the priming procedure is about the hose and not about the pump. Get the water in, keep the air out, and the pump does the rest.
example: You are vacuuming a raised basin and stretch the pole to the far corner. The free end of the hose lifts clear of the surface for a second. The pump changes note, the basket half empties, the discharge goes to a splutter. That is prime gone in one second, and the answer is to stop the pump and re-prime, not to carry on and hope it picks up.

short_definition: A solvent applied before the cement that breaks down the glossy outer skin of the PVC and opens the plastic so the cement can fuse it.
explanation:
Primer is not a cleaner and the purple dye is not the point of it — the dye is there so an inspector can see the step was done. What matters is the chemical state it leaves the surface in, and that state does not last.

Sapphire's sequence is socket, then pipe, then socket again, applied aggressively.
example: You prime a bulkhead fitting, get called to hold a ladder for ten minutes, and come back to a purple ring that is dry to the touch. The purple is still there; the prepared surface is not.

short_definition: A non-toxic glycol antifreeze, sold in marine and RV grades, used to stop residual water freezing in places that cannot be drained.
explanation:
It goes into all sub-grade p-traps and perimeter drains at winterizing. Two limits on it: it is only for the places that cannot be fully drained, and it is never a substitute for draining what can be drained — pouring it into a line you did not blow out buys you nothing.

How much a particular trap or drain takes, and any place beyond the traps and perimeter drains that the design accepts cannot be drained, belong to the system designer and the manufacturer's instructions rather than to habit.
example: Two jugs are on the truck and both say antifreeze. One is pink marine grade and one is the green automotive jug from somebody's car. Only one of them is going anywhere near the feature.

short_definition: Confirming with a meter that a circuit has no voltage on it, using a set sequence rather than a single reading.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a figure of speech - the wire is dead, nothing works. Here it is a named test with a pass and a fail, and a circuit is not dead until that test says so.
explanation:
A meter reading zero is not evidence on its own. A flat battery, a blown fuse inside the meter, or a probe that has come off its lead all read exactly zero as well - the same number a genuinely dead circuit gives you.

So the meter is tested on a source you know is live, then on the circuit, then on the known live source again. If the meter still works at the end, the zero in the middle meant something.
example: You kill the lighting circuit at the panel, meter the junction box in the planter, and read zero. Before putting a hand in it you touch the probes back across the receptacle you know is live - and the meter reads nothing there either. The meter's internal fuse had gone. The box you were about to open was never dead.

short_definition: Pounds per Square Inch: the unit almost every pressure gauge in the equipment room reads in.
explanation: Pressure is force per unit of area, which is why the numbers in this module look so lopsided. A blow-out runs at under 15 PSI and clears a whole manifold; freezing water inside a locked circuit exerts up to 114,000 PSI and splits it.
example: A regulator turned up to give "a bit more push" during a blow-out goes from under 15 to well over it in half a turn. The line does not clear any faster, and there is now real stored energy in a plastic pipe.

short_definition: Thin tape wrapped onto a male thread before assembly to help it seal. It is wrapped in the direction the thread screws in.
explanation: The direction is the part people get wrong. Wrapped clockwise - the way the male thread turns going in - making the joint tightens the tape onto the thread. Wrapped the other way, making the joint unwraps it and bunches it into the first few threads, where it does nothing useful and can hold the joint apart.
example: A joint that will not stop weeping comes apart to reveal the tape balled up in a ragged rope at the leading threads instead of lying flat along them.

short_definition: A place partway along a conduit run where the conductors can be reached, so a long run is pulled in stages instead of all at once.
explanation: Bend allowance is counted between pull points, so adding one resets the count. It is also how a pull that would need dangerous tension becomes two pulls that need very little.
example: A hundred-foot run under a plaza has a box at the halfway island. The crew pulls fifty feet, coils the slack into the box, and pulls the second fifty from there.

short_definition: A slippery compound made for wire pulls, applied to the conductors so they slide through a conduit with less tension.
explanation: It has to be listed as compatible with both the insulation and the conduit. Soap, grease and whatever else is in the truck can attack a jacket, and the damage does not show until years later — by which point nobody connects the intermittent circuit to the day of the pull.
example: A long run to a light vault is going stiff at the second bend. The crew stops, works compound onto the conductors at the feed end, and the pull goes smooth again on steady tension.

short_definition: The perforated basket inside a strainer pot or skimmer that collects leaves and grit before they reach the pump.
explanation:
A basket does not fail gradually. It works, and then it fills, and a full basket starves the pump — it is a restriction on the suction side, so it shows up as a rising vacuum reading and a pot that will not stay full. Vacuuming fills baskets faster than anything else you do, because a vacuum moves more debris in ten minutes than the system sees in a week.

At winterizing, the pump basket has a second job: it is where Sapphire stores the drain plugs, because it is the one container the spring crew opens first.
example: You empty both baskets before starting, vacuum for ten minutes, and the suction reading has climbed noticeably. Nothing is wrong with the pump — the basket you emptied is full of a winter's worth of leaf mat off the basin floor.

short_definition: The manufacturer's chart for a pump: Total Dynamic Head up the vertical axis, flow rate across the horizontal, and a line showing what that pump does at each point.
explanation:
Find your measured TDH on the vertical axis, move across to the pump's line, drop straight down, and read the GPM.

Then look at where you landed. A point out at the extreme right or the extreme left means the pump is running outside the window it was designed for, and it pays for that in motor overheating, cavitation pitting on the impeller, and premature bearing failure. None of which stops it moving water in the meantime.
example: A pump plots hard right of its curve because the system has less resistance than the designer assumed. It looks like it is working beautifully, and it will be on its third set of bearings before anyone connects the two things.

short_definition: Blowing fresh outdoor air through a space with a ventilation blower to clear its atmosphere before it is re-tested.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a purge means getting rid of people or things — a political purge, purging files. Here it means flushing a volume of air, and it is a mechanical operation with a duration and a result you have to measure.
explanation: Sapphire's rule: if the monitor alarms, the vault gets purged, not entered. Deploy an industrial explosion-proof blower and purge with fresh outdoor air for a minimum of 15 minutes before re-testing. Fresh outdoor air is part of the instruction, not decoration. And a purge that ran is not a purge that worked — the only thing that says it worked is the meter afterwards.
example: The blower runs for the full fifteen minutes while the crew has lunch. Before anybody puts a boot on the ladder, the monitor goes back down the hole and all four readings are taken again.

short_definition: Polyvinyl chloride. The rigid white or gray plastic most fountain pipe is made from.
explanation: PVC is an amorphous plastic, which matters in two places in this module: it is why solvent welding works at all, and it is why the material fails the way it does under stored energy.
example: The white 3 inch pipe on the rack and the gray Schedule 80 in the vault are both PVC; the colour is not what tells you the pressure rating.

short_definition: In electrical safety language, a defined status: trained and authorised on the specific equipment and hazard in front of you.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a compliment — experienced, capable, good at the job.
explanation:
It is a defined word rather than a description of how competent somebody feels. Being qualified on one kind of equipment does not make you qualified on another, and Module 9 unpacks what the status actually requires.

If it is not you, the half that still applies is the half that keeps you out.
example: Somebody has opened hundreds of control panels and has never been trained on drives. Those are two different authorisations, and the drive enclosure is not theirs to open.

short_definition: Someone trained on the construction and operation of the specific equipment, trained to recognise and avoid its electrical hazards, and authorised to do the work. All three parts.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English calling someone qualified is a compliment about their general competence and experience. In safety and electrical work it is a defined status tied to particular equipment and particular training — so a very experienced technician can be unqualified for one panel and qualified for another.
explanation:
The definition is narrow on purpose. It is not about how good you are; it is about whether somebody has trained and designated you for this equipment and documented it.

The practical consequence is simple: if you have not been trained and designated for the equipment in front of you, that part of the job is not yours to do, and the right move is to stop and go and get the person it belongs to.
example: You have wired dozens of low-voltage fixtures and you are standing in front of a fountain control panel you have never been trained on. Twenty years of good work does not make you the qualified person for that panel this afternoon.

short_definition: A ninety-degree bend in a conduit run. Bends are counted because each one adds friction to a pull.
explanation: Friction from bends multiplies rather than adds, so the tension needed at the pulling end climbs steeply as bends accumulate. The NEC caps the total bend between pull points at the equivalent of four quarter bends — 360 degrees. The answer to a run that needs more is another pull point, not more rope.
example: A run leaves the panel, turns down, turns along the wall, turns again at the corner and turns once more into the vault. That is the 360 degrees spent, and the offset somebody wants to add at the vault means a conduit body goes in first.

short_definition: The clear tube that separates a UV lamp from the water flowing around it, keeping the lamp dry while letting the light through.
explanation:
Calcium scale attaches to it over time as a chalky white layer, and that layer is insulation: it blocks the UV from reaching the water while the lamp goes on looking fine. Sapphire's document makes descaling a monthly job — isolate the chamber, drain it, carefully extract the sleeve, wipe it clean with a scale-dissolving gel or denatured alcohol.

Handle a new lamp with clean latex gloves. Finger oils left on the quartz cook on at operating temperature and crack the bulb prematurely — the lamp that fails early is usually the one somebody installed barehanded.
example: A sleeve comes out chalky white after a summer, on a feature whose test log has read fine all season. The water was on the scaling side at that hot surface the whole time, and the disinfection went with it.

short_definition: Heat arriving as radiation from the sun and from hot surfaces, on top of the air temperature.
explanation: Concrete, pale stone and water all throw it back at you, so a fountain plaza loads a body from above and below at once. And air temperature is not the whole story in the other direction either: a sealed pump room in August is a heat hazard with no weather in it at all.
example: A shaded thermometer on a plaza reads pleasantly. The technician kneeling on white stone in full sun, with the basin reflecting up at him, is not in that measurement.

short_definition: Bringing a pump up to speed or down again gradually over seconds, rather than switching it straight on or straight off.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a sloped surface you drive or wheel something up.
explanation:
Water in a pipe is heavy and moving, and stopping it abruptly sends that momentum into the pipe as a pressure spike. A ramp changes the speed of the column over seconds instead of instantly, so the momentum change never becomes a shock load on every fitting and check valve in the run. The motor and starter get an easier life from it too.

It is not a substitute for the surge control the system was designed with — check valves and air release are there for the power failure nobody ramps.
example: A feature bangs audibly every time the show ends. The drive is set to wind the pump down over several seconds instead of dropping it, and the bang stops.

short_definition: A pipe passing through a wall or floor that has a fire or smoke rating. It is part of a tested assembly, and only a seal listed for that assembly may be used in it.
ordinary_meaning: Rated sounds like a general quality grade. It means tested as a complete assembly and listed by name — the sleeve, the seal and the installation method together, not the parts individually.
explanation:
A penetration through a rated wall or floor is not a plumbing detail. The rating belongs to the whole assembly, so substituting a component that looks equivalent voids it whether or not the substitute is a better product.

If the drawing calls a penetration rated, the model, the sleeve and the installation are all prescribed. That is an engineering and code question — take it to the project manager rather than fitting what is on the truck.
example: A line has to pass through a wall the drawing marks as rated, and the seal in the van is a perfectly good one that is simply not the listed one.

short_definition: The maximum speed marked on an abrasive wheel. It must be at or above the speed of the tool it is fitted to, never below.
explanation: A wheel spun past its rating comes apart, and the pieces leave at the speed of the rim. Related: a wheel rated for grinding is not a cutting wheel, a wheel that has been dropped is suspect whatever it looks like, and every wheel gets run up to speed clear of the work with everybody standing out of its plane.
example: A small wheel from the bottom of a toolbox fits a high-speed die grinder perfectly. The tool's speed is well above what is printed on the wheel, and it fits perfectly right up until it does not.

short_definition: Of a potting compound: one that sets into a thick, gel-like rubber a person can get back through, rather than curing hard and permanent.
explanation: It is what keeps a potted box honest against the accessibility rule — a potted box is still an accessible box. A box filled with something that cannot be cut, or a potted box buried under a coping, is not.
example: Somebody suggests a rigid epoxy because it would be harder and cheaper. It would also mean the whole box, and the cable back to it, is scrap the first time a fixture fails.

short_definition: Adding water to a mix that has already begun to stiffen, to make it workable again. It is prohibited on this work.
ordinary_meaning: Temper is a mood you lose, or what you do to steel or chocolate to change its hardness.
explanation:
Once cement has begun to hydrate, adding water does not restore the mix, it destroys it, permanently, in a way that will not show until the bed or the tile is loaded.

Sapphire writes the prohibition against mortar that has skinned on a wall, and a mud bed that has started to go off is the same act on the same cement. Throw it out and mix again.
example: Half a batch is left at lunch and splashed back to life at one o'clock. It trowels like new material and it is not new material.

short_definition: Tightening the bolts again after an initial settling period, where the manufacturer's instructions call for it.
explanation:
Rubber relaxes slightly after it is first compressed, so a belt that was at the correct torque on the day can be under it a while later. Skipping the second pass produces a slow weep rather than an obvious failure.

It is a step that lives on a calendar, not on a checklist for the day, which is why it gets lost.
example: A vault penetration is sealed on Thursday and the crew is off that job by Monday. Nobody goes back, and eighteen months later there is a stain under it.

short_definition: The chemical in a test kit that reacts with a water sample to produce the colour or the count you read off.
explanation:
Reagents come as liquid drops, tablets or sealed powder pillows. They carry an expiry date, and that date assumes storage in the dark at sane temperatures — not a season on a dashboard.

The characteristic failure is reading low or not developing at all, so the water looks like it needs more of everything. Hold the bottle vertical when counting drops, too: held at an angle it delivers a different drop size, and a drop count is a measurement.
example: Three visits of dosing against the same stubborn reading, and nothing has moved. A fresh bottle from the shop reads the basin completely differently on the first try.

short_definition: Steel bar cast into concrete. Where it sits in the section is set by the structural drawing.
explanation:
Rebar is not distributed evenly through a section like a filler. It is placed on the side that is going to be pulled, and which side that is does not follow from where the water is. A basin wall bends outward under the water behind it, so the tension at the base is on the wet face.
