A slab spanning between supports is pulled along the bottom in the middle and along the top over a support.

Where the bar sits is the design, not a detail of it. A bar in the wrong half of a slab is a bar that is not in the structure.
example: A mat is tied out beautifully and then the crew walks across it to reach the far form. The bars at the top of the slab are now nearer the middle, and the slab has quietly lost the steel it was counting on.

short_definition: A bottled liquid of a known, certified pH, used as the standard a probe is calibrated against.
explanation:
Sapphire's document gives the order: pH 7.0 first, then pH 4.0 or 10.0. Adjust the controller's offset calibration until the screen matches the value printed on the bottle.

Use fresh buffer. An open bottle contaminated by a dirty probe is a standard that is no longer a standard, and it will calibrate the controller to be wrong with great confidence. Note that "buffer" here means the reference liquid — not the alkalinity reserve in the basin.
example: The 7.0 bottle has been in the kit since last season and a probe went straight into it off the flow cell. Everything calibrated against it since has been calibrated to that mistake.

short_definition: The sealed loop of refrigerant inside a chiller. Opening it, charging it or recovering from it is certified work.
explanation: Venting refrigerant is a federal offence with real penalties. The technician's side of the line is the water side, the electrical disconnect and the airflow, and that is a hard line rather than a preference.
example: A chiller is short of capacity. Before anyone says it is low on gas, check whether somebody has stacked pallets against the condenser: it may simply be breathing its own hot exhaust.

short_definition: A cloth or mesh bedded into a liquid membrane at corners and joints, or the equivalent preformed pieces supplied with a sheet system.
explanation:
Fabric gives the coating something to hold itself together with across a line that is going to move or crack. It also holds a consistent thickness over an edge where the material would otherwise be pulled thin.

It is bedded into the wet coating, not laid on top and coated over — a fabric that is sitting dry on a cured coat is a bond breaker rather than reinforcement.
example: You bed fabric along the floor-to-wall joint, work it down until the coating comes through the weave, and there are no white patches and no bubbles left under it. If you can still see dry cloth, it is not in the system yet.

short_definition: A small switch operated by a coil, so that energising the coil from one circuit changes contacts in a different, electrically separate circuit.
explanation: The separation is the point: one low-voltage signal can switch several things, at a different voltage, without the controller ever seeing that voltage. The contacts have a rating, so a relay is selected for what it switches and how often — not for what fits the empty space on the rail.
example: A single 24 V controller output picks up a relay, and the relay's contacts close a 120 V circuit to the deck lighting. The controller never touches 120 V.

short_definition: Injury that builds up from doing the same movement over and over, rather than from a single incident.
explanation: Overhead work, vibration from a hammer drill, kneeling on concrete and hours of the same grip all do it, and there is no moment to point at afterwards. Rotate the task, use a kneeling pad, put the work at a sensible height where you can. Report the ache while it is still an ache — that is the stage at which it is reversible, and the reason people do not is that it does not feel like an injury yet.
example: A technician's wrist has been sore for three weeks after a run of core drilling. There is no incident to report, which is exactly why he has not reported it.

short_definition: A formal written question to the design team about something the documents do not answer, with a written answer that becomes part of the record of the job.
explanation:
An RFI is the mechanism that moves a decision to whoever owns it. A missing dimension, a conflict between a drawing and a specification, a detail that cannot physically be built - all of those are RFIs rather than field decisions.

It is not an admission that you do not know your trade. A guess costs demolition and rework, and afterwards nobody can say who decided.
example: A nozzle sleeve is dimensioned from a wall face that does not exist on any other sheet. Two days of waiting for a written answer is cheaper than one day of breaking out concrete.

short_definition: The tank holding a feature's water where it is not held in the visible basin - often directly below a deck, or below grade.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary use a reservoir is a lake behind a dam, out in the landscape. Here it is a concrete tank you cannot see into, frequently right under the plaza people are standing on.
explanation:
Because nobody can see it, it is the debris problem that is discovered late - it accumulates quietly for years while everything visible looks fine.

It is also almost always a confined space. Inspect it from outside, and treat entry as a formal procedure rather than an awkward climb.
example: A feature that has never had a debris complaint is opened up for unrelated work, and the reservoir floor turns out to be carrying several seasons of grit that had been slowly starving the suction the whole time.

short_definition: Sanitiser still present and measurable in the body of water, rather than used up or left behind in the equipment.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like leftovers — residue, the useless bit left behind after the useful work is done. In water treatment the residual is the useful part, and it is there on purpose.
explanation:
A residual is protection that travels. Something introduced at the far corner of a basin - a bird, a hand, a leaf - meets sanitiser right there, without having to make it back to the equipment room first.

That is why a target is a range held continuously, not a dose thrown in when the water looks off. A basin with no residual is unprotected between the moment something lands in it and the moment that water reaches the equipment.
example: A hotel feature is dosed hard every Monday morning and reads nothing at all by Thursday. Between Thursday and Monday the far end of the basin has no protection in it whatsoever, however good Monday's number looked.

short_definition: Equipment worn over the airway to filter or supply air. A tight-fitting respirator requires a written program, medical clearance, training and fit testing before it is worn.
explanation: It is not equipment you simply put on. Facial hair at the sealing surface defeats it regardless of how well it seems to fit. And a dust mask is not protection against vapour or gas — believing it is has killed people in exactly the rooms we work in, because a mask makes a person feel protected enough to stay where they should be leaving.
example: Somebody puts a paper dust mask on before going into a pump room that smells of chlorine. The mask does nothing about the gas and everything about his willingness to go in.

short_definition: Controller memory that survives a power cycle. Non-retentive memory comes back at zero.
explanation: Which is which decides whether a runtime total, a backwash count or a latched alarm still means anything after a storm took the site down. Worth knowing before you rely on a number.
example: A technician reads a pump runtime figure off a screen to decide whether a service is due. The site lost power twice in the spring, and that counter started again both times.

short_definition: A harness and line attached to a mechanical device outside the space, so somebody can be lifted out without a second person going in.
explanation: Rescue is decided before the entry, not during it — retrieval equipment where its use is feasible, and rescue services that have actually been contacted and are able to respond. Calling for an ambulance at the moment somebody collapses is not a rescue plan. The reason this is set up in advance is the single most important fact in the module: a large share of the people who die in confined spaces went in to help.
example: Before the hatch opens, a tripod goes over it and the entrant clips into the line. Nobody expects to use it, which is exactly the condition under which it gets skipped.

short_definition: An opening where treated water is delivered back into the basin from the equipment.
explanation:
Water at a return is the output of the treatment equipment, not the body of water. Sample there and you are testing the feeder.

A routine sample goes below the surface, roughly elbow depth, well away from returns and chemical feed points, with the circulation running and having run. The surface film has been baked by sun, concentrated by evaporation and covered by whatever blew in.
example: The easiest place to reach on a raised basin is right beside a return, so that is where the sample has always been taken. The log is a record of what the feeder did, not of what the feature holds.

short_definition: A three-phase motor turning the opposite way to the arrow on its housing, usually because two supply leads were swapped when something was reconnected.
explanation:
The reason it earns its own line is that it hides well. A centrifugal pump running backwards still moves some water and still sounds like a pump - it simply does far less work, and nothing about it looks broken.

So it belongs to the 'what changed' question: it only ever appears after somebody has been into the electrics.
example: A feature is at half its usual height the week after a panel upgrade. Every mechanical check comes back clean, and the arrow cast into the pump housing is pointing the other way to the shaft.

short_definition: A wobbly outline drawn around an area of a drawing that has changed, with a numbered triangle beside it tying the change to a row in the sheet's revision table.
ordinary_meaning: Cloud in ordinary English is weather, or online storage. On a drawing it is a scribbled loop around something that moved.
explanation:
The cloud shows what changed and the table says what and when. But the number that actually matters is the revision of the sheet you are holding, checked against the current issued set.

Changes also arrive as addenda and bulletins that never appear as a cloud on anything. If you are working from paper, you are working from a snapshot.
example: Revision 3 clouds the sump detail. The print in the truck is revision 2, which shows the old detail with no cloud on it anywhere and looks entirely authoritative.

short_definition: Red, green, blue and white — the four emitters in a common type of colour-changing fixture, and therefore four DMX channels.
explanation: Worth knowing because it is the usual reason a fixture consumes four channels rather than one, and because the channel order within that block is a property of the fixture rather than a universal convention.
example: A colour looks wrong on one fixture in a row of otherwise identical ones. It is running a different personality, and the channel that should be white is driving something else.

short_definition: An instrument on a tripod that spins a laser beam to project one flat reference plane across the whole work area.
explanation:
It gives you one thing: a plane. Everything else is arithmetic done with a receiver on a rod — plane height minus your reading at each point.

Self-levelling is not the same as correct. One dropped, rattled in a truck or cooked in a hot vehicle still produces a beautifully flat plane, at the wrong angle, and then every point you shoot is wrong by a different amount. Field-check it against something that is not the laser, and re-shoot your reference if the tripod has been standing a while.
example: The laser lives behind the seat of the van and has done for two years. It self-levels every morning without complaint, which is exactly what it would do if it were out of calibration.

short_definition: An inspection carried out while work is still exposed, before it is covered by concrete, backfill or finishes.
explanation:
Bonding, conduit and buried pipe are all invisible after the pour and the backfill. The rough-in inspection is the only opportunity anybody gets to look at them.

Covering work that has not been inspected means uncovering it, at your cost. It is also a hard dependency in the schedule: you cannot pour until the bonding grid has been signed off.
example: A pour is booked for Thursday morning and the bonding inspection has not been called. Moving the concrete truck is annoying; breaking out a slab to show an inspector a wire is not.

short_definition: The electrical standard DMX is carried on: a differential signal on a twisted pair with a defined impedance.
explanation: This is why DMX runs on proper data cable and not on a spare pair in the power conduit. Put the data alongside a drive's output cable and you are asking the pair to carry that drive's noise as though it were signal.
example: A lighting run was pulled into the same conduit as a pump feed because the conduit was there. The show is fine until the pump starts, every time.

short_definition: Sapphire's name for the set of conditions the concrete has to be in before any membrane goes on it.
explanation:
The name is deliberately blunt because the failure it prevents is blunt. A membrane is only ever as good as the surface under it, and the conditions are not a ranked list where you do the important ones — they all have to be true at once.

The reason it needs a name is that almost every item on it is invisible on a grey slab. A surface with form release on it and a surface without look exactly the same.
example: A basin gets coated on a Thursday because the tile crew is booked for Monday. The slab was poured eleven days earlier. The membrane cures, looks perfect, and the concrete underneath goes on shrinking for weeks with a film stretched across it.

short_definition: One line of a ladder program: a row of conditions running left to right, ending in the thing that happens if all of them are satisfied.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a step on a ladder you climb — which is where the name came from, but a rung here is a sentence, not a height.
explanation: Diagnosis on a controller is usually rung-shaped: follow the rung until the chain of true conditions dies, and you have converted it doesn't work into rung fourteen wants the flow switch and that bit is off. At that point it stops being a program problem and becomes a field question with a meter-shaped answer.
example: Online with the controller, four contacts on the rung are highlighted and the fifth is not. The fifth is the flow switch, and the rest of the afternoon is spent at the flow switch.

short_definition: The manufacturer's document for a chemical, listing what is in it, what it reacts with, what protective equipment it needs and what to do if it goes wrong.
explanation:
It is the authority for the product in your hand, and it outranks anything a course can tell you. What a given oxidiser, acid or organic must not be stored or mixed with is on it, and so is the protective equipment you are expected to be wearing.

Before the product goes in, you should know which product it is and have read both the label and this.
example: A splash goes to a technician's forearm. One person starts flushing him at the hose bib and a second goes to the truck for the safety data sheet, so the sheet arrives with the ambulance rather than being looked for after it.

short_definition: The standard document a chemical manufacturer publishes for a product, covering its hazards, handling, storage, protective equipment and what to do after an exposure or a spill.
explanation:
The SDS is the authority for what is actually on the site - not what the last site used and not what a course says. It is where the storage rules live, and those rules are why oxidisers and acids are kept apart.

Oxidisers and acids stored or mixed together is how equipment rooms catch fire. That is not an abstract warning; it usually happens because two products were put on the same shelf by somebody being tidy.
example: A new drum arrives and goes onto the nearest free shelf, which happens to be above the acid. The SDS for both products, read for thirty seconds, would have stopped that.

short_definition: Equipment that senses a blocked suction outlet and either releases the vacuum or shuts the pump down.
explanation: One of the layered answers to entrapment, alongside certified covers, multiple separated outlets and unblockable designs. It is a backstop for when the others have been defeated, not a substitute for any of them.
example: A sheet of plastic blows into the basin during a windy drain-down and lands flat across a grate. The system sees the vacuum spike and drops the pump before anybody is near the water.

short_definition: Throwing dry silica sand onto a coat of waterproofing while it is still wet, so the grains set into the surface and leave it rough.
ordinary_meaning: Broadcast normally means putting something on the radio or television. The older farming sense, scattering seed by hand, is the one the trade kept.
explanation:
A waterproofed shell is smooth, and a smooth membrane repels thinset and mortar. The bed sits on it rather than bonding to it, and under water pressure it delaminates. The embedded sand turns the surface into a mechanical keyway the bed and the stone mortar can grip permanently.

Two things about it are yours even though the membrane belongs to the waterproofing module. Sweep off all the loose, unbonded sand before you lay anything, because sand that never keyed in is a layer of ball bearings between your bed and the wall. And if you meet a membrane with no broadcast on it at all, stop and ask.
example: The wall feels like coarse sandpaper before the tile goes on, and a stiff broom brings a cupful of loose grains off it. Both of those facts matter.

short_definition: A filter that strains water down through a bed of graded sand. Dirt is trapped between the grains and flushed out by reversing the flow.
explanation: A sand bed catches what will not fit between the grains, which is coarser than people assume. Particles finer than that go through it, back into the basin, and settle again — so vacuuming a silt film through a sand filter can cycle the same dirt round the system all afternoon and leave the floor looking much as it did.
example: You vacuum a fine grey film through the filter and the water goes cloudy rather than clear. Nothing is broken; the fines are passing the bed and coming straight back through the wall inlets.

short_definition: The sewer that carries wastewater to treatment. A storm drain is the other one — it carries rainwater, usually untreated, straight to a creek, river or bay.
explanation:
They look identical from a deck and they end in completely different places, which is why the discharge point for treated water is a rule and not a preference. Water you send to waste carries sanitiser, whatever the pH happens to be, and whatever you just killed. In many jurisdictions it may go to the sanitary sewer or a specific named drain and never to a storm drain or a planting bed.

The answer belongs to the site and the local rule. Find it before you open the valve.
example: There is a grate six feet from the basin and a cleanout twenty yards away at the service yard. The near one is convenient and is very likely the storm drain. The site file names which one to use — read it before the first time, not after.

short_definition: Killing or inactivating living organisms in the water, and keeping doing it continuously everywhere in the body of water.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English sanitation means sewers, drains and rubbish collection - the sanitation department. Here it is a chemical process inside a clean body of water.
explanation:
Sanitation is the job that protects people, and it is the one that has nothing to do with how the water looks. It works through a residual - sanitiser present and measurable throughout the basin, not only in the equipment room.

Clear water is a filtration result. Safe water is a sanitation result. They are different measurements of different things and you need both.
example: Two basins at the same site test the same on clarity. One holds its residual all week; the other is fed by a pump that has been airlocked since the last visit and has nothing in it but clean-looking water.

short_definition: The chemical held in the water to kill microorganisms, most often chlorine. The 'free' part of a reading is what is still available to do that work.
explanation:
A sanitiser reading that will not hold has two ordinary explanations before anything exotic: something is consuming it, or something is shielding it. Organic debris consumes it continuously. Accumulated stabiliser reduces how effective the chlorine you are measuring actually is.

So a reading showing sanitiser present and water that still looks wrong is a real and common combination.
example: The water is glass-clear and the handrail at the edge of the splash zone is slimy to the touch. The filter is doing its job, and nothing is doing the other one.

short_definition: The condition Sapphire's document requires the concrete to be in before the membrane goes on: soaked through and damp on the face, with no standing pooling water anywhere.
ordinary_meaning: The word dry is in the name, so it reads as an instruction to dry the slab out. It means close to the opposite — the concrete is saturated, and only the surface is free of standing water. Every instinct from painting and coating work says get the substrate as dry as you can, and here that instinct is wrong.
explanation:
The reason is that a cementitious membrane needs its own mix water to hydrate. A bone-dry slab is a sponge: it pulls that water straight out of the coating before the reaction has finished, and leaves a chalky, under-cured film that looks perfectly acceptable.

Standing water does the opposite damage — it thins and dilutes the material where it has pooled. Damp, no puddles, is the whole target.
example: You soak a basin floor on a hot afternoon, and by the time the mixer is ready the high spots have gone pale and the low spots are holding water. Neither is SSD. Mist the pale areas, squeegee the puddles, and start when the whole floor is one even dark damp.

short_definition: A material holding as much water as it physically can. Every pore in it is full.
explanation:
A material in a wall gets wet and then dries out again. A material in a fountain never dries. Saturation is its normal condition rather than an event it recovers from, and that one difference is why a unit with fifty good years in a garden wall can fail in a single season at a waterline.

It matters most in a freeze. A pore with room left in it can take the expansion; a full one cannot.
example: You pull a limestone offcut out of the basin after a week of test fill and it is noticeably heavier than the identical piece still on the pallet. Same stone, same size. The difference is water.

short_definition: The hard chalky deposit that comes out of over-saturated water and builds up on surfaces, nozzles, heaters and probes. On the LSI it is the positive side of zero.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily scale means weighing scales, a ratio on a drawing, or the size of something. None of those. In water it is the white crust.
explanation:
It insulates, so a scaled heat exchanger makes the heater work harder and eventually fail. It narrows pipework and blocks nozzles, so a display commissioned symmetrical goes lopsided with no mechanical reason anyone can find. It chalks over a UV quartz sleeve and takes the disinfection with it. And it roughens surfaces, which gives algae exactly the porous foothold it wants.

It also gets harder to remove the longer it sits.
example: A heater that has quietly lost output over a season turns out to be a chemistry finding wearing a mechanical costume - the element is coated, and nothing about the heater was ever wrong.

short_definition: The stated ratio between a length drawn on a sheet and the real length it represents. To scale a drawing is to measure a dimension off the paper.
ordinary_meaning: Scale in ordinary English means size or extent, or a weighing device, or climbing something. It is also what a fountain deposits on tile - a completely different trade word.
explanation:
Every drawing has a stated scale and a scale rule will measure it. Do not build from that. Sheets are printed at reduced sizes, photocopied, scanned, reissued as PDFs and printed again on paper that is not the size the office drew them at. By the time a sheet reaches a truck it may be nowhere near scale.

Written dimensions govern, and every set says so somewhere. A scaled measurement is a sanity check - a way of noticing that a written dimension looks wrong - and never a dimension in its own right. A missing dimension is not a puzzle to solve; it is a question to ask.
example: The sheet in the truck was printed on half-size paper for a meeting eighteen months ago. Everything scaled off it is out by a factor of two, and nothing on the page says so.

short_definition: Describes water that is above saturation with calcium carbonate, so it deposits solid mineral on the surfaces it touches.
ordinary_meaning: Scaling in ordinary English means climbing something, or resizing it - and on a drawing, measuring it. Here it is limescale forming.
explanation:
Scale forms on tile and at the waterline where you can see it, and inside heat exchangers, pipe, nozzles and on probes and sensors where you cannot. A little deposit in a nozzle changes the shape of the visible jet; a little on a probe means it quietly reads wrong.

It forms first on the hottest surface in the system, which is usually the one you cannot see and the one whose failure costs most.
example: A feature whose jets have been drifting off-pattern for months turns out to have a hard white ring inside each nozzle bore, and a UV sleeve with the same bloom on it.

short_definition: The loop a controller runs continuously: read every input into memory, solve the whole program against that frozen snapshot, write every output, start again.
explanation: Three consequences catch people. The program never sees an input change mid-scan, so a contact that pulses shorter than one scan can be missed entirely. An output written early is visible to later rungs immediately, because it is only a bit in memory until the end. And order matters: if two rungs write the same coil and disagree, the last one to execute is the one that survives to the output write.
example: A rung looks perfectly correct on screen and the output never comes on. A rung further down the program writes the same coil and wins, every scan, forever.

short_definition: Establishing that whatever hurt the casualty cannot also hurt you, before you go to them.
explanation: It is the same rule as the confined space lesson and the electrical lesson wearing different clothes, and it is the rule that turns one casualty into two. Before you go to somebody, know what dropped them: a live conductor, an atmosphere, a gas, water.
example: A technician sees a colleague on the ground beside a control panel and takes three seconds to work out whether he is still in contact with anything before moving. Those three seconds are the whole discipline.

short_definition: A pipe's wall-thickness class. Schedule 80 has a thicker wall than Schedule 40 in the same nominal size.
ordinary_meaning: A timetable. This module uses the word both ways within a few paragraphs — the crew's schedule is the calendar, Schedule 80 is the pipe.
explanation:
Schedule sets the wall thickness and therefore the pressure rating and the inside diameter. It does not change the outside diameter: Schedule 40 and Schedule 80 of the same nominal size measure the same across the outside.

That is exactly why it cannot be used to size a penetration seal, and why heavier pipe does not mean a different seal model.
example: Someone measures the OD of a 4 inch Schedule 40 sample in the shop and orders the seal from it, then installs against Schedule 80 in the field. The OD is the same, so this one is fine — which is precisely the coincidence that teaches the wrong lesson next time.

short_definition: A scissor-action clamp that fits through a lock point and takes several padlocks at once. It cannot be opened until every single padlock has been removed.
explanation: It is what lets more than one person work behind the same isolation safely. Each person fits their own lock and takes their own lock off when they are finished, so the isolation can only come off after the last of them has personally cleared it. Nobody else can release your lock for you.
example: Three technicians work on the same pump panel and three padlocks hang off one hasp. The first two finish and take theirs off; the hasp stays shut because the third is still inside the vault.

short_definition: The defined set of work the company has agreed to do on a job. Anything outside it is a change, agreed in writing by somebody with the authority to agree it.
ordinary_meaning: Scope in ordinary English means range or room to manoeuvre - scope for improvement - or a telescope or rifle sight.
explanation:
Scope is one of five things a technician on site does not commit to. The others are price, dates, warranty coverage, and cause or liability.

They slip out as kindness. We will take care of that for you lands as a free scope change; that should be under warranty lands as a promise. The safe shape of the answer is the same every time: here is what I am doing today, I will pass that request on, and somebody will come back to you on it.
example: A client walks over while you are testing and asks if you could just clear the blocked drain at the other end of the terrace while you have the tools out. It is ten minutes of work and it is not today's job - it gets written down and passed on.

short_definition: To strike a bed off to a set of heights by running a straightedge over rails or points. The bed you produce that way is also called a screed.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, a screed is a long, tedious piece of writing that nobody asked for.
explanation:
The sequence is always the same: establish the finished heights you have to hit, set screed points or rails to those heights, fill between them, compact, strike off the rails with a straightedge, then compact and refloat the surface you just cut.

Then check it as a plane, not as two heights. A bed can be exactly right at the perimeter and exactly right at the drain and still have a belly in the middle.
example: Two rails, a straightedge and forty minutes give a surface that is right at both ends. A straightedge laid diagonally across it is what tells you whether it is right in between.

short_definition: A contact of an output's own bit placed in parallel with a momentary start condition, so the rung stays true after the button is released.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like sealing something up — waterproofing or closing it off.
explanation:
Press start, the rung goes true, the coil comes on — and now its own contact holds the rung true. A stop condition in series breaks the seal and it drops out.

That is how every start/stop station in the world works, in relays and in software, and you will recognise it on sight once you have seen it once.
example: A pushbutton starts a feature and it keeps running after your finger leaves the button. Nothing is latching it externally; the rung is holding itself true.

short_definition: A flexible material gunned into a joint to close it while still letting it move. Not the same thing as a sealer.
explanation:
A sealer soaks into a face to slow water going into a material. A sealant fills a gap between two materials and stays flexible. One letter apart, completely different products, and asking for the wrong one at the counter gets you the wrong one.

On this work the sealant for a movement joint is an approved underwater-grade polyurethane or silicone.
example: A tech is sent for sealant for a movement joint and comes back with a stone sealer, because both tins say seal on the front.

short_definition: A liquid applied to a stone or masonry face to slow how much water goes into it.
explanation:
On a fountain, water is also arriving from behind, through the bed, the substrate and the joints. Anything that slows water going in slows it coming out just as well, so a film-forming sealer over a stone that is wet from the back traps the moisture under the film. You get clouding, blushing, peeling in patches, salts crystallising underneath, and a freeze working on a layer of trapped water.

Most sealers are not approved for submerged service, and the only proof is the manufacturer's written statement. Impregnators and colour enhancers often darken stone permanently.
example: A colour enhancer is rolled onto a travertine surround to make it pop. Six weeks later it is blotchy where the stone was still damp from behind, and the darkening does not come back off.

short_definition: A tray, tub or liner placed under a chemical container so that if it leaks, the liquid is caught rather than running loose.
explanation: The container is the primary containment; the tray is the backup for when it fails. On a vehicle it matters twice over, because a leak in a closed load space gives the vapour nowhere to go and you will not find out until you open the doors.
example: A jug of acid rides in a plastic tub strapped to the deck. When the cap works loose on a rough site road, what comes out stays in the tub instead of running down to where the chlorine products are.

short_definition: A drawing of what you would see if the thing were sliced straight through along a marked line.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English a section is just a part of something - a section of a report, the brass section.
explanation:
Sections exist because a plan cannot show depth. On a fountain the section is where the real construction lives: the basin build-up, the waterproofing layers, the sump, the depth of everything.

The section mark on the plan is a cross-reference. It names the sheet the cut is drawn on, and the arrow shows which way you are looking. Read a section from the wrong side and everything on it is mirrored.
example: The section through the basin wall is the only sheet in the whole set that shows the waterproofing turning up behind the coping - and whether it goes behind it or stops under it is the difference between a dry wall and a stained one.

short_definition: A threaded or moving part locked solid so it will not turn. It names the state, not the cause.
ordinary_meaning: Nothing to do with grabbing, confiscating or taking hold of something. And it carries no information about why - scale, corrosion, galling and over-tightening all present as seized, and each one needs a different tool.
explanation:
That is the whole reason the word is worth being careful with. Working out which cause you have is what picks the approach: a scale bond gives way to heat and patience, galling never gives way to anything, and a cross-threaded plastic hub is already destroyed and is coming out in pieces.

Three different jobs, one identical symptom.
example: Two fittings on the same manifold are both described as seized on the ticket. One comes free after penetrant and a back-up wrench; the other is still there at the end of the day, because it was galled the day it went in.

short_definition: The written document that says what a feature is supposed to do — which equipment runs when, on what conditions, and what happens on a fault.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a generic phrase for the order things happen in, rather than a specific document that exists on the job and can be opened.
explanation:
It is the thing the controller's program is measured against. Setpoints, run times and interlock behaviour belong to it and to the commissioning record, not to whoever is at the keyboard.

If the sequence and the program disagree, you have found something worth raising rather than something to quietly reconcile.
example: A technician is asked why the wind interlock drops the feature at one setting here and a different one at the sister site. The answer is in each site's sequence, and neither number is a preference.

short_definition: A product that binds calcium and metal ions so the water can carry more of them without depositing them.
ordinary_meaning: The word sounds like it removes or takes something away — sequestering it. It removes nothing; it holds things in solution that would otherwise fall out.
explanation:
Two honest limits. It suppresses deposition; it does not remove scale that is already there — nothing in a bottle un-deposits a scaled heat exchanger. And it is consumed: chlorine and UV break it down, so it is a repeating program rather than a one-time dose.

When it runs out, everything it was holding can come out at once. On a feature carrying iron or copper that means staining the whole basin in a single episode.
example: A feature on a sequestrant program goes three months without a dose over a quiet winter. It comes back in spring with a rust-coloured stain right around the waterline that was not there in November.

short_definition: A number on a motor's data plate stating how much above its rated power it is built to deliver continuously without damage.
ordinary_meaning: Nothing to do with servicing, a service visit, or a maintenance schedule. It is a motor rating - a multiplier printed on the plate.
explanation: It matters when a measured current is compared with the plate. A motor running into its service factor is not necessarily faulty, but it has no margin left, and margin is what absorbs a hot afternoon or a slightly dirty impeller.
example: A measured draw that sits above the plate's full-load figure looks alarming until somebody reads the line underneath it - and still means the motor is working with nothing left in hand on the hottest day of the year.

short_definition: One of the two waiting periods printed on a solvent cement can, and the shorter of the two.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like the time taken to set the joint in place, or the time you have set aside for the job. It is a property of the chemistry, not of your schedule.
explanation:
Set time answers one question only: how long before the joint can be handled and moved without disturbing it. It says nothing about what the joint can withstand.

Set and cure are two different numbers on the same can answering two different questions, and reading the wrong one is the commonest way a good joint is ruined by the person who made it.
example: A crew moves a solvent-welded rack across the yard shortly after assembly, which set time allows for, and then puts water in it the same afternoon, which it does not.

short_definition: The value a controller is aiming at or acting on — the level that trips a cutoff, the wind speed that drops a feature, the chemical target it holds.
explanation:
Setpoints belong to the sequence of operations, the commissioning record and the manufacturer's instructions for that site. They are not a technician's dial.

Moving one because a sensor keeps tripping is not a repair; it is switching off the thing that was telling you something.
example: A freeze interlock has started shutting a feature down more often than last winter. Raising the setpoint would make the calls stop; finding out why the basin is colder is the actual job.

short_definition: The layer of clean sand or pea gravel placed over the top and sides of a buried pipe, between the pipe and the native backfill.
ordinary_meaning: Blocking sunlight, or pencil shading. It has nothing to do with sun — the pipe is in a trench.
explanation:
Sapphire's figure is a further 6 inches over the top and sides, and where it sits in the sequence is as much the point as the depth.

It is doing its work later rather than now. When the heavy native dirt goes back and gets compacted, the shading is what stands between the compactor's energy and whatever sharp stone happens to be in that spoil.
example: Native fill goes straight onto bare pipe on a Friday because the sand ran out. The compactor pass that afternoon drives a piece of broken brick into the crown of a 2 inch line, and it holds for a year.

short_definition: The seal where the motor shaft enters the pump body, keeping water in and air out while the shaft turns.
explanation: It is a wearing part sitting exactly on the boundary between the suction side and the outside world, which puts it on both lists: the small drip at the back of a pump, and the air source on a system that keeps losing prime with nothing on the floor.
example: A pump that has been drawing air for a fortnight shows a faint rusty halo on the mounting pad below the shaft - the only outward sign, and only visible once the pump is switched off and the drip is not being flung off the coupling.

short_definition: A waterproofing membrane that arrives as a factory-made sheet at a controlled thickness, rolled out and lapped rather than brushed on.
explanation:
A sheet cannot be applied thin, because the factory already decided the thickness. In exchange, every overlap, corner and penetration is a seam you make on site — and the seam is the part that leaks.

Neither type is more waterproof than the other. They move the risk from one place to another: liquid puts it in thickness, sheet puts it in seams.
example: A sheet system goes down over a basin floor in an afternoon with no gauge readings needed. The following week the leak is at one inside corner, where a preformed corner piece was skipped and the installer folded the sheet by hand instead.

short_definition: The structure that holds the water - the concrete, the liner and the waterproofing forming the basin itself, as opposed to the pipework inside it.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a thin outer casing, something you crack or peel. Here it is the whole structural vessel, and a leak through it is the expensive kind - the one that ends with a deck being opened.
explanation: The reason to separate a shell leak from anything else is that it behaves differently. Water leaves through the shell whenever there is water standing against it, running or not, weather or no weather - which is precisely what the second run of a bucket test, with the feature off and the basin still, is testing for.
example: Two bucket tests later, the basin still loses water with the pump idle and the surface flat. Nothing is running, nothing is being thrown anywhere, and the loss is the same. That is the shell, and that is a conversation with the project manager rather than a repair on this visit.

short_definition: A deliberately heavy dose of oxidiser whose purpose is to destroy what is already in the water, not to top the sanitiser up.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like an electric shock, or a sudden jolt for its own sake. Here it names a calculated dose with a chemical target, and the word says nothing about how much.
explanation:
Raising the free chlorine number is the means, not the goal. The goal is breakpoint: destroying the combined chlorine and the organic load that keeps making it.

Which is why the amount is calculated from a fresh combined reading rather than judged by eye, and why the product is pre-dissolved and broadcast at night — sunlight breaks unstabilised chlorine down fast, so a daytime shock spends a share of the dose on the sky.
example: A feature goes in on Monday, gets "a good dose" of granular product tipped in from a bucket at noon, and by Wednesday smells worse than it did before.

short_definition: A small clear window in the waste line that lets you watch how dirty the backwash water is.
explanation:
The whole backwash is timed off it rather than off a clock. It runs dark and dirty as the reversed flow lifts trapped organic matter out of the bed, and the cycle ends when it runs crystal clear, usually in two to three minutes.

Without it you are guessing, and guessing long wastes treated water you have paid to condition.
example: Two identical filters on one site. One clears in just over two minutes, the other has always taken closer to three. The sight glass says when each is done; the clock does not.

short_definition: A silicone-based grease used on threads, O-rings and gaskets in wet plumbing, where petroleum grease would swell and destroy the rubber.
explanation: At spring start-up the winter drain plugs get their threads coated with it before they are re-torqued securely back into their equipment blocks. It does two things: it seals the thread, and it means the plug comes out again next November without galling or stripping the housing — which is usually plastic and far softer than the plug.
example: A plug that went back dry two seasons ago now will not move with a bar on it. The plug is fine and the housing it is threaded into is the expensive part.

short_definition: Very fine settled solids — particles small enough to hang in the water for a long time once they are disturbed, and small enough to pass through some filters.
explanation: Silt behaves differently from leaves and grit and needs a different plan. It settles into a film rather than a pile, it relaunches into the water column at the slightest movement, and it is small enough either to pass straight through a sand bed and come back to the basin, or to blind a cartridge outright. Either way, sending it to the filter does not get it out of the system.
example: A basin floor a week after an algae treatment looks grey and even, and a footstep raises a cloud you can watch drift. That grey film is the reason the job goes to waste or into a silt bag rather than through the filter.

short_definition: A recessed fitting at the water line that draws surface water and floating debris off the top of the basin into the suction side of the system.
explanation: It works by taking water from the surface, which means it stops working — and starts swallowing air — as soon as the level drops to its mouth. Anything that lowers the water while you are working, vacuuming to waste above all, can starve a skimmer and lose the pump's prime for a reason that has nothing to do with the pump.
example: Every leaf on a basin ends up piled against the east wall on a windy afternoon, and both skimmers are set into the west wall. Nobody specified it wrongly on purpose; the prevailing wind was not the one blowing on the day of the site visit.

short_definition: The opening of a skimmer at the water surface. The water level has to sit within it for the skimmer to draw at all.
ordinary_meaning: A throat is a part of a person. On a skimmer it is the mouth of the fitting, and 'the level is below the throat' means the water has fallen too far for the skimmer to pull anything in - not that something is blocked.
explanation: Below the throat, the skimmer starts taking air instead of water, and a pump drawing through it starts losing prime. So a basin that has been quietly losing water all week arrives at a no-flow call on its own, with nothing broken anywhere.
example: A Monday morning no-flow call on a feature that ran perfectly on Friday. Nothing is blocked, nothing is faulty; the level is an inch low and the skimmer has spent the night sipping air.

short_definition: Spread mortar losing its wet sheen as the surface starts to set. It dulls and it stops transferring to a finger touched to a ridge.
ordinary_meaning: A skin is the outside of a person or an animal, and skinning is taking one off.
explanation:
Mortar starts losing its ability to bond the moment it is spread, and when it skins it is finished, whatever the clock says.

A tile set into skinned mortar still sticks. It feels solid, it sounds solid and it survives grouting, because it is genuinely bonded to a skin rather than into the body of the mortar. Sapphire's instruction is to scrape it off, down to the sand-broadcasted base, and apply fresh material. Never re-temper it with water, and pressing harder does not fix it.
example: The wall was combed out ten minutes ahead to save time. The last three tiles go on feeling exactly like the first three, and nothing about them is the same.

short_definition: A short length of larger pipe cast through a wall or slab so that a pipe can pass through it later without anyone drilling the structure.
ordinary_meaning: The arm of a shirt. The shape is the only connection.
explanation:
A sleeve is not a seal. It leaves an annular gap between itself and whatever runs through it, and that gap is an open route through the wall until somebody seals it deliberately.

It also has to be detailed into the membrane, because the membrane has to wrap the sleeve rather than stop at it.
example: A conduit runs through a cast-in sleeve in a basin wall with a finger-width gap all round it. Nothing about that looks wrong on a walk-through, and it is a hole straight through the wall until it is sealed and the membrane is carried onto it.

short_definition: How far a wet mix sags under its own weight. Zero slump means a mix dry enough to hold whatever shape it is compacted into.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, to slump is to slouch in a chair, and a slump is a downturn in business.
explanation:
The commonest single error on a bed is adding water to make it easier to trowel. A wet mix slumps, will not hold the plane you screeded, shrinks as it dries and cures weak. The mix being unpleasantly dry is the point of it.

The penalty is invisible on the day: extra water destroys the compressive strength of the cured product and dramatically increases its porosity, which is a bed weaker and thirstier than the one that was designed, on an assembly that is going to live under water.
example: A batch is improved with half a bucket of water so it trowels nicely. It screeds beautifully and cures into something you can dig out with a screwdriver.

short_definition: A nozzle with a plain tapered bore that throws a clear, solid-looking jet rather than an aerated white one.
explanation:
A smooth-bore jet is meant to hold together in the air as a single clean arc. Too much pressure and it breaks up early into spray instead of arriving where it was aimed; too little and it dribbles and loses height.

Either way the nozzle is fine and the pressure is the finding.
example: An arc that used to land neatly in the receiving basin now breaks into mist halfway across and wets the walkway. Nothing was done to the nozzle - a valve on the return leg was closed part-way during a repair and never reopened.

short_definition: The cup on a fitting that the pipe slides into. It is slightly tapered, narrowing toward the bottom.
ordinary_meaning: A wall outlet you plug something into, or the socket on a wrench.
explanation:
The taper is why a dry fit stops partway, and it is also why a freshly cemented joint tries to push itself back out — the pipe is being squeezed by a cone.

You cannot see inside a socket once the joint is made. Everything that goes wrong in there goes wrong invisibly.
example: You let go of a 4 inch coupling after a couple of seconds and turn to the next one. It looks seated. It has quietly walked a half inch back out of the socket while your back was turned.

short_definition: The underside of a slab, beam or overhang — the surface you see when you stand beneath it and look up.
explanation:
On a raised or podium basin the soffit is where a leak shows itself first, because water that gets through the floor has to come out somewhere and gravity picks the place.

Staining, efflorescence or a damp patch on a soffit is a test result, even when the water level upstairs has not moved enough to measure.
example: The level in a rooftop basin looks stable through a flood test. The parking level below it has a dark patch on the ceiling about three feet across that was not there on Monday. The test failed; the tape just could not see it.

short_definition: A valve opened and closed by an electric coil. The controller energises the coil; the coil moves the valve.
explanation: It is the muscle at the water end. The coil is the part that fails: a few tens of ohms of fine copper wire living in a wet vault. It has two ways to die, and they present completely differently — melted windings behave as a near short across a 24 VDC output and take the controller's circuit fuse with them, so one drowned coil can look like a controller that has stopped doing anything at all. A snapped winding just goes open, and nothing happens and nothing else is damaged.
example: Every effect on a manifold stops at once, and the controller looks dead. One valve in the vault has flooded, its coil has gone to near zero ohms, and the fuse it took with it is the reason the other five are silent.

short_definition: The solvent product applied to a pipe and fitting to make a solvent weld. Commercial fountain work uses heavy-bodied gray cement.
ordinary_meaning: The gray powder that goes into concrete. It has nothing to do with that, and it is not an adhesive either.
explanation:
Heavy-bodied gray cement is formulated for Schedule 80 and high-pressure systems. It is not a filler — it cannot bridge a gap, because there is nothing on the far side of a gap for the plastic to fuse into.

PVC, CPVC and ABS take different cements and they are not interchangeable. Every can also carries a maximum pipe size, and there are separate formulations for wet and for cold conditions.
example: The only can on the truck is a small-diameter product and the joint in front of you is 4 inch. That is a stop-and-ask, not a judgement call — the size limit is printed on the can for a reason.

short_definition: Joining plastic pipe by softening both mating surfaces with cement so they fuse into a single piece, rather than by threading or clamping.
explanation: It appears in this module as an atmosphere hazard rather than a piping technique. The vapour is heavier than air, so it settles into the bottom of a vault or a pit and stays there — which means gluing a joint changes the air in a space that tested clean an hour earlier, and is one reason the atmosphere is monitored during an entry rather than only before it.
example: A technician glues three joints at the bottom of a vault with the hatch open above him and no ventilation running. The meter on his belt is the only thing in the vault that notices.

short_definition: Joining two pieces of plastic pipe by chemically softening both surfaces so they flow together and set as one piece.
explanation:
It is a weld, not a glue. Nothing is stuck to anything; the solvent dissolves the surface of the pipe and the surface of the fitting and the two plastics mix. When the solvent leaves, what is left is a single piece of PVC.

Every rule in the procedure comes from that one fact. The surfaces have to touch, both surfaces have to be wetted, both have to be clean and dry, and the solvent has to be given time to leave.
example: A new tech cements one side only, reasoning that the cement will squeeze around anyway. The pipe and the fitting never fuse on the dry side, and the joint holds until the first pump start puts a pressure spike through it.

short_definition: The moulded tabs on top of a pedestal that hold the pavers apart, setting a consistent open joint between them without anyone measuring.
explanation:
The open joint is what lets the deck drain straight through to the sloped sub-slab, and the tabs make it uniform. Sapphire's typical gap is 1/8 to 3/16 inch.

Whether that width is acceptable underfoot on a particular deck is an accessibility question with a code answer behind it, not something the tabs decide for you.
example: Four pavers meet over one pedestal and the tabs hold all four apart at the same gap. A setter working by eye gets four different gaps and a deck that looks handmade from ten feet away.

short_definition: A flake or a crater where the face of a material has come away.
explanation:
Freeze-thaw does it, salt crystallising inside a pore does it, and a rusting reinforcing bar does it. All three are pressure generated inside the material, which is why the face comes off in sheets and craters rather than wearing down evenly.

So spalling is a clue about what is happening behind the surface, not a finish problem to patch.
example: A strip of basin wall sheds palm-sized flakes along one horizontal line, and the same line has a faint orange stain above it.

short_definition: The written document that says what things are made of, which standards they must meet, which products are acceptable and how the work is to be executed.
explanation:
Drawings and specifications are two different documents doing two different jobs. The drawings show geometry - arrangement, location, size, how it goes together. The specification says what it is. A drawing may show a pump; the specification says which pump.

They disagree more often than anyone would like, and when they do there is an order of precedence written into the contract documents. That is not resolved on site by whoever is holding the wrench.
example: The drawing shows a stainless grate over the sump. The specification names a grade of stainless and a fixing method, and the grate that turned up on the pallet is neither.

short_definition: Eye protection that seals against the face, so liquid cannot get in from below or the side.
explanation: Impact and splash are different protections. Safety glasses with side shields stop a flying fragment and do nothing about a liquid arriving from underneath — which is the direction a splash comes from when you are pouring, or when something is above you. The sealing is the whole point of goggles.
example: A technician wearing safety glasses tips a jug and catches a drop on the cheekbone that runs straight up behind the lens. The glasses did exactly what glasses do.

short_definition: The controller panel that runs a feature's program — which zones fire, in what order and for how long, plus lighting scenes and any sensor inputs. Its sequence triggers are the events that start each step.
explanation:
At start-up the whole program is run, not spot-checked: every zone, every effect, the lighting scenes, the autofill through a cycle, the wind sensor if there is one, with you standing there. A program that was correct in October can have been edited, power-cycled or partially lost, and the faults that hide in a sequence are the ones that only appear at step nine.

The zones, timings and scenes themselves belong to the design and the program for that feature, not to a general rule.
example: A feature has gone completely dead. Putting the leads across an output relay shows no 24 V appearing when the schedule says it should, which puts the fault upstream in the controller rather than out in the vault.

short_definition: The band of a feature that is alternately wet and dry: the level the water sits at, and anywhere spray lands.
explanation:
The worst place on a whole feature is not the bottom of the basin, which at least stays at one condition. It is here. Wet, dry, wet, dry, freeze, thaw, and evaporating all day.

Evaporation is the part people miss. Water leaves and salts do not, so this band concentrates whatever the water is carrying.
example: The tile a hand's width above the water is chalky and edged with white. The tile two feet under it, in the same batch and the same bed, looks new.

short_definition: Water thrown clear of the basin by the display, or carried out of it by wind, that lands on the deck instead of returning.
explanation: It is one of the three ways water leaves a basin, and it is the one that moves with the weather and the spray height. That is exactly what separates it from a leak: it changes week to week, and it leaves evidence outside the basin rather than none at all.
example: A feature loses noticeably more water in the week the wind turns, and the pavers downwind of it carry a chalky ring that was not there in still weather.

short_definition: A joint where two or more conductors are connected together.
explanation: A splice is the most likely place on a circuit for it to fail, which is why splices live in boxes, why those boxes have to stay accessible, and why underwater ones get potted.
example: A circuit reads continuous on the buzzer but the light is dim under load. The splice in the vault has corroded down to a few strands, which beeps happily and drops voltage the moment current flows.

short_definition: A heavy clamp that joins two conductors mechanically by squeezing them between the two halves of a slotted bolt.
explanation: On Sapphire work every mechanical structural connection beneath the water line is made with a solid copper or bronze split-bolt. Steel fasteners are forbidden outright below the water line, because they rust out and sever the loop — and a severed bonding loop has no symptom at all.
example: A stainless clamp in the van would hold that joint perfectly well today. It is still the wrong material, because nothing will tell anybody the day it finally fails.

short_definition: The material dug out of a trench, piled beside it and usually put back as the upper backfill.
ordinary_meaning: To ruin something, or to indulge a child. Here it is just the dirt that came out of the hole.
explanation:
Spoil contains whatever the ground contained — stones, brick, roots, old concrete. That is fine above the shading and not fine against the pipe.

Pipe is also never set on loose spoil to hold grade. Loose material settles under the first compactor pass and takes your pitch with it.
example: A pipe is propped to grade on small heaps of spoil between the bedding, because it was quicker than dressing the bed. The laser says it is perfect right up until the plate compactor runs.

short_definition: Setting a tile or a stone on separate dabs of mortar instead of a full bed.
explanation:
Five dabs will hold a tile on a dry wall and it is quick. Submerged it fails every way at once. It builds a continuous void between the dabs that fills with water and connects the whole wall behind the finish, so a leak at one tile tracks sideways to somewhere else entirely. It hands freeze-thaw a reservoir immediately behind a rigid finish, leaves the tile edges and corners unsupported so a point load cracks the tile, and gives salts a chamber to concentrate in.

The same objection applies to the variations: setting on a mound and tapping it down, bedding only the perimeter, and worst of all filling the void afterwards by working grout in from the front.
example: One cracked tile in a cold-climate basin comes off and there is a connected air space behind half the panel.

short_definition: Chlorine products that carry cyanuric acid with them, so every dose adds stabiliser as well as sanitiser. Dichlor and trichlor are the two.
explanation:
A feature dosed on these accumulates stabiliser as a side effect of ordinary sanitising, and nobody ever decides it should. Cyanuric acid does not evaporate, does not burn off and is not consumed — practically, it leaves only with the water.

They are also acidic, so they pull pH down, where calcium hypochlorite and liquid sodium hypochlorite are alkaline and push it up. And trichlor combined with calcium hypochlorite in a bucket, a feeder or on a damp scoop can ignite.
example: Nobody at the site has added stabiliser in two years, and the stabiliser reading has doubled. Every tablet that went into the feeder brought some with it.

short_definition: Steel alloyed with enough chromium, conventionally at least about 10.5 per cent, that a very thin oxide film forms on the surface and protects it.
explanation:
The name describes a mechanism, not a guarantee. The film is the entire corrosion resistance, and the film has two well-known ways of being defeated in treated water.

The 300-series is the austenitic family and it is what most fountain hardware is made of. It is tough, ductile, non-magnetic and soft enough at the surface that contamination embeds in it easily.
example: A brand new stainless nozzle body develops a weeping pinhole in its second season, and the metal around it is still mirror-bright.

short_definition: Tightening a ring of bolts by jumping to the one opposite each time rather than working round in order.
explanation:
Exactly like the lug nuts on a truck wheel. Going round in sequence pulls one side up tight before the other side has moved, and the belt ends up loaded unevenly no matter what the final readings say.

You are finished when the rubber links visibly bulge uniformly all the way round, checked against the manufacturer's torque rating.
example: A seal tightened bolt by bolt around the ring bulges hard at the twelve o'clock position and barely at all at six, and it was never going to end anywhere else.

short_definition: The channel number a fixture is set to listen from. It reads that channel and as many consecutive ones as it needs.
explanation:
Two fixtures set to the same start address do exactly the same thing forever, perfectly. They are not faulty; they were told to.

A partial overlap is nastier — if one fixture starts on a channel inside another's block, only some channels are shared, so one light does something odd on one axis and behaves normally on the rest. That reads as an intermittent fault and it is arithmetic.
example: A fixture is replaced and set to the number written on the old one's label, which was wrong. Now it moves in colour with a light at the other end of the basin and nobody can see why.

short_definition: A component on a single-phase motor that provides the extra push needed to get the motor turning from rest.
explanation:
A failing one gives a characteristic picture: the motor hums, struggles to get away, may start if the shaft is nudged, and heats up doing it. It is on the list of reasons a motor overheats and drops out.

Capacitors hold a charge after the supply is removed, which is one more reason this is work with a procedure attached.
example: A pump that started fine all spring now sits humming for a second or two before it gets away, and cuts out on a hot afternoon. Nothing in the water has anything to do with it.

short_definition: A state-run occupational safety programme approved to operate in place of federal OSHA, with rules that can be stricter than the federal ones.
explanation: It is why 'the OSHA rule is X' can be incomplete. A state plan can add requirements federal OSHA does not have — heat illness rules are a common example — and where it is stricter, it is what applies to the work.
example: A crew that works across a state line finds the requirements for a task are not identical on the two sides of it. Both are OSHA; one is a state plan with more in it.

short_definition: Energy still held in a system after the power is disconnected — water standing above the equipment, pressure, springs, or charge in a capacitor.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like electricity in a battery. On a water feature most of the stored energy is not electrical at all — the largest source is usually water sitting somewhere above you.
explanation: The disconnect handles electricity arriving. It does nothing about what is already in the system: water head and gravity drain-back that will come back through whatever you open, air pressure in a bladder tank or a pneumatic actuator, chemical under pressure downstream of an injector, springs in check valves and actuators, and capacitors — including the DC bus in a VFD, which stays charged after the disconnect is open. Stored energy is released or restrained before work starts.
example: A technician opens a union on a discharge line with the pump locked out and takes the contents of the header and the basin above it across his chest. Nothing electrical was involved at any point.

short_definition: A length of uninterrupted straight pipe immediately before a pump inlet or a fitting, specified as a multiple of the pipe's own diameter.
explanation:
It is written in diameters rather than inches so it scales with the pipe: a 4-inch line needs more of it than a 2-inch line. Sapphire's requirement into a pump inlet is at least five times the pipe diameter.

What it buys is an even, laminar delivery into the eye of the impeller. It is also the first thing sacrificed when an equipment pad turns out to be smaller than the drawing.
example: Two identical pumps on one site. One has a sweep and then a length of straight pipe into the inlet; the other has an elbow bolted to the port. Only one of them makes its numbers, and nobody can hear the difference.

short_definition: A thread of constant diameter that seals on a gasket or an O-ring face rather than on the threads themselves.
explanation:
The distinction is practical rather than academic. If a straight-thread joint weeps, more torque will never fix it - the sealing face or the O-ring is the problem, and more force damages both.

Treating one like a tapered thread and winding it up is how an O-ring groove gets crushed.
example: A union under a filter weeps a slow drip and gets tightened a little more on each visit. It is still weeping in the autumn, and now the O-ring is flat and the face is marked.

short_definition: An arrangement that makes any pull on a cable act against the gland body or a clamp, rather than against the seal or the terminations inside.
explanation:
Without it, every tug on a cable — a foot, a pressure washer, a maintenance lift — drags the jacket a little further through the seal. Each movement is small and none of them is the one that causes the failure.

It protects two things at once: the seal at the entry, and the conductor terminations inside that would otherwise take the load.
example: A light cable gets stood on during a seasonal clean-out. With the gland properly gripping the jacket, the pull stops at the enclosure body. Without it, the jacket moves a few millimetres through the seal and stays there.

short_definition: A removable basket on the suction line that catches debris before it reaches the pump.
explanation:
The strainer protects the pump from leaves, gravel and anything else that gets past the drain. It is the cheapest part on the loop and the one most often neglected.

A clogged strainer does not simply slow the water down. It starves the pump on its suction side, which is exactly where pumps get damaged. Symptoms show up everywhere else first - low nozzle heights, poor filtration, a pump that sounds wrong.
example: A feature under a row of oaks in October loses half its jet height in a week. The strainer basket comes out packed solid with leaf litter, and the display comes straight back the moment it goes back in clean.

short_definition: The basket housing on the suction side of a pump, usually with a clear lid, that catches debris before it can reach the impeller.
explanation:
It is also the best window into the system you have without opening anything: you can see whether the pot is full of water or carrying air, and you can see what the site is delivering.

A missing, cracked or badly seated basket is a fault in its own right, because everything it should have caught is now going through the impeller instead of sitting in front of it.
example: You lift the lid to empty a basket and find the basket split down one side with half a season's grit sitting in the pot below it. Nothing about the feature looked wrong from the plaza.

short_definition: A wrench that grips with a band wrapped around the part rather than with teeth, so it can turn a fitting without marking the finish.
explanation: It gives less bite than a pipe wrench, which is the trade being made deliberately: it is the tool for a polished or plated fitting that will be visible when the job is finished.
example: A polished bronze nozzle body that sits above the waterline in full view of the lobby. A pipe wrench would move it and would also leave four bright scars on it forever.

short_definition: Gases settling into layers inside a space instead of mixing evenly, according to whether they are heavier or lighter than air.
explanation: Solvent vapour and many fuel vapours are heavier than air and sit in the bottom of a vault — which is where you will be kneeling — while others collect at the ceiling. This is the reason a test is taken at the top, the middle and the bottom, lowering the probe slowly, rather than once at the hatch.
example: A monitor held at the hatch of a vault reads clean. The same monitor lowered slowly to the floor alarms two feet from the bottom, where the vapour has been sitting all morning.

short_definition: The conductive body of the structure itself — the shell, its reinforcing steel and the metal tied to it — used as the reference point when measuring for a leak.
explanation: Measuring from the hot line to structural ground on the megohm range asks the question the GFCI is asking: is there a path out of this circuit into the thing people are standing on?
example: The technician puts one lead on the suspect conductor and the other on bonded steel at the shell, and reads the megohm range. A low figure means water has found a way in.

short_definition: Below ground level. A sub-grade trap or vault is one buried under the deck or paving rather than sitting on it.
explanation: Sub-grade is where the parts you cannot see, cannot drain and cannot easily reach all live. It is also where the residual water that no blow-out reaches sits, which is why the glycol goes into sub-grade p-traps and perimeter drains specifically.
example: Two drains in a plaza look identical from above. One runs to a trap set below the paving with a permanent water seal in it, and that is the one that gets glycol.

short_definition: A distribution panel fed from a larger one, splitting that supply into circuits and holding the overcurrent device for each.
explanation: Sapphire's rule is that lock-out and tag-out come before any sub-panel or control enclosure is opened. A pump sub-panel is also one of the two places named in this module where a GFCI that keeps tripping gets worked through systematically.
example: The equipment room has a main panel and a smaller one feeding the basin. Locking the main does not necessarily de-energise everything in the smaller one, which may have a feed of its own.

short_definition: The waterproofed concrete slab underneath a pedestal deck. It is pitched, and it carries the water back to the holding tank.
explanation:
This is the detail that gets inverted in the field. The finished deck is set level, because people walk on it and it has to look flat. The sub-slab beneath it is pitched, because water has to leave.

Adjustable pedestals exist to take up the difference. Pitching the deck to match the slab gains nothing - the open joints already pass water straight through - and gives you a walking surface that slopes where it should be flat.
example: A run of pavers gets set to follow the fall of the slab beneath. The deck drains no better than it would have, and the edge of the plaza is now half an inch out of level across a seating area.

short_definition: Somebody going under water — a real hazard on our sites, and one that does not need deep water.
explanation: Drowning is quiet. There is no shouting and no splashing, which is why people nearby miss it entirely. Do not enter the water to reach somebody unless you are trained for it — reach or throw instead — and anyone who was submerged needs medical assessment even if they were pulled out and seem recovered.
example: A child goes into a shallow basin at a public plaza while the crew is working twenty feet away. Nobody hears anything, because there is nothing to hear.

short_definition: The package a contractor sends the design team showing the exact products and fabrications intended, for review and approval before anything is ordered or built.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a generic word for anything somebody submitted. It is a specific, named document set with a review and approval history attached, and it is the record of what was actually accepted for this job — which is not always the same as what is on the truck.
explanation:
The approved submittal is the closest thing to a statement of what is actually going in. It carries the model numbers, the data sheets, the cut sheets and the fabrication drawings, and it can differ from both the drawings and the specification because it came later and was reviewed.

It is also where the real numbers live - the torques, cure times, dose rates, flows and clearances that this course deliberately does not print. Together with the O and M manual and the as-builts, it is the document set for a feature you have never seen before.
example: A fixture is leaking and the obvious next step is to open it, dry it and reseal it. First find out whether it is one that may be opened at all — because if it is not, you have just turned a warranty replacement into a bill.

short_definition: A person, a limb, hair or clothing being held against a submerged suction outlet by the water flowing into it.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English entrapment is luring somebody into doing something wrong — the police sense. Here it is physical: a body held under water by suction.
explanation:
The holding force is beyond what anyone can pull against. It has drowned people, including children, and it has caused disembowelment injuries.

Every engineering answer is a version of one idea: never let one outlet take the whole flow, and never let one outlet be fully blocked. Certified covers, multiple separated outlets, unblockable designs, and a safety vacuum release system. Covers are rated for a flow and carry a life span and a date; they are a wear part.
example: A compliant two-grate design gets throttled at the manifold until one grate is taking effectively all of the flow. Every cover is in place, everything looks correct, and it is a single-point suction hazard again.

short_definition: An arrangement where the pump sits above the water it draws from, so the air in the suction line has to be got out before water will follow.
explanation:
There is a hard physical limit on how high this can work, and it gets worse with altitude, with warm water, and with every foot of pipe and every fitting on the suction side.

A pump on lift has no margin to lose. Anything that adds resistance or lets air in on the suction side shows up as a pump that will not pick up.
example: The pump sits on a pad at deck level and the balance tank is eight feet down in a vault. Every call on that site that starts with 'it will not pick up' starts there.

short_definition: Everything on the inlet side of a pump — the pipework, hose and fittings between the water and the pump's intake. The pump pulls through it.
explanation:
The suction side is below atmospheric pressure while the pump runs, which reverses everything you expect about leaks: a bad joint on the suction side does not drip, it draws air in. It is also where restriction hurts, because a pump can push against an obstruction but it cannot pull harder than the atmosphere lets it.

When you vacuum with a portable pump, your flexible hose becomes part of that suction line. Every weakness the pump has on the suction side, it now has through however many feet of hose you are dragging round the basin.
example: A pump keeps losing prime and the floor under it is bone dry, so nothing is leaking. The pot lid O-ring is the culprit: on the suction side it lets air in instead of letting water out. The tell is a steady stream of fine bubbles arriving at the wall inlets.

short_definition: The set of pipes and valves where the skimmer lines and the main drain lines come together before the pump, with a valve on each leg.
