explanation:
How much of the pump's draw each leg gets is set by hand on those valves. It is a real adjustment with a right answer, not a set of valves to leave wide open.

Both errors announce themselves. Too much skimmer draw and the skimmers vortex, pulling air into the lines. Too much main drain draw and the surface goes stagnant, which is the one the client sees first.
example: The valve handles are all wide open because more seemed better. The skimmers are pulling a visible funnel and the pump burps air every few minutes.

short_definition: Everything between the water and the impeller. The discharge side is everything after the impeller, on the way back out to the feature.
explanation:
The distinction decides what a leak looks like. Downstream of the impeller the line is above atmospheric pressure, so a leak pushes water out and you can see it. Upstream it usually runs below atmospheric while the pump runs, so a leak pulls air in: bubbles at the returns, a pump that loses prime, and nothing on the floor.

Usual suspects upstream: the pump lid O-ring, the drain plugs, a threaded fitting, the union, and the shaft seal itself.
example: A fountain loses prime every afternoon and the floor is bone dry. The tech shuts it down and comes back in ten minutes to find a bead of water under a threaded fitting ahead of the pump. On a flooded-suction system, that weep with the pump off is the confirmation.

short_definition: A milder, thickened acid cleaner used where a stronger acid would attack the surface underneath the deposit.
explanation:
This is Sapphire's product family for limestone, travertine and other porous natural stone. It loosens the scale without dissolving the soft stone beneath it.

The gel body matters as much as the chemistry: it clings to a vertical face and to the underside of a coping long enough to work, instead of running off onto whatever is below.
example: The scale band under a travertine coping is softened with a gel, left to work, then lifted with a stiff nylon brush and vacuumed up before it can drip into the basin.

short_definition: The low point of a tank or basin, where water and everything that settles out of it collects.
explanation:
The sump is where the loop starts. It holds a reserve of water so the pump has something to pull from while the basin level swings with wind, splash and evaporation. On anything the public can reach it is also where suction entrapment protection lives.

If the sump uncovers, the pump is pulling air instead of water, and the pump is what gets damaged even though the sump was never the fault.
example: A plaza basin looks fine from the deck on a windy Tuesday, but the sump behind the weir wall has drawn down far enough that the pump is gulping. You hear it before you see it - the note changes and the jets start pulsing.

short_definition: Replaced by a newer issue. A superseded drawing is one that is no longer the current version of that sheet.
explanation:
Building from a superseded sheet is one of the most expensive mistakes available on a construction site, and it gives no warning at all. An old print looks exactly as authoritative as a new one, it is often cleaner, and it is frequently the one that has been living in the truck.

Two habits fix it: check the revision before you build from a sheet, and destroy superseded prints rather than rolling them back up.
example: A crew sets sleeves from a print that has been in the van since the pre-construction meeting. The sleeve locations moved eighteen inches on the reissue, and the slab is already poured.

short_definition: The roughness of a concrete surface, and the act of producing it by grinding or shot blasting so a coating has texture to key into.
ordinary_meaning: Profile in ordinary English is an outline seen from the side, or a description of somebody. Here it is nothing to do with shape — it is how coarse the surface is, measured against a standard set of reference textures.
explanation:
A steel-trowelled floor is polished. It looks like the best-finished concrete on the job, and it is the worst thing to bond to. Grinding or shot blasting takes off the laitance and any contamination at the same time as it opens the surface up, so profiling usually solves three items on the Rule of Clean at once.

How rough is not a judgement call. Membrane data sheets specify a profile, and that is the figure to work to.
example: The contractor is proud of a glass-smooth basin floor and asks why you are about to grind it. Because the membrane needs somewhere to hold on, and right now the best-looking slab on the site is the slickest one.

short_definition: A compound that lowers water's surface tension — the active idea behind soaps and detergents, and the reason a liquid foams when it is agitated.
explanation:
A pool agitates gently. A fountain drives water through high-pressure nozzles, so a surfactant that is harmless in a pool produces mounds of foam over the weir borders.

It is not only cosmetic: the foam carries product out of the basin, so the dose leaves with it, and a foaming feature usually gets shut off while somebody works out what happened.
example: Somebody washes a vacuum head with dish soap and rinses it over the basin. The display comes on at dusk and the plaza looks like a bubble bath.

short_definition: A vessel of trapped air or a cushioned device fitted near a valve or pump to absorb a pressure spike instead of letting the pipework take it.
explanation:
Air compresses and water does not, so a pocket of air gives the surge somewhere to go. This is the tool for the case the other measures cannot cover: a pump tripping on a power failure, where nothing closes slowly and the drive has no power either.

The failure mode is worth knowing. A plain air chamber gradually water-logs as the air dissolves into the water, and once it is full it is doing nothing at all - while looking exactly like one that works.
example: A feature has banged on every power blip for years. The air chamber on the discharge is solid with water when you tap it, and it has been that way longer than anyone remembers.

short_definition: A separate holding tank, often below grade, that carries part of a feature's water outside the basin you can see.
ordinary_meaning: "Surge" suggests an electrical spike and "vault" suggests a bank or a leap. Both are just parts of the water system — a tank that absorbs level changes, and the below-grade room the equipment lives in.
explanation:
When a feature starts, a lot of water goes up into the air and stays there for as long as the show runs. When it stops, all of that comes back down at once. A surge tank absorbs that swing so the basin does not run dry on start-up or flood over on shutdown.

It is also a common place for make-up water, level probes and chemical feed to live, so it is worth finding before you start chasing a level problem in the basin.
example: A technician eyeballs a basin at a few thousand gallons and doses for that. The tank under the plaza holds a meaningful share of the system, so the whole feature receives a fraction of the breakpoint dose — which is worse than not dosing it.

short_definition: Solid particles floating in the water rather than resting on the floor. Material goes into suspension when it is disturbed, and comes out of it again when it settles.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English, a suspension is a car's springs, or being sent home from work or school.
explanation: Everything worth vacuuming off a basin floor got there by settling out of suspension, sometimes over weeks. A slow head lifts it into the hose; a fast head puts it back into suspension, where it hangs for as long as it takes to settle again — on ground you have already covered.
example: You do the near half of a basin carefully and then hurry the last few passes. Next week the clean half has a fresh grey bloom on it and the corner you rushed is clean. That is the same silt, settled somewhere new.

short_definition: A hardened cutting tool that cuts an internal thread in a drilled hole.
ordinary_meaning: A tap in ordinary English is a faucet, or a light knock, or tapping a phone. On a fountain site the faucet sense is in play constantly, so context matters.
explanation:
A tap removes metal. It is not a cleaning tool, and running a cutting tap down a dirty thread to tidy it up takes away metal that was doing work and leaves the thread loose.

Technique is the same everywhere: cutting fluid, keep the tap square to the work, cut a little and back off to break the chip, and never force it. A tap started crooked cuts a crooked thread and that hole is not recoverable.
example: A blind hole in a bronze housing gets tapped square, slowly, with fluid, backing off every half turn. The identical job done fast and dry snaps the tap off flush, and now the part needs a machine shop.

short_definition: A table giving the correct hole size to drill before cutting a given internal thread.
explanation:
The hole has to be right. Too large and there is not enough thread left to hold the load. Too small and the tap has more metal to cut than it was built for: it binds, and it snaps off inside the hole, which is a far worse afternoon than starting over.

There is usually a chart printed inside the lid of the tap set. Use it every time - the sizes are not intuitive and they are not worth remembering wrong.
example: Somebody reaches for the next drill down because the right one is dull. The tap goes in three turns, binds, and breaks off flush in a casting that is now a warranty conversation.

short_definition: A pipe thread whose diameter increases along its length, so it seals by wedging into the matching thread as the joint is made up.
explanation:
The wedge is the whole behaviour. It is why the joint seals on the threads themselves and needs a sealant, and it is why there is a limit to how far it can be made up: past that point the friction becomes greater than the strength of the material and something breaks before it turns.

On plastic what breaks is the female hub. The course gives hand-tight plus one to two turns with a wrench as the general standard for plastic-to-plastic and plastic-to-metal.
example: A plastic tee is nipped up 'just a bit more to be sure' on a Friday afternoon. It does not weep - it splits, two weeks later, along the line of the thread.

aliases: total dissolved solids in the basin
short_definition: Total dissolved solids — everything dissolved in the water added together: minerals from the fill, the residue of every chemical ever added, and whatever evaporation has concentrated.
explanation: It appears in the LSI as the constant that gets subtracted. Practically, it is the number that only ever goes up while a basin is in service — evaporation takes the water and leaves the solids behind — and the only thing that brings it down is replacing water with fresh. A full winter drain and spring refill does that wholesale, which is one more reason the water in April is not the water from October.
example: A feature that has been topped up all season rather than drained reads noticeably higher than the one next to it that was emptied for a repair in June. Same site, same fill water, different history.

short_definition: A pulling force in a structural member: the section is being stretched apart rather than squashed together.
ordinary_meaning: In everyday English, tension is nervous strain between people, or just how tight a rope feels.
explanation:
Concrete carries compression extremely well and tension very badly, on the order of a tenth as well. So nobody designs concrete to be pulled. Wherever a section will be pulled, steel goes there instead.

Every structure in this trade has a tension side somewhere, and finding it is not intuition. It is on the drawing.
example: A basin wall full of water bows outward at its base, so the base is being stretched on the wet face. That is where the steel is, which surprises anybody expecting it on the dry side.

short_definition: Tiles lifting clear of the bed in a ridge along a line, popping up into a shape like a tent.
explanation:
It is what an assembly does when it needs to expand and has nowhere to go, typically because a movement joint was filled with grout or never left at all.

The failure is not where the pressure came from. It comes out at the weakest line, which can be metres away.
example: One morning in high summer a row of tile is standing proud of the floor in a ridge, with sound tile either side of it and no impact anywhere near.

short_definition: The row of screw or clamp terminals in a panel or box where field wiring lands and is joined to internal wiring.
explanation:
It is the boundary between the panel and the field, which makes it the place most tests start: lifting a lead there isolates whatever is out in the vault from everything inside the enclosure.

It is also a row of bare metal points close together, which is why water arriving inside a box only has to bridge a terminal strip once.
example: A technician proves 0 volts on the two conductors he expects to be live and never touches the third, which is fed from a control transformer somewhere else in the building.

short_definition: A resistor fitted across the data pair at the very end of a DMX chain, matched to the cable — 120 ohms.
explanation:
It matches the impedance of the cable, so the signal arriving at the end is absorbed there instead of bouncing back down the line and colliding with data still coming the other way.

Leave it off and fixtures flicker, jump to colours nobody asked for, or freeze holding the last value they understood — worst at the far end, and worse as the chain grows.
example: A run behaved perfectly for two seasons and started misbehaving the week two more fixtures were added at the end. That is a termination and topology story, not a fixture story.

short_definition: A mechanical plug or a temporary glued-on cap that closes off the end of a run so a section can be pressurised on its own.
explanation:
Isolating the section matters because pumps, filters and electronic control valves are rated far below typical test pressures. Testing through them destroys them.

A plug is also the most likely thing on the system to let go, and it lets go along the pipe axis. Nobody stands in front of one, and nobody stands over a joint or a thrust point either.
example: A crew caps both ends of a 60 foot buried run so the vault equipment never sees the test pressure, and works from the side of the trench while it comes up.

short_definition: A protective device that opens a motor's circuit when the motor gets too hot - either built into the motor itself or fitted in its starter.
explanation:
Some reset themselves once cool and some have to be reset by hand. Either way, a motor that runs, cuts out, and comes back after cooling has reported a condition rather than developed a mystery fault.

The question then becomes why it is overheating: blocked airflow, a high ambient, low or unbalanced supply voltage, a mechanical load it was not chosen for, a failing bearing or a failing capacitor. Resetting it repeatedly cooks the windings, and when they fail the cause is still there waiting for the new pump.
example: A pump drops out every afternoon and runs happily all morning. Its cooling grille is packed with cottonwood and it sits in a box with no ventilation, in full sun from noon.

short_definition: The cement-based adhesive that sticks tile to a surface, spread thin and combed out with a notched trowel.
explanation:
Thinset is designed to bond to porous, textured surfaces. A smooth cured waterproofing membrane is neither, and standard thinsets are actively repelled by one — the bed sits on the film rather than gripping it.

Some tile-industry membranes are sold as accepting thinset directly on the cured film. Sapphire's document does not offer that as a choice on a submerged basin: the sand broadcast goes in.
example: On a dry test patch the thinset seems to be sticking to a smooth membrane just fine. Fill the basin and leave it a season, and the same bed lets go in sheets — water pressure is the load that finds the difference.

short_definition: A brand of cementitious waterproof coating, named alongside Basecrete in Sapphire's document as an example of the material class.
explanation: Same point as Basecrete: the name in the course identifies a type of product, and the data sheet for the pail on the truck identifies everything else about it.
example: Someone on site calls every grey cementitious waterproofer Thoroseal, the way people call every adjustable wrench a Crescent. Fine in conversation; not fine when you are reading a cure time off the wrong sheet.

short_definition: A tool that reforms a damaged existing thread by pushing metal back into shape instead of cutting metal away.
ordinary_meaning: A chaser in ordinary English is somebody in pursuit, or the drink you have after a shot.
explanation:
This is the right tool for a thread that is dirty, corroded or lightly bruised - which on a fountain is most of them. It leaves the thread its original size and strength.

The wrong tool for that job is a cutting tap. A tap run down a dirty thread to clean it up removes metal that was carrying load and leaves a thread that is loose.
example: A pump flange stud on a coastal site is crusted and will not take a nut. A chaser run down it brings it back in seconds, where a tap would have quietly taken a size off it.

short_definition: Paste thread sealant, brushed onto a thread instead of tape or as well as it.
ordinary_meaning: Dope here is not slang and not an insult. It is the paste in the tin, and 'tape or dope' is an ordinary question with a manufacturer's answer behind it.
explanation: Which to use on a given joint - and whether both together are acceptable - comes from the manufacturer of the part in your hand, because some compounds attack some plastics and some are not rated for potable water.
example: A technician reaches for the tin out of habit on a plastic fitting, and the fitting crazes around the thread within a season. Nothing was wrong with the product; it was the wrong product for that plastic.

short_definition: A sleeve fitted into an oversized tapped hole to restore the original thread size in material that has been stripped.
explanation:
This is how a stripped hole is actually repaired: the hole is drilled out, tapped oversize, and the insert restores the thread the fastener needs. It is often stronger than the material it replaced, especially in soft castings.

The alternative that people try first - a bigger bolt, more thread locker, more effort - does not work and usually takes the part with it.
example: A stripped hole in an aluminium pump adapter gets an insert and goes back into service holding torque properly. The same hole with the next size up bolt forced into it lasted a month.

short_definition: An adhesive applied to a thread that cures in the absence of air and stops the fastener rotating loose under vibration.
explanation:
Grades differ mostly in how hard they are to undo afterwards - the stronger ones need heat to break. Which grade a given assembly takes is a manufacturer's call.

It is the exact opposite of anti-seize, and the two never go on the same fastener. One is there to stop the bolt moving; the other is there to make sure it can.
example: A set screw on a coupling backs out every few months on a feature that runs sixteen hours a day. The fix is the right grade of locker, not another quarter turn.

short_definition: How far apart the turns of a thread are - stated as threads per inch on inch fasteners, or as a distance in millimetres on metric ones.
ordinary_meaning: Pitch in ordinary English is a sales pitch, a musical note, a sports field, or throwing a ball.
explanation:
A fastener is defined by diameter, pitch and which standard it belongs to. Inch fasteners come in UNC coarse and UNF fine; metric ones are named by diameter and pitch. Both families live in the same toolbox and some near-miss combinations will start and turn a couple of times before they bind.

Coarse tolerates dirt, damage and corrosion and holds better in soft castings. Fine adjusts more precisely and resists loosening slightly better, but cross-threads easily. Around water and outdoors, corrosion usually argues for coarse.
example: A bolt out of the bin goes in two turns by hand on a pump housing and then stiffens. It is the right diameter and the wrong pitch, and the next quarter turn with a wrench would cost a casting.

short_definition: A supply with three live conductors, used for larger motors. Swapping any two of them reverses the direction the motor turns.
explanation:
Rotation has to be proved at the first run because it can be wrong without looking wrong. A centrifugal pump running backwards still moves water and still builds some pressure — it does not sit there doing nothing and it does not announce itself. It just underperforms, quietly, all season, while every reading you take looks vaguely plausible.

Any electrical work done over the winter can have swapped two legs, so "it was right last year" is not evidence.
example: A feature comes up in spring looking a bit tired — the display is shorter than the client remembers and the filter pressure sits low. Nothing has failed. The panel was replaced in February and two legs landed in the wrong order.

short_definition: Deliberately part-closing a valve to add resistance and reduce how much water gets past it.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like strangling somebody, or the pedal in a vehicle that makes it go faster.
explanation:
A throttling valve is built to sit part way: the control is smooth and spread across the travel, and the internals tolerate the fast stream squeezing past. A globe valve is the classic example.

Throttling also costs energy. The pump still turns at full speed and still draws most of its power, and the energy you took out of the flow is spent as friction that ends up warming the water. Changing pump speed with a drive is the efficient alternative.
example: A branch is running too hard, so somebody nips the ball valve on it to about a third open. Two years later the seats are cut, the valve weeps when shut, and the branch is still not at its design flow.

short_definition: The engineered detail that stops a pressurised line pushing itself apart at a bend or a tee — a concrete block behind the fitting, or joints mechanically locked together.
explanation:
Water changing direction in a pressurised pipe pushes hard and continuously outward at the turn. Underground there is nothing holding the fitting in place except the soil and the restraint.

It is an engineered detail with a size on it, off the civil drawings. If the drawing does not say, that is a question for the project manager before the trench is open, not after.
example: A 4 inch supply takes a 90 toward the basin and the drawing shows a block behind it. Nobody has poured it, and the trench is due to be closed tomorrow.

short_definition: A rated strap, chain or device used to restrain a load to the vehicle so it cannot move.
explanation: Secure against all four directions: forward, rearward, sideways and upward — a load that lifts off the deck over a bump is a load that is no longer tied to anything. In a hard stop the truck decelerates and an unrestrained load does not; it keeps travelling at the speed you were doing and stops against the bulkhead, or the back of your head. A length of pipe lying loose in a bed is a spear.
example: A pallet strapped down tight side to side but with nothing over the top hops on a speed bump, lands an inch further forward, and by the second site is resting against the cab with the straps slack.

short_definition: A test where you add a reagent drop by drop until the sample changes colour, and the number of drops is the result.
explanation:
Hardness and alkalinity tests work this way, and they are genuinely quantitative — the count is the measurement, not an eye matching a printed block.

Which means the sample volume has to be right. Fill past the line or stop short of it and the reagent-to-sample ratio is wrong, so every drop after that is counting against the wrong denominator.
example: Two technicians titrate the same basin and get results two drops apart. One of them read the meniscus from above while filling the vial.

short_definition: A discharge route — a position on a multiport valve, or a dedicated drain valve — that sends water out of the system to a drain instead of returning it to the basin.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like squandering something, or like rubbish. Here it is simply a valve position: the name of where the water is going.
explanation:
Vacuuming to waste means the dirt leaves the site instead of being handed to a filter that may not hold it. That is the whole reason to choose it — and it costs you water, so the level falls while you work, and it means treated water is leaving the property, which is a legal question and not a convenience one.

Not every system can do it. A cartridge filter with no multiport has nowhere to send it.
example: You are clearing fines from a hotel basin and the multiport goes to waste. Twenty minutes in, the level is visibly down and the skimmer is starting to gulp, so you shut down, top up from the fill, and take the second half in a fresh pass.

short_definition: The downward weight the front of a loaded trailer presses onto the hitch ball.
ordinary_meaning: Nothing to do with a tongue in the body sense — the trailer's 'tongue' is the drawbar at its front end that reaches to the hitch.
explanation: A trailer tows straight because some of its load bears down on the hitch. Too little — load piled behind the trailer axle — and the trailer starts to sway, the sway feeds itself and gets worse with speed rather than damping out. Too much and the back of the tow vehicle squats, which lifts weight off the steer axle and takes your steering and braking away together. The fix for both is where the weight sits: heavy low, slightly forward of the trailer axle, balanced side to side, and tied so it cannot migrate rearward on the first hill.
example: A trailer loaded with a pallet of stone pushed right to the back tows fine at 30 mph and starts a slow wag at 60 that grows every second. Nothing has broken — the load is simply behind the axle and there is almost no weight on the ball.

short_definition: Said of a gasket or O-ring that has been squashed in one position for long enough to stay that shape. It no longer springs back, so it no longer seals.
ordinary_meaning: "Set" in ordinary English is a collection of things, or putting something down. Here it describes rubber that has given up its springiness and kept the shape it was squeezed into.
explanation: A winter does this: months of compression plus drying out, and the seal that was fine in October is a flat, hard ring in April. It will often look perfectly serviceable. The failure shows up as a weep at a lid or a housing on the first fill, or as air drawn in on the suction side, which then reads as a pump that will not hold prime.
example: The strainer pot lid goes back on at start-up with its original O-ring, which looks fine. The pot will not stay full and there is no visible leak anywhere — the ring is flat on one face and has stopped sealing against air.

short_definition: The twisting force applied to a fastener, set with a torque wrench. It is the means, not the thing the joint actually needs.
explanation:
Torque is only an indirect way of producing clamp load, and a lossy one: most of what you apply is spent overcoming friction under the head and in the threads, and only a fraction becomes tension.

Which is why a real torque figure always arrives with a condition attached - dry, oiled, anti-seized, plated, galvanised. Change the friction and the same torque produces a very different clamp load. The figure and its condition belong to a specific fastener on a specific assembly, and they come from the manufacturer or the engineer.
example: A set of head bolts is given the dry figure off a chart, but every one of them was anti-seized on the way in. They are now stretched well past what anybody intended, and they all looked fine going together.

short_definition: The water's capacity to absorb acid or base without the pH moving. It is a reserve held in the water, not a position on the acid-base scale.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a measure of how alkaline the water is — the opposite end of the scale from acidic. It is not. That is what pH reads. Alkalinity is about how stubborn the pH is, not how high.
explanation:
The reserve is mostly carbonate and bicarbonate. Too little of it and pH bounces — every dose swings it, rain swings it, the aeration from the display swings it. Too much and pH locks high and resists correction no matter how much acid you pour at it.

So correct alkalinity first, then pH. The two are coupled: muriatic acid pulls both down at once, so expect to come back and re-read.
example: A rill has read a different pH on every visit for a month. The technician keeps correcting it and it keeps moving. The alkalinity is on the floor, so each correction is being made into water with nothing to hold it.

short_definition: Free chlorine and combined chlorine added together.
explanation: On its own it is close to useless — it cannot tell you whether the water is well sanitised or full of spent byproduct. Its value is as one half of a subtraction: combined equals total minus free.
example: A borrowed kit reports only total chlorine. You can tell the supervisor what is in the water and nothing at all about whether the feature needs shocking or how hard.

short_definition: The total amount of dissolved material the water is carrying, from all sources together. It is one of the terms in the saturation index.
explanation:
It climbs as water evaporates and the make-up keeps arriving, so on an outdoor feature it is a rough measure of how long the water has been recycling.

Worth knowing what it is not used for here: Sapphire's saturation index method does not carry a TDS term. It works from five site readings instead, with cyanuric acid subtracted from total alkalinity.
example: Somebody brings a saturation index worksheet from a pool background that asks for TDS. It is not the arithmetic this course uses, and mixing the two methods gives an answer that belongs to neither.

short_definition: The total quantity of dissolved material carried in the water, and a term subtracted in the saturation index.
explanation:
TDS climbs as a feature evaporates, because water leaves as vapour and everything dissolved in it stays behind. Every dose of chemical adds to it too.

It is one of the reasons the index drifts on its own and has to be measured and trended rather than set once. It is also the reason an old body of water behaves differently from a fresh one at the same pH.
example: A feature that has not been drained in four summers reads high on TDS and responds sluggishly to everything. It is not one bad reading - it is four years of concentration.

short_definition: The whole resistance a pump is working against on a particular installation, expressed in feet of head.
explanation:
Its value is that it is measured live, on this system as built, rather than taken off a drawing. Two conversions do it: discharge PSI x 2.31, suction inHg x 1.13, added together.

Once you have it, the manufacturer's pump curve turns it into a flow rate without a flow meter.
example: 20 PSI on the discharge and 5 inches of mercury on the suction works out at about 52 feet of head. Take that to the curve and the GPM comes off the bottom axis.

short_definition: The voltage difference between two things a person is in contact with at the same time.
ordinary_meaning: Potential in ordinary English means possibility or promise - somebody with a lot of potential. Here it is an electrical level, and a difference in it is what pushes current.
explanation:
Current flows through a body when one part of it touches something at one voltage and another part touches something at a different voltage. The body bridges the gap. The absolute voltage is not what hurts somebody; the difference across them is.

Bonding exists to drive touch potential to nearly zero. A tingle in the water, on a rail or on the deck is touch potential you can feel, and it is often the only warning anybody gets.
example: A visitor standing in an interactive feature with one hand on a stainless bollard reports a faint buzz that stops when they let go. Everybody comes out of the water, the feature is de-energised, and it stays off.

short_definition: A device tightened around a limb to stop severe bleeding. It is a real tool with a right way to use it and a wrong way, and using it is trained-skill territory.
explanation: For bleeding that keeps coming rather than oozing, the move available to everybody is firm, direct pressure with whatever clean material is to hand, while somebody calls. The tourniquet is in the glossary so you recognise the word, not so you feel ready to use one — that is the certified course rather than this page.
example: A technician gets a deep cut from sheet metal and it is not slowing down. Hard direct pressure and a phone call are the two things that are definitely correct.

short_definition: A sensor that reports a continuous value — a level, a pressure, a temperature — rather than simply switching at a threshold.
explanation:
More information, and more ways to be quietly wrong. A switch that has failed usually reports the same state forever; a transducer that has drifted still reports a number, and the number still looks like a measurement.

Depth and pressure are the same fact in different units — water weighs about 62.4 pounds per cubic foot — so a transducer at the bottom of a basin can be read as a continuous level, which is what makes leak detection possible.
example: A basin level has read the same figure for a fortnight, through a hot week that should have cost it some evaporation. The level did not hold steady; the transducer port has silted up.

short_definition: A device that switches a load between the normal supply and a standby source such as a generator.
explanation: It matters for lock-out because it can energise a circuit from a direction nobody was thinking about, automatically, with nobody present. The utility going off is the event that makes it operate, so the moment your circuit unexpectedly comes alive is the moment everything else went dark.
example: A storm drops the site power while a technician is working in a plant room with one breaker open. The generator starts, the transfer switch operates, and part of what he thought was dead is not.

short_definition: One of several selectable connection points on a transformer winding, used to raise or lower its output voltage a little.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily a faucet, or a light knock.
explanation: Taps are how a lighting transformer compensates for the voltage lost along a long run, so the far fixtures see what they should. Which tap belongs to which run is a design decision — it is fixing an engineered problem, not turning something up.
example: A run to the far side of a plaza arrives visibly low. The designer's answer is a different tap on that circuit plus a conductor size change, not a brighter lamp.

short_definition: Water held in a closed space with nowhere to expand into — a capped line, a plugged pump housing, the low spot of a sagged run, a length of pipe between two shut valves.
explanation:
Water expands by roughly 9% in volume when it freezes, and inside a locked plumbing circuit that expansion exerts up to 114,000 PSI of bursting force. No pipe wall, pump volute, heater coil or filter body argues with that.

Which is why freezing is only a problem where water is trapped. Ice in an open basin at least has a free surface to rise into, though it still pushes outward against walls, coping and tile as it grows — which is why a basin is drained rather than left full.
example: A run of pipe between two valves that were both closed "to be safe" in October. It is drained at neither end, it has nowhere to expand to, and it is the one length on the site that splits.

short_definition: The engineered means of stopping a trench wall collapsing on people — cutting the walls back, stepping them, or putting a shield in.
explanation:
Sloping cuts the walls back to a safe angle, benching steps them, shielding drops a box in that holds the soil off the people. Which applies depends on the soil, the depth and the loads beside the trench.

Excavation safety is its own standard and its own training, and this program is not it.
example: The excavator finishes a five foot trench and the crew wants two minutes in the bottom to make one joint. Two minutes is how long the collapses take too.

short_definition: How long it takes for a volume of water equal to the whole feature to pass through the treatment equipment once.
ordinary_meaning: In ordinary English turnover is staff leaving a company, a business's revenue, or a folded pastry.
explanation:
Everything that happens inside the equipment room - filtration, UV, ozone, heating - only happens to water that actually gets there. Turnover is the measure of how quickly that comes round.

It is set in the design and it is one of the things a feature's classification drives: the more public contact there is, the faster the required turnover. Slowing a pump down to save energy changes it.
example: A basin is shut down to one pump over a quiet winter and the turnover halves. Nobody notices until spring, when the water starts going off faster than the same dose used to hold it.

short_definition: A field check of a level's accuracy: read two fixed points from one position, move the instrument, and read them again to see whether the difference between them changed.
explanation: The trick is that it checks the instrument against itself from a different place, so a tilt in the plane shows up as a disagreement. Checking a single point proves nothing, because a tilted plane is still perfectly flat and can be right at any one spot.
example: A laser reads a coping and a stake, gets carried across the pad and reads the same two points again. The difference between them should be identical. It is off by a quarter inch, and that laser does not get used today.

short_definition: A load that one person should not handle alone — because of its weight, its shape, or where it has to come from and go to.
explanation: Most of what hurts people in this trade is awkward rather than heavy: a pump lifted out of a wet pit at arm's length, a length of pipe carried one-handed up steps, a drum on a tailgate. Water makes it worse because it is deceptive — at about 8.34 lb per gallon, a bucket, a sump full of debris and water, or a partly full container weighs far more than the same volume of almost anything else you handle. Plan the lift and the route before you pick it up, keep the load close, let your legs do the work, and do not twist while loaded — turn your feet. The honest answer is very often that it is a two-person lift, or a cart, or a hoist, and the cost of saying so is a minute.
example: A technician bends over the lip of a wet pit to lift out a submersible that is still half full, at arm's length, and twists to set it on the deck. Every part of that is the wrong way round, and the pump was never the problem.

short_definition: A secondary sanitation circuit: water passes through a chamber where a lamp emitting at 254 nm destroys the DNA of what goes through it.
explanation:
It reaches bacteria, viruses and chlorine-resistant pathogens — Cryptosporidium above all — and stops them reproducing or infecting guests. What it does not do is leave anything behind it. The basin is still protected by the free chlorine in the water, so a UV system is a reason for confidence about pathogens and never a reason to let the residual fall.

Two quiet failures: scale on the quartz sleeve blocks the light, and lamps lose intensity after roughly 9,000 to 12,000 operational hours. Both leave a lamp that still looks exactly as lit as on day one. Track the hours; do not judge it by the glow.
example: A splash pad's UV has been in service three seasons and the lamp lights every morning. Nobody has tracked the hours, and it has been doing very little for months.

short_definition: A lamp in a sealed chamber that shines ultraviolet light on water flowing past it, inactivating organisms as they go through.
explanation:
UV is real and effective, and it is a point-of-treatment device: it works on the water that is inside the chamber at that moment. Whatever is happening out in the basin is happening where the lamp is not.

It has a specific failure mode worth knowing. Lamp output falls as it ages and the quartz sleeve between the lamp and the water fouls with scale and film. Both happen slowly and neither raises an alarm, so the lamp goes on glowing while inactivating very little.
example: A controller shows the UV lamp lit and no fault, and the lamp has been in since two summers ago. Pulling the sleeve shows a grey film you can scrape with a thumbnail. Nothing on the panel was ever going to tell you.

short_definition: A mortar bed deliberately not stuck to what is underneath it, so the two can move independently.
explanation:
It is placed over a cleavage membrane or slip sheet, usually with reinforcement in it, and it isolates the finish from substrate movement and cracking. The price is thickness: it has to work as a slab in its own right, so it cannot be thinned down.

The membrane, the reinforcement and the thickness are one decision made in the assembly detail. A thin bed built unbonded is neither thing.
example: A detail calls for a floating bed and the build-up available is half what it asks for. Thinning it to fit produces something that is not either kind of bed.

short_definition: The two common inch thread series - UNC is the coarse one and UNF the fine one - identified by diameter and threads per inch.
explanation:
Knowing which series a fastener belongs to is how you avoid the near-miss that strips a hole. Identify a thread by measuring and by a thread gauge, never by eye and never by whether it feels about right.

Metric fasteners sit in the same drawers on most sites, and several metric and inch combinations are close enough to engage before they seize.
example: Two bolts in the same tray look identical on the bench. One is a half-inch coarse and one is a metric size a hair under it, and only one of them belongs in the hole you are looking at.

short_definition: The supply conductor — the hot. The word describes its relationship to earth, not a defect in the installation.
ordinary_meaning: Reads like a fault report — a conductor that should have been grounded and was not.
explanation: A GFCI watches the current leaving on the ungrounded conductor and the current returning on the grounded conductor. On a healthy circuit those are equal. The difference between them is the only thing the device measures.
example: A technician reads a note saying the leakage was measured from the ungrounded conductor to structural ground and starts looking for a missing ground connection. Nothing is missing; that is just the name for the hot.

short_definition: A three-piece pipe fitting with a threaded collar, letting a joint be taken apart and put back without cutting anything.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a labour union, or just 'a joining'.
explanation:
Every pump, filter, heater, valve and controller in the system will be serviced or replaced. Unions or flanges on both sides of anything that comes out is what decides whether that is a twenty-minute swap or half a day of cutting and re-piping.

The decision is made at installation, by you, for the price of a fitting.
example: A pump fails in December. The crew that installed it put unions either side and an isolation valve on each line, so it comes out in twenty minutes without draining the system. The identical pump on the next site is glued in solid.

short_definition: One complete DMX data stream, carrying 512 channels. A system needing more than 512 channels needs more than one.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily means everything that exists — the cosmos.
explanation: The controller is broadcasting all 512 values over and over, very fast, to everything on the run. It is not talking to fixtures; it is shouting numbers, and each fixture picks out the ones it was told to listen to.
example: A designer adds a row of colour-changing fixtures late in the job and the channel count runs past 512. That is a second universe and a second run, not a longer chain.

short_definition: In controller work, upload means copying the program out of the controller onto a laptop, and download means sending one from the laptop into the controller.
ordinary_meaning: On the internet the directions are the other way round — you upload to a server and download to your own machine. Here the controller is the reference point, not you.
explanation: Getting the direction wrong is not a vocabulary slip; it is the difference between saving the working program and overwriting it. An online edit also acts on live equipment the moment it is accepted or downloaded, and staging an edit is not the same as testing it — nothing simulates what the machine will do.
example: Somebody means to save what is running and instead sends the laptop's copy in. Whatever field change was living in that controller is gone, and nobody knows what it was.

short_definition: Uninterruptible Power Supply: a battery-backed unit that keeps equipment running when the incoming supply goes away.
ordinary_meaning: Outside a plant room, UPS is a parcel company. Here it is a box full of batteries that will happily keep a circuit live after you have opened its breaker.
explanation: A UPS is a source inside the building, so opening the supply breaker does nothing to what it is feeding. Control cabinets on water features often have one for the controller, which means the panel you just isolated can still have live control wiring in it.
example: A technician kills the feed to a control cabinet and the display on the controller stays lit. That is not a puzzle — it is a small UPS on the shelf below, doing its job.

short_definition: The marking out of buried services before excavation, required before you dig. The marks are approximate and they expire.
ordinary_meaning: Locate sounds like finding the exact spot. A locate gives an approximate position inside a marked tolerance zone, not a pinpoint.
explanation:
Because the position is approximate, anything inside the tolerance zone is exposed by hand before machinery goes near it.

Hitting a gas line or a primary electrical feed is not a bad day. It is a fatality, potentially somebody else's.
example: Paint marks from a job three weeks ago are still faintly visible across the lawn. They are decoration now, not a locate.

short_definition: A sealed housing the circulating water passes through, where an ultraviolet lamp inactivates organisms as they go by.
explanation: For this module it matters as a vessel rather than as a sanitiser: it holds water, it carries a drain plug, and it is one of the handful of places to inspect for freeze damage in spring. The quartz sleeve around the lamp is glass and does not forgive being left full over a winter.
example: The chamber drained fine in November and in April there is a wet ring on the pad beneath it as soon as the system fills. The housing let go at a seam where the last inch of water sat.

short_definition: A gauge on the suction side of a pump, reading how hard the pump is having to pull. A rising reading means restriction between the water and the pump.
explanation:
Suction vacuum and filter pressure are two different instruments telling you two different stories, and they call for opposite actions. Vacuum climbing means something ahead of the pump is choking it — a loading basket, a blocked hose, the head sitting on a leaf. Pressure climbing means the filter behind the pump is loading with what you are sending it.

Both are only readable against the baseline someone wrote down when the system was clean.
example: Mid-vacuum the suction reading climbs steadily while the filter pressure barely moves. The filter is fine. The head is parked on a sodden leaf mat in the corner.

short_definition: The weighted tool on the end of the pole that runs along the basin floor with the suction hose attached to it.
explanation:
It is also your air gauge while priming: bubbles coming out of the submerged head mean air is still being pushed out of the hose, and bubbles stopping is the signal that the hose is full. Nothing about that is a count of seconds.

Keep it on the floor. A head skipped along, or lifted clear while the pump is drawing, is the commonest way to lose prime on a vacuum job.
example: You set the head down, hold the hose on a wall inlet, and watch a steady boil of bubbles come off the head across the basin. They thin, then stop. Now the hose goes on the pump — quickly.

short_definition: The pressure at which a liquid at a given temperature turns to vapour. Lower the pressure on water far enough and it boils without being heated at all.
explanation: This is the piece that makes cavitation make sense. Boiling is not only about temperature - it is about the relationship between temperature and pressure. Water in a suction line starved by a blocked basket can reach its vapour pressure at ordinary basin temperature.
example: Nothing in the system is hot, the water is cool to the touch, and the pump is full of bubbles that were not there five minutes ago. Nothing heated the water; something restricted the suction.

short_definition: A controller that varies a motor's speed by varying the frequency of the power it feeds it — so a pump can run at part speed rather than only on or off.
explanation: Because it controls speed rather than just state, it can ramp flow up and down instead of stepping it. Avoiding instant 0% flow steps — even a fraction of a second of programmed deceleration — eases the velocity change that generates water hammer.
example: A display pump programmed to fall from full to nothing in one step is retimed to ease down over a moment instead, and the bang at the end of the show stops.

short_definition: An electronic drive that runs a motor at a chosen speed rather than only at full speed, and ramps it up and down over a set period.
explanation:
A VFD changes flow by changing how fast the pump turns, instead of making the pump fight a part-closed valve. For a centrifugal pump the relationships are steep and universal: flow falls roughly in proportion to speed, head falls roughly with the square of speed, and power falls roughly with the cube - so a modest slowdown is a large saving.

It is also the gentle way to start and stop a pump, which takes one of the main causes of water hammer off the table. But there is a floor: below some speed the pump no longer makes the head the feature needs. That minimum and the ramp times are commissioning settings, not knobs to explore.
example: A plaza feature is set to run at reduced speed after the offices close. Somebody drops it a little further to quieten it, and the tallest jet collapses to a dribble while the small ones look fine.

short_definition: A below-ground concrete chamber holding a water feature's pumps, valves and controls, reached through a hatch.
ordinary_meaning: A bank vault, or to jump over something.
explanation: Sapphire's own training document classifies its below-ground vaults as permit-required confined spaces, on the grounds of toxic gas accumulation and oxygen depletion. So a vault is not a space you assess and form a view about at the lip — it starts permit-required, and the pre-entry gas test applies every time, including the ones where the hatch has been open all morning.
example: A technician needs thirty seconds inside a vault to read a gauge. The thirty-second job is the one where the monitor does not come off the truck, and it is the same vault it was yesterday.

short_definition: Speed a fluid up through a narrow point and its pressure drops. The low pressure at that point will pull in whatever is next to it.
explanation: It is how a hydro-vac does an impeller's job without being one, and it is worth recognising elsewhere: chemical injectors, some air features and jet nozzles all use the same trick. Nothing is being pushed into the stream — the stream's own low pressure is doing the pulling.
example: You put a thumb over the end of a running garden hose and the jet sucks a leaf in off the deck alongside it. Same effect, same reason, no moving parts.

short_definition: A variable frequency drive — an electronic device that changes the frequency and voltage supplied to a motor, and therefore its speed.
explanation: In a safety context the relevant fact is the DC bus inside it: the drive's capacitors stay charged after the disconnect is open, so the enclosure holds a shock hazard after everything has been locked out correctly. The drive's own instructions give the wait time before it is safe to open, and that figure belongs to the drive in front of you rather than to any course.
example: A technician locks out the feed to a pump drive, waits while he fetches his meter, and opens the cover. The right wait is whatever the label on that drive says, which is why he reads it rather than counting.

short_definition: An unfilled gap under or beside buried pipe, where the support the pipe needs is simply missing.
ordinary_meaning: Cancelled or invalid, as in a void cheque. Here it is literally empty space.
explanation:
A void is a channel, and a channel is exactly the thing you poured the compound to prevent. It is invisible once the surface skins over, so the pour looks perfect from above.

Voids come from two things, and both happen before the pour: dust or moisture left in the shell that stops the compound bonding where it lands, and pouring too fast so air is trapped against the splices rather than pushed out.
example: A box is potted on a dusty afternoon without wiping the shell out first, and poured quickly because the crew is leaving. The top looks flawless. Water finds the gap behind the terminal strip that winter.

short_definition: The loss of voltage along a conductor, so that equipment at the far end of a long run receives less than was sent.
explanation: On a lamp it reads as dim and yellow. On an LED it more often shows as a colour shift, a flicker, or a fixture that simply drops out. It is a design problem solved by conductor size and transformer taps, not by turning something up.
example: A run of submersible LEDs is correct in colour for the first few fixtures and goes visibly cooler toward the end of the basin. Nothing is faulty; the far end is receiving less than the near end.

short_definition: The spiral water passage inside a pump housing, wrapped around the impeller. It collects what the impeller throws out and turns speed into pressure.
explanation: For winterizing, the shape is the point: the volute sits below the level of the pipes connected to it, so it holds water after everything else has gravity drained. Nothing about a system looking empty tells you the volute is empty. That is what its drain plug is for.
example: A pump room in April with a hairline split along the seam of a pump housing and a dark stain down the pad below it. The plug is still in, finger-tight, exactly where somebody left it in November.

short_definition: A funnel forming over a suction fitting when the draw is stronger than the water above it can feed, carrying air down into the pipe.
explanation: Air on the suction side costs the pump its prime, so a vortexing skimmer is not a cosmetic problem. The fix is at the manifold, not at the pump.
example: You can see a dimple over the skimmer throat that stretches into a little tornado every few seconds, and every time it does the returns spit.

short_definition: A fitting set into the wall of the basin where filtered water comes back in from the system.
explanation: It is the only place on a running system where a decent stream of water is being pushed out under pressure and you can get a hose end onto it. That is why it is the priming tool: hold the free end of the vacuum hose tight against it and the return flow fills the hose from the wrong end, pushing the air out ahead of it.
example: You hold the hose end hard against the inlet and watch the vacuum head at the other end of the basin. Bubbles boil out of it, slow, and stop. The hose is full — and the moment they stop is the moment to move, because everything you dawdle over is air coming back in.

short_definition: The body of water standing between the floor of a basin and its surface, considered as a whole. Clouding the water column means putting material into suspension all through that depth.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a pillar or jet of water. Confusingly, plumbers also use "water column" as a pressure unit — inches w.c. on a gas or low-pressure gauge — which is a different thing entirely.
explanation: It is the phrase for what you are trying not to spoil. The sediment on the floor is only visible and only liftable while it stays on the floor. Once it is distributed through the depth above, you cannot see what you have cleaned, and it will settle again wherever it drifts to.
example: Ten minutes of fast passes and the far half of a knee-deep basin has gone the colour of weak tea from floor to surface. Nothing has been removed — it has just been moved into the water you are standing in.

short_definition: The pressure spike produced when moving water is stopped or started abruptly, heard as a bang in the pipework.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like something striking the pipe from outside. Nothing hits it — the water inside does all of it.
explanation:
A column of water has mass and speed, and stopping it turns that momentum into pressure. The wave travels up the pipe, reflects off the far end and comes back, banging until friction kills it. The spike can be several times normal working pressure and lasts a fraction of a second, which is why a gauge on the wall almost never shows it.

Two things make it bigger: how fast the water was moving and how fast you stopped it. Common causes on a fountain are a slammed ball valve, a snapping solenoid, a pump started or stopped across the line, a check valve closing late, and a pump tripping on power loss.
example: A feature bangs once, hard, every time the evening shutdown sequence runs. Eighteen months later you are sent to look at a cracked fitting, loose pipe supports and a weeping threaded joint, and every one of them gets written down as age.

short_definition: A device fitted to a manifold that gives a pressure shockwave a compressible chamber to push into — commonly a sealed air chamber or a nitrogen-charged bladder.
explanation:
The wave carries energy that has to go somewhere. Without a suppressor it goes into the fittings, the valve internals and the joints. With one it goes into a gas volume that can be squeezed, which is exactly the compressibility water does not have.

Worth fitting on manifolds feeding fast-cycling interactive nozzles, where the shockwave happens over and over rather than occasionally.
example: A splash pad manifold with eight fast-cycling zones gets a commercial-grade arrestor at the head of the run, and the bang becomes a thud.

short_definition: The pressure created by water standing above a point in the system — the higher the water sits, the more force it arrives with.
ordinary_meaning: 'Head' in everyday English is the thing on your shoulders, or the top of something. In a piping system it means a height of water expressed as a pressure, and it is a force that is still there when everything is switched off.
explanation: Head is the most underrated stored energy on a water feature because nothing about it looks energetic. A basin, a riser or a header standing above the equipment will empty through whatever you open — and a basin above a vault can empty into that vault with you in it.
example: A vault sits eight feet below a raised basin that is still holding water. Everything down there is switched off, locked and tagged, and the head in that basin has not noticed any of it.

short_definition: The level below ground at which the soil is fully saturated — the depth you would find standing water if you dug a hole and waited.
ordinary_meaning: It sounds like a piece of furniture, or a table of figures about water. It is neither. Table here is used in its old sense of a flat level surface, like a plateau — the level the groundwater sits at.
explanation:
The water table decides which job you are doing. Above it, you are keeping water in and the membrane goes on the positive side. Below it, groundwater is also trying to get in, and that is a different, engineered system.

It is not fixed. It rises after rain and with the season, so a basin that was dry ground in August can be sitting in water in February.
example: A basin is excavated in dry ground in late summer and everyone builds on the assumption that this is what the ground is like. The following spring the same excavation would have been standing in water, and the structure was never detailed for it.

short_definition: A sealed mechanical connector used to join conductors in a wet location, crimped rather than twisted.
explanation: Every splice inside a potted box is made with these before any compound is mixed. Splices made with anything else are asking the compound to do a job it was only ever meant to back up — and a wire nut in a puddle is not a connection at all.
example: A crew is one connector short at the end of a light install and there is a bag of wire nuts in the van. That box waits for the right connectors, because the compound going over the top of it will hide the shortcut perfectly.

short_definition: A strip cast into a concrete joint so that it is embedded in both pours and blocks water from travelling along the joint.
explanation:
A waterstop only exists if it went in with the pour. It cannot be added afterwards — there is no way to get it into the middle of a wall once the wall is there.

So when one was left out, the recovery is a surface system and a repair detail rather than the thing that was designed. That is worth saying out loud at the time rather than discovering it at the flood test.
example: You arrive at a basin after the pours are done and ask what is in the wall-to-floor joint. If the answer is nothing, that is information the whole waterproofing approach needs, and it needs it today rather than in three weeks.

short_definition: A mechanical anchor that grips by expanding against the walls of a drilled hole as it is tightened.
explanation:
It can be loaded as soon as it is torqued, which is its advantage. The cost is that it puts outward force into the concrete, so edge distance and spacing matter a great deal.

Set too near an edge, it blows a cone of concrete out sideways instead of holding.
example: Four anchors along the top of a basin wall and the end one lands a hand's width from the edge, because that is where the bracket fell. It holds through installation and lets go the first time the equipment vibrates against it.

short_definition: A deliberate opening that lets water out of an assembly, usually at a drain and at the level of the mortar bed.
ordinary_meaning: To cry. Which makes it sound like a fault being described rather than a feature somebody designed in.
explanation:
Water gets past tile: grout is porous and tile joints are not a seal, so water reaches the bed and soaks into it. That is expected. What is not expected is the water having nowhere to go.

So the assembly drains twice. The membrane below the bed slopes to the drain as well as the finished surface above it, and the weep openings must be open and stay open. Weeps packed solid with mortar during the pour is one of the most common failures in this trade, and it is invisible the moment the tile goes down.
example: A drain body is set and the mud goes in around it. The small openings around its base are full of mortar, and the bed above them can now only fill.

short_definition: An edge or wall built so water flows over it in a controlled sheet. The weir wall is the structure carrying that edge.
ordinary_meaning: A small dam across a river. Same idea, but on a fountain it is a designed architectural edge, and the top of it is a precise elevation rather than a rough one.
explanation:
Sapphire's tolerance is that the top overflow edge must be level to within 1/16 inch across its entire length. That is the specification for the edge, not a target to aim at and miss politely.

The reason is that water does not average, it goes to the low point. If one side of the weir dips even slightly, all of the flow funnels through that dip, the sheet breaks up, and the rest of the edge beads or runs dry. Nothing downstream rescues it: more pump does not fix it and a bigger basin does not fix it.
example: A run of coping is levelled piece to piece down its length, each joint matched to its neighbour. The finished edge is a smooth curve out by a hair, and the whole sheet pours out of one corner.

short_definition: The hinged, floating flap across the mouth of a skimmer. It rides up and down with the water level and accelerates the top layer of water over its lip.
ordinary_meaning: A weir in ordinary English is a low dam built across a river.
explanation:
That acceleration is what creates the localised surface-tension draw pulling floating debris off the water and into the basket. A weir door that is jammed, missing or installed backwards turns a skimmer into an ordinary suction port.

It follows the level by itself, but only across the range it was set for. Too low and it gulps air past the flap; too high and the surface layer stops accelerating over it, so debris drifts past.
example: A weir door goes back in upside down after a basket clean. The fountain still circulates, and from that day leaves drift past the skimmer mouth and sink to the floor.

short_definition: A small notched or toothed gauge pressed into a freshly applied coating to read how thick the wet film is.
explanation:
The word wet is the operative part. It only works while the material is still liquid, and once the coat has cured there is nothing left to measure without cutting into it and destroying what you are checking.

So thickness is not something you verify at the end of the job. It is something you check repeatedly while you are working, and it is the only honest number you will ever have about the coat.
example: Take a reading, then take another one four feet away, then another over a high spot in the slab. If they disagree, the coat disagrees — and the thin reading is the one that matters, because that is where the pinhole will be.

short_definition: A code classification for a place exposed to water — including the inside of a buried raceway. Wiring methods and fittings have to be listed for it.
ordinary_meaning: Sounds like a judgement you make by looking — somewhere that is currently wet, as opposed to somewhere that looks dry today.
explanation: Treat every buried raceway as though it has standing water in it, because it does. Conduit joints are not watertight the way pressure pipe is, the ground around them is wet, and warm air drawn into a conduit condenses on the inside overnight. The wire that is acceptable in a dry indoor wall is not the wire that goes underground.
example: A trench is bone dry the week the conduit goes in, in the middle of a drought. It is still a wet location, and the conductors pulled into it still have to be listed for one.

short_definition: The small cap that fits over a probe's tip and holds it in liquid while it is out of service. The liquid it is filled with is the reference solution the probe is designed to sit in.
explanation: The cap is what makes indoor winter storage safe for a probe: filled with reference solution, it keeps the glass membrane and the reference junction wet for six months. Plain water is not the same thing and a rinse-and-box is not storage at all. Not a bucket, not a toolbox.
example: Two probes come off the system in November. One goes into its cap topped up with solution and onto a shelf indoors; the other goes into a zip bag in a tool tray in the van. In April only one of them is an instrument.

short_definition: Shutting a water feature down for the freezing season so that nothing anywhere in it is left holding water.
explanation:
It helps to treat it as one goal rather than a list of products: there is no trapped water anywhere in this system. Every step — draining, opening plugs, blowing lines, glycol in the traps, removing what cannot drain — exists to serve that sentence, and any step you are unsure about can be judged against it.

It is also work whose mistakes are invisible. A missed low-point drain looks exactly like a finished one in November.
example: Everything on the list is ticked and the cover is on. In April the system fills, holds for an hour, and then the pressure will not come up because a line under the paving has been split since January.

short_definition: The maximum load a strap, chain or anchor point is rated to hold, stamped or labelled on the item itself.
explanation: Every tie-down and every anchor has one, and a securement is only as good as the weakest item in the chain — a rated strap on an unrated anchor secures nothing. Damage takes the rating away without taking the label away: a cut edge, a frayed web or a strap that has been abraded on a sharp corner no longer holds its stamped figure.
example: A strap with a clean-looking buckle turns out to have a nick two feet up the webbing where it ran over the edge of a steel plate. It goes in the bin — the number printed on the tag stopped being true when the web was cut.

short_definition: The point at which stretched metal stops springing back and stays deformed. Past it, a bolt is on its way to snapping.
ordinary_meaning: Ordinarily, to yield is to give way at a junction, or a yield is what a harvest produces.
explanation:
A fastener is designed to stretch a little and stay elastic, like a very stiff spring. That stretch is the clamp load. Past yield it is not a spring any more.

The dangerous part is that it does not announce itself. A bolt taken past yield can look completely normal and be sitting at a fraction of the strength anybody thinks it has.
example: A stainless bolt is pulled up hard on a stone coping with compound on the threads and a number from the last job. It does not snap on the day. It is already stretched.

short_definition: The tension at which a fastener stops springing back and stays permanently stretched.
ordinary_meaning: To yield in ordinary English is to give way or surrender, or what a crop produces. Here it is a precise point on the way to breaking.
explanation:
Below yield a bolt behaves like a spring: stretch it, it pulls back, and that pull is your clamp load. Past yield it deforms permanently and there is almost nothing left in it - a little more turning, or the next shock load, necks it and snaps it, or tears the thread out of the casting.

And it cannot be trusted again. A bolt stretched past yield will not reliably reach the specified clamp load a second time, so it is replaced, not re-used.
example: A bolt comes out noticeably longer than its neighbour and its threads look slightly drawn near the shank. That one does not go back in, however good it looks otherwise.

short_definition: A feature with no standing water on the surface people walk on: a splash pad, or a dry-deck plaza fountain.
explanation:
Everything drains straight off the surface, so all the water in the system is either in the pipes or in the balance tank. There is no pool to buffer anything.

It also means everything that lands on the deck ends up in the tank with the water.
example: A plaza is a dry, usable public space at nine in the morning and a water feature at noon. Same surface, and the entire system is under a floor people are standing on.
